case20v1-res.qual.quant:
Navkar Pantry Works: Counting or Listening

A teaching case on qualitative and quantitative research in product discovery

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday 15 October 2026, Tanvir Chaubey sat in a glass meeting room on the third floor of Navkar Pantry Works' office in Baner, Pune, looking at a chart that had been falling for six weeks. Tanvir was the senior product manager for the retailer app. On Monday 19 October he was due to present a recovery plan to the chief executive, Tarak Chakradeo, and the leadership team. Diwali falls on 8 November, and Tarak had been clear that stocking season could not begin with two cities still drifting away.

Tanvir had three days and a choice that was really about order. He could act on the numbers he had, send out a bigger count, or go and talk to the people who had stopped ordering.

2. Company background

Navkar Pantry Works was founded in 2019 by two former distribution managers who had watched Pune kirana owners phone in their weekly orders. Its app lets a store owner order staples from partner warehouses, pay by UPI or on short credit, and receive delivery the next day. Navkar keeps about 6 per cent of order value.

By September 2026 the company had 36,000 registered stores across five cities: Pune, Nashik, Indore, Lucknow and Coimbatore. It competed with Udaan and Jumbotail in app-based wholesale, with Flipkart Wholesale and the JioMart partner network of Reliance Retail at larger scale, and with the local distributor's salesman who had known a shopkeeper for twenty years. Navkar defines an active store as one that places at least one order in the calendar month.

3. The situation

The decline was uneven. Exhibit 1 shows active stores by city in August and September. Across the five cities the active count fell from 20,825 to 17,680, a drop of 3,145 stores or 15.1 per cent. Pune, Nashik and Coimbatore each lost 5 per cent; Indore lost 20 and Lucknow 40. Indore and Lucknow account for 2,530 of the 3,145 lost stores, about four in five.

Exhibit 1: Active stores by city, August and September 2026

Source: Navkar order database. The total-row change is computed on the summed store counts (17,680 divided by 20,825), not as a mean of the five city percentages. Active means at least one order in the calendar month.

Two operational changes had been made in those cities, and Exhibit 2 places them on a timeline. On Monday 17 August the Lucknow warehouse moved to a new site, and morning delivery windows became a single afternoon window from 2 to 6 pm. On Monday 24 August, to control bad debt, the Indore team cut the credit limit for stores from ₹25,000 to ₹15,000. Neither was made elsewhere. A list-price revision in July applied to all five cities alike.

Tanvir's team had already tried to count its way to an answer. Between 1 and 8 October an in-app exit survey went to the 3,400 stores that had ordered in August and not in September; the net fall of 3,145 is that 3,400 less 255 stores that began or resumed ordering. Exhibit 3 shows the 212 stores that replied, a response rate of 6.2 per cent. The questionnaire offered a fixed list of reasons the team had drafted in one afternoon. A third of respondents picked price.

Exhibit 3: Reason selected in the exit survey (one answer per respondent)

Source: Navkar in-app exit survey, 1 to 8 October 2026. Of 3,400 lapsed stores invited, 212 replied (6.2%). Shares are of the 212 respondents, not of all lapsed stores.

The three global colleagues read this evidence differently. Tara Chandak, the data scientist working from Montreal, saw a weak sample that could not tell her how many of the lapsed stores shared any given reason. Tavish Chaphekar, who leads customer support from Manila, had listened to six recorded calls from Lucknow stores and heard the word "morning" in four of them, which no survey option captured. Tikam Chhatre, the head of operations in Lucknow, heard in the same calls only stores cross about price.

4. The people

  • Tanvir Chaubey, senior product manager, Pune. Owns the recovery plan and wants a decision he can defend.
  • Tara Chandak, data scientist, Montreal. Wants evidence she can size, and prefers a larger structured sample.
  • Tikam Chhatre, head of operations, Lucknow. Defends the new warehouse and believes a modest price cut would win stores back.
  • Tavish Chaphekar, customer support lead, Manila. Wants someone to visit the stores, since the calls suggest reasons nobody asked about.

Tarak Chakradeo, the chief executive, wants a plan that is neither reckless nor slow. One owner, Tahir Chhipa, who runs a store near Aminabad in Lucknow and ordered every week until mid-August, told a support agent: "I open at seven. If the sack comes at four, my customers have already gone to the other shop."

5. The options

Tanvir saw three courses, set out with their costs in Exhibit 4. An average active store orders about ₹20,000 a month, so the 2,530 stores lost in Indore and Lucknow represent ₹506 lakh of monthly order value and, at the 6 per cent take rate, ₹30.36 lakh of Navkar revenue.

Exhibit 4: The three options compared
OptionCostTime to answerWhat it can tell him
A. Cut prices 2% on all items in Lucknow and Indore now₹34.1 lakh a monthImmediateWhether orders return, but not why
B. Interview 14 lapsed store owners in the two cities, then decideAbout ₹1.2 lakh9 daysWhy stores left, in their words; not how many
C. Survey the 8,525 stores in both cities that were active in August, using the existing reasonsAbout ₹0.16 lakh6 daysHow many pick each listed reason; nothing beyond the list

Cost of A: 2% of August order value for the 8,525 stores active in August in Indore and Lucknow (4,400 + 4,125), at ₹20,000 each, which is ₹1,705 lakh. Cost of C: an expected 529 replies (8,525 at the 6.2% response seen in the exit survey) at a ₹30 credit each, which is about ₹15,870. Cost of B is a team estimate covering travel to Lucknow and Indore and a ₹1,000 thank-you for each owner. Revenue at risk: 2,530 stores x ₹20,000 x 6% = ₹30.36 lakh a month.

Option A is quick and would please Tikam, but it costs more each month than the lost stores earn Navkar even if every one returned, and it changes only price. Option B is the slowest of the three and gives no counts. Option C is quick and comfortable for Tara but can only reproduce the team's own guesses at scale.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish, and what does it leave open?
  2. For each of the exit survey (Exhibit 3) and the six support calls, what kind of question is it good at answering, and what are its limits?
  3. Which question does Tanvir face first: "why did stores leave?" or "how many left for each reason?" Why does the order matter before Diwali?
  4. Which option, or sequence of options, would you present on Monday, and what would you say to Tikam and to Tara?

7. A note for the learner

This topic frames the decision through a simple division of labour. Qualitative research answers "what is going on and why", and it is the right tool when you do not yet know what the possible reasons are. Quantitative research answers "how many, how much, how often", and it is the right tool once you know which reasons exist and want to size or rank them. The common mistake is counting before listening, which yields precise answers to possibly wrong questions.

Applied here, Exhibit 3 looks like quantitative evidence but is mostly a record of what Navkar chose to ask. The "Other" box is the only place where an unexpected reason could surface, and Tavish's four mentions of "morning" in six calls suggest one that Navkar did not list. The 33.5 per cent figure for price describes 71 people, not the 3,145 missing stores. Exhibit 1 does give a real quantitative clue: the two cities with extra operational changes fell far more, pointing toward delivery and credit rather than the July price revision shared by all five.

One defensible path is Option B first, followed by a short version of Option C. Tanvir would start interviews on Friday 16 October with around 14 owners in Lucknow and Indore, finishing by Saturday 24 October. The findings then become the answer list for a sharpened survey to the 8,525 August-active stores in both cities, read within six days, giving a sized ranking by Friday 30 October, over a week before Diwali. Meanwhile Tikam can test a morning slot in a few Lucknow pin codes. Option A fails on arithmetic, since a blanket cut costs more than the revenue recoverable, and Option C alone counts only what was already suspected.

What matters is the reasoning: separating what numbers show from what they cannot, and matching each method to its question. Interviews with 14 people prove nothing about proportions; their job is to find the right questions.
exp40v2-res.qual.quant:
Interviewing or Counting: The Order of Evidence in Customer Discovery

Discovery & Design · Qualitative Research · near-expert treatment

1. Two decisions, two kinds of evidence

On 14 July 2026 Qaisar Mobedji, product head at Qiyaas Diagnostics Network in Bengaluru, opened the review for the quarter ended 30 June. Qiyaas sells home blood collection, booked in an app. Of 12,40,000 installs in the quarter, 3,72,000 users opened an account — 30.0 per cent. Of those, 74,400 booked a first test: 20.0 per cent of accounts, 6.0 per cent of installs, ₹5.80 crore at an average bill of ₹780. Of them, 13,392 booked again within ninety days: a repeat rate of 18.0 per cent.

The board had set a target of 25 per cent repeat within two quarters. The growth team's plan came off the dashboard, with no account of why 61,008 people who had paid Qiyaas once had not paid again. Qaisar's objection: 18.0 per cent is an average of something, and nobody could say of what. He gave Qaneez Bharucha, the first research hire, eighteen days — 20 July to 7 August — and held the roadmap slot open.

Four hundred kilometres away Xavera Dastur had the opposite problem. She leads product at Qandeel Grid Industries in Pune, which sells solar-hybrid inverters with monitoring software to small manufacturers: textile processors, moulders, cold stores. The base on 30 June 2026 was 268 sites, and two quarters of engineering would go to one module. The favourite, pushed by the founder and by Ximena Ferrol, a firmware contractor in Valencia, was predictive maintenance: battery-string degradation forecasting at ₹1.35 lakh per site per year, ₹1.9 crore to build.

Xavera could not survey her way to an answer. With 268 customers a questionnaire returning seventy replies carries error wide enough to swallow any decision, and the people who answer vendor surveys like the vendor. She had a ticket census, a field-service head named Qasim Sanjana, and August on site. The question due with the 7 September board paper was whether the problem predictive maintenance solves is the one that costs her customers money.

Qaisar had measurement without meaning; Xavera had meaning without measurement. Interviewing or counting is a question about which inference the decision requires.

2. The idea, stated precisely

Qualitative research studies a few cases in depth, with open instruments, to establish what a phenomenon is: its structure, mechanism, boundaries and vocabulary. Quantitative research studies many cases with closed instruments — survey items, logged events — to establish magnitude: how large, how common. Qualitative work buys construct validity — the thing measured is the thing meant; quantitative work buys statistical and external validity. The dependency follows: you cannot count a category you have not constructed, and the construct comes either from the field or from whoever wrote the instrument.

The intellectual history is that dependency being rediscovered. Paul Lazarsfeld, at the Office of Radio Research in the 1930s and 1940s, called the missing step the reduction of indicators: a concept is elaborated into dimensions, then indicators, then items, and that step is qualitative by necessity. Campbell and Fiske named construct validity in 1959: the instrument that measures reliably and measures the wrong thing. Glaser and Strauss published grounded theory in 1967 to generate theory from data rather than test theory brought to it. Beyer and Holtzblatt made it contextual inquiry for software; Christensen and Moesta moved the unit of analysis to the switching episode. The lineages disagree, and an expert can say what each will and will not sign.

Sequentialists sign: a survey whose terms were not harvested from interviews measures its author. Not: interviews can establish how many.
Behaviouralists sign: revealed preference dominates stated preference at every sample size. Not: nine site visits justify reallocating two quarters.
Continuous discovery signs: a quarterly research project is an organisational failure; the unit is a weekly habit of contact. Not: saturation is a stopping rule — you never stop.
The jobs school signs: with the episode as the unit, ten to twenty switch interviews generalise, because the forces acting on progress recur. Not: generalisation needs a representative sample.
Mixed-methods formalists sign: integration must be designed before collection, not improvised afterwards from whatever is to hand.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Qaneez did not begin with interviews. She began by taking the 18.0 per cent apart: a blended rate is a weighted average, and the weights are an empirical claim. Her construct ladder decomposed "repeat behaviour" into "reason the first test existed at all", operationalised from prescription uploads, booking codes and who was tested.

Two segments account for 33,480 of the 74,400 bookers, 45.0 per cent, and for 10,490 of the 13,392 repeat bookings, 78.3 per cent. Their combined repeat rate is 31.3 per cent; the other three, 40,920 bookers, repeat at 7.1 per cent. The 25 per cent target on the blend asked certificate users to behave like chronic-illness patients.

The second-order effect catches competent teams. A weighted average moves when the weights move, with no change in behaviour. Hold every segment's rate at its Exhibit 1 value and shift the mix so prescribed panels rise from 30 per cent of bookers to 40 while routine self-monitoring falls from 25 to 15. The arithmetic is 11,160 × 0.34 plus 14,880 × 0.28 plus 29,760 × 0.07 plus 11,160 × 0.06 plus 7,440 × 0.09, giving 11,383.2 repeats on the same 74,400 bookers: a blended rate of 15.3 per cent. The headline falls 2.7 points while every segment is flat.

Only now do interviews earn their place. Qaneez recruited eleven participants purposively — six from the high-repeat segments, five from the low-repeat, including four who had not returned; recruiting from the return channel would have guaranteed the finding. Her guide asked about past episodes, not intentions: walk me through the last time you decided it was time for a test. By the eighth conversation the structure was stable. For chronic-panel users the repeat decision was not the user's; a physician wrote "repeat after three months", and the user's problem was remembering the date and finding a lab with comparable reference ranges. For certificate users there was no repeat decision to influence: the job was finished.

The formal treatment of "how many interviews" is simple. If a theme is present in a fraction p of the sampled population and n participants are drawn independently, the chance at least one exhibits it is 1 − (1 − p)n.

Two things follow. First, small samples are not a scandal: eleven conversations are near-certain to surface anything common. Second, the table assumes independent draws from a population of uniform prevalence, and purposive recruiting violates both deliberately. The p is prevalence in the pool recruited from. Had Qaneez used an in-product prompt her pool would have been active users, and a theme at 25 per cent prevalence among all bookers might sit at 3 per cent among actives — at which point eleven interviews have a 28.5 per cent chance of catching it. Recruitment, not sample size, is where qualitative inference is lost.

4. Conditions, stated as testable claims

One: if the terms of the question are not fixed, counting is premature. Test: can every noun in the instrument be traced to something a customer said unprompted? "Repeat intent" was Qiyaas's phrase; the user's was "when my doctor said to come back". "Predictive maintenance" is likewise a vendor category.

Two: if the decision turns on magnitude, interviews cannot close it. Test: does the decision change if prevalence is 8 per cent rather than 40? For Qaisar yes — a scheduling spine is worth building for 33,480 bookers, not for 3,000. For Xavera too, which is where her situation bites: with 268 sites she must substitute a ticket census for a survey.

Three: if the mechanism is unknown, a magnitude is uninterpretable. Test: state the causal story the number implies, and name the step you have evidence for. The 18.0 per cent implied motivation; the evidence supported calendars.

Four: if being wrong is cheap and reversible, measure instead of asking. Test: what does one wrong iteration cost? For a consumer checkout an experiment beats a study. At Qandeel, where modules ship on a quarterly firmware train, iteration is not an available epistemology.

The idea can also mislead: where the question is purely magnitude within a settled construct, interviews add delay, and where "we must talk to users first" is a procedural veto, the argument has stopped being methodological.

5. Hard edge cases

Qandeel is hardware plus software, which changes the economics of evidence, not its logic. Xavera's starting point was a census: every ticket from all 268 sites in the twelve months to 30 June 2026.

The census settled nothing on its own. Reconciliation led on both denominators, but a ticket is a request for help, not a measure of harm. So Xavera and Qasim visited nine sites between 3 and 28 August, chosen to span three load profiles. Six of the nine raised bill reconciliation unprompted, usually with a folder of disputed statements. Two raised battery degradation, and both were cold stores running deep cycles. When Ximena's mock-up was shown, the reaction was that predicting failure in six weeks did not help a manager who could not get a credit note approved in six months.

Three further seams recur. Two-sided: Qiyaas has phlebotomists as well as patients, and a pool that blends them averages away the tension that is the product. Regulated: clinical disclosure wording is not open to free experimentation, so qualitative evidence carries weight that elsewhere would go to an A/B test. AI-native: at Qaayda Tax Systems, a filing copilot for chartered accountants, the quantitative instrument is an evaluation set built from transcripts. The model handled 186 of 240 sampled real queries acceptably, 77.5 per cent, and review of the 54 failures traced 31 of them — 57.4 per cent — to one root cause, a misread of amended-return context.

At the organisational seam, mature companies say mixed methods. In fact research reports into design and analytics into data, on different cadences with different definitions of evidence, and the general manager trusts whichever function was right last. Those that genuinely integrate hold a single evidence review: both halves of a question, one owner, the decision written at the top.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The construct precedes the count

A competent practitioner asks which method to use; an expert asks whether the category being counted exists. The tell is a metric whose definition needs the company's own invented noun — engagement, repeat intent. Definitions look like a documentation problem; in fact the team's assumption is being measured very precisely.

The denominator is a finding, not a given

Exhibit 5 is the general case: the same facts ranked by tickets and by hours give different priorities. The tell is a priority list nobody can reorder, because only one denominator was computed. The choice encodes what the business conserves, which is a strategy question in an analytics costume.

A blended rate has weights that move on their own

The 15.3 per cent calculation above is the point. The tell is a headline metric that moves while nobody claims credit or blame. An expert's reflex on any aggregate change is to ask whether the mix moved before asking whether behaviour did.

Recruitment is where qualitative inference is won or lost

Exhibit 3's prevalence term belongs to the recruited pool, not the user base. The tell is a study whose participants were all reachable through the product, the mailing list or the account manager. Reachable users look like users; in fact the frame excludes those whose absence is the finding — the 61,008 who did not come back.

Saturation is relative to your own coding frame

Teams reach saturation on schedule because they saturate the categories they brought. The tell is that no interview produced a category without a heading waiting for it. Genuine saturation arrives only after some conversation forced a rewrite; "no new themes" is indistinguishable from having stopped listening.

Logged behaviour is also stated, by whoever named the event

Instrumentation feels like unmediated reality; it is an interpretive artefact. Someone decided what counts as a session and which taps deserve a name. The tell is an event taxonomy nobody can trace to a decision. The correction is not to distrust logs but to read the taxonomy as a document with authors.

Stated intent is valid about some things and not others

"What people say is not what they do" is too coarse. Stated evidence is strong on completed episodes, constraints, approval chains and vocabulary, weak on future behaviour and willingness to pay. The tell is a guide that mixes the two and treats the answers alike. Xavera asked who signs a credit note; asking what the plant would pay for forecasting would have bought only courtesy.

The unit of analysis is usually chosen by default

Person, episode, account, site-year, session: each gives a different answer. Qandeel's unit is the site-year, because a factory's problems recur seasonally; Qiyaas's is the testing episode, because one person is a chronic-panel user in March and a certificate user in September. The tell is research that counts people when the phenomenon is episodic. The jobs school's contribution is this choice of unit, not its interviewing style.

7. Product type and company stage

In consumer products behavioural volume makes measurement nearly free, which is why construct errors survive: nobody interrogates a daily number. In B2B and enterprise sampling collapses — 268 sites support no survey at useful precision — so censuses and deep access replace statistics, and the buyer-user split means two pools. In platforms and marketplaces each side must be studied separately before any blend is believed. In hardware plus software the release train removes iteration as a learning strategy. In AI products the modes fuse: the eval set is the instrument and the transcript its source.

By stage the difference is real but smaller than claimed. Before product-market fit there is no behavioural data, so the discipline is to act on eleven conversations; at scale the risk inverts to dashboard substitution. Stage changes what evidence is available, not what a decision requires.

8. Three worked examples

Qiyaas, succeeding. The interviews and Exhibit 1 together produced a scoping decision rather than a growth tactic. The target became the 33,480 bookers in the two chronic segments, repeating at 31.3 per cent. The build was a due-date spine: capture the physician's review interval at booking, remind against it, hold results at one lab. Moving that cohort from 31.3 per cent to 38 per cent yields 12,722 repeats against 10,490 — 2,232 extra bookings at ₹910, or ₹20.31 lakh a quarter, ₹81.24 lakh annualised.

Qandeel, choosing against the favourite. Predictive maintenance at ₹1.9 crore, recovered through a ₹1.35 lakh annual uplift, earns ₹2.70 lakh per adopting site over two years and so needs 71 sites to break even — 26.5 per cent of 268. The visits placed likely adoption in the cold-store slice, a fifth of the base. A reconciliation module, scoped at ₹1.1 crore because it reuses meter telemetry, breaks even at 41 sites, 15.3 per cent, against six of nine sites naming the problem unprompted.

Qismat Audio House, failing and recovering. On 12 January 2026 the podcast app surveyed its 2,00,000-subscriber mailing list and received 4,100 responses, a 2.05 per cent response rate. Sixty-eight per cent agreed that they wanted full-season offline downloads. Build ran eleven weeks from 2 February, shipping on 20 April at ₹46 lakh. At the ninety-day review on 19 July, 6,510 of 3,10,000 monthly actives — 2.1 per cent — had used it once. Fourteen interviews found two compounding errors: the frame was the mailing list, whose respondents averaged 7.4 listening hours a week against 1.9 for the base; and the instrument asked for agreement with a pleasant proposition rather than an account of a past episode. Data already held would have raised the alarm — 3.22 crore of the 4.6 crore listening sessions that quarter, 70.0 per cent, ran under twelve minutes with the network available. The recovery was an ₹18 lakh cross-device resume feature, used by 1,27,100 of 3,10,000 monthly actives, 41.0 per cent, within sixty days. The failure was not "they used a survey": the frame and the verb tense were both wrong.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The premature survey. Sign: instrument language appearing in no transcript. Diagnostic: read every noun aloud and ask who said it first. Caught late, the cost is a shipped feature — ₹46 lakh at Qismat.

Managing a blend. Sign: a target on an aggregate never shown decomposed. Diagnostic: ask for the metric split five ways and see whether anyone can produce it in a day. Caught late, a quarter goes on moving a mix.

Qualitative theatre. Sign: the recommendation deck predates the transcripts. Diagnostic: ask what finding would have cancelled the project, and whether anyone looked. Caught late, the organisation learns that research is ceremony.

The analytics veto. Sign: a mechanism question answered with a dashboard — "why are they not coming back?" met with a cohort chart. Diagnostic: ask what the number would look like under two competing mechanisms; if identical, it cannot arbitrate between them.

Synthesis at volume. Sign: four hundred interviews reduced to theme counts and percentages. Diagnostic: ask what the denominator is; usually "transcripts we happen to hold".

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

How many interviews. The fixed-n position — five is enough, and has been since usability testing established it — rests on evidence that defect discovery saturates fast for bounded tasks. The saturation position rests on discovery rate depending on heterogeneity, which five cannot establish. Exhibit 3 does not settle it: five interviews catch a 50 per cent theme 96.9 per cent of the time and a 10 per cent theme 41.0 per cent of the time — an argument for five if your themes are common, against it if they are not, and you learn which only afterwards.

Whether qualitative evidence generalises. The jobs school argues that with the episode as the unit, the forces acting on a switching decision recur, so ten interviews describe a mechanism holding beyond them. Survey methodologists reply that this is an untested claim about a population dressed as a definition. The jobs position fails if one job produces different forces across segments — which is what Exhibit 1 looks like read as five jobs rather than one.

Whether revealed preference dominates. The behaviouralist case is strong: stated intent has a replicable optimism bias, and logs are census-scale and cheap. The counter is that logs record only what the product made possible, so they are silent about what it does not yet do — and new products are made of that. The generative position fails if stated problems rarely convert into usage, which is what Qismat's 2.1 per cent looked like.

Whether machine synthesis substitutes for the researcher. One camp holds that transcript volume has been the binding constraint on rigour and automated coding removes it. The other holds that the value of synthesis is judgement about which surprise matters, not summarisation. For the first to be right, coding would have to elevate the single disconfirming case over twenty confirming ones — the opposite of what summarisation optimises for.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this writes the decision and its falsifier before choosing a method, so the research has something to fail against. They refuse to present an aggregate without its decomposition, and treat unexplained movement as a mix question first. They can state what a number would have to be before it changed the decision. And they can say that a question cannot be answered with the access available, then name the access that would.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On 20 August 2026 Qaisar took the repeat target off the blend. The metric became repeat rate within the two chronic segments, reported alongside the mix, with certificate users measured on first-booking volume instead. The roadmap slot went to the due-date spine, underwritten by ₹81.24 lakh of annualised incremental second bookings and by eleven transcripts showing the mechanism to be a calendar and a reference range, not a price.

On 7 September 2026 Xavera's board paper recommended the reconciliation module: a lower break-even, 41 sites against 71, confirmed on six of nine visits and in a census of 1,748 tickets. Predictive maintenance was re-scoped to the cold-store cohort and deferred, with a note that Qandeel did not yet know how many of its 268 sites ran the deep cycles that make forecasting valuable — and that finding out was a two-week data exercise.

Three questions worth sitting with. First: take the aggregate your team is accountable for and say how much of its last movement was behaviour and how much was mix — and if you cannot, what does that imply about the target? Second: for the last study your organisation ran, name the people the sampling frame excluded, and say whether including them would have changed the recommendation. Third: Xavera had 268 customers and could reach significance on nothing. Was her nine-site evidence weaker than Qismat's 4,100 responses, and how would you defend that to a board?

13. Going deeper

  1. Interview fundamentals — what makes a past episode recoverable rather than reconstructed.
  2. Designing an interview guide — how a guide encodes the construct ladder and still leaves room for a rewrite.
  3. Recruiting research participants — the highest-leverage topic here: Exhibit 3's prevalence term belongs to the channel.
  4. How many interviews — the arguments behind section 10, including stopping rules needing no number up front.
  5. Survey design — closed items built from interview vocabulary, without the author's construct smuggled back in.
  6. Cognitive biases in research — how both modes confirm prior belief, and what blunts each.
  7. Synthesising research — transcripts into a problem memo with evidence traceable to source.
  8. AI-assisted synthesis — where automated coding extends reach and where it buries the disconfirming case.
case40v1-res.qual.quant:
Osai Health Works: The Night Before the Board

A case on evidence, order and the gap between what people say and what the ledger records

1. Sunday night, Hyderabad

On the evening of Sunday 29 November 2026 the Osai Health Works office in Hyderabad held a security guard and Vismaya Datar, its Director of Product. In fourteen hours she had thirty minutes with the board to defend the fourth-quarter engineering plan: eleven people for twenty weeks at ₹4.2 crore: ₹2.20 crore of salary at a loaded ₹1.00 lakh per person-week and ₹2.00 crore of vendor and certification work.

She had four studies and no settled account of why members stopped paying. A survey of 12,740 people said price. A ledger of 30,976 non-renewals said payments. Fourteen home visits said something neither had asked about. An experiment said a new screen worked, then said it did not. The plan locked on Monday 14 December, and the Orvaan Industries Group contract renewed on 31 January 2027, sixty-two days after the meeting she had not yet written.

What she kept returning to was not which study was right, but that she had spent ₹52 lakh of a ₹1.10 crore research line on the study she now trusted least, and had approved its questionnaire herself in an August afternoon without a pilot.

2. Osai Health Works, 2018 to 2026

Osai was founded in 2018 by Vyjayanthi Deulgaonkar, a former hospital administrator, with two payments engineers. For a monthly subscription a person with diabetes or hypertension gets a coach on the phone in their own language, quarterly laboratory tests collected at home, reminders and a glucometer with free strips. By 30 September 2026 Osai had 2,60,000 paying members, 79,000 on Osai Care Plus at ₹599 a month and 1,81,000 on Osai Care Counter at ₹349: a blended ₹425 and monthly revenue of ₹11.05 crore, ₹132.6 crore annualised. The year ended 31 March 2026 brought ₹96 crore.

The decision that shapes what Vismaya can do today was taken in March 2023. App growth had stalled, and Osai signed the Otla Chemists Network, 1,900 pharmacy counters across Maharashtra, Telangana and Madhya Pradesh, to enrol members at the till for ₹120 an enrolment. To make counter selling work, Osai dropped the requirement that a member authorise a UPI AutoPay mandate at signup: the chemist took cash or a one-time UPI collect and the member was prompted later, the plan assuming most would set one up at their first renewal. The contract runs to 31 March 2027 and specifies that enrolment at the counter shall not require a bank mandate.

That assumption was first tested in September 2026. Of the 29,432 members enrolled at Otla counters in the April–June quarter, 11,479 ever created a mandate (39.0 per cent). The other 17,953 paid, when they paid, by walking back into a shop.

3. The industry

Chronic-care subscriptions sit between three larger businesses. Apollo 24|7, Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Practo own the habit of refilling medicine; Dr Lal PathLabs, Thyrocare and Metropolis own the test; HealthifyMe, BeatO and Fitterfly own the daily nudge. Osai competes on the bundle and on language, so its churn is exposed to any of them unbundling it cheaply.

Two pieces of regulation bear on the decision. UPI AutoPay, run by NPCI under the RBI's recurring-payments framework, requires a member to approve a mandate and to re-approve it if the amount changes: a reprice is a fresh consent event, not a database update. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act governs what Osai may record in a member's home: compliance has ruled that a member's photograph of a kitchen shelf cannot be retained if other household members appear in it. Abroad, Orvaan Industries Group in Muscat covers 9,400 employees at ₹675 each a month, ₹7.61 crore a year, 5.7 per cent of annualised revenue and Osai's only contract outside India. Orvaan judges renewal on measured improvement in annual health checks, not on renewal rates.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Figure A sets out the sequence. Osai enrolled 62,000 new members in the April–June 2026 quarter; by 28 September their day-90 outcomes were complete, and 31,024 of the 62,000 had renewed, 50.0 per cent. Exhibit 1 breaks that down by app language, and Exhibit 2 charts those rates for the board pack. On 14 July, before any cohort data was in, Vyjayanthi had written to the board that the dip was festival-cycle seasonality.

In August Vismaya commissioned Oppam Research Collective, which fielded a single-choice questionnaire between 2 and 16 September to 2,10,000 members lapsed since 1 January 2026 or flagged at risk; 12,740 completed it, 6.1 per cent of those invited, and a third of them chose price (Exhibit 3).

Two things about Exhibit 3 have since turned out to be wrong. The first is linguistic. The English item read “The monthly price is more than I can keep paying”; the Hindi and Marathi renderings said, in effect, “the price is high” — a judgement about value a satisfied member can also make — while the Telugu kept the affordability sense. Price selection by language: Hindi, 2,127 of 5,065 (42.0 per cent); Marathi, 920 of 2,300 (40.0 per cent); Telugu, 850 of 3,400 (25.0 per cent); English, 435 of 1,975 (22.0 per cent). The second is the ₹50 pharmacy credit per respondent, which Oppam's own note concedes attracts price-attentive members.

Vinutha Diwate's team then ran fourteen home visits over the nineteen days from 21 September to 9 October, and nine members kept a two-week photo diary. In nine of the fourteen visits, Exhibit 4 records, the member did not know a bank debit had failed. On 12 October Vetri Devadiga circulated the mandate ledger for the same cohort, Exhibit 5: of the 30,976 members who did not renew, 24,781 either had no mandate or a failed debit, 80.0 per cent of that group, the largest single category being the 30.0 per cent for whom no mandate existed to attempt. Renewal, he concluded, was a payments problem.

Vanaja Dias had meanwhile redesigned the renewal screen, and Exhibit 6 reports the test, run from 24 August to 20 September. Variant B won at fourteen days; on 10 November, when the first fortnight's day-60 outcomes were pulled, B was behind.

8. The options as Vismaya sees them

A. Price. Launch a ₹299 counter tier in January in place of Osai Care Counter at ₹349. Across the 1,81,000 members on that plan the ₹50 reduction is ₹90.5 lakh a month, 8.2 per cent of the ₹11.05 crore monthly total, and break-even needs 30,268 new members a month at ₹299. It also needs re-approval from the 1,12,000 counter-plan members holding an active mandate, 61.9 per cent of that plan: at June's rate 69,440 would re-approve within thirty days and 42,560 would not. Whether an unbundled tier keeps the healthcare GST exemption is unsettled.

B. Payments. Spend the ₹4.2 crore plan on the mandate layer: retry logic, a failed-debit notice, mandate creation at the counter, a pay-at-counter fallback. This follows Exhibit 5, runs into the Otla contract, which forbids requiring a mandate at the counter until 31 March 2027, and treats the 9,293 members with no mandate as a failure when 8,660 of their cohort peers renewed without one.

C. Evidence. Re-field the survey with corrected wording and a telephone mode for the unreachable: ₹46.5 lakh and five weeks, which from 1 December lands on 5 January 2027, after the plan locks. D. Instrument and wait. Two engineers for six weeks, ₹12 lakh of capacity, to log what a member sees after a failed debit, shipping variant B meanwhile. Vairam will support it for the wrong reason: he has shown Orvaan the 40.0 per cent.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board sits at 9.30 on Monday 30 November. The plan locks on Monday 14 December, and engineering will not hold eleven people idle past it. ₹58 lakh remains in the FY27 research line after the ₹52 lakh paid to Oppam. The Otla contract, which produced 29,432 of the 62,000 cohort enrolments and earned Otla ₹35.32 lakh that quarter at ₹120 an enrolment, bars a mandate requirement at the counter until 31 March 2027. A reprice is a re-consent event under the NPCI mandate rules, and the DPDP Act limits what the diaries may retain. Orvaan renews on 31 January 2027: ₹7.61 crore a year, 5.7 per cent of annualised revenue, turning on evidence Osai has not gathered.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 establish about the April–June cohort, and what does it leave open? What does Exhibit 2 remove?
  2. Write down the population behind the 34.0 per cent in Exhibit 3 and behind the 80.0 per cent in Exhibit 5. What can each support, and what has each been used to support?
  3. Exhibit 4 reports counts out of fourteen and no percentages. Is that a weakness of the method or a property of the question it answers?
  4. For each of the four studies, state the question it could answer. In what order should they have been commissioned, and at what cost?
  5. Before acting on the six-point fourteen-day difference in Exhibit 6, what must you establish about the two arms? Does the day-60 reversal change the decision or the confidence?
  6. What should Vismaya do on Monday morning, and what should she say to the board about the ₹52 lakh already spent?

11. The rest of the night

At eleven Vismaya wrote one sentence on the whiteboard — members are leaving because — and left it unfinished. Vetri's ledger could tell her how many debits failed and never what a member believed had happened. Vinutha's fourteen households could tell her what a member believed and never how many believed it. Oppam's 12,740 answers told her only what people chose from a list she had written herself in an afternoon, in words that shifted between languages. The board wanted the sentence finished by half past nine; Orvaan wanted a different one by the end of January. She turned off the light.
exp20v2-res.qual.quant:
Qualitative vs Quantitative Research:
Should I Be Interviewing People or Counting Them?

Discovery & Design — Qualitative Research module

1. The Scene: Lumenate, March 2024

Maya Odiya is the product lead for Shift Swap, a proposed feature inside Lumenate, a workforce-scheduling platform used by roughly 1,100 mid-size retail and hospitality employers to build staff rosters. Lumenate has 40,000 named end users — the shift workers who log in to see their schedules — and the company's engineering backlog has one open slot for Q2 2024. Two features are competing for it. One is a reporting dashboard that three enterprise accounts have explicitly requested in writing. The other is Shift Swap: a marketplace inside the app where a worker who cannot make a shift could post it and a coworker could claim it, without a manager playing switchboard operator.

The idea for Shift Swap came from a single comment on a support ticket, amplified by the VP of Product, who liked it. No customer has asked for it by name. Building it will cost an estimated $280,000 in engineering time over one quarter. Maya has been given until April 15 — five weeks — to tell the leadership team whether Shift Swap deserves the slot, and she has a budget for exactly one research activity before that meeting. She is tempted to write a ten-question survey, blast it to all 40,000 users, and report back a clean percentage: "62% of workers say they would use shift swapping." It would look rigorous in a slide. It would also, she suspects, tell her almost nothing about whether the thing is worth building — because she does not yet know what "shift swapping" even means to the people doing the swapping, how often the underlying problem actually bites, or what they currently do instead. She has a passing sense that there is a "right order" to this kind of inquiry — talk first, count second — but she has never had to defend that order to a room that wants a number by name.

2. The Idea, Precisely

Qualitative research is the systematic study of a small number of cases — typically people, through interviews or observation — to understand the structure of a problem: what it is, why it occurs, in what words people describe it, and what they currently do about it. Quantitative research is the systematic study of a large number of cases, using closed, pre-defined questions or instrumented behavior, to measure how big, how common, or how correlated something is. The difference is not "squishy versus rigorous" — both, done properly, are disciplined methods with their own standards of evidence. The difference is what kind of question each can answer. Qualitative work answers what is going on, and why. Quantitative work answers how much, how often, and for how many people.

The intellectual lineage matters because it explains why the two were never meant to compete. Qualitative inquiry, as a formal discipline, descends from anthropological fieldwork — Bronisław Malinowski's immersive studies of Trobriand Islanders in the 1910s–20s — and from grounded theory, a method Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss codified in 1967 specifically to let researchers build explanatory theory from unstructured observation rather than testing a theory they already held. That lineage entered software through contextual inquiry, a technique Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt formalized in the 1990s for watching people use tools in their own workplace rather than in a lab. It entered product management specifically through Steve Blank's customer-development method (mid-2000s) and Eric Ries's Lean Startup (2011), both of which insisted that founders talk to customers before building, not after. Quantitative research, by contrast, descends from statistics and survey methodology — the apparatus of sampling, confidence intervals, and significance testing built up across the twentieth century precisely to let a researcher generalize from a sample to a population without talking to every member of it. Both toolkits are old and well tested. The error Lumenate risks is not choosing the wrong one — it is reaching for the counting tool before anyone has defined, in the customer's own words, what is worth counting.

"Interviews tell me what the problem is and why it matters; a survey can only tell me how many people have it — and that number is meaningless until the interviews have told me what to ask."

3. How It Actually Works

The mechanics run in a specific order, and the steps practitioners skip are usually the connective ones, not the glamorous ones. First, Maya writes down the decision the research must inform — not "learn about scheduling pain" but "decide whether Shift Swap deserves the one open Q2 engineering slot." Second, she drafts a working hypothesis of the problem, stated as a guess she intends to disprove: "Workers who need to swap a shift currently resort to personal group chats and lose time or pay when no one responds." Third, she recruits five to eight people who have recently lived the situation — not a random sample, but a purposive one, chosen because they are close to the problem, not because they represent the population statistically. Fourth, she writes a discussion guide: a short list of open-ended prompts ("Tell me about the last time you needed someone to cover your shift") rather than closed ones ("Would you use a shift-swap feature?") — because a closed, hypothetical, future-tense question reliably produces polite overclaiming, not evidence.

Fifth — and this is the step most often skipped — she conducts the interviews one at a time and updates her guide between them, following up on surprises instead of running every session identically like a script. Sixth, after each interview she writes a short synthesis note within an hour, while memory is fresh, capturing the person's actual words. Seventh, after five to eight interviews she looks for saturation: the point at which new interviews stop producing new themes. Saturation, not a target sample size, is what tells a qualitative researcher to stop — this is the detail that separates people who understand the method from people who think "small sample" is just a budget constraint. Eighth, she writes a problem memo: a one-to-two-page document stating what she now believes the problem is, in the customers' vocabulary, with direct quotes as evidence, and an explicit statement of what remains uncertain. Only after that memo exists does a quantitative instrument — a survey, an A/B test, a funnel analysis — make sense, because only then does Maya know which questions are worth asking at scale, and in what words her own customers would recognize them.

4. A Worked Example, With the Arithmetic Shown

Maya runs seven interviews over nine days with workers who recently needed a shift covered. By interview five, the same three behaviors keep recurring: people text a personal group chat (6 of 7), they lose pay if no one answers in time (4 of 7), and several mention they have, at least once, simply not shown up and eaten a point against their attendance record (3 of 7) — a cost nobody on the leadership team had mentioned. By interview seven, no new behavior category appears; she has reached saturation. Her problem memo states the finding plainly: the pain is not "I wish there were a marketplace," it is "I lose money or standing because my informal coordination channel is slow and unreliable," and it concentrates among hourly workers with unpredictable personal schedules, not among salaried team leads.

Now a survey becomes meaningful, because Maya knows what to ask and in what words: "In the last 30 days, how many times did you need someone to cover a shift?" and "What did you use to find a replacement?" with answer options drawn directly from her interview transcripts (group chat, asked manager, posted on a board, other). To report a result with confidence across her 40,000-user population, she needs to know how many responses she needs. The standard formula for a simple random sample is:

n = (Z² × p × (1−p)) / e²

where Z is the confidence multiplier (1.96 for 95% confidence), p is the expected proportion answering a given way (0.5 is used when unknown, because it is the most conservative, largest-sample assumption), and e is the margin of error she is willing to accept. At a ±5% margin: n = (1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5) / 0.05² = (3.8416 × 0.25) / 0.0025 = 0.9604 / 0.0025 = 384.2, rounded up to 385 completed responses. Out of 40,000 users, that is under 1%, achievable with a well-targeted email campaign and a modest incentive.

A second pass shows why this matters operationally. If the leadership team insists on tighter precision — say ±3% instead of ±5%, because they want to distinguish 60% from 63% confidently — the arithmetic becomes n = (1.96² × 0.25) / 0.03² = 0.9604 / 0.0009 = 1,067.1, rounded to 1,068. That is a near-threefold increase in required responses for a survey whose questions only became answerable because seven conversations happened first. The lesson is not "more precision is always better." It is that precision has a price, and the price is only worth paying once you know you are measuring the right thing.

5. Nuances a Learner Must Catch

Saturation, not sample size, governs qualitative stopping rules

A common tell of someone who has only the vocabulary is treating "8 interviews" as a magic number. The actual stopping rule is saturation: stop when new interviews quit producing new themes. Eight is a typical count at which saturation tends to occur for a reasonably bounded problem — it is a rule of thumb born of experience, not a statistical requirement, and a messier problem space may need twelve or fifteen before it stabilizes.

What people say is not what people do

Interviews are strongest at surfacing attitudes, motivations, and vocabulary; they are weak at predicting future behavior, because people are poor forecasters of their own actions, especially under hypothetical framing ("Would you use X?"). The fix is to ask about specific past instances ("Tell me about the last time...") rather than future intentions, and to treat any claim about future use as a hypothesis for the survey or the prototype to test, not as a finding.

Qualitative work cannot tell you how many — and should not be asked to

Seven interviews cannot support the sentence "62% of users want this." That is a category error, not a small-sample problem: no amount of interview rigor converts a purposive sample of seven into a statistically representative one. If the sentence "how many" needs to appear in the board deck, qualitative research alone cannot supply it.

Quantitative work cannot tell you why — even with a huge n

A survey can report that 40% of respondents cite "group chat" as their coordination method, but it cannot explain what makes that method fail, what workers tried before settling on it, or what they would accept as a replacement. Large numbers answer "how much"; they are silent on mechanism, and teams that mistake a big dataset for understanding routinely build the technically correct answer to the wrong problem.

Generative versus evaluative is a separate axis from qual versus quant

Generative research discovers problems you didn't know you had; evaluative research tests a solution you've already designed. Both can be done qualitatively (interviews to generate hypotheses; usability tests to evaluate a prototype) or quantitatively (surveys to generate at scale; A/B tests to evaluate at scale). Conflating "qualitative" with "early-stage only" is a common and costly confusion — usability testing, a qualitative method, belongs right before launch, not just at the start.

An unstructured conversation is not rigorous qualitative research

People who merely use the vocabulary often equate "I talked to some customers" with qualitative rigor. Rigor requires a written guide, consistent documentation, a defined unit of analysis, and some form of coding or theme-tagging across interviews so conclusions trace back to evidence rather than to whichever conversation the researcher remembers best.

Triangulation means independent methods converging, not two surveys

True triangulation pairs methods with different blind spots — interviews plus usage logs plus a survey — so that each method's weakness is covered by another's strength. Running two surveys, or two rounds of interviews, checks reliability but is not triangulation in the methodological sense.

Bias lives in recruitment before it lives in analysis

The single biggest threat to both methods is who gets studied. Interviewing only enthusiastic power users, or surveying only an email list of engaged customers, biases the sample long before any question is asked. A thoughtful researcher asks, before recruiting: who is missing from this sample, and would their absence change the conclusion?

6. How This Differs by Context

ContextWhat changes
Consumer productLarge user base makes quantitative instruments (A/B tests, funnel data) cheap and fast to run, which tempts teams to skip interviews entirely — yet consumer behavior is driven by motivations users rarely articulate in a survey, so generative interviews remain essential before a redesign.
B2B (Lumenate's case)User counts are small, access to the right person is hard-won, and the buyer is often not the user — so qualitative access is precious and should be spent on decision-makers and end users separately; quantitative surveys often lack the n for tight confidence intervals, so B2B teams lean more heavily on qualitative evidence and triangulate with account-level usage data instead of survey statistics.
MarketplaceTwo sides (e.g., shift-posters and shift-takers) can have opposite problems; a single survey or interview pool that blends both sides will average away the real tension, so research must be run and analyzed per side before being combined.
Early-stage companyNo usage data exists yet, so qualitative work is close to the only evidence available, and the discipline is to treat five good interviews as sufficient to act, rather than waiting for a sample size that will never come.
Large companyAbundant quantitative data creates the opposite risk: treating dashboards as a substitute for talking to anyone, so the discipline is scheduling qualitative check-ins deliberately rather than assuming the numbers already explain themselves.

7. Common Mistakes

Mistake one — the premature survey. Symptom: a survey goes out with questions like "How important is feature X to you, on a scale of 1–5?" before anyone has defined X in the customer's own words. Underlying misunderstanding: treating quantitative research as cheaper and more objective, when in fact a poorly grounded survey simply produces precise-looking nonsense. Cheapest diagnostic: ask whether every term in the survey appeared, unprompted, in at least one customer interview; if not, the survey is measuring the researcher's assumptions, not the customer's reality.

Mistake two — treating seven interviews as a statistic. Symptom: a slide states "most customers want this" based on five conversations. Underlying misunderstanding: conflating a purposive sample with a representative one. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "most, out of what denominator, selected how?" — if the honest answer is "seven people I thought to call," the claim needs rewording to "this pattern appeared in the small group we spoke with" and a quantitative follow-up before any "most" claim is made.

Mistake three — leading questions dressed as neutral ones. Symptom: interview transcripts are full of confirming nods and short agreeable answers. Underlying misunderstanding: the interviewer asked "Would a shift-swap marketplace help you?" instead of "Tell me about the last time you needed coverage." Cheapest diagnostic: read the guide aloud and count how many questions could be answered with a single word — a well-built guide has almost none.

Mistake four — stopping at the first comfortable theme. Symptom: research "finds" exactly what the team already believed going in, on schedule. Underlying misunderstanding: confirmation bias in both recruitment and coding — the researcher heard what they expected and stopped listening for disconfirming cases. Cheapest diagnostic: before synthesis, have someone write down the three findings that would most threaten the existing plan, and check the transcripts explicitly for evidence of each.

8. What Good Looks Like

At a comparable company, a product lead facing the same fork — reporting dashboard or new marketplace feature — spends week one writing a one-page decision brief and a discussion guide, then conducts seven interviews with workers who recently needed shift coverage, recruited across both power users and infrequent ones. She writes a synthesis note after each conversation, reaches saturation by interview six, and produces a two-page problem memo with verbatim quotes showing that the dominant cost is lost pay and attendance penalties, not inconvenience. In week two she fields a 12-question survey built entirely from that vocabulary to a stratified sample of 500 users (yielding 190 usable responses, still informative for directional comparison across worker types even short of the full 385), confirming that the pattern concentrates among hourly workers with variable schedules — about a third of the user base. She walks into the leadership meeting with both: a quote-backed account of the mechanism and a number that bounds its size, and recommends the feature for exactly that third of users rather than the whole base, reshaping the build to a lighter scope that ships in six weeks instead of a full quarter.

9. Maya's Decision

Maya runs the interviews first. By April 3 she has her saturation point and her problem memo: the real cost is lost pay and attendance penalties among hourly staff with unstable personal schedules, roughly 35% of Lumenate's user base by her interview sample's composition — a number she flags explicitly as a hypothesis, not a finding. She spends the remaining ten days fielding a targeted survey to confirm prevalence and size, reaching 410 responses, comfortably past her 385 threshold for ±5% confidence. She walks into the April 15 meeting able to say not "62% of users want shift swapping" but "among hourly staff with variable schedules — about a third of our base — 71% report losing pay or an attendance point in the last quarter from coverage failures, and group chat is the dominant workaround today." The reporting dashboard loses the slot; Shift Swap, scoped specifically to the segment the evidence supports, wins it.

The next things worth learning, in order, are Interview Fundamentals — how to write a guide that doesn't lead the witness, and how to run a conversation that surfaces what someone actually did rather than what they'd like to believe about themselves — and Survey Design, which governs how to turn an interview's vocabulary into closed questions without smuggling in bias through answer-option wording. Both depend on the sequencing argument made here: a survey is only as good as the interview that preceded it.

Two questions worth sitting with: when you last reported a number from customers in a meeting, could you trace every word in the question back to something a customer actually said first — or had you supplied the vocabulary yourself? And the next time a stakeholder asks for a survey "to be sure," what would you need to already know before that survey could be sure of anything at all?
case20v1-res.ai.synthesis:
Jantar Udhar Exchange: Trusting the Synthesis

A decision case on AI-assisted synthesis in qualitative research

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Oorvi Tembe sat in the Mumbai office of Jantar Udhar Exchange with two documents open side by side. The left screen held a nine-theme research synthesis, produced in an afternoon by a large language model from twenty-four merchant interviews. The right held a six-page audit memo from a colleague in Montreal, listing where that synthesis did not match the raw transcripts.

Tembe, a group product manager, owned the festive-season credit-limit feature. It had to be live by Thursday, 5 November, three days before Diwali. Engineering needed ten working days to build it, and the design brief depended on the synthesis. Sprint planning was on Friday, 16 October, and she had to say that morning which version of the research the team would build from.

2. Company background

Jantar Udhar Exchange, founded in Pune in 2019, runs a mobile app on which kirana owners record customer credit, order from wholesalers and draw short-term working capital from partner lenders. About 62,000 merchants across nine cities were active in September 2026. It competes for the same shopkeeper with Khatabook and OkCredit in credit ledgers, with PhonePe for Business and Paytm for payments and soundbox devices, and increasingly with lenders reaching merchants through ONDC-linked apps. Its lending is subject to the RBI's digital lending directions, and the personal data in its interviews to the DPDP Act, 2023.

The festive quarter matters disproportionately. Shopkeepers stock up for Dussehra, Dhanteras and Diwali, and the company had set a target of ₹60 crore in working-capital disbursals for the quarter. The feature in question lets a merchant raise a credit limit in three taps before a wholesale purchase. Early tests showed many eligible merchants opening the offer and never accepting it; the research was meant to learn why.

3. The situation

Between 14 September and 2 October, Tembe's research team interviewed twenty-four merchants in four cities (Exhibit 1). Interviews ran in Hindi, Marathi and English-mixed speech, and each was transcribed. On 5 October, Tembe asked a data scientist to run all twenty-four transcripts through a general-purpose LLM, operating under an enterprise agreement with India-hosted processing and with names and phone numbers masked first. It returned nine themes and fifty-four supporting quotations in about three hours. The same work had taken her team three weeks the previous year.

The synthesis read well. Its headline said merchants declined the offer because of interest-rate sensitivity. Odette Tremblay, the company's senior researcher in Montreal, did not trust a conclusion she had not seen earned. Between 12 and 13 October she hand-coded six transcripts and checked every one of the fifty-four quotations against the raw files. Exhibit 2 sets out what she found.

Most quotations were sound, but three did not exist, and the unmatched ninth theme, a supposed fear of GST notices, rested on exactly those quotes. The three missed themes shared a pattern: each concerned how a shopkeeper's spouse or elder relative shaped borrowing decisions, voiced in Marathi and Hindi phrases that the model had flattened into generic remarks about "trust". In her coding the most recurrent finding was that merchants felt wholesalers' informal credit was cheaper and less risky than a formal limit, whatever the interest rate; rate sensitivity appeared, but as a secondary theme.

4. The people

Oorvi Tembe, group product manager, Mumbai, owns the feature and the sign-off. She wants a design that fixes the real reason for non-acceptance, and she wants it in market before 5 November.

Omvir Thakkar, chief business officer, Mumbai, owns the ₹60 crore festive target. He points out that the synthesis already supports a clear idea (a lower-rate festive offer), and that the company cannot afford a second year of reports that arrive after the season.

Odette Tremblay, senior researcher, Montreal, wrote the audit. She does not oppose the tool; she opposes shipping its output unverified, and she is willing to extend the audit to the remaining eighteen transcripts if given four working days and a Marathi-speaking colleague.

Otto Thorsen, designer, Copenhagen, is three and a half hours behind Mumbai. He needs a brief by Monday 19 October to begin screens. He does not want to redraw the flow twice.

5. The options

Tembe saw three courses (Exhibit 3).

Option A: ship the synthesis as it stands. The brief goes to Copenhagen on 19 October, building starts the same day and finishes on 30 October, leaving a week of buffer. It costs nothing extra. But the plan rests on a synthesis whose ninth theme has no support in the sample, whose quotations three times cannot be found, and whose rate-sensitivity headline Tremblay's coding ranks below other findings.

Option B: audit the rest and then build. Tremblay and a Marathi-speaking researcher trace every theme and quotation in the remaining eighteen transcripts back to the raw lines, and re-code the family-decision material by hand, using the LLM to propose and the people to confirm. The audit takes four working days, 19 to 22 October. The build starts on 23 October and ends exactly on 5 November, with no slack.

Option C: discard the synthesis and code all twenty-four transcripts by hand. This is the old method, three researchers for three weeks. It produces the most trusted result, but ends on 6 November, so build starts on 9 November and finishes on 20 November, after Diwali.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, what does 83 per cent of quotes verbatim tell you, and what does it hide? How should one untraceable quotation change the way you treat the theme that depends on it?
  2. Theme precision is 89 per cent and recall 73 per cent in the sample. Which of the two matters more for a design brief, and why does the pattern in the three missed themes matter more than the percentage?
  3. Omvir Thakkar argues that speed is the point of using an LLM. What exactly was sped up, and what was never sped up?
  4. Which option would you take on 16 October, what would you ask Tremblay to do first, and what would make you switch?

7. A note for the learner

This case is about the difference between synthesis and evidence. An LLM compresses transcripts quickly, but it cannot show that its compression is faithful. The method this topic teaches is to treat the model as a fast junior analyst whose output you audit against the raw notes: trace every quote, check coverage on a hand-coded sample, and look for patterns in what is missed, not only for how much.

A well-reasoned answer separates three claims. First, the model's themes are hypotheses, not findings. Second, the audit has already told Tembe where the weaknesses are: invented quotes and lost family-decision material, concentrated in code-mixed speech. Third, the sample recall of 73 per cent cannot be projected onto the remaining eighteen transcripts without more checking.

One defensible path is Option B. It costs ₹2.40 lakh, a fifth of Option C's ₹12.00 lakh, and still reaches the market before Diwali. It also removes the specific defect, untraceable quotes, while adding human coding where the model was weakest. Option A saves the audit cost but builds a festive offer on a lower interest rate when the audited evidence points to wholesaler credit and family decisions. Option C buys certainty after the season has gone.

The path is not risk-free: Option B leaves no slack. Tembe should therefore commit Thorsen to a flexible brief on 19 October, with the rate-sensitivity theme excluded and the offer framed around wholesaler credit, and confirm the remaining themes on 22 October. If the audit of the eighteen transcripts finds a failure rate of unsupported quotes far above Tremblay's sample, she should fall back toward a hand-coded core. Cheap synthesis makes evidence checking the scarce skill.
exp20v2-res.ai.synthesis:
AI-assisted synthesis

Using a language model to code and cluster interview transcripts, and auditing it against the raw notes

1. The Monday committee

On Thursday 24 September 2026, Nayana Bhalla, a product manager at Banjara Exchange, opened a spreadsheet and found a problem she had wanted for months. Banjara runs a B2B marketplace in Indore that connects small truck operators, most of whom own between two and ten vehicles, with manufacturers and traders who need goods moved. Between 7 and 18 September she and the research analyst Navin Bhide had held 18 discovery interviews with operators. The audio was transcribed, and the roadmap committee, chaired by head of product Bharat Naik, met on Monday 28 September.

The committee had ₹90 lakh to spend that quarter and two candidate bets. An escrow-based payment guarantee, which holds the shipper's money until delivery and releases it to the operator, was costed at ₹86 lakh. A load-verification feature, which checks that a posted load and its shipper are real, was costed at ₹64 lakh. The budget allowed one. Hand-coding 18 transcripts would take Navin most of a week, and the committee would meet before he finished.

She pasted the transcripts into a language model and asked it to find the themes. Forty minutes later it returned six themes, each with quotations and a count, in confident prose. Nayana now faced the decision this page is about, and it was not which feature to build. It was how much of the model's synthesis she was entitled to put in front of a committee that would commit ₹86 lakh on the strength of it. If she trusted it blindly, she risked building the wrong feature on a pattern the model had half invented.

2. The idea

A language model (LLM) is software trained on large quantities of text to predict plausible continuations of a passage; given a transcript and an instruction, it can summarise, label and group. AI-assisted synthesis is the practice of using one to perform the mechanical labour of qualitative analysis, while a human keeps responsibility for checking the result against the raw evidence. Coding means attaching a short label, called a code, to a passage that expresses an idea (for example, "waited 40 days for payment"). Clustering means grouping codes that belong together into themes.

The problem is old: interviews generate more material than a person can hold in mind. Thematic coding, developed through grounded theory (Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, 1967) and later thematic analysis (Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, 2006), made the process disciplined but slow. General-purpose language models, available widely from late 2022, removed much of the slowness. They made the discipline easy to skip.

That gives Nayana her sentence for the meeting: "The model proposed the themes, I checked a sample of its evidence against the transcripts, and here is how much of it held up." It names a division of labour and a measured result: the model supplies speed, the human judges whether a quotation supports a label.

3. How it actually works

The workflow has seven steps, shown in Figure 1. Most descriptions leave the last three implicit, which is where the risk lives.

Step 1: each transcript is given an identifier and speaker labels, so every later claim can be traced to a file and line.

Steps 2 and 3 are the model's core work. It works by similarity of meaning, not a rulebook, so two runs can group slightly differently. Step 4 produces the summary Nayana first saw.

Step 5 is the heart of the audit. A person draws a random sample of coded excerpts, opens the raw transcript beside each, and judges whether the excerpt genuinely supports its theme. Step 6 recounts the themes by person, not by excerpt,. Step 7 asks the question models are worst at answering: what did the interviews contain that no theme captures, and what did the interviews never reach? A model cannot tell you about people you did not interview.

4. A worked example

The model coded 240 excerpts into six themes. Table 1 shows its counts. Nayana then drew a sample of 40 excerpts, about one in six, allocated across themes in proportion to size and rounded to whole excerpts. Navin read each against the transcript and marked it supported or not.

The overall support rate is 35 ÷ 40 = 87.5 per cent, which sounds reassuring, but the figure that matters is by theme. Projecting the sample rate onto the full theme gives a rough corrected count. Payment delay: 78 × 12 ÷ 13 = 72 supported excerpts. Load-matching trust: 62 × 0.70 = 43.4, call it 43.
