Navin traced the cause: two operators contributed 34 of the 78 payment excerpts, 43.6 per cent of that theme, so the remaining 44 came from seven other interviews. Payment delay is intense for a few; load-matching trust is a mild worry for nearly everyone. Which matters more is a genuine judgement, but the model's first output hid it.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Fluency is not accuracy

The model writes the same polished paragraph whether its theme is solid or invented, so the reader must create evidence of reliability through audit, as Table 1 did.

Counts are derived, not observed

A model asked "how many times was this raised" will often produce a number, but it is estimating from text it may have only partly attended to. Recompute counts from exported excerpts in a spreadsheet.

Excerpts and people are different units

This was Table 2's lesson. Frequency of mention mixes talkativeness with importance; the number of people who raised a theme measures breadth.

A quotation can be real and still mislead

Models sometimes trim a sentence so that a hedge disappears: "I wait for payment, but honestly it comes on time with regular shippers" becomes "I wait for payment". Check the surrounding lines.

Sampling has to be random

If the auditor checks the excerpts that look most interesting, the audit measures the auditor's taste. Draw it by random number, stratify by theme, and say how many you checked. Ten items is a spot check, not a statistic.

Synthesis is not discovery

The model can only group what was said. It cannot tell you that the 18 operators were all recruited from Indore, that none had yet been burned by a fraudulent load, or that a question you forgot to ask would have changed everything.

6. How it differs by context

In consumer products, interviews are numerous and short; clustering many small utterances is the model's strength, and the main risk is mistaking vivid quotes for prevalence. In B2B products, interviews are few and long, and each participant may represent a firm. Count by account and role too, since the buyer who signs and the operator who uses may want different things.

In marketplaces, there are at least two sides, and synthesis must be run separately for each. Operators' payment complaints and shippers' no-show complaints may be one incident seen from opposite ends.

Scale matters too. An early-stage company with 18 interviews can audit every theme; the model accelerates a team of two. A large company with hundreds of interviews cannot hand-check everything, so it builds a standing audit: a fixed sampling rule, a recorded support rate per theme, and a threshold (say 80 per cent) below which a theme goes back for human recoding.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting the model's summary as the finding

Symptom: a slide of themes with percentages and no mention of any audit. Misunderstanding: that the model's output is data, when it is a hypothesis about the data. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "which ten excerpts did a person read against the transcript?" If nobody can name them, the synthesis is unaudited.

Counting excerpts and calling it prevalence

Symptom: a top theme resting on a handful of people. Misunderstanding: that quotation volume equals prevalence. Cheapest diagnostic: recount by interview, as in Table 2.

Leading the model with the answer

Symptom: themes mirroring the existing roadmap. Misunderstanding: that a model reads neutrally. Cheapest diagnostic: rerun with a neutral prompt; themes appearing only under the leading one are suspect.

Treating a clean synthesis as a complete one

Symptom: confidence about operators nobody interviewed. Misunderstanding: that more efficient analysis means more representative evidence. Cheapest diagnostic: list who is absent from the 18, such as operators who left the platform.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Nayana's Friday looks like this. She keeps the model's six themes as a draft. She asks Navin for a stratified sample of 40. She recomputes counts from an exported spreadsheet, not the model's prose, and recounts by interview. She reruns the synthesis with a neutral prompt; the same six themes return. Since the decision turns on load-matching trust, she asks Navin to read all 62 of its excerpts, because the sample leaves a range of 25 to 55.

The committee deck then carries one slide of themes, with counts by excerpt and by interview, audited support rate and sample size; a second slide listing who was not interviewed; and a third giving the recommendation and what would change it.

9. Closing

When the full read of load-matching trust finished on Saturday, Navin found 41 of its 62 excerpts supported, which is 66.1 per cent, consistent with the sample. Nayana recommended the load-verification feature at ₹64 lakh, leaving ₹26 lakh of the ₹90 lakh budget, and proposed using part of that to run a two-week payment-timing pilot with the nine operators who raised delay. Her reasoning: load-matching trust touched 14 of 18 operators, payment delay 9 at higher intensity, so the cheaper bet reached more people while the pilot tested whether intensity justified the ₹86 lakh escrow later. She told the committee what she could not claim: the interviews showed the problems exist, not that either feature would change behaviour.

To go further, read next about AI-assisted persona synthesis, which applies the same audit logic to a riskier output, a composite character that can feel more real than any evidence behind it. Then study discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't, where the scarce resource is good conversations.

Two questions to sit with. First, if load-matching trust had a 95 per cent support rate but all 14 interviews that raised it came from operators recruited by one sales manager, what would you trust? Second, at what support rate, and from what sample size, would you let a theme reach a roadmap without a full read, and what does your answer reveal about how much a wrong decision would cost you?
exp40v2-res.ai.synthesis:
AI-assisted synthesis

Coding and clustering transcripts with a language model, and auditing it well enough to spend money on

1. Two decisions, four days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, Iravati Dange opened a file of 46 transcripts. She is principal product manager at Lipi Learning Works, a Pune company whose Android app teaches children to read in four Indian languages. Lipi has 2.40 crore lifetime installs, 11.6 lakh monthly active users — 4.8 per cent of installs — and 1.42 lakh paying subscriptions, 12.2 per cent of those actives, at ₹249 a year: ₹353.6 lakh of subscription revenue. Her researcher Imtiaz Belgaumi had interviewed parents in Nashik, Hubballi and Howrah between 14 September and 2 October; a Nairobi vendor team under Lydia Wambui transcribed them.

Her quarter held ₹96 lakh of engineering capacity and two bets: a typography and legibility overhaul at ₹58 lakh, and a rebuild of offline downloads at ₹71 lakh — ₹129 lakh together, so only one would fit. Lajwanti Kher, head of product, had set the choice for Monday 19 October, fourteen days away; hand-coding 46 transcripts would take Imtiaz about 161 hours. So Iravati ran them through a language model and had, by that evening, nine themes, 612 coded excerpts, counts and prose that read like a finished finding. Her question was not which feature to build, but how much of that output she could carry into a room committing ₹58 or ₹71 lakh.

Lakshmikant Gharpure faced the same question from the other end of the scale. He is vice-president of product at Iqraar Claims Systems in Bengaluru, selling claims-adjudication software to seven Indian general insurers. His evidence was 19 interviews run between 1 and 11 September 2026 — seven claims managers, five surveyors, four IT heads, three subrogation-recovery heads — each about seventy minutes. His quarter held ₹340 lakh; a subrogation module was costed at ₹290 lakh, a surveyor-scheduling module at ₹175 lakh. The model made subrogation the largest theme by a clear margin, conveniently: his chief revenue officer had wanted it for a year. Before the meeting on Friday 23 October, Ishrat Munshi asked the question he could not dismiss. Largest by what unit?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

AI-assisted synthesis is the use of a language model to do the mechanical labour of qualitative analysis — attaching short labels (codes) to passages, grouping codes into themes, counting, drafting — while a human remains responsible for verifying the output against the raw material. A model predicts plausible continuations of text, so it produces labels that look like codes whether or not the passage supports them. The practice has two halves and only the first is automated.

The discipline it accelerates was built slowly: Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss set out constant comparison in The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967), Matthew Miles and Michael Huberman codified the audit of qualitative data (1994), Richard Boyatzis formalised codebooks (1998), Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke published reflexive thematic analysis (2006). Alongside ran a measurement tradition — Jacob Cohen's kappa (1960), Klaus Krippendorff's alpha — letting coders show that two people reading one transcript would label it alike. All of it addressed one problem: interviews generate more material than a person can hold in mind, so the analyst's expectations fill the gap. Language models, available widely from late 2022, removed the labour but not the expectations. Four positions on what follows divide competent practitioners.

The reflexive school is not squeamish about computers; it denies that any correct theme set exists to score the model against, which makes "support rate" incoherent. Iravati's reply: her committee will act on counts regardless.

3. Mechanics: what the audit consists of

The automated part is understood: label transcripts, code each passage, cluster, count, draft. The implicit part has five steps, each yielding a number.

Prompt isolation. Transcripts go in; the roadmap, the strategy memo and the feature names do not, because a model shown a feature list returns themes shaped like it. The cheapest step, most often skipped.

Stratified precision sampling. Draw a random sample of coded excerpts, allocated across themes in proportion to size, and have a human read each against the surrounding lines. Precision is supported divided by sampled. Iravati drew 90 of the 612, one in 6.8.

Multiplying each count by its precision gives 86 × 8 ÷ 13 = 52.9 for price against 58 × 9 ÷ 9 = 58.0 for narration speed, three ranks below it on raw counts.

Sampling error, stated. Thirteen items is a spot check. For price, precision is 8 ÷ 13 = 61.5 per cent and the standard error is the square root of 0.615 × 0.385 ÷ 13 = 0.135, so a 95 per cent interval runs 35.1 to 88.0 per cent — 30 to 76 of the 86 excerpts. Price could rank third or seventh, and thirteen reads cannot say which.

A gold set, for the error nobody measures. Precision catches excerpts the model should not have coded; it cannot catch passages it should have coded and did not. For that you need transcripts a human codes from scratch, blind to the model. Imtiaz hand-coded 6 of the 46 interviews, drawn by random number — 13.0 per cent of the corpus — marking 104 passages as code-worthy. The model had coded 83 there, of which 71 matched one of his: recall 71 ÷ 104 = 68.3 per cent, gold-set precision 71 ÷ 83 = 85.5 per cent, F-measure 75.9 per cent. The 33 misses mattered more than the twelve false attachments: fourteen, 42.4 per cent, concerned one thing — grandparents objecting to a child holding a phone unsupervised — for which there was no theme. Projecting 14 misses from 6 interviews to 46 gives 14 × 46 ÷ 6 = 107.3 passages, the second-largest theme in Table 2. A precision-only audit scores 82.2 per cent and misses it.

Agreement, properly computed. Lakshmikant ran the stricter version: for one binary code, "this passage expresses a regulatory or audit constraint", Ishrat coded the same 400 passages blind.

The economics explain the appeal. Hand-coding 46 transcripts at 3.5 hours each is 161 hours; at a fully loaded ₹1,100 an hour, ₹1,77,100, and at 35 productive hours a week, 4.6 weeks of one analyst — longer than Iravati had. The audited model path cost 90 excerpt reads at four minutes each (6.0 hours) plus 6 gold-set transcripts at 3.5 hours (21.0 hours): 27.0 hours or ₹29,700, plus ₹9,600 of model usage across three runs, so ₹39,300, which is 77.8 per cent below ₹1,77,100, in four working days. That saving is also the size of the temptation to skip the 27 hours and bank ₹39,300 as ₹9,600.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: reading everything is infeasible. True for Iravati at 161 hours. False for Lakshmikant: Ishrat could read all 19 transcripts in 66.5 hours, cheap against ₹340 lakh. For him the model is a search index.

Claim two: the question is prevalence, not one decisive observation. True for Iravati. Partly false for Lakshmikant: a constraint mentioned once by one compliance head can veto a module, and clustering buries singletons by design.

Claim three: one coding frame fits the corpus. True of Lipi's parents; false of any two-sided corpus, and of four roles in one file.

Claim four: the decision can wait for the audit. Both pass, barely: fourteen days for Iravati, six weeks from 11 September to 23 October for Lakshmikant. Where this fails, the right move is a smaller claim, not a faster audit.

It actively misleads in three cases. On a convenience sample it makes unrepresentative voices look like a measured population; polish is the problem. Shown the roadmap it returns the roadmap, and the agreement reads as confirmation. Asked "why" rather than "what", it supplies a mechanism from plausibility, not from the transcript.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Lakshmikant's corpus shows the commonest edge case: 19 interviews from only 7 accounts and 4 roles, so three denominators compete.

Subrogation leads on excerpts at 32.7 per cent and loses on accounts at 4 of 7; scheduling is second on excerpts and reaches all seven. The mechanism is visible once you look: 59 of the 100 subrogation excerpts, 59.0 per cent, came from the three recovery-head interviews, 3 of 19 or 15.8 per cent of the sample, arranged by sales because the chief revenue officer wanted the module. The sampling frame produced the theme, and the model faithfully reported the frame.

Two-sided businesses must be synthesised per side and joined afterwards, because one incident appears twice from opposite ends and a single frame merges them into false consensus. In regulated products no code may be invented where a regulator has fixed the vocabulary; Iqraar maps each compliance code onto its insurers' audit-checklist wording. In hardware plus software — Lohagarh Pump Industries in Rajkot, irrigation pumps with a telemetry app — half the evidence is not text, so a text-only synthesis drops failure logs and warranty returns. At AI-native firms such as Iksha Agent Labs in Hyderabad, whose corpus includes the product's own conversation logs, a model synthesising complaints about a model is correlated-blind. What mature companies do, as against what they say, is audit only what a decision turns on: Iqraar's standard demands kappa above 0.70 on every code, but it computes kappa only on the codes that carry funding.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Fluency is uncorrelated with accuracy

The model writes the same confident paragraph at 100 per cent precision and at 50. The tell: prose quality uniform across themes while audited precision ranges from 50.0 to 100.0 per cent.

Instability is a free diagnostic

Iravati ran the prompt three times; six of nine themes recurred in all three. By membership overlap between runs one and two — intersection over union — font size scored 101 ÷ (112 + 109 − 101) = 84.2 per cent and price 58 ÷ (86 + 73 − 58) = 57.4 per cent. Price, the weakest on audit of the five largest themes, was also the less stable of the two measured, and stability needs no reading. Spend the audit where the runs disagree.

Recall is the half never measured

Precision is easy because the model hands you the items to check; recall needs a gold set, 21.0 of Imtiaz's 27.0 audit hours. The tell: a support rate quoted with no recall figure. Recall was 68.3 per cent against a blended 82.2, and the missing third held a whole theme.

A missing theme does not look like an error

False attachments announce themselves on reading; an absent theme looks like silence. The tell is a gold set whose misses cluster: 14 of 33 on one subject is not noise. Random misses mean imprecision, correlated misses blindness, which more sampling cannot fix.

Excerpts, people and accounts are three populations

Counting excerpts weights the talkative, people the recruited, accounts the sold-to. The tell: a theme's shares under two denominators differing by more than about fifteen points, as for Lipi's offline downloads (15.8 of excerpts against 58.7 of interviews, a gap of 42.9) and Iqraar's subrogation (32.7 of excerpts against 57.1 of accounts, a gap of 24.4).

Trimming changes meaning without inventing text

Models rarely fabricate quotations; they truncate. "The download fails, though only on my mother's phone, not mine" becomes "the download fails". Every word is real; the prevalence claim is not. The tell: audited excerpts that are short, clean and end without a subordinate clause. Audit the window.

The sampling frame usually decides the answer

A model cannot know who was not interviewed, which is why Lipi's missing theme belongs to grandparents, never in the room. The tell: a theme whose excerpts concentrate in a few interviews one stakeholder arranged. The obvious reading is a strong signal; the accurate one is recruitment.

Audit depth must be pre-committed

If sample size and threshold are set after the themes are known, the audit measures the auditor's preferences. Lipi's standard, written beforehand, was 90 excerpts, a 75 per cent precision floor and a full read of any theme a funding decision turned on. The tell it is absent: no theme ever fails.

7. Differences by product type and stage

In consumer products the corpus is large and the interviews short, so clustering earns its keep and the risk is mistaking a vivid quotation for prevalence. In B2B and enterprise the corpus is small and the units nested — person inside role inside account — so the risk is unit confusion, and the fix is Table 3's extra columns, not a bigger sample. In hardware, text is a minority of the evidence, so a text-only ranking favours problems customers can articulate.

Stage changes the protocol more than product type does. At 19 interviews you can read everything and should. At 46, auditing is a choice, and the choice is the discipline. Above roughly 150 interviews a quarter it must become standing process: a fixed sampling rule, recorded precision per theme, a quarterly gold set, a recoding threshold. The overstated difference is the arithmetic, identical everywhere; only sample sizes and the cost of error move.

8. Three worked runs, including one that failed

Lipi, consumer, succeeded with a surprise. Nine themes, 612 excerpts, 82.2 per cent blended precision, 68.3 per cent recall, a tenth theme found only by reading, projected at 107.3 passages, ₹39,300 spent against ₹1,77,100. The value was the reordering: price fell from third to fifth, and the theme that would have justified a pricing experiment rested on 11 interviews.

Iqraar, enterprise, succeeded by changing the denominator. Five themes, 306 excerpts, kappa 0.642 on the compliance code — below the written 0.70 floor, so that code was recoded by hand. The decisive finding needed no model at all: 59 of 100 subrogation excerpts came from 3 of 19 interviews.

Imarat Property Network, marketplace, failed. Imarat, a Chennai platform matching commercial landlords with small-business tenants, is the counter-case. In November 2025 its head of product, Irfan Kazi, ran 58 transcripts through a model in one pass, landlords and tenants together, with the roadmap pasted into the same prompt. It returned 217 excerpts, and the second-largest theme, 41 excerpts or 18.9 per cent, was demand for a verified-tenant badge — already item two on that roadmap. Imarat built it for ₹190 lakh and shipped on 12 February 2026. Eleven weeks later, on 30 April 2026, 2,840 of 61,500 active listings had adopted it: 4.6 per cent against a 25 per cent plan.

The post-mortem ran three tests. Separated by side — 34 landlord and 24 tenant transcripts, 58 in all — the badge appeared in 5 of 34 landlord transcripts (14.7 per cent) and 2 of 24 tenant (8.3 per cent), so 7 of 58, 12.1 per cent, against the 18.9 per cent excerpt share that carried the decision. Concentration: 23 of the 41 badge excerpts, 56.1 per cent, came from two transcripts. Contamination: re-run with the roadmap removed, the badge did not emerge as a theme at all, its excerpts dispersing into deposit disputes and tenant churn. Recovery cost ₹14 lakh and a quarter of delay; the module was withdrawn on 7 August 2026. The model hallucinated nothing: it was shown the answer and asked to find it, and two talkative landlords supplied the evidence.

Six of the seven are process-design failures, not model failures, and cost less to prevent than to detect.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether reliability statistics belong here. The measurement position, steelmanned: decisions are made on counts, counts carry error, unreported error is not absent error, and kappa and precision are the only instruments, so refusing to compute them makes a synthesis less accountable, not more interpretive. It is wrong if error runs systematically in the decision's direction rather than randomly — as at Imarat, whose badge theme would have passed any precision audit because its excerpts genuinely said what the model claimed.

The reflexive position, steelmanned: there is no correct theme set, so precision against a gold set measures agreement with one analyst's reading, and calling that accuracy imports confidence the method cannot support. Its evidence is the variance between expert human coders on one corpus, often larger than the model's error. It is wrong if practitioners can be trusted to treat themes as provisional — they cannot, because themes go on a slide and the slide decides a budget.

The second disagreement is where the marginal hour goes. Depth: 21 hours of Lipi's reading found a theme worth 107 passages. Breadth: evidence, not analysis, is now the bottleneck, and those 21 hours would have bought four grandparent interviews, which would have surfaced the same theme and sized it. Breadth is wrong only if the missing voices were not identifiable in advance; at Lipi they were. The third, unsettled, is whether a model should propose the coding frame or only apply a human codebook: open coding sometimes finds framings a human would not, closed coding is auditable and immune to drift, and no evidence settles which decides better.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this runs the synthesis and spot-checks a few quotations. Someone who has internalised it designs the audit first, writing down sample size and precision floor so the audit can fail; computes what is free — three runs, stability overlap, each theme's concentration; buys a gold set, the only instrument that detects absence; and reports in units, plural. The tell is what they say about what they cannot measure: an expert reports that one theme rests on eleven of forty-six interviews at 61.5 per cent precision, interval 35 to 88, then declines to rank it. The studied practitioner ranks everything, because the model did.

12. The decisions

On Monday 19 October 2026 Iravati recommended the offline-download rebuild at ₹71 lakh over the typography overhaul at ₹58 lakh, leaving ₹25 lakh of the ₹96 lakh. Her reasoning turned on the unit: font size led on excerpts (112, adjusted to 105.0) but appeared in 19 of 46 interviews, 41.3 per cent, while offline downloads reached 27 of 46, 58.7 per cent, at 92.9 per cent precision. She withdrew the pricing work on 61.5 per cent precision and 11 interviews, and asked ₹9 lakh of the remaining ₹25 lakh for eight grandparent interviews.

On Friday 23 October Lakshmikant chose surveyor scheduling at ₹175 lakh over subrogation at ₹290 lakh, leaving ₹165 lakh of ₹340 lakh. Scheduling reached 7 of 7 accounts and 13 of 19 interviews; subrogation reached 4 accounts, drawing 59.0 per cent of its excerpts from 3 interviews the sales team arranged. He committed ₹40 lakh of the remainder to six weeks of paid discovery with those three insurers: if subrogation is real there, ₹290 lakh is better spent next quarter with evidence than this quarter without. He gave the chief revenue officer the finding, not the conclusion — the model ranked subrogation first, and the sampling frame wrote the ranking.

  1. Iravati measured 82.2 per cent precision and 68.3 per cent recall. If you could improve only one before 19 October, which, and at what cost?
  2. Imarat's badge theme would have survived a precision audit. Which of Table 4's seven diagnostics would have caught it, and why was none in Irfan's process?
  3. Iqraar requires kappa above 0.70 and the compliance code scored 0.642. Suppose it had scored 0.71 at a prevalence of 4 per cent rather than 31. Would you trust it more, and what does that imply about one threshold for every code?

13. Going deeper

Synthesising research is the prerequisite: if you cannot judge a theme by hand you cannot audit a machine's. AI-assisted persona synthesis applies this logic to a riskier output, a composite character that feels more real than its evidence. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't takes up section 10's breadth-versus-depth argument. Qualitative vs quantitative research clarifies what a count of excerpts can claim. Interview fundamentals and designing an interview guide fix the transcript's contents, which no synthesis repairs. Recruiting research participants is where Iqraar's answer was decided, how many interviews explains Lipi's 46, and cognitive biases in research explains why a model shown the roadmap returns it.

One question to sit with. Imarat's synthesis was precise, well written and wrong. If the one error a precision audit cannot detect is introduced before the model runs, where in your process is that decision made, and who audits it?

Thikana Housing Network: What the Machine Heard

An ambiguous case on AI-assisted synthesis, qualitative evidence, and a roadmap that locks in nine days

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Thikana Housing Network's fourth floor off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru held Dipanwita Issar alone. Three windows were open: a six-theme synthesis a large language model had built from ninety-six interviews; an audit memo from Pune arguing that two of those themes were artefacts of how the model had been asked; and a slide she could not write, titled H2 roadmap: one recommendation.

By nine the next morning she had to name one of two bets for November to March: a deposit-relief product code-named Tijori, or a landlord-trust stack built on tenant verification and arrears cover. The board pack closed on Monday, 19 October, and capacity locked on the 23rd, after which nothing could move without missing the April–June leasing peak. She had a synthesis she could not defend, an audit she could not trust, and a chief executive who had already said the word deposit in front of an investor.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2021

Thikana was founded in Pune in 2017 by two engineers who had each lost a security deposit. It let owners list directly, handled the agreement and e-stamping, and charged one tenant fee instead of two months' brokerage. By September 2026 it carried 2,04,000 active listings, of which 44,900, or 22 per cent, belonged to non-resident Indians.

The decision that constrains Issar was made in March 2021, when field visits stopped and city teams began recording every conversation as a voice note, consented by one checkbox permitting use "for product improvement". Tokri was built in six weeks and deliberately given no tagging schema: structure imposed early encodes the wrong categories, the founders argued, and search could be added later. By October 2026 Tokri held 1,41,000 voice notes and some 14,200 hours of audio, almost none searchable, and only 38,500 notes, or 27 per cent, carried 2025 consent broad enough for a third-party model. Thikana owns the largest body of Indian rental conversation anyone has assembled, and can lawfully read almost none of it.

3. The industry

Thikana competes on three fronts. For tenants it meets NoBroker, Housing.com, MagicBricks and 99acres on listing quality and the no-brokerage promise; for managed-rental owners, Stanza Living and Colive; for the rent transaction itself, CRED Rent Pay, Paytm and the UPI autopay rails NPCI opened to recurring mandates. Brokerage attracts 18 per cent GST, which flatters Thikana's single fee.

Regulation shapes the product more than competition does. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021, caps deposits in the states that adopted it; Karnataka and Telangana have not, and a ten-month Bengaluru deposit remains ordinary. Rent paid to a non-resident owner attracts tax deducted at source at 31.2 per cent under Section 195, with Forms 15CA and 15CB. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, governs the Tokri archive; deposit financing sits under the RBI's digital lending directions. Thikana's NRI owners sit in Melbourne, Muscat, Nairobi and Chicago, and churn without complaining.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

In March 2026 the research function, then six people, was cut to three and the saving redeployed into a licence with Turiya Labs, a model vendor offering India-hosted processing under a no-training guarantee. Danish Iqbal, Head of Data Science in Hyderabad, built the pipeline: transcription, masking, then coding and clustering under a prompt he kept in version control.

Between 14 July and 25 September 2026 the team ran ninety-six interviews in six cities and six languages (Exhibit 1). On 28 September the pipeline returned nine clusters in under four hours, against three weeks in 2025. Nine clusters is not a choice, it is a list; Issar asked for a re-run merging near-duplicates into no more than six. On 1 October version two came back with deposit burden at the top, in sixty-one of the ninety-six transcripts, or 64 per cent (Exhibit 2).

Three things were believed then: that the synthesis described the interviews; that deposit burden was the largest tenant problem, since "deposit is 41 per cent of churn" had already reached the August board pre-read; and that the base was representative.

All three have since been complicated. Durva Itagi, Principal Researcher in Pune, hand-coded a stratified sample of twenty-four transcripts between 5 and 9 October and circulated her memo on the 12th (Exhibits 3 and 4). The model merged and dropped, she found, and what it dropped was patterned. Version two's leading cluster was the union of three version-one clusters: deposit size (38 transcripts), the overlap month in which a tenant pays old rent and new deposit together (24), and advance borrowing against the broker fee (19). Those are three products, not one. Iqbal rebutted on the 13th: agreement with the human coder was 85 per cent on the deposit label, and nine of the twenty-four transcripts, or 38 per cent, were interviews Itagi had run herself.

Meanwhile the exit-survey belief had collapsed. Exhibit 5 shows the survey fires only when a tenant cancels in the app, and that 61 per cent of terminations were landlord-initiated, with no reason captured at all.

5. The people

Dipanwita Issar, Senior Director of Product, Bengaluru, owns the recommendation, and her promotion case rests on H2 shipping something measurable. She has not told anyone that the instruction to merge near-duplicates and return six was hers.

Dushyant Isloor, co-founder and chief executive, wants the biggest theme built: a company that researches one quarter and ships the next has lost the season. His incentive is a Series C conversation in January, and he has not said that both investor meetings were built around the deposit product.

Durva Itagi, Principal Researcher, Pune, holds that nothing should be committed until the 102 unchecked quotations are traced to source lines — four weeks for two people and a translator. Her function was cut from six to three to pay for the licence she audits, and she does not volunteer that the nine transcripts she coded herself weaken her numbers.

Danish Iqbal, Head of Data Science, Hyderabad, holds that 85 per cent agreement is production-grade and the misses are a translation problem a Tulya Language Services glossary would fix for under ten lakh. His 13 October note omitted that only five of the nine version-one clusters survived into version two, a stability of 56 per cent nobody above him has seen.

Disha Indorkar, Head of Landlord Success, Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead of Bengaluru, says the base is upside down: landlords are forty of the ninety-six interviews, or 42 per cent, while landlord-initiated terminations are 61 per cent of the total, and the tax theme her owners raise appears nowhere. What she does not say is that she has been forwarding complaints to Isloor directly for five months.

Delna Ichhaporia, General Counsel, Mumbai, sets the boundary: the ninety-six interviews were consented cleanly, the archive was not, and re-consent at scale is a fantasy. She has not circulated that counsel gave a split opinion and she quotes the conservative half.

Dhiraj Ikkeri, Design Director, Lisbon, four and a half hours behind Bengaluru, thinks the question is wrong: a two-micro-market pilot offering a deposit in three instalments would settle live, in six weeks, what neither model nor audit can. He has not mentioned that his team has already built the screens.

Dolly Immanuel, Vice-President for City Operations, Bengaluru, carries the number everyone repeats, and her city accounts improve the moment conversion does. She has not said that her teams chose who was put forward, and that forty-four of the ninety-six participants, or 46 per cent, came from six micro-markets holding 38,800 of the 2,04,000 listings.

Bet A, Tijori. A deposit paid in three instalments, funded by a partner non-banking financial company whose term sheet expires on 30 November. It follows the leading theme, satisfies Isloor and Immanuel, and leaves room for half of Bet C. Against it: the leading theme is a merge Issar herself requested, its label carries precision of 64 per cent, and the three problems inside it point at three products with three different partners.

Bet B, the landlord trust stack. Tenant verification, an arrears guarantee, and an NRI compliance pack covering TDS. It serves the 61 per cent of terminations for which no reason is recorded, and it is what Toofan's procurement asked for in writing. Against it: it is the dearest bet, it consumes the budget alone, and its evidence is what the model handled worst — recall of 40 per cent on the verification label.

Bet C, fix the evidence. Rebuild Tokri with a coding schema, trace the 102 unchecked quotations, re-consent what it can, and keep the model as a proposer whose output people confirm. Nothing reaches a customer before the peak.

The framing has soft joints. It treats synthesis and audit as rivals when both rest on the same ninety-six interviews, nominated by city teams. Ikkeri's pilot is not on the list, although a live test would answer for less what the exhibits cannot. And the choice is written as A or B when Exhibit 6A shows capacity permits A and C, or B and C: money, not people, forbids the pair.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board pack closes at nine on Monday, 19 October; the board sits on the 22nd; capacity locks on the 23rd; notice on the Turiya licence must be served by the 24th or it renews at ₹31 lakh. The lender's term sheet for Bet A expires on 30 November, Toofan's letter of intent on 15 December, and Bet B must be live by 31 March 2027 to hold it. The budget is ₹215 lakh against 260 delivery weeks, research is three people, and Ichhaporia will not sign off processing beyond the 38,500 re-consented notes.

  1. Exhibit 3B prints raw agreement of 85 per cent and κ of 0.58 for one label on 600 passages. What does each measure, why do they diverge where a label is rare, and which belongs in a board pack?
  2. Exhibit 5 states one count of 173 as 41 per cent, 14 per cent and 5 per cent. Which of the three, if any, describes Thikana's deposit problem, and what would you need to answer the landlord side at all?
  3. Exhibit 2's leading cluster unions three earlier clusters, and run-to-run stability was 56 per cent. How much of what the team calls a finding is a property of the prompt, and how would you detect that beforehand?
  4. Exhibit 4 shows recall falling from 77 per cent on English-mixed transcripts to 39 per cent on Malayalam, on bases of 96 and 18 passages. Iqbal says small bases cannot carry the pattern; Itagi says the pattern is the finding. What would settle it?
  5. Itagi coded nine of her own twenty-four transcripts and her function was cut to pay for the licence she audits; Immanuel's teams nominated the participants; Issar wrote the merge instruction. Whose evidence should be discounted, and what design would have avoided all three?
  6. It is Monday morning, 19 October, and the pack closes in an hour. What does Issar submit, what does she tell the board about how this company knows what it believes, and what does she do about the Turiya notice?

Late that night

Issar closed the memo at twenty to one and opened her own message to Iqbal from 28 September: Nine is too many. Merge the near-duplicates, give me six. Eleven seconds to write. In a few hours Indorkar would be at her desk in Melbourne; by nine the executive group would assemble expecting a recommendation.
case40v1-res.truth.curve:
The Reserve Slot

Chowk Energy Network, Hyderabad — October 2026

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Wednesday 21 October 2026, Iniya Melkote was still at the Chowk Energy Network office in Gachibowli, Hyderabad, with four printouts on the desk. The board met at ten and she had to open the second item: whether Chowk should commit ₹2.60 crore and nine engineers for two quarters to build Reserve.

Reserve was a simple promise: a rider taps a station in the Chowk app and a charged battery is held in a numbered slot for twenty minutes. Chowk would sell it at ₹449 a month to riders, by UPI Autopay mandate, and ₹399 a vehicle a month to fleets.

The four printouts were the four ways Chowk had asked whether riders wanted it: a survey of 1,240 riders, two eight-week pilots at 26 stations, and two pre-payment cells, the second closed five days earlier. Read as four measurements of four different things, they did not agree; and which number she said aloud turned on a question nobody at Chowk had settled: what counts as evidence that a person wants something.

Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November; the engineering freeze ran 1 to 15 November, and Chenab Growth Partners' term sheet had to be signed by Monday 30 November.

2. How Chowk came to be constrained

Chowk was founded in 2021 by Ivaan Mewada, who had spent nine years in two-wheeler distribution in Mumbai, on the observation that gig riders do not want to own a battery; they want the next one. By October 2026 it ran 612 swap stations in Hyderabad, Jaipur, Lucknow and Coimbatore and served 18,400 active riders: 15,900 on two-wheelers, mostly delivery partners on the quick-commerce and food platforms, and 2,500 driving fleet-owned three-wheelers. Revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹21.4 crore, the loss ₹29.6 crore.

One decision from March 2023 constrains everything after it. Rather than wait for an interoperable swappable-battery specification, Chowk committed to a proprietary 2.4 kWh pack co-developed with Corvus Cell Industries in Osaka. It was cheaper per cycle than anything open to a company of its size and has never caught fire. But a Chowk pack fits only a Chowk cabinet: the company owns 9,200 packs at a gross block of ₹42.32 crore and cannot borrow a charged unit from Battery Smart, Sun Mobility or Honda's network when a station runs dry. Every slot Reserve blocks is one of 7,344.

3. The industry around the decision

Swapping sits between two industries it does not control. Upstream are the vehicle makers — Ola Electric, Ather, TVS, Bajaj, Hero MotoCorp, Mahindra with the Treo, Piaggio — whose pack choices decide what a network can serve. Downstream are the aggregators: Zomato, Swiggy, Blinkit, Zepto and Flipkart's logistics arm, whose rider apps set the clock that makes a dry station expensive. Battery Smart, Sun Mobility and Honda Power Pack Energy India want the same kerb space.

Policy pushes both ways. PM E-DRIVE and the Telangana and Rajasthan EV policies subsidise the vehicles and, in part, the stations; the Battery Waste Management Rules place extended producer responsibility on the pack owner, which is Chowk; AIS-156 means any firmware change, which a lockable slot requires, triggers fresh certification. Because holding a battery implies continuous location, the DPDP Act requires a consent flow and a retention policy. The RBI's recurring-payment framework makes a ₹449 mandate easy and a one-off charge awkward, which is why the pay cells were run by hand.

4. What happened, and what has since come apart

Reserve began as a complaint: through the spring of 2026 the commonest message in the Jaipur support queue was a rider who had travelled to a station and found no charged pack. Iniya's team built a reservation flow and tested demand four times.

Wave 1 ran from Monday 1 June to Sunday 26 July at 26 stations in Hyderabad and Jaipur, free and opt-in: a rider had to find Reserve in the app and switch it on. Of 1,460 riders at those stations, 403 switched it on at least once and 118 used it in six or more of the eight weeks. Idalina was asked to make it easier to find.

She did more than that. In Wave 2, from Monday 10 August to Sunday 4 October, Reserve was on by default for the 980 riders at those stations who had not opted in earlier. Usage jumped. Without quite deciding to, the team had changed the question from whether riders would choose Reserve to whether they would switch it off.

The survey ran from Monday 3 to Friday 21 August, fielded by Cinnamon Field Services by telephone in Telugu, Hindi and Tamil. Riders heard a description and were asked whether they would pay ₹449 a month: 879 of the 1,240 who completed the call said they would, or 70.9 per cent. Only two-wheeler riders were sampled.

Two facts have since undermined the sequence. On Tuesday 1 September the swap price rose from ₹55 to ₹62 in Hyderabad and Jaipur and from ₹52 to ₹58 in the newer cities: Wave 1 and the survey sit in a ₹55 world, Wave 2 straddles the change, both pay cells sit after it. And the cells differ. Cell A, 21 September to 2 October, offered ₹449 for the first month and ₹8 off every swap that month; cell B, 5 to 16 October, offered ₹449 alone. At the network's average of 25.9 swaps a month that discount was worth about ₹207, so cell A's payers bought Reserve at an effective ₹242.

5. The people in the room

Iniya Melkote, 38, Head of Product, Hyderabad, owns the recommendation and has never taken a board item this size. Her bonus is tied to shipped roadmap items.

Ivaan Mewada, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai, wants Reserve announced before Diwali. His memo of Friday 9 October applies the survey's 70.9 per cent to all 18,400 riders, giving 13,043 subscribers and "upwards of ₹7 crore of recurring revenue". He has not said that Chenab's diligence lead keeps asking for a subscription line.

Iftekhar Mutalik, Head of Network Operations, Jaipur, is against, and his argument is physical: a reservation creates no battery, it reserves a slot, and the rider who arrives without one finds the cabinet emptier. He puts the buffer at one spare pack per 22 subscribers, not 36. His bonus runs on completed swaps.

Itishree Methil, chief financial officer, Chennai, is formally neutral and wants the cheapest defensible number. She would rather not document a low willingness to pay while a term sheet is open.

Ibrahim Momin, Head of Fleet Partnerships, Delhi NCR, is strongly for. He quotes the pay result as 16.5 per cent, not 14.3, since riders who never answered should not count, and points to nine letters of intent from fourteen operators approached, covering 1,310 vehicles and ₹62.72 lakh a year. His variable pay runs on LOI vehicles; two of the nine also asked for a price concession.

Iwona Mazur, lead data scientist, Krakow, insists on 14.3 per cent — 86 of the 600 riders cell A set out to charge — and that cell A measured a discount as much as a feature. The one-per-36 buffer model was fitted on default-on Wave 2 data, which she has not volunteered.

Idalina Monteiro, design lead, Lisbon, argues that Reserve is a service promise and should be free to everybody, paid out of swap margin. She has not said that her team has already merged the reservation screens into the app shell behind a flag.

Itsuki Morikawa, battery systems engineer, Osaka, is careful: slot-lock firmware needs fresh AIS-156 certification, nine weeks on the queue. He has not told the board that Corvus's 2027 pack reports slot state natively, removing a third of the build.

She wrote one line on the back of Exhibit 6 and left it for the morning: whose arrival are we holding a battery against? Outside, a rider pulled up at the cabinet, opened the app, and waited.
case20v1-res.truth.curve:
Eighty-Two Per Cent Said Yes

Banjara Provisions Network and the question of Auto-Reorder

1. Opening

On Monday 5 October 2026, Hemlata Lohiya sat in the Pune office of Banjara Provisions Network with three printouts and a deadline. The leadership council would meet on Friday 9 October, and Hemlata, Head of Product, had to say whether to commit ₹180 lakh and a nine-person team to building Auto-Reorder, a feature that would place a grocer's weekly stock order automatically.

The three printouts were a survey, a beta and a payment test whose last payment window had closed three days earlier. They did not agree. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and the chief executive wanted the roadmap announced before the festival orders began.

2. Company background

Banjara supplies packaged staples to kirana stores through a retailer app and a fleet of leased vans. It was founded in 2019 by Hasmukh Ladhani, a former regional distributor for a large food company, and serves about 12,000 active retailers across Pune, Nashik, Nagpur and Indore. "Active" means at least one order in the last 30 days.

The competitive field is crowded. Udaan and Jumbotail pursue the same retailers with wider catalogues, Flipkart Wholesale and JioMart Partner have very large parents, and DealShare competes on price. Banjara's edge is reliability in smaller cities: a van that arrives on the day promised, and store-by-store credit terms. Many retailers reorder the same twenty or thirty items weekly and pay through UPI.

3. The situation

Drivers kept hearing the same list dictated over the phone each Tuesday, so Hemlata's team built a prototype and tested demand three ways before committing engineers. The first was a phone survey run by an agency between 10 and 28 August. Four hundred retailers were asked whether they would use a feature that reordered their usual items automatically, and 328 said yes, or 82.0 per cent. The second was a beta. From Monday 3 August, 60 stores in Pune and Nashik were given a working prototype for six weeks, ending on Sunday 13 September. Twenty-one stores switched it on at least once, which is 35.0 per cent of the 60. Nine stores, 15.0 per cent of the 60, used it in three or more consecutive weeks.

The third was a payment test. Between 14 and 25 September, 150 other retailers, drawn at random from the 12,000 active base, were told by phone that Auto-Reorder would cost ₹599 a month and sent a UPI link to pay the first month in advance. The last payment window closed on Friday 2 October. Twelve paid within a week, or 8.0 per cent of the 150. Exhibit 1 sets the three results beside each other, and Exhibit 2 shows the dates.

Each global colleague read these numbers from a different place. Hanneke Laan, a researcher in Amsterdam, listened to forty survey recordings and noticed that most "yes" answers came within two seconds, before the question about price was finished. Hermie Lacson, who leads retailer support from Manila, found that the nine persistent users were mostly stores that already phoned in an identical order every week. In Nashik, a grocer named Haribhau said he checked every item because prices moved with the wholesale market.

4. The people

Hemlata Lohiya, Head of Product, Pune. She owns the recommendation and has to defend it to the council.

Hasmukh Ladhani, founder and chief executive, Mumbai. He wants a visible launch before Diwali and reads the 82 per cent as a mandate.

Harmeet Lashkari, head of sales, Nagpur. His field team earns incentives on subscriptions, and he believes retailers who say yes will pay once it is polished. He distrusts the payment test because the offer reached retailers by phone, with no demonstration.

Hanneke Laan, researcher, Amsterdam. She argues that the survey measured politeness and that the payment test, though small, is the only evidence in which retailers risked something. Hermie Lacson, support lead, Manila, adds the field detail. Hetvi Lahoti, data scientist in Pune, prepared the figures in Exhibit 3.

5. Exhibits

Hetvi asked what each result would mean for revenue if it were the true share of the 12,000 active stores. The annual price per store is ₹599 times 12 months, or ₹7,188. Exhibit 3 shows the result.

In Exhibit 4, building Auto-Reorder costs ₹180 lakh, which finance spreads over three years, or ₹60 lakh a year. Running it, including hosting, support and a share of the van-routing team, adds ₹36 lakh a year. Annual cost is therefore ₹96 lakh, and at ₹7,188 per store the feature needs 1,336 paying stores to cover it (₹96 lakh divided by ₹7,188 is 1,335.6, rounded up to whole stores). That is 11.1 per cent of the 12,000.

6. The options

Option A: build now. Commit the ₹180 lakh and the nine-person team and announce Auto-Reorder in October. The upside is speed. The cost is that the measures clearing break-even by a wide margin are the survey and the beta's tried rate, which asked little of retailers; if the payment test is nearer the truth, the feature loses money from the first year.

Option B: run a paid concierge test first. Spend about ₹22 lakh over six weeks. Operations staff would place reorders by hand for 300 stores paying ₹599 a month, with no engineering. The upside is a sturdier read on payment, since 300 stores is double the earlier test. The cost is a delay of about six weeks, which pushes the build decision to Friday 20 November, after Diwali.

Option C: build a light version and give it away. Spend ₹45 lakh on a basic reorder button bundled free into the existing app, to raise order frequency rather than earn subscriptions. The upside is that it is cheap, quick and consistent with what the nine persistent users valued. The cost is that it abandons subscription revenue and could lower stores' willingness to pay later.

7. Questions for discussion

1. For each result in Exhibit 1, what did the retailer give up to produce it, and what does that say about trust?

2. Exhibit 3 ranges from ₹69.0 lakh to ₹707.3 lakh. Which rows describe stores that paid, which stores that behaved, and which only what stores said?

3. Twelve of 150 stores paid. How far would you trust the 8.0 per cent, and does Harmeet's objection about the phone pitch change that?

4. Which option would you take to the council, and what result would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

This topic offers a simple rule for weighing evidence: what people say counts least, what they do counts more, and what they pay for counts most. Saying is free and shaped by courtesy; doing costs time; paying costs money and exposes a person to regret, so it is hardest to fake. Payment evidence is imperfect, since twelve payers is a thin base, but the rule says which way to lean when signals disagree.

Applied here, the results fall in a clear order. The 82.0 per cent survey sits at the bottom, and Hanneke's finding that answers arrived before the price was stated explains why. The beta sits in the middle: 35.0 per cent tried the feature, but only 15.0 per cent kept using it, mostly stores that already phoned in a fixed order. The payment test sits at the top, and at 8.0 per cent it falls below the 11.1 per cent break-even. The beta's 1,800 stores clear the line only on the assumption that every such store would pay, which nobody has tested.

One defensible path is Option B. It does not reject the feature, since the beta shows real persistence among a minority. It turns the largest uncertainty, whether enough stores will pay, into a measured number at modest cost. Hemlata can set the rule in advance: if at least 11.1 per cent of the 300 concierge stores, which is 34 stores, are still paying after six weeks, the council funds the build; if fewer, it chooses Option C or shelves the idea. Setting the threshold before the data arrives guards against the pull of the 82.0 per cent figure. The cost is some weeks and a founder's impatience, small beside ₹180 lakh.
exp40v2-res.truth.curve:
Evidence strength: say, do, pay — in depth

Discovery & Design, Qualitative Research. What separates a practitioner who ranks evidence by its price tag from one who ranks it by how differently buyers and non-buyers behave.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Monday 12 October 2026, Rohini Parulekar, vice-president of product at Raseed Expense Systems in Pune, had to allocate fourteen engineer-months. Raseed sells spend-management software to Indian firms of 200 to 2,000 employees: 310 customers, 2,32,500 covered employees, ₹41.85 crore of recurring revenue at ₹150 per employee per month. The candidate was Auto-Reconcile, which matches corporate-card statements to expense claims without a human, priced at ₹60 per employee per month. Its rival for the same fourteen engineer-months was a GST e-invoicing connector that eight enterprise accounts had made a renewal condition, worth ₹30 lakh each, or ₹2.40 crore. That set the hurdle: Auto-Reconcile had to beat ₹2.40 crore of year-one recurring revenue to deserve the quarter beginning Monday 2 November.

Parag Pingle, the research lead, had spent twelve weeks — Monday 13 July to Monday 5 October — producing four numbers from the same 62 finance leaders. Forty-eight said in interviews that reconciliation was their worst monthly job and that they would buy a module to end it. Twenty-seven of those 48 uploaded a real card statement into a prototype between Monday 17 August and Friday 4 September, at a cost of forty minutes and an IT clearance. Nine of the 27 signed a letter of intent for a three-month paid pilot between Monday 7 and Friday 18 September. Invoices went out on Monday 21 September on net-fourteen terms; by the due date, Monday 5 October, four of the nine had paid. Pranjal Rahalkar, the chief executive, read the 48; Qaizar Patrawala, the finance chief, read the four.

Renuka Pethe, co-founder and head of product at Prakriti Solar Industries in Coimbatore, faced a harder version of the problem on Monday 26 October. Prakriti installs rooftop solar on knitwear and dyeing units in the Tiruppur cluster. Its new proposal was a zero-upfront five-year lease: it funds the array at ₹38,000 per kilowatt and charges ₹1,150 per kilowatt per month, maintenance costing ₹160. A module supplier had offered to hold ₹13,900 per kilowatt if Prakriti committed to 8,000 kilowatts by Friday 30 October — take-or-pay, worth ₹11.12 crore. Rutuja Pawaskar had visited 54 units between Monday 3 August and Friday 4 September. Prasanna Rangnekar, who ran sales, wanted the full 8,000; Renuka wanted less.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

The claim is narrow: a statement about future behaviour is weaker evidence than an observation of present behaviour, which is weaker than an irreversible transfer of a scarce resource. Say evidence is a report of an intention, elicited by a researcher. Do evidence is an act taken in the person's own work, which nobody had to request twice. Pay evidence transfers something not easily recovered — money, a budget line, a binding signature.

The history is older than product management. Allan Wicker's 1969 review put attitudes' share of the variance in behaviour below a tenth. Icek Ajzen and Martin Fishbein then showed attitudes predict behaviour well when the measure matches it in action, target, context and time. Paschal Sheeran's 2002 meta-analysis put intention's share of variance at roughly 28 per cent, a correlation of about 0.53: far from nothing, far from enough to size a factory. Vicki Morwitz and co-authors found intention surveys predict sales tolerably for established categories and badly for new ones. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test of 2013 made the finding a discipline, and the lean-startup writers a ritual.

Four schools disagree substantively. The behavioural-commitment school signs the proposition that no unpaid signal should size a capital commitment, and refuses the proposition that a survey can estimate a price. The stated-preference school — discrete-choice experiments, Gabor-Granger ladders, the Juster scale — signs the proposition that properly specified stated preference beats a badly specified pre-sale, and refuses the proposition that payment is self-validating. The jobs-to-be-done school of Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta signs neither: the strongest evidence is what the person already paid for in a real past switch. The design-research school — Steve Portigal, Erika Hall — holds that payment tests answer a commercial question while destroying the conditions for a generative one.

The sentence that holds the page together: evidence is strong in proportion to how differently buyers and non-buyers behave, not in proportion to what it cost the person.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has seven steps; two are usually implicit and decide whether the exercise is worth anything. First, name the behaviour and its unit: Raseed's question was not whether finance leaders dislike reconciliation but whether one would cause ₹60 per employee per month to be paid. Second, keep the funnel nested and the denominators explicit, as Figure 1 does. Each rate is conditional on the one before, so the four must multiply to the end-to-end rate: 0.774194 × 0.5625 × 0.333333 × 0.444444 = 0.064516, which is 4 ÷ 62.

Third, carry each rate into the quantity under decision. Raseed's 310 customers are exactly five times its sample of 62, so each tier scales cleanly. The 310 hold 2,32,500 employees — 125 averaging 360, 115 averaging 760, 70 averaging 1,430, which is 45,000 + 87,400 + 1,00,100 = 2,32,500, an average of 750. Assuming attached customers carry the same mix, each is worth 750 × ₹60 = ₹45,000 a month, ₹5,40,000 a year.

BasisAttach rateCustomers of 310Add-on revenue, ₹ lakh/monthYear-one ARR, ₹ crAgainst ₹2.40 cr hurdle
Say: would buy77.4%240108.0012.96clears by ₹10.56 cr

Check: 240 × ₹5,40,000 = ₹12.96 cr; 135 × ₹5,40,000 = ₹7.29 cr; 45 × ₹5,40,000 = ₹2.43 cr; 20 × ₹5,40,000 = ₹1.08 cr. The say forecast is twelve times the paid, since 240 ÷ 20 = 12.

Fourth — the first implicit step — carry the interval, not the point. Four of 62 is 6.45 per cent, with a standard error of the square root of (0.064516 × 0.935484 ÷ 62), or 3.12 percentage points, so a rough 95 per cent band runs from 0.34 to 12.57 per cent. The top of that band is 39 customers, ₹2.11 crore, still under the ₹2.40 crore hurdle. The nine letters give 14.52 per cent, a standard error of 4.47 points and a band from 5.75 to 23.28 per cent: 18 customers and ₹0.97 crore at the bottom, 72 and ₹3.89 crore at the top. A tier readable across that range is a prompt for a better test, not a forecast.

Fifth, pre-register the threshold: Raseed's hurdle existed before the invoices went out, the only reason the arithmetic above is believable. Sixth, specify the counterfactual population — a ladder built only on eventual buyers tells you nothing, because what you need is not what buyers did but how much more often they did it than non-buyers. Seventh, back-test against a resolved cohort, which Prakriti had done and Raseed had not.

4. The quantitative treatment: likelihood ratios

In 2025 Prakriti had approached 180 Tiruppur units with an outright-purchase offer; 24 bought and 156 did not, a base rate of 13.3 per cent. Because that cohort was resolved, Renuka could compute for each act the share of eventual buyers and of eventual non-buyers who performed it. That ratio is the likelihood ratio: the factor by which the act multiplies the odds that this person is a buyer.

Act of evidenceBuyers who did it (of 24)Non-buyers who did it (of 156)Likelihood ratioProbability of purchase after the act
Said they would go solar this year22 — 91.7%108 — 69.2%1.3222 of 130 — 16.9%

Prior odds 24 ÷ 156 = 0.1538; base rate 24 ÷ 180 = 13.3 per cent. Last row: 0.1538 × 9.75 = 1.50, and 1.50 ÷ 2.50 = 60.0 per cent, matching 18 ÷ 30.

Two rows should unsettle anyone who ranks evidence by what it cost the person. The refundable ₹25,000 fee is real money and multiplies the odds by 4.19; writing down a month and the budget owner's name costs two minutes and multiplies them by 9.75. The costly act is the weaker signal, and the reason is in the non-buyer column: 19.9 per cent of non-buyers paid a fee they could get back, while only 7.7 per cent would write a date against a colleague's budget. An act is diagnostic because non-buyers decline it; refundability makes payment easy.

A likelihood ratio can also be computed for a negative result. Two of the 24 buyers did not say they would go solar that year, and 48 of the 156 non-buyers also did not; (2 ÷ 24) ÷ (48 ÷ 156) = 0.083 ÷ 0.308 = 0.27, so a no cuts the odds from 0.1538 to 0.0417 and the probability to 4.0 per cent. Interviews are weak at confirming demand and strong at ruling it out, and most teams use them the other way round.

5. When the hierarchy applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions, each testable. One: the payment must be refusable without penalty to the relationship. Raseed passes; a vendor asking a captive customer for a fee learns nothing, because the customer is buying goodwill. Two: non-buyers must be able to decline the act, which Prakriti's refundable fee fails more than its written commitment does. Three: the thing paid for must resemble the thing you will sell — a survey fee buys a survey, not a lease.

The hierarchy misleads in three settings. In low-salience, high-frequency purchases nobody deliberates, so paying is nearly as cheap as saying. In mandated purchases payment reflects compliance: a firm buying e-invoicing software because the GST Network requires it has said nothing about valuing yours. In new categories, asking for money before the person can imagine the product measures trust rather than need.

6. Hard edge cases

In two-sided markets the ladders interact: a factory will sign only if a lease exists, which needs a bank lending against five-year receivables. A pay signal from one side, with the other absent, is evidence about a hypothetical.

In hardware-plus-software businesses the hardware half dominates: Prakriti can revise its app in a fortnight and 8,000 kilowatts of modules not at all. The evidence standard should rise with irreversibility, not product size.

In regulated and enterprise settings the organisational seam is the problem: the person who feels the pain, the one who signs and the one who releases the purchase order are three people, and two of Raseed's five non-paying letters were blocked by procurement. An LOI is a pay signal from the champion and a say signal from the company.

In multi-product firms the bundle contaminates: if Auto-Reconcile ships free for a quarter, adoption says nothing about ₹60. Mature firms claim to use holdouts; most read a renewal rate that conflates everything.

In AI-native products usage is cheap to observe and nearly worthless; but inference costs money, so a customer who buys credits or tolerates a cap gives a real pay signal. The question is not usage but whether they paid to raise their limit.

7. Eight nuances that separate an expert

Refundability destroys diagnosticity

The tell is a rate that falls hard at the second gate: Prakriti's fee converted 52.2 per cent of the 23 bill-senders into payers, then only 41.7 per cent of those 12 into signers, and four of the 12 asked for their ₹25,000 back. The obvious reading is a wrong price; the expert reading is that a recoverable payment recruits tyre-kickers nearly as fast as buyers.

The negative is often the strong signal

The tell is a team that reports only the yes count. A no in a Prakriti interview carried a likelihood ratio of 0.27 and dropped the probability to 4.0 per cent — more movement than a yes produced. Weak tests have asymmetric power, favouring exclusion.

Specificity, not sincerity, makes a statement useful

The tell is a quote with no date, amount or name. "We'd buy this" predicts nothing; "we approved ₹4 lakh for an OCR tool in March and the controller signed it" reports a purchase, and belongs in the do tier, not the say tier.

Past payments outrank future ones

The tell is a discovery plan with no question about incumbent spend. A unit already paying ₹2.40 lakh a year for diesel has shown willingness to pay for reliable power with no researcher involved — the cleanest evidence available, and free.

Asking for money changes the sample you can keep learning from

The tell is a research pipeline that dries up after the pre-sale. Of Prakriti's 54 units, the 42 who declined the fee became harder to re-interview: the relationship had turned from inquiry into sales. Pay evidence is bought with access, the scarcer asset early on.

A paid pilot creates a customer who captures the roadmap

The tell is a backlog driven by a handful of accounts. Raseed's four payers were all in the 1,000-to-2,000 band; building for them tunes Auto-Reconcile to the 70 largest customers and away from the 240 smaller ones. It cuts the other way too. Table 1 prices every attached customer at the 750-employee average; price the same 20 at the top band's 1,430 and they are worth 20 × 1,430 × ₹60 × 12 = ₹2.06 crore, not ₹1.08 crore, narrowing the shortfall against the ₹2.40 crore hurdle from ₹1.32 crore to ₹0.34 crore. That reading demands 20 of the 70 top-band customers, a 28.6 per cent attach rate against 6.5 per cent overall. The verdict is assumption-dependent, not arithmetic.

Rate chains hide rounding that changes decisions

The tell is a deck whose tier percentages do not multiply to the end-to-end rate. Raseed's four rates give 0.064516, exactly 4 ÷ 62; rounded to 77, 56, 33 and 44 they give 0.062610, implying 19 customers rather than 20 and ₹1.03 crore rather than ₹1.08 crore.

The hierarchy is about purchase and silent about retention

The tell is a payment number justifying a five-year commitment. Prakriti's lease recovers ₹1,150 per kilowatt per month for 60 months, ₹69,000, against ₹38,000 of capital and ₹9,600 of maintenance — ₹21,400 per kilowatt of undiscounted surplus, but only if the unit survives five years in a cluster where dyeing units fail. A first payment is evidence about month one.

8. How the pattern changes across settings

In consumer products the ladder is steep and the money small, so the constraint is test cost. In B2B and enterprise the ladder looks shallow and is steep: the champion's enthusiasm is cheap and the purchase order is not, and Raseed's data prices the gap — four payments from nine signatures, so a letter of intent is worth 0.44 of a purchase order. In marketplaces the ladder runs per side; in hardware irreversibility dominates; in AI products nobody has settled what a pay signal is when price is per token.

Stage changes less than people claim. A seed-stage firm can ask a stranger for ₹25,000 and a listed firm cannot without legal review, so large firms substitute paid pilots and deposit-backed letters — which is why Figure 2's written-commitment row matters more to them than its deposit row.

9. Three worked examples

Raseed's price question, answered badly. In the interviews, 31 of the 48 who said yes also called ₹60 per employee per month reasonable. Pirjo Rautio, a pricing econometrician in Helsinki, noted that the question followed a demonstration of the module's best case, and that the four payers had bought a three-month pilot, not the per-employee subscription — so ₹60 was never tested. The payments showed demand exists, and nothing about price.

Prakriti's capital arithmetic. The addressable set is 1,458 cluster units with connected load above 100 kilowatts — 648 averaging 30 kilowatts of usable roof, 540 averaging 55, 270 averaging 88, which is 19,440 + 29,700 + 23,760 = 72,900 kilowatts, an average of 50.0 per unit. The sample of 54 is one twenty-seventh of 1,458, so each tier scales by 27.

Check: 0.759259 × 0.560976 × 0.521739 × 0.416667 = 0.092593, which is 5 ÷ 54. Year-one capital is ₹6 crore of equity plus an ₹18 crore facility — ₹24.00 crore, enough for 6,316 kilowatts, about 126 units.

The inversion matters: for Raseed weak evidence overstated demand, while for Prakriti every tier exceeds the balance sheet, so the question is not whether demand exists but how much to serve.

The failure: Pragyaa Skills Network. Ruchika Pastakia's Jaipur company sells examination preparation. In mid-2026 it ran a landing-page test for a ₹3,600 course: 18,400 visitors, 2,840 of whom paid a ₹49 refundable pre-order token, a rate of 15.43 per cent. Pastakia read a paid signal and committed ₹1.40 crore to build the course. At launch, 212 of the 2,840 paid the full ₹3,600 — 7.46 per cent — producing ₹7.63 lakh against that ₹1.40 crore. The visitor-to-buyer rate was 1.15 per cent, so the token had over-predicted buyers by 13.4 times, which is 2,840 ÷ 212.

The recovery was a re-test. Pragyaa replaced the token with a ₹500 non-refundable credit against the ₹3,100 balance. Of 12,600 visitors, 310 paid the ₹500 — 2.46 per cent — and 198 of the 310 paid the balance, 63.87 per cent. The visitor-to-buyer rate was 1.57 per cent, so the new test over-predicted by 1.57 times rather than 13.4, and revenue per visitor rose from ₹41.48 to ₹56.57. At ₹49, a non-buyer's false yes cost 1.4 per cent of the price: a say test with a payment gateway attached. The ₹500 credit was 13.9 per cent of the price and non-refundable, and that is what made it discriminate.
