11. Where experts genuinely disagree

Only money counts; the rest is theatre. The strongest form rests on Pragyaa's 13.4-fold over-prediction. For it to be wrong, free written commitments would have to out-predict payments — which Figure 2 shows in one resolved cohort.

A well-specified stated-preference study beats a badly specified pre-sale. Rautio's version: a choice exercise holds price, bundle and alternative constant, while a pre-sale confounds all three with urgency and vendor trust. Raseed is her exhibit — four payments that tested a pilot fee and never ₹60. For it to be wrong, such designs would have to fail in new categories, as Morwitz's results suggest.

The ladder is the wrong instrument; the circumstance is the right one. Forecasting attach rates assumes a stable population of buyers, when purchase is triggered by events. Prakriti's 9.3 per cent would then be an artefact of how many units received a TANGEDCO demand notice that quarter. For this to be wrong, conversion would have to be stable across triggers, and nobody has shown it is.

Payment tests cost more than they yield early on. The 42 units that declined Prakriti's fee had the most to teach, and turning them into declined prospects destroyed the cheapest learning channel a seed-stage firm has. Its weakness: no answer for Figure 4.

12. Mastery, and what each protagonist decided

Someone who has merely studied this ranks evidence by price and reports the strongest tier. Someone who has internalised it designs the act so non-buyers refuse it, insists on a resolved cohort before quoting a ratio, reports the interval, treats the negative result as the more powerful one, and fixes the threshold before the data arrives — spending more time on who the non-buyers are than on what the buyers said.

Rohini Parulekar did not build Auto-Reconcile. She committed four engineer-months, ₹10.40 lakh, to a narrow version serving only the four paying pilots, moved the remaining ten engineer-months and ₹26.00 lakh to the GST connector, and pre-registered a gate: 18 paid customers, a run-rate of ₹97.20 lakh, by Friday 29 January 2027, or the module stops. Eighteen is a 5.8 per cent attach rate, just below the measured 6.5 per cent — achievable if the paid tier was honest, a clean failure if not. Rahalkar accepted on condition that the pilots be re-priced per employee at ₹60, so that the next quarter would at last test the price.

Renuka Pethe committed 6,000 kilowatts rather than 8,000, at ₹14,600 per kilowatt instead of ₹13,900 — ₹8.76 crore instead of ₹11.12 crore, a price penalty of ₹42.00 lakh. The reasoning was arithmetic: 8,000 kilowatts needs ₹30.40 crore of installation capital against ₹24.00 crore available, a gap of ₹6.40 crore, and if only the signed-lease tier of 6,750 kilowatts materialised, 1,250 kilowatts of modules worth ₹1.74 crore would sit unplaced. Paying ₹42.00 lakh to avoid ₹1.74 crore of exposure is 4.14 to one. Six thousand kilowatts is 88.9 per cent of the conservative tier and fits ₹22.80 crore, leaving ₹1.20 crore of headroom. She also made the ₹25,000 survey fee non-refundable, credited against the first lease invoice. Rangnekar objected that this would halve the surveys, and the pipeline.

Three questions for discussion. First: Raseed's letter-of-intent tier cleared the ₹2.40 crore hurdle by ₹3 lakh. Is a margin of 1.25 per cent, on a tier whose 95 per cent band runs from ₹0.97 crore to ₹3.89 crore, grounds for anything but another test? Second: Prakriti's free written commitment out-predicted its ₹25,000 deposit — does that generalise, or is it an artefact of a cluster where a written date binds socially? Third: when does a stronger test on fewer people become worse than a weaker test on many?

13. Going deeper

How many interviews supplies the denominator this page depends on, and argues that strength beats count — four payments from 62 outrank 48 statements. The evidence ladder extends the logic above purchase to renewal and referral, where Prakriti's ₹21,400 per kilowatt of surplus is decided. Reconciling contradictory research findings is what Rahalkar and Patrawala needed. Qualitative vs quantitative research shows the likelihood-ratio treatment to be quantitative work on qualitative acts. Interview fundamentals and designing an interview guide decide whether a statement lands in the say tier or, through specificity, the do tier. Recruiting research participants decides whether a counterfactual population exists, cognitive biases in research explains why the ₹49 token felt like evidence, and synthesising research turns the tiers into a memo a finance chief will interrogate.
exp20v2-res.truth.curve:
Evidence strength: say, do, pay

Discovery & Design, Qualitative Research. How much should you trust what someone says, compared with what they do or pay for?

1. Thirty-four yeses

On Monday 28 September 2026, Hemalatha Kondapalli, head of product at Hamsafar Exchange, walked into a conference room in Hyderabad with a one-page memo and an unpleasant choice. Hamsafar runs a commuter-pooling service in the HITEC City corridor: office workers book a seat on a shared tempo-traveller or van that runs a fixed route between a residential cluster and a tech park. Until now, seats were sold ride by ride. The founder, Ishaan Mallampati, wanted to launch a monthly pass at ₹1,500 that guaranteed a seat, and a fleet lessor had offered thirty vehicles on a twelve-month lease at ₹36 lakh a month. The offer lapsed on Friday 2 October.

The twelve-month commitment came to ₹4.32 crore, and Hamsafar would owe it whether or not passengers appeared. Govardhan Tummala, the research lead, had gathered three kinds of evidence from the same forty commuters, and they pointed in different directions. In interviews held from Monday 17 to Friday 28 August, 34 of the 40 said they would definitely buy a guaranteed-seat pass. In a two-week trial from Monday 31 August to Friday 11 September, 22 of those 34 actually booked a seat. When a pre-sale opened on Monday 14 September, with the first month payable in advance by UPI and non-refundable, 6 of the 22 paid.

Ishaan read the first number and said that 85 per cent was a launch. Hemalatha read the third and saw a different company. The topic of this page is how to decide which of those numbers deserves belief, and by how much, when they disagree.

2. The idea

Evidence about a customer's future behaviour comes in three grades. Say evidence is what a person tells you: an interview answer, a survey response, a stated intention. Do evidence is what the person is observed doing without being asked: using a prototype, returning to a product, switching from what they currently use. Pay evidence is what the person gives up that they cannot easily get back: money, but also time, data, a signed commitment or a favour called in from a colleague. The grades are ordered by cost to the person. Saying is nearly free, doing costs effort, and paying costs a scarce resource that has other uses.

The problem the idea was invented to solve is old. Usability researchers in the 1990s, Jakob Nielsen among them, argued that observing behaviour beats collecting opinions. Rob Fitzpatrick's 2013 book The Mom Test turned it into a practical discipline for founders: ask about the past and about real behaviour, because people will lie to be kind about your idea even when you ask them not to. The logic: telling a friendly interviewer you would buy is a courtesy, while paying is a decision.

The sentence Hemalatha could repeat in a meeting: "Weight each claim by what it cost the person to make it."

3. How it works

The method has five steps, and practitioners usually leave the first and last implicit. First, fix the question in terms of a behaviour. Hamsafar's question was not "do commuters like a pass?" but "will commuters hand over ₹1,500 a month?" A claim can only be graded against a behaviour, so this step comes before everything else. Second, collect the cheap evidence first. Third, convert each tier into a rate of the people who reached the previous tier. Fourth, carry each rate forward into the quantity you are deciding, here passes sold and monthly revenue. Fifth, state what would change your mind before the result arrives, so that the ladder is not read generously after the fact.

Figure 1 applies the first four steps to Hamsafar's forty commuters. Each bar is scaled at 8 pixels per person, so 40 people span 320 pixels, 34 span 272, 22 span 176 and 6 span 48. The funnel is nested: those who booked in the trial all came from the 34 who said yes, and those who paid all came from the 22 who booked. That nesting matters, because it means each rate is conditional on the one before.

Table 1 gives the same numbers with both denominators. The last column is what the forecast will use, because it answers the only question that matters to the lease: out of every forty people we spoke to, how many gave us money.

TierPeopleShare of previous tierShare of all 40
Say: would buy3485.0%85.0%
Do: booked in trial2264.7%55.0%
Pay: bought pass627.3%15.0%

Check: 0.850 × 0.647 × 0.273 = 0.150, which is 6 ÷ 40.

4. A worked example

Hamsafar's corridor has about 12,000 office employees who commute alone and live within reach of its pickup points. Each forecast below multiplies that population by one tier's share of the forty, then by ₹1,500 per pass. Ishaan's number comes from the first row. Revenue is shown in ₹ lakh per month, and 1 lakh is 1,00,000, so 10,200 passes at ₹1,500 is ₹1,53,00,000, or 153.0 lakh.

BasisShare of 40Passes (of 12,000)Revenue, ₹ lakh/monthMargin over ₹36 lakh cost
Say85.0%10,200153.0+117.0
Do55.0%6,60099.0+63.0
Pay15.0%1,80027.0-9.0

The say forecast is 5.67 times the pay forecast (153.0 ÷ 27.0), and it would have sanctioned the lease without hesitation. Only the pay row notices that the lease costs ₹36 lakh a month. Dividing that cost by the pass price gives the break-even: 36,00,000 ÷ 1,500 = 2,400 passes, or 20 per cent of the corridor. The pay rate of 15 per cent sits five points below it.

Figure 2 makes the same point visually. The pay bar ends before the red cost line, while the say and do bars overshoot it so far that the line is irrelevant to them.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose Hamsafar leases twenty vehicles instead of thirty, at the same ₹1.2 lakh per vehicle (36 ÷ 30). Cost falls to 20 × 1.2 = ₹24 lakh a month, and break-even falls to 24,00,000 ÷ 1,500 = 1,600 passes, or 13.3 per cent of the corridor. The pay forecast of 1,800 passes (₹27.0 lakh) now clears it by ₹3.0 lakh, and the margin rows become +129.0, +75.0 and +3.0. The say forecast approved both leases, so it carried no information about which to choose. The pay forecast flipped, because it was the only one that behaved like evidence.

A caution about precision. Six of forty is an estimate, not a fact. Its standard error is the square root of (0.15 × 0.85 ÷ 40), about 5.6 points, so a rough 95 per cent range runs from about 3.9 to 26.1 per cent. Both break-evens, 13.3 and 20 per cent, lie inside it. The business is plausible but unproven, a more useful finding than "85 per cent said yes".

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Cost is the real axis, not the label

The words say, do and pay are shorthand. A person who rearranges a morning routine for a trial has paid in effort, and a person who pays a refundable deposit has paid very little. Grade each piece of evidence by what it cost the person and how hard it would be to reverse. Hamsafar's pre-sale was non-refundable for the first month, which is why six payments counted for more than twenty-two bookings made on free seats.

Do evidence can be a favour

The 22 trial bookings were free, and free things are taken at rates that say little about willingness to pay. Observed behaviour is strong only when it is spontaneous, repeated and costly.

Say still has a job

Nothing here says interviews are useless. Statements are excellent for discovering the problem, the vocabulary and the objections, and for choosing what to test. The error is using statements to estimate quantities such as demand and price, which they are poorly suited to do.

Absence of payment is not proof of absence of demand

Sixteen people who booked in the trial did not buy. Some may simply have postponed it. Pay evidence is conclusive when it is positive, and ambiguous when it is negative. That is one reason to read the rate as a range and not as a point.

Selection decides what the sample can say

Govardhan recruited the forty from three tech-park cafeterias, which over-represents people who linger at lunch and are therefore somewhat sociable and time-rich. The 15 per cent should not be projected to 12,000 people without a haircut. forty signals from the wrong people can mislead as surely as none.

What it cannot tell you

Even perfect pay evidence cannot tell you why people paid, whether they will renew, or whether they will refer a colleague. A first payment is a purchase, and renewal at month two is retention. The evidence ladder, which this topic unlocks, extends the same idea upward to renewal and referral.

6. How the pattern differs by setting

In consumer products, saying is cheap and paying is small, so the ladder is steep and conversion is often below a fifth of stated intent. In B2B products, the money sits with a buyer who is not always the user. The cheap tier is a user saying "this is great", and the strong tier is a procurement officer signing a pilot order, a letter of intent that names a budget, or an employee lending an internal champion's hours. In marketplaces there are two ladders at once, one per side, and each side's willingness to pay depends on the other being present, so a seat pass that sells to passengers fails if vehicles are not on the route.

Company size changes the cost of pay evidence: an early-stage firm can ask a stranger for ₹1,500 on a Tuesday, while a large one often substitutes deposits or paid pilots.

7. Common mistakes

Averaging the tiers. Symptom: a deck shows a single "interest score" blended from survey answers, trial usage and payments. Misunderstanding: treating the tiers as three noisy measurements of one quantity. They measure different things, and the weaker ones are biased upward. Diagnostic: ask which number would change if you removed the survey. If none would, the survey is decoration.

Accepting enthusiasm as behaviour. Symptom: the team quotes interviewees verbatim ("I'd pay double for this!") as proof. Misunderstanding: a vivid statement feels like strong evidence because it is memorable. Diagnostic: ask what the speaker has done in the last three months about this problem. People with a real problem usually have a workaround, and it has a cost.

Designing a payment test nobody can fail. Symptom: a "pre-order" with free cancellation reports 70 per cent conversion. Misunderstanding: confusing a gesture with a commitment. Diagnostic: ask what the customer loses if they walk away. If the answer is nothing, it was a say test with a button.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version would have written, before any interview, that a pass is worth launching if the paid share reaches the lease's break-even. Interviews would have found pickup points and objections, not estimated demand, and the trial would have used discounted paid seats. The memo would then carry one table: forecast on each tier, break-even for each lease size, a range and a recommendation.

9. Closing

On the afternoon of 28 September, Hemalatha recommended against the thirty-vehicle lease. Ingrid Halvorsen, a finance contractor in Oslo who had built the model, confirmed the break-even arithmetic on a call, and Harini Ravipati, who ran operations, confirmed that the lessor would offer twenty vehicles at ₹1.2 lakh each on a three-month term with a break clause. Ishaan accepted, with one condition: that the first renewal rate, measured in the last week of the first month, would decide whether Hamsafar ordered more. The pay forecast cleared a 20-vehicle fleet by ₹3.0 lakh a month, a margin thin enough to need monitoring, but it was the only forecast that a lease could be sized against.

What to learn next: the evidence ladder, which extends say-do-pay to renewal, referral and unprompted return, and the discipline of reconciling contradictory findings, which asks what to do when two credible sources of evidence disagree and no extra test is affordable.

Two questions to sit with. First, if the 16 trial users who did not pay were called tomorrow and half said price was the barrier, would you lower the price or accept the 15 per cent? Second, think of a decision in your own work that rests on stated intent. What is the cheapest payment you could request from the person before you commit?
exp40v2-res.synthesis:
Synthesising Research: From Notes to Claims Worth Money

An analytical treatment for product managers who must referee the argument, not just run the workshop.

1. Two rooms, two piles, one question

On Monday 5 October 2026, in a co-working room in Baner, Pune, Meera Natu stood in front of 412 sticky notes. Natu is group product manager at Maatra Nutrition Works, which sells a personalised eating plan in an app with a monthly supplement box. The September quarter brought 2,40,000 installs, 48,000 activations at 20.0 per cent and 9,600 paying subscribers, 20.0 per cent of activations and 4.0 per cent of installs. At ₹780 a month they produced ₹74.88 lakh of monthly revenue; churn of 11.0 per cent took 1,056 subscribers and ₹8.24 lakh of that revenue out every month.

Maatra held ₹1,040 lakh of cash against a burn of ₹52 lakh a month: twenty months of runway. The December-quarter budget was ₹120 lakh, and four proposed programmes cost ₹86 lakh, ₹54 lakh, ₹22 lakh and ₹40 lakh, a total of ₹202 lakh. A wrong quarter would consume ₹156 lakh, 15.0 per cent of the company's cash. Nakul Godbole, the founder, wanted a one-page problem memo by Friday 16 October, eleven days away.

Four days later, on Friday 9 October, Nirupama Lele faced a different pile in Coimbatore. Nipun Machine Industries builds filling and sealing machines for dairies and sells telemetry alongside them; 1,420 machines run in 186 plants, from co-operatives of the kind Amul and Hatsun run down to single-line district units. Her team had made 26 site visits to 18 plants, interviewed 41 people across five roles and produced 306 notes. Against an annual engineering budget of ₹240 lakh, bearing-failure alerting was costed at ₹165 lakh and a changeover wizard at ₹95 lakh: ₹260 lakh together, ₹20 lakh more than existed. Mohanraj Thangavel, the managing director, would lock the plan on Tuesday 27 October, eighteen days later.

Both decisions reduce to one question, not about empathy: which pile is a market pattern, and which an artefact of who talked most?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Synthesis is the disciplined reduction of raw research material to a few named patterns, each traceable to the people who produced it, each carrying a strength of evidence, each stated so it could be shown false. Three things make it hard: memory over-weights the vivid and the recent; the notes a cluster attracts reflect the interviewer as much as the customer; and the synthesiser has a favoured answer.

The lineage is real. Jiro Kawakita formalised bottom-up grouping of field notes in the 1960s as the KJ method, insisting a group be named only after it exists. Glaser and Strauss published The Discovery of Grounded Theory in 1967, with its practice of constant comparison, each observation tested against the category it is about to join. Beyer and Holtzblatt carried the affinity diagram into software work in Contextual Design in 1998. Tversky and Kahneman supplied the reason it is needed at all: availability, not frequency, is what an unaided mind reports.

Three schools disagree. The interpretive school holds that the value of qualitative work lies in mechanism, not incidence; it will sign that one well-understood case can justify a roadmap, and will not sign that cluster size ranks priority. The decision-analytic school treats synthesis as estimation under uncertainty, to be counted, weighted by segment value and audited; it will sign that an unweighted theme list amplifies the bias of whoever held the marker, and will not sign that a vivid interview is grounds for spending. The design-ethnographic middle holds that extreme users reveal what the median user cannot articulate; it will sign that frequency is a poor proxy for importance, and will not sign that the largest pile is where to start.

3. Mechanics, including the steps usually left implicit

The visible craft is three moves: dump one observation per note with a source code, sort in silence, name each stable group as a problem rather than a topic. Maatra's 34 interviews split into 18 subscribers retained three months or more, 11 who had cancelled and 5 who never paid. Malati Risbud, who ran research operations, tagged every note with a source code and one of three verbs: the person said it, did something about it, or paid to work around it. That tagging makes the implicit steps possible.

The first implicit step is declaring the unit of count before sorting. Table 1 gives both.

Table 1. Maatra: seven clusters from 34 interviews, 412 notes

The second implicit step is capping. One subscriber produced 19 of M1's 84 notes, 22.6 per cent of that pile from one of 34 people. A cap of three notes per person per cluster is crude but honest: it changes nothing about who was in the room, and much about which pile looks tallest.

The quantitative treatment is worth working rather than naming. First, saturation: Risbud recorded how many new candidate clusters each batch produced.

Raw agreement is the diagonal, 26 plus 78, or 104 of 120, which is 86.7 per cent and sounds comfortable. Chance agreement is not zero, because both coders said "paid" rarely: Natu marked 35 of 120, or 29.2 per cent, Myklebust 33 of 120, or 27.5 per cent. Expected chance agreement is 0.292 times 0.275 plus 0.708 times 0.725, or 0.594, so Cohen's kappa, agreement above chance as a fraction of the room above chance, is (0.867 minus 0.594) divided by (1 minus 0.594), which is 0.67: short of certainty, since on about one note in seven two competent readers disagreed about whether money had changed hands.

4. When the method applies, as testable claims

Three conditions can be stated so either protagonist can check them. First: the problem space is unknown enough that categories must come from the data. True at Maatra, where M4 appeared in no plan and was raised by 17 of 34 people; only narrowly true at Nipun, where all six clusters were known before the visits, though their weight was not. Second: the people were selected on a frame you can defend. Maatra's frame was its own subscriber and canceller lists, which cannot speak for the 1,92,000 installs that never activated; Nipun's was 18 plants of 186, chosen because they had reported incidents, over-sampling failure by construction. Third: the decision turns on which problem, not how many customers have it. Both passed; a pricing or forecasting decision would not, and synthesis misleads there, because a ranked list invites readers to read cluster shares as market shares. Saying 61.8 per cent of Maatra's market has a travel-routine problem misuses Table 1: it is a fact about 34 people.

5. Hard edges: roles, plants, regulation and models

Nipun shows what happens when respondent and customer are different objects. Its 41 interviewees were 16 operators, 9 maintenance technicians, 6 plant managers, 5 quality heads and 5 procurement staff, so counting people counts operators twice over.

Table 5. Nipun: six clusters, three units of count
ClusterNotesPeople (of 41)Plants (of 18)People per plant raising it
N1. Bearing seizure, no warning7123141.64
N2. Changeover overruns the shift6417161.06
N3. Spare-part identification is guesswork5215111.36
N4. Alarm codes mean nothing481992.11
N5. No proof the batch met the quality spec419100.90
N6. Service arrival unpredictable301281.50
Total memberships30695681.40 (95 ÷ 68)

By people, N1 leads with 23 of 41 and N4 is second with 19. By plants, N2 leads with 16 of 18, or 88.9 per cent, N1 follows with 14, and N4 falls to fifth with 9. The last column explains it: N4 drew 2.11 people per plant raising it, against N2's 1.06. Alarm-code frustration is felt intensely by the role with the most bodies; changeover overrun by almost every plant. For a company that sells to plants and renews with plants, the plant count matches the money, and the blended 1.40 people per plant-cluster pair is what a head-count ranking omits.

Three further seams matter. In regulated contexts the account is partly a compliance performance: Nipun's quality heads describe practice as Legal Metrology and FSSAI auditors would wish it, so N5 reads better from logbooks than words. In hardware-plus-software businesses the halves have different clocks, firmware on a six-month train and an app screen in a fortnight, so a synthesis that does not say which half owns a cluster yields a roadmap nobody can build. In AI-native products the reported failure is rarely the one that occurred, so clusters need logs too. At the seam, mature companies say they run a research repository; mostly they run decks whose claims cannot be traced to a source code in a minute, the only test that matters.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

One talker can own a pile. At Maatra one subscriber supplied 19 of M1's 84 notes. The tell-tale is notes per person above the page average: M3's 4.4 and M1's 4.0 against 3.8. The obvious reading, that a big pile means a big problem, confuses how much a person talks with how many are affected.

Said, did and paid are different evidence classes. Economists separate stated from revealed preference; someone who drove to a chemist and paid retail has shown what a sigh does not. Figure 1 is the argument: M1 and M2 broad and lightly paid, M3 narrower and paid. The tell-tale is a memo where every cluster carries the same confidence.

Negative space is evidence. No Maatra cluster concerned the app's first run, which is suspicious given that 1,92,000 of 2,40,000 installs never activated and none of that group was interviewed. The expert reads the holes as a map of the recruiting channel.

A cluster name that is a noun is not a finding. "Delivery" is a topic; "the box arrives after the last runs out" is a problem with a victim and a consequence. The tell-tale is a cluster list matching the interview guide's headings, which means the sort merely recovered the team's prior structure.

Saturation is a property of the frame, not the number. Figure 2 flattens after 24 interviews, licensing a claim about Maatra's subscriber list and none about non-activators. The tell-tale is "we reached saturation at twelve", said without a frame.

Agreement should be measured, and above chance. Raw agreement of 86.7 per cent flattered Natu; kappa of 0.67 was the honest figure. The tell-tale is a team that has never had a second person re-sort a sample, a twenty-minute exercise almost nobody performs.

Frequency, severity and willingness to pay rank differently, and arithmetic beats salience. At Nipun, seizures were described vividly in 14 plants, changeover overruns flatly in 16; section 8 shows the money runs 2.4 times the other way. Rare catastrophes dominate recall, chronic losses the ledger. The tell-tale is a cluster everybody can tell a story about and nobody can size.

Quotes are illustrations; source codes are evidence. The expert's artefact is a claim register showing each claim's denominators and its disconfirming test, quotes attached afterwards for persuasion. The tell-tale is a deck whose quotes are beautiful and whose counts are missing.

7. How it changes by product type and stage

In consumer products the respondent describes an idealised self, so the paid column carries the weight, as at Maatra. In B2B and enterprise the account is the customer and the respondent is not, so counts belong at account level with the role mix recorded, as in Table 5. In platforms and marketplaces each side is synthesised separately, because a blended ranking hides that the sides' problems differ. In hardware the cost of error is tooling and inventory rather than a sprint: Nipun's bearing programme at ₹165 lakh is 68.8 per cent of a year's budget. In AI products the honest corpus is logs plus interviews, since users cannot report a failure they did not detect. Across stages the risk inverts: at Maatra's size the danger is three people confirming each other; at Nipun's 1,420 machines it is synthesis by people who attended none of the 26 visits. What does not change is the arithmetic: denominators, capping and the said-did-paid ladder apply identically to a ₹22 lakh app change and a ₹165 lakh firmware programme.

8. Three worked examples

One: Maatra's cheap cluster. M3 is narrow, 14 of 34 people, and strong, 9 of 14 paid. Nidheesh Karve, who ran support, estimated that fixing dispatch timing would cut monthly churn from 11.0 per cent to 9.5 per cent. On 9,600 subscribers those 1.5 percentage points are 144 subscribers retained a month, worth 144 times ₹780, or ₹1.12 lakh a month and ₹13.48 lakh a year on a static base. Against the full ₹22 lakh build that is a payback of 19.6 months. Karve held that the gap sits on the long routes, so an ₹8 lakh version dispatching a week earlier for the 2,000 subscribers on those routes alone would retain about 100 of the 144, worth ₹0.78 lakh a month and a payback of 10.3 months. The arithmetic did not choose the cluster; it chose the size of the bet.

Two: Nipun's quiet problem. Mythili Ganapathy priced the clusters at one rate agreed with three plant managers: ₹0.45 lakh of lost output per machine-hour stopped.

Table 6. Annual avoidable loss, 18 plants studied
ClusterEvents a yearMean minutes per eventHours lostValue at ₹0.45 lakh per hour
N1. Bearing seizure112192358.4₹161.28 lakh
N2. Changeover overrun4,68011858.0₹386.10 lakh
N3. Spare-part search9690144.0₹64.80 lakh
N6. Waiting for a service engineer54360324.0₹145.80 lakh
Total4,94220.45 (101,064 ÷ 4,942)1,684.4₹757.98 lakh

The ranking by money is N2, N1, N6, N3. N2's 4,680 changeovers at 11 minutes of overrun are 51,480 minutes, or 858.0 hours, worth ₹386.10 lakh; N1's 112 seizures at 192 minutes are 358.4 hours, worth ₹161.28 lakh. The quiet cluster is worth 2.4 times the loud one. Across the 18 plants the total is ₹757.98 lakh, an average of ₹42.11 lakh and 93.6 machine-hours per plant. Ganapathy also produced the number Lele refused to circulate: 12 per cent of N2's loss captured as subscription revenue is ₹46.33 lakh a year across 18 plants, ₹2.574 lakh per plant, which over 186 plants gives ₹478.76 lakh, nearly ₹4.79 crore. Those plants were chosen because they had reported incidents, so that is arithmetic on a biased frame, and such a figure, once on a slide, becomes a commitment nobody withdraws.

Three: where it failed. In March 2026, Mrinalini Satoskar at Nartan Fitness Network synthesised 28 interviews into 196 notes and concluded that social challenges were the leading unmet need: that cluster held 54 of 196 notes, 27.6 per cent of the wall and the largest pile. The feature cost ₹70 lakh and fourteen weeks of six engineers. On 2,80,000 monthly active users, 5,320 used it once, 1.9 per cent, and 1,064 used it twice, 0.38 per cent of the base and 20.0 per cent of those who tried it. The post-mortem found the 54 notes came from 6 of 28 interviewees, 21.4 per cent, and 38 of the 54, or 70.4 per cent, from three people recruited through the company's community group, its most social users. Satoskar re-sorted the same notes with a cap of three notes per person per cluster and a people denominator; the social cluster fell to fifth of seven, and resuming after a break in training, sixth on notes, rose to first on people. The error cost ₹70 lakh and a quarter; the correction took two days.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Ranking by pile height. Early warning: the biggest cluster wins every argument and nobody quotes a denominator. Diagnostic: how many distinct people, and what is the most any one contributed? Caught late, it costs a build cycle, as Nartan shows.

Synthesis by the absent. Early warning: the slide author attended no interviews and the notes are summaries of summaries. Diagnostic: pick a claim and ask for its source codes. Caught late, the organisation loses the ability to tell evidence from folklore, costlier than any feature.

Confirmation sorting. Early warning: no cluster contradicts the plan the team has. Diagnostic: before the sort, what result would have made you drop it?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The counting position. Synthesis without denominators is bias with better typography; Nartan is the evidence, where three enthusiasts produced 70.4 per cent of a pile that drove ₹70 lakh of spending. It would be wrong if the decisions that mattered turned on mechanism rather than incidence, where counting measures the wrong thing precisely.

The interpretive position. Counting qualitative material imports the authority of statistics into data that cannot bear it, and a count of 34 invites the extrapolation section 4 forbids. Its evidence is insight from single cases: one dairy's changeover log revealed the mechanism behind N2 before anyone counted plants. It would be wrong if uncounted teams over-weighted vivid minorities, as Nartan shows.

The log-first position, newest and strongest in software. Interviews are weak where behaviour is already instrumented: Maatra could read dispatch timing for all 9,600 paying subscribers rather than infer M3 from 14 people. It would be wrong where the question is why, where no log exists, or where the metric encodes the team's assumptions, as for the 1,92,000 installs that generated no events.

Two questions are open rather than contested: nobody has a defensible rule for the weight a paid workaround deserves, and nobody has shown that model-assisted clustering preserves what synthesis exists to protect, traceability to a person.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. They declare the unit of count and the frame before the first note moves, so the method cannot be chosen to suit the answer. They carry three numbers for every claim: people, people who acted or paid, and the most any one person contributed. They can produce the source codes behind any sentence in a minute, and expect to be asked. And they state, unprompted, what would make them abandon their own recommendation. The merely studied practitioner runs a good workshop and cannot say how many people stand behind the largest cluster.

12. What each protagonist decided

Natu's memo of 16 October recommended neither large programme. She proposed ₹22 lakh for the dispatch-timing fix behind M3, the only cluster with paid evidence above 60 per cent; ₹18 lakh for an instrumented pilot of progress measurement with 500 subscribers, since 9 of the 11 cancellers raised M2, 81.8 per cent, while its paid share was 15.8 per cent; ₹12 lakh for twelve interviews with family cooks and with installs that never activated; and ₹68 lakh unallocated until those were synthesised. The four amounts total the ₹120 lakh available. Breadth without payment is a hypothesis, payment without breadth a niche, and the cheapest way to tell which M2 was cost 15.0 per cent of the quarter rather than 45.0 per cent.

Lele's plan for 27 October also split: the changeover wizard at ₹95 lakh, on the plant count of 16 of 18 and ₹386.10 lakh of avoidable loss; ₹35 lakh for vibration sensors on 40 machines to collect the data predictive alerting would need, without building the alerting; ₹30 lakh for alarm-code translation, cheap and what operators asked for; and ₹80 lakh held for a mid-year re-decision, together the ₹240 lakh she had. Nagarajan Velayutham, who ran field service, dissented, and Lele's minute recorded the objection rather than resolving it: if a seizure caused a milk spoilage claim, the ranking by hours is the wrong ranking.

Three questions. First, Lele ranked by plants and Velayutham by consequence; what evidence obtainable before 27 October would settle which unit is right? Second, Natu's ₹12 lakh buys twelve interviews with people who never activated, a group no cluster describes; what would she have to find for the ₹68 lakh to leave M2 and M3? Third, had the kappa come back at 0.35, which claims in Tables 1 and 2 should have been withdrawn, and which survive?

13. Going deeper

  • Interview fundamentals — note quality caps synthesis quality.
  • Designing an interview guide — topic headings guarantee clusters mirroring them.
  • Recruiting participants — the frame decides what cannot be discovered.
  • How many interviews — enough that new clusters stop arriving in one frame.
  • Cognitive biases in research — what counting blunts.
  • Evidence strength: say, do, pay — the ladder behind Figure 1.
  • Qualitative versus quantitative — what a count of 34 cannot answer.
  • Survey design — turns a cluster into an incidence estimate you may quote.
  • Validating a problem hypothesis — is the cluster worth paying for?
  • Reconciling contradictory findings — when operators and managers disagree.
  • Building personas — how segments harden, then decay into fiction.
  • Translating research into design — problem to specification, evidence intact.
  • Mining tickets, reviews and sales calls — where capping matters more, not less.
  • AI-assisted synthesis — models compress the dump and sort; counting stays human.

Synthesising Research: From a Wall of Notes to a Decision

1. A wall of 168 notes

On the morning of Thursday 8 October 2026, Disha Karmarkar, the only product manager at Fasal Setu Exchange, stood facing 168 yellow sticky notes in a rented room above a seed shop in Latur. Fasal Setu runs a marketplace, a service that connects two groups who need each other, in this case farmers in Marathwada and the licensed input retailers who sell them seed, fertiliser and crop-protection chemicals. Between 8 September and 3 October, Disha and two colleagues had interviewed 22 people: 14 farmers and 8 retailers.

The company held ₹640 lakh in cash and spent ₹40 lakh a month, which is 16 months of runway. The engineering budget for the coming quarter was ₹60 lakh. The founder, Darius Pavri, wanted a recommendation for the board on Monday 19 October, eleven days away. Two proposals were on the table: a pay-after-harvest credit ledger at ₹38 lakh, and a seed-authenticity verification feature at ₹22 lakh. A quarter spent on the wrong one would burn ₹120 lakh of company cash (three months at ₹40 lakh), which is 18.75 per cent of everything the company had.

Two trusted colleagues read the wall differently. Faraz Siddiqui, who had joined the farmer visits, was certain that counterfeit seed was the issue: "Nearly every farmer I met brought it up." Elisha Thomas, who had transcribed all 22 interviews, had counted the notes in each pile and pointed out that credit was the largest. Each method was quietly biased. Disha needed a method, not seniority, to settle it. That method is called synthesis.

2. The idea

Synthesis is the disciplined process of reducing a large pile of raw research material (notes, quotes, observations) to a small number of named patterns, each tied to traceable evidence, and then judging which patterns deserve action. Three verbs carry it: reduce, name, test. It exists because human memory is a poor filter. We remember the vivid interview and the recent one; 168 notes cannot be held in one head, so the loudest voice stands in for the whole.

The central technique is affinity mapping: sorting notes into groups by similarity, from the bottom up, and writing each group's name only after the group exists. Jiro Kawakita, a Japanese anthropologist, developed it in the 1960s to organise field notes (the KJ method). Glaser and Strauss described a cousin, coding, in 1967, and Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt carried affinity diagrams into software design in Contextual Design.

The sentence Disha could repeat in the board meeting without sounding glib was this: "We count people rather than quotes, and we trust what people did more than what they said."

3. How it actually works

Step 1, dump. Every observation goes on its own note, one idea each, tagged with a source code: F07 for the seventh farmer, R03 for the third retailer. Elisha had also marked each note as something the person said, did or felt. Without the source code, later counting is impossible.

Step 2, sort. The team moved notes into groups without talking, so no first speaker named the categories.

Step 3, cluster and name. Each stable group was named as a problem the customer has, not a topic. Six clusters emerged, labelled A to F below.

Steps 4 to 6 are the implicit ones. Step 4 counts distinct people in each cluster, not notes. Step 5 separates what people reported from what they had actually done, such as borrowing, travelling or paying extra. Step 6 invites a challenge: Freya Lindqvist, a contract researcher in Stockholm who had never seen the wall, independently sorted a random sample of 40 notes into the six cluster names. She matched Disha's placement on 34 of them, which is 85.0 per cent agreement, and the six disagreements showed that clusters B and D blurred at the edges, so their boundary was rewritten.

4. A worked example, line by line

Table 1 is what the wall looked like when Elisha counted the way most teams count: notes per pile.

Counting notes, cluster A, credit until harvest, leads with 41 of 168, or 24.4 per cent, as Elisha saw. Counting people, cluster B, counterfeit seed, leads: 12 of 22 interviewees, or 54.5 per cent, as Faraz saw. The last column explains the gap: A produced 4.6 notes per person raising it, against 2.8 for B. One retailer, Dattatray Mhaske, supplied 14 of the 41 notes, which is 34.1 per cent of the pile from one of the 22 interviewees. Notes reward verbosity; people reward breadth; neither measures importance.

The notes sum exactly (41 + 33 + 29 + 27 + 22 + 16 = 168). The interviewee column is not additive, since one person can raise several problems: the six counts give 50 memberships across 22 people, or 3.4 notes per membership (168 ÷ 50 = 3.36).

Now the second pass, changing one input. Instead of asking who mentioned a problem, Disha asked who had acted on it at their own cost, which Elisha's said, did and felt tags made possible.

Counterfeit seed falls from first (12 people) to third (3 people acted), and only 25.0 per cent of those who raised it had done anything about it, such as driving to a trusted town shop. Credit rises to first: 7 of the 9 who raised it, or 77.8 per cent, had acted, mostly retailers extending a tab from their own working capital. Delivery is second, with 4. The credit problem sits mainly with retailers: 6 of 8, or 75.0 per cent. The counterfeit problem sits with farmers: 11 of 14, or 78.6 per cent. What survives all three tables: retailers finance the farmers' season and resist an app that cannot track what is owed, while counterfeit seed is a widespread worry that costs people little to tolerate.

5. Six nuances

Counting people versus counting notes

The unit of count must be chosen on purpose. Notes measure how much a topic was discussed, which depends on the interviewer's questions and the interviewee's talkativeness. People measure how many separate lives contain the problem.

Said versus did

Economists call the first stated preference and the second revealed preference. A problem someone has spent money or time working around is stronger evidence than one they sigh about; stated problems are not false, merely unproven.

A cluster is a hypothesis, not a finding

The name you give a pile is an interpretation. Freya's 85.0 per cent agreement still leaves 15.0 per cent contested; if a second person would sort differently, the clusters are the team's opinion.

Frequency is not importance

Cluster F had only 5 of 22 people, or 22.7 per cent, yet if they were the largest buyers it could outweigh a cluster twice its size.

Qualitative counts do not generalise as percentages

Twenty-two people recruited by a small team are not a random sample of Marathwada. Saying that 54.5 per cent of interviewees worry about counterfeit seed is a misuse: the figure describes your interviewees only. Interviews show what problems exist; a later survey shows how common each is.

What it cannot tell you, and what to ask first

No clustering can tell you whether a proposed solution will work or whether anyone will pay for it. Before relying on a synthesis, ask who was interviewed and how (Fasal Setu recruited through existing retailers, so departed ones went unheard), who sorted, and what evidence would change the team's mind.

6. How it differs by product and by stage

Table 4. Where the unit of count and the main hazard change
Product typeWhat you countCharacteristic hazard
ConsumerIndividualsInterviewees describe an idealised self
B2BAccounts and rolesBuyer, user and payer differ
MarketplaceEach side separatelyAveraging sides hides that their problems differ

In consumer products the polished self-portrait is the danger, so said-versus-did matters most. In B2B, one customer organisation holds several people with different stakes, so count accounts as well as individuals. In a marketplace, as Table 3 shows, synthesise each side alone before comparing; agri-input platforms such as DeHaat and BigHaat share this two-sided structure.

Stage changes the rigour you can afford. An early company like Fasal Setu can sort 168 notes with a wall, and its risk is bias from three people in the room. A large company has specialists and thousands of notes, and its risk is the opposite: synthesis by people absent from the interviews, producing slide-ready themes with the evidence stripped out.

7. Common mistakes

Ranking by pile height. The symptom is that the biggest cluster wins every argument. The misunderstanding: more notes means more customers. Diagnostic: divide notes by distinct people and look for a high ratio, like A's 4.6.

Naming clusters before sorting. Symptom: clusters match the interview guide's headings. Misunderstanding: synthesis is filing. Diagnostic: ask which pile holds what surprised the interviewer; if none, nothing was learned.

Treating one segment as everyone. Symptom: the story changes with the teller. Misunderstanding: one group's pattern is the product's. Diagnostic: cut every cluster by segment, as Table 3 does.

Reading only confirmation. Symptom: no cluster contradicts the favoured plan. Misunderstanding: evidence is gathered in support. Diagnostic: write down beforehand what result would make you drop your option, then check the notes.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Disha's output is one page, not a deck: each claim carries its people count, action count and what would overturn it.

Table 5. The one-page evidence ledger
ClaimEvidenceConfidenceWould change my mind if
Retailers who carry farmer credit resist app-only ordering9 raised credit, 7 actedModerate: 8 retailers, one-segment skewFresh retailers report no tab at all
Counterfeit seed is a common worry but a low-cost one to tolerate12 raised it, 3 actedLow to moderateFarmers who bought fake seed describe lost crop

Nothing is quoted as a market statistic, and any sentence traces to source codes within a minute.

9. What Disha decided

She chose neither feature outright. She recommended to Darius a staged commitment: ₹15 lakh for a minimal credit ledger piloted with the 6 retailers who raised credit, ₹5 lakh for low-cost authenticity measures (photographing batch labels at dispatch), and ₹40 lakh held back until a second round of eight interviews, aimed at counterfeit seed buyers and at retailers outside Latur, had been synthesised. The three amounts total ₹60 lakh. Her reasoning: credit had behavioural evidence but a narrow segment, counterfeit seed had breadth but little behavioural proof, and the cheap test would show which mattered.

Read next on validating a problem hypothesis (is the pattern serious enough to pay for?), reconciling contradictory findings (when segments disagree), and AI-assisted synthesis, which speeds steps 1 and 2 but leaves steps 4 to 6 to human judgement.

Two questions to sit with. First: if Freya had agreed with Disha on 40 of 40 notes, what additional assurance would that have bought, and what would it still have left uncovered? Second: recall a decision you made on one loud person's word. What had that person actually done?
case20v1-res.synthesis:
Vyanjan Kirana Network: Thirty-One Interviews

A decision case on synthesising qualitative research

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Ekambar Jhaveri sat in a glass cabin at the Pune office of Vyanjan Kirana Network, with a wall of yellow sticky notes behind him and a roadmap that had to be locked by Friday, 23 October. Between 7 September and 9 October he had run, or sat in on, thirty-one interviews with neighbourhood grocers in four cities. The notes were still on the wall, and the company's chief executive, Elavarasi Jain, wanted one answer by the Friday review: what should the product team spend the next quarter building?

Two proposals were already circulating. The sales head said the interviews proved that retailers wanted credit. The data scientist said the order logs pointed somewhere else. Ekambar, a senior product manager, owned the synthesis, and the room expected him to settle the argument with evidence rather than with seniority.

2. Company background

Vyanjan Kirana Network, founded in 2021, runs a mobile ordering app through which small grocery retailers, the kirana stores that still sell most of India's packaged food, buy stock from nearby wholesalers and distributors. A retailer in Indore who once phoned a salesman each evening now sends an order from a phone and receives goods the next morning. Vyanjan earns a margin of a few per cent on each order and charges distributors a listing fee.

By September 2026 the app had about 14,000 active retailers across Pune, Nagpur, Mysuru and Indore. The company competes with Udaan and Flipkart Wholesale, which offer wider catalogues, and with JioMart Partner, which offers its own supply chain and aggressive pricing. Retailers also still order the old way, by phone and through the visiting salesmen of Amul and other brands. Vyanjan's pitch is local: trusted distributors, Hindi, Marathi and Kannada interfaces, and a cash-friendly rhythm built around the festival season. Diwali falls on Sunday, 8 November 2026, and the weeks before it carry the largest order volumes of the year.

3. The situation

Ekambar ran the research as a discovery sprint. He and two colleagues conducted the interviews in the retailers' own shops, often between customers. Each session produced a page of raw notes, and afterwards the team transcribed every observation onto a separate sticky note. The wall held 412 of them. Ekambar first dumped them without ordering, then sorted them by who said what, and then clustered them into themes, discarding the labels he had walked in with.

The clustering produced five themes, shown in Exhibit 1. Ekambar added two columns to the usual count of mentions. The first recorded whether the retailer raised the topic unprompted. The second recorded whether the interviewer saw something that backed up the claim, such as a ledger, a photograph of rejected goods or an order history on the retailer's phone.

Credit was the most frequently mentioned theme, and it was the figure that had travelled around the company. Yet fourteen of the nineteen credit mentions came after an interviewer asked a version of "would you like to buy on credit?" Only five retailers raised it on their own. Short and wrong deliveries had fewer mentions, but eleven of the twelve who raised the topic did so unprompted, and nine could show something. A retailer in Nagpur called Eknath had opened his phone to a folder of photographs of cartons that arrived with the wrong flour. "I do not need credit," he said. "I need what I ordered."

Edmundo Jumde, the data scientist, had meanwhile analysed 1,86,000 orders placed in August and September 2026. Of these, 11,160 carried a shortage or wrong-item complaint, which is 6.0 per cent of orders. He then split the 14,000 active retailers by whether any of their first three orders had been short, and compared how many placed another order within thirty days. Exhibit 2 shows the result.

The global team saw the question differently from where each of them sat. Eleni Jasani, the designer in Lisbon, had watched recordings of six interviews and told Ekambar that credit appeared mostly where the salesman was in the room. Edmundo, in Santiago, trusted the logs but warned that retailers who suffered shortages might also be the newest and least committed. Distance shaped the conversation too: Lisbon is four and a half hours behind Pune and Santiago eight and a half, so both joined the Friday review in their early mornings.

4. The people

Ekambar Jhaveri, senior product manager, Pune, owns the synthesis. He wants a conclusion he can defend line by line to the board.

Ehsaan Juneja, head of sales, Bengaluru, joined eleven of the interviews as the account owner. He wants a credit product, because distributors have asked for one and his team's targets depend on distributor growth.

Eleni Jasani, designer, Lisbon, wants the team to read the notes for what retailers did, not what they agreed to when asked.

Edmundo Jumde, data scientist, Santiago, wants any chosen investment to be measurable within a quarter.

Elavarasi Jain, chief executive, Bengaluru, wants one clear decision and does not want to enter Diwali with a half-built product.

5. The options

Ekambar framed three courses of action and costed each, as in Exhibit 3.

Option A follows the loudest request and would please distributors, but it carries lending risk under RBI's digital lending rules and rests on a theme with thin unprompted support. Option B addresses the quietest and most consistent complaint. If shorted retailers reordered at 71.0 per cent rather than 44.0 per cent, about 1,134 more of the 4,200 would remain active, which at an assumed ₹2,500 of net revenue per active retailer per month is about ₹28.35 lakh a month. That is an upper bound that assumes shortages fully explain the gap, and on it the ₹65 lakh pays back in about 2.3 months. Option C is cheap but costs three weeks, from Friday, 23 October to Friday, 13 November, which means missing the Diwali window.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 1 tell you that a raw count of mentions hides? Which themes would you call signal and which false positives, and why?
  2. How should Ekambar weigh Ehsaan's presence in eleven interviews when reading the credit evidence?
  3. What does Exhibit 2 establish, and what can it not establish? What second explanation would Edmundo want ruled out?
  4. Which option would you take to the Friday review, and what would make you reverse that choice?

7. A note for the learner

Synthesis exists to turn a pile of notes into patterns someone can act on. The method is dump, sort, cluster, and then test each cluster. A theme earns trust from how it was raised, whether behaviour backs it, and whether independent data agrees. A count of mentions alone measures what the interviewer asked about as much as what the customer feels.

Applied here, credit is the weaker signal. Most mentions were prompted, the evidence seen was thin, and the loudest voice in the company had been in the room for eleven of the conversations. Short and wrong deliveries are the stronger signal, because unprompted mentions, photographs and order logs all point the same way, three methods agreeing.

One defensible path is Option B now, with a gate on credit. Ekambar commits ₹65 lakh to order accuracy, and tells Elavarasi that credit is a hypothesis rather than a finding. He then asks Ehsaan and Eleni to design a short, unprompted test of credit with a few dozen retailers, which costs a fraction of ₹6 lakh and need not wait for the full eight interviews. Option A fails because it spends ₹240 lakh on the thinnest evidence, and Option C fails because it delays a fix whose cost of delay is already visible in Exhibit 2. The reasoning has a limit, since Exhibit 2 shows association and not cause. He should say so at the review and track the reorder rate of shorted retailers after launch.
case40v1-res.synthesis:
ISB · Software Product Management · Case 40

Atulya Care: Three Syntheses, One Roadmap

An unresolved case on turning a pile of research into patterns someone can act on

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 25 October 2026, Ghazal Koul was still at her kitchen table in Indiranagar, Bengaluru, with three decks open. The board of Atulya Care Services Private Limited met at eleven the next morning, and it had asked for one thing: the roadmap for the two quarters to 31 March 2027, and the evidence behind it.

Ghazal, the vice-president of product, had spent six weeks on that evidence. Forty-two members of the chronic-care programme had been interviewed in their homes and shops in Lucknow, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Guwahati and Pune; 1,310 support tickets had been coded, 68 coach calls transcribed, 2,140 members surveyed. Nothing in it had converged.

The affinity map built on a wall in Hyderabad said the coach kept changing. The machine-assisted clustering her design head commissioned said medicine refills and money. The survey said members wanted the same coach and plans in their own language. The churn model said something subtler that Ghazal suspected was partly circular. The board had approved ₹3.6 crore; each candidate bet cost more than a third of it, and two together more than all of it.

2. How Atulya Care came to be shaped this way

Atulya Care was founded in Bengaluru in November 2019 by Garvita Kunnath and two colleagues from a diagnostics chain. The first product was a direct-to-consumer diabetes coaching app at ₹1,499 a quarter. It reached about 31,000 paying subscribers and stopped, because Indian households do not habitually pay subscriptions for health behaviour.

In March 2021 the founders made the decision that still governs everything. Employers and health insurers would buy the programme for their people, and Atulya would be paid per enrolled member per month. It worked: revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹74 crore, and September 2026 billing ran at ₹6.671 crore across 2,41,000 enrolled members, a blended ₹276.80 per member per month.

Two consequences constrain the present. The price is per enrolled member, so the engine rewards enrolment drives at employers rather than engagement by members; the exception is a service level in the insurance contracts. And the app was rebuilt around a logging-centric data model in which a member is a sequence of readings: streaks, prompts, risk scores and insurer reports all compute from logged readings. Anything that reduces logging touches everything, which is why the cheapest-sounding idea here is the most expensive to build.

3. The industry

Chronic care in India is contested from three directions. Apollo 24|7, Practo and Tata 1mg sell consultations and medicines at national scale and treat coaching as an attachment. HealthifyMe and the fitness apps own habit logging. Insurers and third-party administrators run their own wellness benefits and, under the IRDAI's rules, can reward members directly, which makes Atulya one option inside a policy rather than the policy. Avasar Health Labs, a Gurugram competitor, sells a thinner product: no coaches, automated nudges, a third of the price.

Two regulatory facts bear on the roadmap. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act requires purpose-specific notice and consent for health data, so a new category of collection — voice recordings, for instance — needs fresh consent in every language the app supports. And integration with the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, now expected by large insurers, is mid-flight.

Atulya is exposed outside India too. Arkaan Industries LLC, a contracting group in Muscat with a largely Indian and Nepali workforce, enrols 11,500 lives at ₹420 per member per month: ₹48.3 lakh a month, ₹5.796 crore a year. The team itself sits in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad, Krakow, Manila, Melbourne and Montreal, so the synthesis argument has run in writing, across up to fifteen hours of time difference.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In April 2025 Atulya signed Apeksha General Insurance, its first insurer. The contract put a tenth of the fee at risk against a service level: at least 45 per cent of each monthly cohort must still be active at month three, as measured by the method in force at signature. That method was generous — any app open inside thirty days counted.

On 1 July 2026 the analytics team replaced it: active now required a logged reading or a completed coach call inside thirty days. It was made for honesty, documented in a data dictionary, and connected by nobody to the contract clause. Month three of the April cohort fell in July, so every cohort from April onwards is measured on the new rule and every earlier one on the old. Exhibit 1 carries the break.

Through August the pack looked alarming. Garvita asked for discovery, and Ghazal ran it from 24 August to 2 October: interviews in five cities, Gulf members by video, tickets and coach calls for the surrounding two months. On 10 August, unnoticed, the Manila team merged its pharmacy and order-status ticket categories into one bucket called refills.

Gisha Kilaru's team clustered the notes by hand on 7 and 8 October, reporting on the 9th: Exhibit 2. Grazyna Kozlowska had engaged Asmaan Analytics, a Bengaluru research-operations vendor, on 14 September to transcribe everything and cluster the whole corpus with a language model; that came back on 12 October: Exhibit 3. The two passes rank the themes differently, and both are faithful to what they were given. Exhibit 4 reports how far the coders agreed.

Guhan Kommineni's churn model of 16 October found the strongest predictor of month-three inactivity to be the number of coach changes in the first ninety days. Of the 148,500 members in the January-to-June cohorts, 18,900 (12.7 per cent) had three or more changes; 31.0 per cent of that group were active at month three against 50.0 per cent of those with no more than one. He also split the cohorts another way: newly diagnosed members, 56,430 of 148,500 (38.0 per cent), were active at 60.0 per cent and the remaining 92,070 at 39.6 per cent, which is how Exhibit 1's blended 47.4 per cent arises.

Two beliefs have since broken. The cliff is partly definitional: the old rule applied to the June cohort gives 45.2 per cent, not 39.0. And Apeksha's renewal letter of 2 October, quoting “49.0 per cent, per your mid-year pack of 6 August”, is quoting the April cohort; the insurer has not seen the September pack of 6 October.

5. The people

Ghazal Koul, vice-president of product, Bengaluru, wants a recommendation she can defend line by line. Unsaid: in August she told the sales head refill visibility was “basically next quarter”, and she no longer trusts the map.

Garvita Kunnath, co-founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants one bet and a story for the next round. Unsaid: an investor's interest is conditional on the Apeksha renewal, which makes the insurer's view of the numbers worth more than the numbers.

Gisha Kilaru, principal researcher, Hyderabad, holds that coach continuity is the finding; her incentive is a function that must justify six weeks. Unsaid: she set aside 78 notes as venting and coded seven in ten herself.

Grazyna Kozlowska, head of design, Krakow, commissioned the machine-assisted pass and argues the logging burden is the cause. Unsaid: her prompt named five candidate themes as examples, and she engaged the vendor without procurement review.

Guhan Kommineni, director of data science, Montreal, wants whatever is chosen to be measurable inside a quarter. Unsaid loudly enough: coach changes are partly downstream of inactivity, since coaches leave quiet members.

Glenda Katigbak, customer-success lead, Manila, says the queue has been shouting about refills for a year. Unsaid: her own August taxonomy change inflated that bucket, and only one member in nine has ever raised a ticket.

Gemma Kirkland, head of enterprise sales, Melbourne, carries Arkaan and the insurer channel and wants the refill work. Unsaid: the demand comes from Arkaan's procurement manager, not its finance chief, and her variable pay turns on renewals signed by 31 December.

Granth Kubal, director of engineering, Pune, says seven of his 23 engineers are on the Ayushman Bharat migration until 15 December and nothing ships before it. Unsaid: a side project has taken vernacular voice logging to sixty per cent, tested with 40 volunteers.

7. Voices

“Seventy-eight notes were people blowing off steam about the hospital, their son. Leave them in and the wall is noise. I made a judgement and wrote it down.”

Gisha Kilaru, synthesis review, 9 October

“This is not human against machine. The model read everything we collected. The wall holds what three people wrote on cards, minus what one of them called venting.”

Grazyna Kozlowska, product channel, 12 October

“My queue is not your sample. And fair warning, we merged two buckets in August, so do not read the trend line.”

Glenda Katigbak, from Manila, 13 October

“Coach changes is the top feature and I would not bet a quarter on it. When a member goes quiet we move the coach to someone active. The feature is partly the label.”

Guhan Kommineni, email, 16 October

“Four coaches in five months. Every time I explain my tablets again, my readings again, my mother's cooking again. The fourth was good. Then she also went.”

Ghulam Kazmi, 58, member since November 2025, Lucknow

“I enter the reading twice, in the machine and in the app. If the app wants it, let the app take it. I stopped for two weeks, nobody noticed, so I stopped properly.”

Ganpat Kunte, 42, member since March 2026, Nagpur

“If someone does not log for three weeks the system moves them off my list. I did not stop caring; the list stopped showing them.”

Golap Konwar, coach, Guwahati, recorded call

8. The options as Ghazal sees them

Exhibit 6 costs the four. Option A buys coach continuity: pods of four coaches on a shared panel, a scheduling rebuild, 14 hires. It answers the most unprompted theme on the wall, the strongest statement in the survey and the top feature of the churn model Guhan has himself warned may read the outcome backwards.

Option B attacks the logging burden with device pairing and vernacular voice entry. It answers the theme named in the most interviews and backed by the most artefacts, and Ganpat Kunte's double entry is exactly it. It also collides with the 2021 data model, the Act's consent work and Granth's migration — and its cost is the one Granth knows to be overstated.

Option C builds refill reminders, pharmacy status and a benefit explainer with claim status. It answers the largest cluster in Exhibit 3, Arkaan's request and Gemma's renewal, and is the cheapest and fastest of the three builds. Its evidence leans hardest on a channel re-bucketed in August that only a ninth of members use.

Option D spends ₹0.35 crore restating the question: fix both definitions, re-run month three on both rules for every cohort, re-code a sample against a shared codebook, re-cluster with a prompt that names nothing. It produces no feature and lands the decision six days after Arkaan's window shuts.

Three things sit outside the frame. Nobody interviewed a buyer: not one benefits owner at the 86 employer accounts, not one product owner at Apeksha, though they renew and pay. The research studied members, who do not pay, and 26 of the 42 (61.9 per cent) were newly diagnosed, the easier half. And it treats month-three activity as the thing to fix, when a tenth of one contract's fee turns on it and a definitional change explains much of the fall.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Apeksha open-enrolment pack, which carries the service-level reporting, locks on Friday, 20 November, and Arkaan's signature window closes on Tuesday, 1 December. Apeksha is 64,000 insured members at ₹185 per member per month: ₹1.184 crore a month, ₹14.208 crore a year, of which a tenth — ₹11.84 lakh a month, ₹1.42 crore a year — is at risk against the 45 per cent service level.

The money is ₹3.6 crore. A and C together come to ₹5.30 crore and B and C to ₹4.50 crore, so no pair of the build options fits; C with D fits at ₹2.25 crore, B with D at ₹2.95 crore, A alone with ₹0.20 crore to spare. Capacity is not what binds: from 1 November to 31 March there are about 449 engineer-weeks (16 engineers until 15 December, 23 after), of which Granth reserves roughly 300 for run-rate, support and the migration, leaving about 150 discretionary — enough for any two of A, B and C that the budget would never allow. Cash was ₹46.2 crore on 30 September against net burn of ₹5.5 crore a month: 8.4 months, into the second week of June 2027. Counsel's memo of 9 October holds voice capture to be a new purpose, requiring fresh notice and consent in all eight supported languages.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 2 and 3 cluster overlapping material and rank the themes differently. Reading both as honest work, what accounts for the difference?
  2. Which columns of Exhibit 2 would you trust, and why, and what does Exhibit 4 do to that answer?
  3. Exhibit 5's strongest result is the one Exhibit 3 ranks fourth. Set out the sampling and base differences. Which number would you put on a slide, and which would you refuse to?
  4. Guhan's warning and Golap Konwar's remark describe one mechanism from two directions. Design a test, inside a quarter, that separates coach churn as a cause from coach churn as a symptom.
  5. Suppose the June cohort's 45.2 per cent under the old rule is the right number. Does Atulya owe Apeksha anything, does it owe the board a restatement, and who decides which definition it reports on?
  6. Monday morning: what does Ghazal put in front of the board, in what order, and with which exhibit on the screen? What does she say about the ₹3.6 crore, the 1 December window and the six weeks she is standing on — and what if Garvita asks whether she believes her own researcher?

It was past one. Ghazal had moved Exhibit 3 to the front of the deck, then moved it back. Somewhere in the 1,082 cards in Hyderabad, the 3,010 units in a vendor's spreadsheet and the queue in Manila there was one true account of why a man in Lucknow stops logging in his third month. She had three accounts, four options, a budget that fitted none of the combinations she wanted, and nine hours.
exp40v2-res.observation:
Observation and Contextual Inquiry

Discovery & Design › Qualitative Research. What would I learn by watching users that they would never tell me?

1. Two decisions waiting on something nobody had said

On Thursday 22 October 2026, Yashada Yeole will sit in a capital review at Yakeen Diagnostics Labs in Bengaluru and argue against her own operations counterpart's proposal. Yakeen runs home blood collection in the market Dr Lal PathLabs and Thyrocare opened up: 420 phlebotomists, eight completed visits each per working day, 25 working days a month, ₹640 a collection — 10,08,000 collections and ₹64.512 crore of annual revenue. On the table is a ₹2.4 crore route-optimisation engine, justified by the claim that phlebotomists lose the day to traffic, which every phlebotomist surveyed confirmed.

She did not disbelieve them; she noticed they had been asked a leading question. Between Monday 14 September and Friday 2 October 2026, Yagnesh Zilpe, a design researcher, and Zaina Yerunkar, who runs field operations, rode along on 34 collections with eleven phlebotomists in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Kochi. Zdenka Zelenkova, who runs Yakeen's analytics from Brno, had the dispatcher logs ready.

Zubeda Yalgi faced the mirror image. Zehen Shopfloor Systems sells a manufacturing execution system to auto-component plants supplying Tata Motors and Bajaj Auto: 38 plants live at an average licence of ₹46 lakh a year, or ₹17.48 crore of recurring revenue. Yatindra Zope, her engineering lead, had proposed a ₹1.9 crore classifier to predict a stoppage's cause from sensor data, trained on 4.38 lakh stoppages already labelled in Zehen's database. Her doubt was narrow: she did not know how those labels got there. Between 21 and 30 September 2026 she and Zakir Yelgaonkar stood through six shifts at Yojak Axle Industries in Chakan, Zor Gears Forge in Aurangabad and a third plant.

Both decisions turn on one question: what does watching work tell you that asking about it cannot?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Observation is the recording of behaviour as it occurs, where it occurs, without steering it. Contextual inquiry is a structured use of it: the researcher watches a real task in the user's own setting and interrupts to ask what the person was just doing — past tense, concrete act. It exists because routine competence becomes automatic, invisible to its owner: a phlebotomist who hand-writes a label forty times a week does not call that a workaround.

The lineage has two incompatible roots. The industrial one runs from Taylor and the Gilbreths, who watched work in order to standardise it, through the Hawthorne studies of 1924–32 to the method's founding embarrassment: being watched changes what you do. The anthropological one runs from Malinowski to Garfinkel's ethnomethodology, which treated the orderliness of ordinary action as the thing to explain. They met product work in Lucy Suchman's Plans and Situated Actions (Xerox PARC, 1987): users of a copier's help system were not executing the designers' plan, because plans are resources people improvise against. Holtzblatt and Beyer made that a method in Contextual Design, on a master–apprentice stance and four principles: context, partnership, interpretation, focus.

SchoolWill signWill not sign
Contextual design (Holtzblatt, Beyer)The worker cannot narrate the work; it is co-interpreted in placeThat a remote interview yields the same data
Ethnomethodology (Suchman, Garfinkel)The plan is not the work; improvisation is the unitThat field data becomes a ranked backlog
Outcome-driven innovation (Ulwick)Outcomes are stable, articulable, sizeable on a sampleThat you must be present to know what matters
Behavioural telemetryThirty-four visits cannot establish magnitudeThat a field study should gate a roadmap
Naturalistic decision making (Klein)Expertise is cue recognition, recovered by probing one past incidentThat it must be witnessed live

Exhibit 1. Section 10 returns to the two that decide where money goes.

Interviews tell you what people believe about their work. Observation tells you what the work is. Telemetry tells you how much of it there is.

3. Mechanics, worked through

What separates expert practice from a ride-along is instrumentation and sampling discipline. Yagnesh carried a stopwatch, a grid with one row per step, and the printed SOP. The stopwatch is the cheapest instrument in research and the most often left behind, because timing feels like appraisal. Yakeen's SOP describes a collection in five steps totalling 17.0 minutes. The observed median across 34 visits was 38.0 minutes in nine steps, four unnamed by the SOP.

Step, in observed sequenceIn SOP?SOP minObserved min

Exhibit 2. The SOP column sums its five named steps only.

Exhibit 3. The maroon blocks are work the organisation had no vocabulary for.

Two readings follow, differing in kind. The five named steps alone took 22.2 minutes against 17.0 documented, an overrun of 5.2 minutes or 30.6 per cent: an estimation error, the sort a planner finds. The four unnamed steps took 15.8 of the 38.0 observed minutes, or 41.6 per cent — a representation error no planning against the SOP can find, because the SOP is what is wrong. Traffic lies outside these 38 minutes.

The formal treatment: when have you seen enough?

The one quantitative question here is saturation. Yagnesh defined a breakdown as a point where the work and the system's model of it diverge, counting instances and types separately.

BlockVisitsNew distinct typesBreakdown instancesInstances per visit
Visits 1–668111.83

Exhibit 4. 61 instances in 19 types. The pooled rate is 61 divided by 34, or 1.79, not the 1.81 mean of the block rates.

Exhibit 5. The curve flattens after visit 30; the singleton count is the stronger test.

Flattening is the usual stopping rule and too generous: a curve flattens when the researcher stops noticing as readily as when the population runs out. The sharper test comes from species estimation. Seven of the 19 types appeared exactly once, and those seven singletons are 7 out of 61 instances, or 11.5 per cent — the Good–Turing estimate of the share of future breakdowns belonging to a type not yet seen. Coverage is therefore about 88.5 per cent: Yakeen misses roughly one event in nine. It equally argues against over-reading the tail, since singletons should not drive a ₹1.75 crore decision.

4. When the method applies, as testable claims

ClaimYakeenZehen
The behaviour recurs inside the windowHolds: eight collections a dayHolds: 73 stoppages in six shifts
The gap is between what people say and doHolds: everyone blamed trafficHolds: the database claims the cause
The setting can lawfully be enteredMarginal: a home, consent per visitHolds, with safety induction
Being wrong costs tenfold the visits₹2.4 crore against ₹6.4 lakh₹1.9 crore against ₹3.1 lakh

Exhibit 6. Failing the third is a hard stop; failing the first points to a diary study.

Observation is actively misleading in three common situations: when the behaviour answers a constraint about to vanish, so you optimise a workaround the next release removes; when the value is not in watchable work, because a category whose economics turn on rare events — a claim, a line changeover — will not perform them on a Tuesday; and wherever present behaviour anchors the team to the present workflow, since watching a dispatcher work a whiteboard yields a better whiteboard.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies do

Zubeda's six shifts are the cleanest illustration of the AI-native edge case, because they tested a premise nobody had stated: that the labels describe reality. Her team timed 73 stoppages, recorded what caused each, and compared that against the code the operator had chosen — in all three plants at shift end, from memory.

Observed cause → code loggedTool changeMachine faultNo materialOtherNot loggedRow total
Tool change (planned)14001217

Exhibit 7. Observed cause against logged code. Rows and columns both total 73.

Read down the diagonal and 31 events carry the right code: against all 73 that is 42.5 per cent, and against the 50 logged at all it is 31 of 50, or 62.0 per cent. The structural finding is worse. Zehen's list has no code for an absent operator and none for a quality hold, so 19 of 73 events, 26.0 per cent, have no correct answer available, and at most 54 of the 73, 74.0 per cent, could ever be labelled right. Those two causes are 273 of the 1,284 observed stoppage minutes, 21.3 per cent; the 23 unlogged events carry 258 of those 1,284 minutes, 20.1 per cent.
