Exhibit 8. The total row's 17.6 is 1,284 divided by 73, not the mean of the row averages. Against 11,520 machine-minutes — four machines, six eight-hour shifts — 1,284 lost minutes are 11.1 per cent.

The other edge cases rhyme. In a two-sided business the friction sits in the seam and neither side can describe it, so teams that watch only their accessible side reach confident wrong answers. In regulated settings observation is constrained rather than forbidden: Yakeen's observers took consent at each door and recorded no audio, while Zehen's needed a safety induction and the works committee's agreement. In hardware-plus-software products the environment is part of the product, so what must be observed is water quality, dust or a missing plug point. In multi-product companies the finding belongs to a team that did not pay for it.

Mature companies say they run a research function with trained ethnographers. What they often do takes one of three degraded forms: the sales ride-along, where the account manager grants access and the sites are the happiest customers; the research deck, rigorous and unread; and the annual immersion, where executives spend a morning in a shop and return with an anecdote that outranks the data for a year. Organisations that get value differ in one unglamorous way: the engineer who will write the code is present. Yatindra stood through two shifts himself, which is why the proposal died quietly.

6. Eight distinctions that mark an expert

The absence is the finding

Competent practitioners record what happened; experts also record what they expected and did not see. None of the 34 Yakeen visits touched the suggested route; none of the 73 Zehen stoppages drew a glance at the wall dashboard. The tell-tale sign is notes with a section for absences, because the obvious reading inverts the truth: a praised feature nobody opens is the surest sign the stated problem is the wrong one.

Watch the artefact, not the screen

Paper survives where software has not earned trust, so the expert photographs the receipt book, the sticky note on the bezel, the laminated code card, the WhatsApp group carrying the handover. The tell-tale sign is a parallel record: where a second book is kept, your product is not the book of record. Such users are not old-fashioned; the paper does a job, usually recoverability, that software does not.

A workaround is a vote on trust, not a feature request

Stepping outside the system to finish or verify work says the system cannot be relied on there. The tell-tale sign is duplication rather than substitution: the step happens inside your product and outside. The obvious response is to build the outside step inside, when often the right move is to make the existing path trustworthy: a duplicate is dropped only when one step survives challenge.

Credit the messy finding, discount the tidy one

The observer effect runs one way: people tidy up when watched, so evidence deserves asymmetric weight. The tell-tale sign is a first hour unlike the fourth. A clean process teaches little, being performance for a guest; a shortcut teaches much, since it was taken despite your presence. Treating both as equally good data understates the shortcut.

Saturation is about kinds; magnitude needs another method

Thirty-four visits establish that a breakdown type exists and roughly what triggers it, not how many of Yakeen's 10,08,000 annual collections contain it. The tell-tale sign is a field percentage with no denominator. A careful 34 does not generalise, for a nameable reason: field access is never random, because it is granted. Observe, instrument, size — which is why Zdenka had the logs ready first.

Who opened the door determines what you see

Access is a sampling instrument, and sales usually holds it. Zakir offered Zubeda the five best reference plants; she took two and insisted on one renewal-risk account. The tell-tale sign is a site list correlated with account health. Any customer will not do: the mechanism you want is made by strain, and happy accounts have absorbed theirs through unpaid effort.

Your own data is a behaviour, not a fact

Every field in your database was filled by a person under conditions you can watch. Zehen's reason codes were one operator's end-of-shift reconstruction, and no model trained on them can exceed them. The tell-tale sign is a label entered late by someone who did not witness the event. Scale does not fix bias: habits are systematic, so more data makes a model confidently wrong.

Leave with a sequence, not a list

The mechanism lives in order and interruption. Yakeen's 5.1 minutes of waiting matter because of where they fall: before verification, after travel, with the next appointment slipping. The tell-tale sign of expert output is a timeline, not a list of pain points. A prioritised list looks more actionable, but sends each item to a different team in a different quarter, which is how a sequence problem becomes tickets.

7. Differences by product type and company stage

ContextWhat is actually different
ConsumerPrivate, brief, interleaved with other apps. Shifts towards diary studies; the unit is the moment.
B2B and enterpriseBuyer is not user, so two programmes. Work is continuous and watchable: easiest case, hardest access politics.
Platform and marketplaceObserve both sides, then the handoff. The seam makes the friction; neither side can narrate it.
Hardware and physical goodsThe environment is a variable: water, dust, power, bench height.
AI productsTwo new objects: how labels are produced, and what a user does with a half-trusted output — a check the product never sees.

Exhibit 9. Real differences only: sampling and timing discipline do not change here, but access and the window do.

By stage the difference is failure mode, not method. In a company of fifteen the founder observes constantly and writes nothing down, so the same discovery is made three times and credited to intuition. In a company of fifteen hundred the fieldwork is better and travels worse: studies reach a roadmap three quarters after a sales anecdote decided it. The remedy in both is organisational: put the builder in the room.

8. Three worked examples

Yakeen: what the 38 minutes were worth

ChangeStep attackedMin saved per visit₹ lakh
Narrowed slots, automated confirmationWaiting at the door3.538
Patient-kitted, pre-printed labelsHand-written labels, prescription reconciliation5.4115
In-app receipt with a UPI deep linkDoor-step payment2.422
Total11.3175

Exhibit 10. Each saving reduces an observed median; none eliminates a step.

At a median of 38.0 minutes in the home and 22.0 minutes of travel between homes, the cycle is 60.0 minutes, and a 480-minute shift yields exactly the eight visits operations reports. Remove 11.3 minutes and the cycle falls to 48.7 minutes, or 9.86 visits a shift — a capacity rise of 23.2 per cent for ₹1.75 crore. The route engine attacks only the 22.0-minute travel leg; a creditable 15 per cent cut there gives a 56.7-minute cycle and 8.47 visits, a rise of 5.8 per cent for ₹2.4 crore. Capacity is not demand, so Yashada models one extra visit per phlebotomist-day — 1,26,000 collections, ₹8.064 crore of annual capacity — only where booking is supply-bound.

Yugma Water Works: when the user is not the variable

Yugma Water Works of Chennai rents purifiers to 28,000 households at ₹399 a month, or ₹13.4064 crore a year, and had 3,100 cancellations in twelve months citing taste. Its filter-life model assumed municipal supply at 340 ppm of total dissolved solids and a cartridge change at 180 days. Zeenat Yadkikar's team visited fifteen homes and measured the tap: eleven days in thirty, these households were on tanker water at about 760 ppm. The load-weighted average is (11 × 760 + 19 × 340) ÷ 30 = 14,820 ÷ 30 = 494 ppm, 45.3 per cent above the modelled figure, so the cartridge is exhausted at 340 ÷ 494 of that interval — 124 days. The reminder arrived 56 days late, matching complaints peaking around day 130. No interview would produce this: no customer knows their TDS. The fix was firmware plus one onboarding question: ₹22 lakh against the ₹1.48 crore those cancellations represented.

Zaamin Freight Exchange: the expensive failure

Zaamin Freight Exchange in Indore matches shippers with fleet owners. In nine working days between 13 and 23 January 2025, Yatish Zinjurde observed four commission agents' desks in transport nagar and judged the constraint to be call volume. Zaamin built auto-dial and bid-matching for ₹2.1 crore, shipping on 23 July 2025, six months after the last visit. In the four weeks to 20 August 2025, listed loads rose 34.0 per cent, from 2,450 to 3,283 a week; matched trips rose 6.0 per cent, from 1,078 to 1,143, so fill rate — matched divided by listed — fell from 44.0 per cent to 34.8 per cent. The study was rigorous and one-sided: Yatish never watched a shipper's dispatch dock. Eleven dock visits between 8 September and 10 October 2025 found the mechanism: a load could not be committed until a quality hold was released, so loads carried a two-hour window no fleet owner could serve. A tentative-load state with a 90-minute confirmation window cost ₹34 lakh, shipped on 17 November 2025, and in the four weeks to 15 December 2025 produced 1,441 matched trips on 3,120 listed — a fill rate of 46.2 per cent and 33.7 per cent more matched trips than before. The recovery cost 16 per cent of the failure.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Interviewing while pretending to observeNotes full of "she said she would"How many lines record a timed act?A roadmap built on stated preference
Access-driven samplingSite list matches the reference accountsWho nominated each site?Strain invisible; churn blamed on price
One-sided study of a two-sided systemAll sites on one sideWhich side's constraint binds?Zaamin's ₹2.1 crore
Field counts used as population ratesA percentage with no denominatorWhat population is that denominator?Mis-sized investment, found late
Fix-as-you-seeA prototype after visit threeWhat would visit twenty have to show?Tail breakdowns built as core features

Exhibit 11. Each is cheap to catch in week one, expensive after a build.

None of the six is subtle once named, and all six survive for one reason: nobody asks the third column's question while the study can still be redirected. Ask it after visit two, when the sample can change and no code is written. The last column is the price of asking late.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is observation against instrumentation. The telemetry position, at its strongest, holds that products now emit so much behavioural data that field visits are a romantic indulgence: Yakeen's logs cover 10,08,000 collections, the visits 34. It rests on evidence: the history of analytics is full of field findings that proved rare. It is wrong when what matters is systematically unlogged, as Exhibit 7 shows: 23 stoppages generated no record, and the two costliest causes had no field to appear in. Instrumentation ranks only what it can represent, and representation is fixed before the data exists.

The second is contextual inquiry against outcome elicitation. The outcome-driven position holds that what a customer is trying to accomplish is stable, articulable and quantifiable: ask about outcomes, size them on 400 respondents, and you get the magnitude 34 visits cannot. Its evidence is a record of expensive ethnography that produced vivid stories and no prioritisation, and Yakeen's phlebotomists would have rated "arrive at a patient who is ready" high-importance and low-satisfaction without leaving the office. It is wrong wherever the respondent cannot name the step: nobody lists "the barcode roll is missing" as a desired outcome, since it is an artefact of a supply chain nobody designed. Both are one point from opposite ends: observation finds what you did not know to ask, and cannot size it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the method returns with insights. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They fix the stopping rule and sampling frame before the first visit, and can say what would make them stop early. They write down what they expect, so absence becomes evidence rather than silence. They time things, and carry the sequence — not a list — into the room where money is allocated. And they treat their own company's data as a behaviour, the highest-leverage habit in an era of models trained on operational labels.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Yashada will take Exhibits 2, 3 and 10 to the 22 October review and ask for ₹1.75 crore instead of ₹2.4 crore, on condition that Zdenka first verifies two things across the base: the share of collections closed more than fifteen minutes after the draw, and the share with cash or UPI taken at the door, which was 18 of the 34 observed visits, or 52.9 per cent. Zubeda has withdrawn the classifier and funded a ₹52 lakh change over ten weeks: capture at the moment of stoppage on the machine's panel, three taps, plus two new reason codes for operator availability and quality hold — the 19 events, 26.0 per cent of the 73, her list could not express. Her argument was not that the model was bad but that its supervision was.

  1. Yakeen's fieldwork cost ₹6.4 lakh and reframed a ₹2.4 crore decision. What is the rule for how much observation to buy before a capital decision?
  2. Good–Turing put coverage at 88.5 per cent, with seven singleton types as the unseen tail. Should any of the seven influence the roadmap?
  3. Zubeda's finding condemns Zehen's own data. What should she tell 38 customers whose downtime reports under-count by a fifth, and in what order?

13. Going deeper

  • Interview fundamentals — the past-tense probe that makes behaviour explicable.
  • Diary studies and longitudinal research — for what one visit cannot hold.
  • Field research for physical and hardware products — the environment as the variable.
  • Lightweight ethnography — most of this value in two days, when no study is funded.
  • Qualitative vs quantitative research — why reversing observe, instrument, size wastes both.
  • Designing an interview guide — the field grid behind Exhibit 2 is its analogue.
  • Recruiting research participants — how to take the sampling instrument from sales.
  • How many interviews — the singleton arithmetic of Exhibits 4 and 5.
  • Cognitive biases in research — the observer effect; confirmation in notes.
  • Synthesising research — how 61 instances become 19 types, sequence intact.
case20v1-res.observation:
Lifafa Works: Watching the Counter

A teaching case on observation and contextual inquiry

1. Opening

On Monday 26 October 2026, Rajni Abhyankar, head of product at Lifafa Works, sat in the company's Pune office with a roadmap spreadsheet open and a deadline on the calendar. The engineering plan for January to March 2027 had to be frozen by Friday 13 November. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and the office would be thin for days afterwards.

One item stood at the top of the draft plan: bulk GST invoice import, a feature that let a shop owner upload a supplier's invoices in one step. Nine of the fourteen store owners interviewed in September had asked for it. Yet something Rajni had seen behind a counter in Nashik would not leave her alone. She had to decide whether to commit the quarter to what customers said they wanted, or spend the days before the freeze finding out what they did.

2. Company background

Lifafa Works sells a billing and credit-ledger app to neighbourhood retailers: kirana stores, small chemists and general stores in Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities. Founded in Pune in 2019, the company charges ₹200 a month, or ₹2,400 a year, per store. About 38,000 stores bill on it each month.

The category is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the idea of the digital credit notebook. Vyapar and Zoho Books serve owners who want proper accounting. PhonePe and Paytm put a QR code and a soundbox on nearly every counter, and ONDC-linked apps court the same shopkeepers with commerce rather than billing. Lifafa's pitch was narrower: a single screen that bills a customer in under ten seconds on a modest Android phone.

Growth had come from field sales in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Acquisition was working; staying was the difficulty.

3. The situation

Radhika Amte, the company's data scientist in Montreal, pulled the retention numbers on 15 October. Of 6,000 stores onboarded between April and June 2026, 4,500 sent at least one bill in their first week, but only 2,160 were still billing at day 90 (Exhibit 1). The 2,340 stores that started and then stopped represented about ₹56 lakh a year in list-price subscriptions.

Source: Lifafa product database, pulled 15 October 2026. Annual value of the 2,340 stores that stopped = 2,340 × ₹2,400 = ₹56.16 lakh. Of the 4,500 stores that started, 48% were still billing at day 90.

To find out why, Rajni's team had phoned fourteen owners between 7 and 18 September. Their top requests are tallied in the first table of Exhibit 2. Rutvik Alurkar, the engineering lead in Bengaluru, read the tally as settled: build the bulk GST import. His estimate was twelve weeks of work and ₹42 lakh fully loaded.

Then, in the week of 19 October, Rishika Adkar, the designer who normally works from Lisbon, was in Pune for three weeks. Rajni took her on five unscripted shop visits in Nashik, Indore, Coimbatore, Pune and Nagpur, each lasting about two hours at the counter. They asked few questions; they watched, and photographed the screen and the notebooks beside it.

What they saw is in Exhibit 2. Every one of the five shops kept a paper notebook of udhaar, goods sold on credit, next to the phone. Four of the five owners re-entered the day's bills into Lifafa after closing, because the app's credit ledger demanded the customer's mobile number and regular customers would not hand it over mid-rush. Nobody had mentioned this on the phone; it did not feel like a complaint. As Raghubir Ambre, who runs the Nashik store, put it: "That is just how the evening goes." Only one of the five shops, in Indore, issued GST tax invoices at all. The other four were composition-scheme dealers who issue a bill of supply.

4. The people

Rutvik Alurkar, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He wants a plan he can staff. His team has carried the bulk-import design since July, and he fears a research detour will cost the quarter.

Rishika Adkar, designer, Lisbon. She believes the credit notebook is the product's real competitor and wants a larger, planned programme of visits. She flies home on Saturday 7 November.

Rukmani Ajgaonkar, customer-success lead, Manila. Her team works a late shift to cover Indian business hours. She hears the churn first, in support tickets, where "how do I add credit without a number" recurs.

Radhika Amte, data scientist, Montreal. She can tell Rajni how many stores stop billing but not why, and she is wary of reading five visits as proof of anything.

5. Timeline

Figure 1. Key dates. Positions are schematic and not drawn to scale.

6. The options

Rajni saw three courses of action, compared in Exhibit 3.

Option A: build bulk GST import as planned. The request has the most backing in the interviews, Rutvik's team is ready, and the work is well defined. But it addresses a need seen in one of five shops and does nothing about the evening re-entry.

Option B: run a short, structured round of shop visits before the freeze. Rajni, Rishika and Rukmani's field agents would visit twelve shops between Monday 2 and Saturday 7 November, in the run-up to Dhanteras on Friday 6 November, when counters are at their busiest. Each visit would follow a common protocol: watch the whole billing cycle, photograph the workarounds and ask owners to explain what they did. Twelve visits at ₹30,000 each come to ₹3.6 lakh. The cost is a week of the team's attention.

Option C: instrument the app more heavily and wait. Radhika would add event tracking on the credit screens and test variants. It costs ₹6 lakh and six weeks, which would carry the answer to the first week of December, after the freeze. It would count taps but not explain why a shopkeeper picked up a pen.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared

Costs are fully loaded estimates by Lifafa finance, October 2026. Option B is ₹30,000 per visit × 12 visits.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why did fourteen interviews and five visits point in different directions? What can a person say about their work, and what can they only show?
  2. Read Exhibit 1 alongside Exhibit 2. Which story about the 2,340 stores that stopped is each source able to support, and which can it not?
  3. Five visits were chosen for convenience. How much weight should Rajni put on them, and what would twelve more visits need to show to change her mind?
  4. Using Exhibit 3, which option should Rajni choose, and what would she tell Rutvik, whose team has waited since July?

8. A note for the learner

Interviews record what people believe and are willing to say. Observation records what they do, including the habits so familiar that they no longer register as problems. The question this topic asks is: what would I learn by watching users that they would never tell me? Here the answer sat beside every phone: a paper notebook, and an evening ritual owners treated as the cost of business.

A well-reasoned answer separates three things. First, the weight of evidence: nine of fourteen owners asked for bulk GST import, but the visits suggest the request came from the buyer and not the daily user, and describes a task only one of five shops actually performs. Second, the cost of being wrong: Option A commits ₹42 lakh of a quarter to a guess, while Option B costs under a tenth of that. Third, the limits of the evidence: five convenience visits show a pattern exists, not how common it is.

One defensible path is Option B, scoped tightly. Rajni should run the twelve visits in the festival week, with a written protocol that includes a deliberate search for shops that do not keep a notebook, so she can find out whether the pattern is general. Radhika should add a single cheap measure alongside: the share of stores that open the credit screen and then abandon it. On Monday 9 November the team would reconvene and decide whether the freeze carries a credit-entry fix, bulk import, or both. If the twelve visits show no notebook pattern, Option A goes ahead on 13 November with a week lost and ₹3.6 lakh spent. If they confirm it, Lifafa avoids shipping a quarter's work to a minority of shops while 39% of its newest cohort quietly goes back to paper.
case40v1-res.observation:
Mojni Works: The Button Nobody Chose

A case on what a factory tells you, and what it only shows you

1. The night before

At twenty to midnight on Wednesday 18 November 2026, in a flat in Baner, Pune, Shivani Bhondve had two documents open on one screen: a forty-one page agreement from Mabrook Metals Group, a pipe and fittings maker with two plants outside Riyadh and one each in Jubail and Muscat, and a memo from her data lead in Krakow, subject line "before you sign: which baseline".

The agreement paid Mojni Works, which Shivani had co-founded in 2017, a small fee for every machine it monitored and a large fee for every percentage point by which the monitored plants' availability improved, availability computed by Mojni's software from stop reasons entered by Mabrook's operators on its tablets. Mabrook's board met on Tuesday 24 November and wanted signature by Friday 20 November; Shivani's board met at half past nine the next morning.

Three weeks earlier her implementation lead had sent a photograph from Chakan: a slate propped against a press, six stop times chalked on it in a fitter's hand, the Mojni tablet on its post fourteen metres behind. Shivani could not decide whether it was an anecdote or the whole story.

2. How Mojni got here

Mojni Works sells downtime measurement to small and mid-sized Indian engineering plants. A clamp on the machine's supply cable detects a stop; a tablet at the head of the line asks the operator why; a dashboard turns that into availability and loss hours. It installs in a day and costs ₹3.2 lakh per line per year plus ₹1.4 lakh of hardware. In October 2026 it ran on 420 lines in 54 plants: ₹1,344 lakh, or ₹13.44 crore, of recurring revenue.

One decision from 2024 shapes what is possible tonight. On Friday 9 August, to win Mavla Forge Industries and its eleven lines at Chakan, Mojni adopted the twelve-code taxonomy Mavla's works manager, Satish Bongirwar, had written for his own whiteboard. Eight codes went onto the tablet's buttons; the other four sit behind a sub-menu needing two taps and a three-second hold. Code 7, "Material awaited", became the leftmost and largest button, because material shortage was what Satish wanted counted. Figure 2 shows that panel, and the bay it stands in.

The contract defined availability as scheduled run hours less unplanned stop hours over scheduled run hours, stops coded 7, 8, 11 and 12 treated as planned and excluded; that definition went into the firmware, the billing engine and the licence. Mavla prepaid three years, eleven lines at ₹2.8 lakh a year, ₹92.4 lakh, and its counsel made any change to the taxonomy or the definition a material change, with termination rights. Soumitra Bhisey promised Satish no new hardware for five years.

3. The industry around it

Mojni's customers are Udyam-registered component makers who supply Tata Motors, Bajaj Auto and Mahindra. The large plants in that chain buy platforms from Siemens, Bosch and Rockwell, integrated by L&T Technology Services or Tata Elxsi, at prices Mojni's customers cannot consider; Zoho and Tally own the back office, Jio and Airtel sell the SIM. Mojni's wedge is the gap below them: measurement cheap enough that a promoter signs for it himself.

Two forces press on that wedge. Outcome pricing has become fashionable: Mabrook's procurement team, on a localisation agenda that rewards measurable productivity, asked for it unprompted, and two Indian groups have since asked the same. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has made customers' counsel careful about anything identifying a worker, which an operator login and a camera both do. Mojni has never put a camera on a floor.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The relationship began as a pilot: thirty lines at Riyadh, the eighty-nine days from Monday 16 March to Friday 12 June 2026. Shaurya Biradar, who runs international sales from Muscat, reported on Friday 10 July a gain of 6.1 points and recommended outcome pricing. Nobody in Pune had been on the Riyadh floor. The reference account at home was performing: in Exhibit 1, Mavla's eleven Chakan lines move from 71.2 per cent in the quarter Mabrook's draft proposes as a baseline to 82.3 per cent in the quarter ended 30 June 2026, a gain of 11.1 points weighted by scheduled hours. Shaurya put that deck in front of Mabrook.

Then two things came apart. On Monday 21 September, Shamika Bhamare drove to Moraya Precision Castings in Solapur to replace a clamp and stayed eleven hours, watching one moulding line and counting stops herself. The tablet stood twenty-one metres from the far machine, and the night shift's reasons had all been entered between 5:40 and 5:55 that morning by one man reading a chalk slate. Between 28 September and 23 October she and Sofie Bakker, the design lead, observed nine shifts across three plants: Exhibit 4 is their tally. On 12 November Szymon Bielak reconciled sensor events against logged reasons for the week of 5 to 10 October on three Mavla lines, then asked what the baseline window was worth: Exhibit 2 is the reconciliation, Exhibit 3 the window.

Four beliefs have not survived. That a logged reason means a known stop: Exhibit 2 shows 275 of the 371 detected stops carried any reason, 74.1 per cent, and 172 of those were coded 7. That the sensor sees the floor: Exhibit 4 records 320 stops witnessed in 75.0 hours at the machine, 4.3 an hour, against the clamp's 0.86, because it ignores anything under two minutes, where the jams live. That the taxonomy was the operators' language: nine of Exhibit 5's 143 respondents recall being asked what the buttons should say. And that a new machine lifts the number: Line 7 took a new press in February 2026 and is the one line in Exhibit 1 whose availability fell. Figure 1 sets out the sequence.

5. The people

Shivani Bhondve, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, sold the first fifty lines herself. Her position: Mojni cannot be paid on a number it cannot defend. Her incentive: she has told Moksha Growth Partners that international revenue opens the next round. Unsaid: she thinks the Chakan gain real and its measurement not.

Soumitra Bhisey, co-founder and chief technology officer, Pune, owns the firmware, the taxonomy and the no-new-hardware promise. The fix is a sensor change, he says, not research: a vibration channel would catch stops under two minutes. Unsaid: it invalidates every baseline Mojni has quoted, Mavla's included.

Shaurya Biradar, head of international sales, Muscat, has carried Mabrook for fourteen months and is paid on contracted value, not recognised revenue. The Gulf buys outcomes, he says, and India follows. Unsaid: he has never spent a shift on the Riyadh floor, and the pilot's reasons were entered by supervisors.

Shamika Bhamare, implementation lead, Chakan, has installed clamps in forty-odd plants and is the one person at Mojni whom operators telephone. She wants five weeks and nine plants to learn what the buttons should have been. Unsaid: the Solapur shift was her own initiative and cannot be repeated alone.

Sofie Bakker, design lead, Amsterdam. Two weeks in Maharashtra changed her view: Mojni shipped a vocabulary, and it belongs to a works manager. Unsaid: she argued for operator research in 2024, lost, and kept the email.

Szymon Bielak, data lead, Krakow, has two findings and no conclusion: the logging is thin, and the Riyadh gain cannot be separated from the maintenance contract Mabrook signed in January 2026. Unsaid: he built the availability formula he is now criticising.

Son Bui, customer-success lead, Ho Chi Minh City, covers Indian hours. For two quarters his commonest ticket has been a request to rename the buttons; they close as working as designed, and his team is measured on closure time.

Seema Biswas, partner at Moksha Growth Partners and board member, holds that the Series B needs ₹20 crore of recurring revenue at 31 March 2027, and outcome fees are not recurring. Unsaid: her fund's own vehicle is raising, and she would take a clean metric over a large one.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Eleven points at Chakan, and every line improved. Mabrook has seen the deck. If we start explaining our own numbers now, we will be explaining them to Siemens' sales team next week."

Shaurya Biradar, email to Shivani, 16 November 2026

"My people log everything. The report is the report. If you want to change the buttons, that is a new contract, and honestly, the old ones are what my seniors understand."

Satish Bongirwar, works manager, Mavla, 23 October

"Madam, the post is near the gate. If the strip jams I clear it in forty seconds; by the time I walk there and back the machine has run three strokes. So I write the time on the slate and Sakharam enters it in the morning, as we have since the Diwali before last."

Soham Bhoir, press operator, Mavla Chakan, to Shamika Bhamare, 13 October

"Material awaited is the big button. When the supervisor asks why the line is down, that answer does not come back to me."

Sakharam Bhutada, fitter, Mavla Chakan, same visit

"The logging is thin. I cannot tell you the gain is false, nor that it is ours: Mabrook signed a maintenance contract with its press maker in January. Choose a baseline window and I will give you any improvement between five and eleven points, honestly computed."

Szymon Bielak, memo of 12 November

"I will count ₹54 lakh from this contract at 31 March, because that is what will be live and invoiced. Shaurya is counting ₹7.92 crore. One of those numbers goes in a data room."

Seema Biswas, board call, Friday 13 November

8. The options as Shivani sees them

A. Sign the draft as it stands. Take Mabrook's baseline window, keep the taxonomy, bank ₹216 lakh of base fee and up to ₹576 lakh of outcome fee, and fix the data later. Exhibit 6 gives the exposure: ₹360 lakh of delivery cost against revenue that could be ₹120 lakh if the measured number moves the wrong way. Shaurya argues that a number which has risen for two years will keep rising.

B. Sign, but change the measurement. Insist on a sensor-only definition, with a vibration channel for short stops and no reason codes in the formula. Soumitra puts the firmware and billing work at fourteen weeks and ₹190 lakh, plus ₹105 lakh to re-baseline 420 lines at ₹0.25 lakh each: ₹295 lakh in all. It cannot be done by Friday, and it changes the availability definition in Mavla's licence, which Mavla's clause makes material.

C. Hold the deal and go and look. Five weeks of structured observation in nine plants, twenty-seven shifts at ₹1.2 lakh a shift, with ₹8 lakh of interpretation and ₹5 lakh of contingency: ₹45.4 lakh. Mabrook's board sits on 24 November, and its procurement team has a competing proposal.

The page troubles her. Each option asks which measurement Mojni should sell, and Exhibit 5 suggests the floor was never asked what it would want measured. Soumitra's cheapest answer, a camera inferring cause from a stopped machine, is not on the page: counsel's reading of the data protection Act and Satish's view of a camera arrive at the same place. And a fourth framing is not written down: Mojni's buyer is the promoter, its user is the operator, and no option changes which of the two the product serves.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Mabrook requires signature by Friday 20 November for its board on Tuesday 24 November, and the file closes either way. Mojni holds ₹11.4 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹1.35 crore a month, which is 8.4 months, to mid-July 2027. Moksha's term sheet is conditioned on ₹20 crore of recurring revenue at 31 March 2027. Today's ₹13.44 crore plus the domestic plan of ₹3.10 crore reaches ₹16.54 crore; Mabrook's base fee adds ₹0.54 crore if only Riyadh is live and invoiced by then, ₹2.16 crore if all four plants are, giving ₹17.08 crore or ₹18.70 crore. Neither reaches ₹20 crore, and the outcome fee is invoiced after 31 March 2028. Against that sit Mavla's prepaid ₹92.4 lakh and its material-change clause.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of Exhibits 2, 4 and 5 measure, and which could have been produced without standing on a factory floor?
  2. Exhibit 5 reports 131 of 143 operators saying they log every stop; Exhibit 2 finds a reason on 275 of 371 detected stops. Are these in conflict? What is the population in each?
  3. Code 7 was made the largest button in 2024 for a reason that made sense. Trace what that one decision now does to Exhibit 1, to Exhibit 6 and to Mojni's valuation.
  4. Szymon says he can produce any improvement between five and eleven points honestly. If so, what is Mojni selling to Mabrook, and what should the contract measure?
  5. Nine shifts overturned four beliefs. What would Shivani have to believe about observation for that to be luck rather than method, and how would she tell the difference?
  6. It is Monday 23 November and Shivani has either signed or not. Set out what she does that morning, what she says to Satish Bongirwar, and what she tells her board she knows now that she did not know in July.

At one in the morning she opened the photograph again: six times chalked on the slate, 2:10, 2:48, 3:05, 3:31, 4:02, 4:40, and a fitter's initials. In the event store, that night was 91 per cent available. She closed the laptop with the agreement unsigned and the memo unanswered.

Observation and Contextual Inquiry

Discovery and Design, Qualitative Research: what would I learn by watching users that they would never tell me?

1. Nineteen of twenty-two said the billing was fine

On Monday 5 October 2026, Tanishka Rawool, head of product at Tantu Billing Works in Pune, had one slot in the quarterly roadmap review and a decision she could not defer. Tantu sells a GST billing application to small shops, mostly garment retailers and general stores, at ₹7,200 per shop per year. It had 14,000 paying shops, which is ₹10.08 crore of annual recurring revenue. Annual churn, the share of shops that fail to renew, had risen from 16 per cent to 24 per cent.

Uday Kasbekar, the head of sales, had a diagnosis: shops left because they could not import their customer and item lists from Tally, the incumbent accounting package many of their accountants use. His proposal, a bulk-import module, would take five months and ₹1.2 crore. Tanishka had also asked a support analyst to phone 22 lapsed or wavering customers. Nineteen said the billing itself was "easy" and "fine". The interviews supported Uday's story by default, since nobody mentioned anything else.

She distrusted that silence. Ulrike Haas, a data analyst in Graz who supports Tantu's analytics, had noticed that invoices created inside the app per active shop were falling even in shops that said they loved it. So between 7 and 25 September, Umesh Lingayat, a product designer, had sat in eight shops for most of a working day each, in Surat, Pune and Hyderabad, watching real invoices being raised. This page follows what he saw, because it is the cleanest way to understand what observation can do that questioning cannot.

StakeFigureHow derived
Annual recurring revenue₹10.08 crore14,000 shops × ₹7,200
Extra churn1,120 shops(24% − 16%) × 14,000
Revenue at risk each year₹80.64 lakh1,120 × ₹7,200
Bulk-import proposal₹120 lakh₹1.2 crore, five months

Exhibit 1. The stakes. The import module costs more than a year of the extra churn it is meant to stop, so being wrong about its premise is expensive.

2. The idea

Observation means watching people do real work without steering them, and recording what happens. Contextual inquiry is a disciplined form of it: the researcher visits the person in their own setting, watches them do an actual task, and interrupts at moments of interest to ask what they were just doing and why. It was invented to solve a specific gap. People cannot report most of what they do, because routine behaviour becomes automatic and invisible to its owner; and they report what they believe a polite answer looks like. Anthropologists had long worked this way, and in the 1980s researchers such as Lucy Suchman at Xerox PARC showed that people use machines in ways their designers never planned. Karen Holtzblatt and Hugh Beyer then turned the practice into a repeatable method for product teams in the late 1980s and 1990s, described in their book Contextual Design.

Their central device is the master and apprentice relationship: the user is the master of their own work, and the researcher is an apprentice who learns by watching and asking. Four principles follow: stay in context, form a partnership with the user, interpret what you see together, and keep a focus so that you do not drown in detail. The sentence Tanishka could repeat in the meeting without sounding glib is this: interviews tell us what shopkeepers believe about their work; observation tells us what the work is.

MethodWhat it capturesWhere it misleads
InterviewBeliefs, memories, reasonsOmits the habitual and the embarrassing
SurveyFrequency of stated opinionsOnly answers the questions you thought to ask
ObservationActual sequences, interruptions, workaroundsSmall sample; the observer alters behaviour

Exhibit 2. Three methods answer different questions. Observation is not better, only complementary.

3. How it actually works

Exhibit 3. The loop. Steps 1 and 6 are where practitioners are least explicit.

Frame. Umesh began with a focus, not a hypothesis to prove: "how does an invoice actually get made and filed?" The implicit work is deciding what you will ignore. Recruit. He asked Ulrike for shops across the engagement range, from daily users to near-dormant ones, rather than letting Uday nominate friendly accounts. Sales had offered the six best-renewing shops; he declined, and took two of those among his eight.

Watch. He arrived before opening, sat beside the counter rather than across it, and asked the owner to work as normal. The first hour is mostly the shopkeeper performing for a guest, so useful data starts later. Probe. When he saw something odd he asked a past-tense question: "What did you just do there?" never "Why don't you like the app?" Record. He logged each invoice and each departure from the app's intended path, with the time, in a fixed grid, plus photographs of notebooks and sticky notes with permission. Interpret. That evening he reviewed the log, separating what he saw from what he inferred, and next morning showed the owner a one-line reading of the day to check it. Shopkeepers corrected him twice, which is the partnership principle working.

4. A worked example

Umesh defined a workaround as any step the shopkeeper took outside the app to complete or verify an invoice. Over 44 observed hours he counted invoices and workarounds per shop. The rate is workarounds divided by invoices.

Exhibit 4. Observation log. The final rate is 64 divided by 310, pooled across shops, not an average of the eight rates.

Exhibit 5. The four garment shops (A, C, E, G) sit at 21 to 37 per cent; the four general stores (B, D, F, H) at 11 to 15 per cent.

The workarounds fell into four kinds. Of the 64: 23 were looking up a tax classification code (the HSN code, which sets the GST rate) on a sticky note or a phone; 17 were writing the sale into a paper tally notebook; 14 were photographing a printed bill and sending it by WhatsApp to the accountant; 10 were recalculating a discount on a calculator. These sum to 64.

The notebook entries mattered most. The shopkeepers did not trust the app as their book of record, so they kept two. That explains falling in-app volumes among happy users and why none mentioned it: to them the notebook is simply how a shop works. Import from Tally appeared nowhere in the 44 hours.

Second pass: change one input. The sample is half garment, half general stores (170 invoices and 46 workarounds against 140 and 18). Garment is 27.1 per cent and general stores 12.9 per cent. Tantu's base is 35 per cent garment. Weighting each type by its share of the base gives 0.35 × (46/170) + 0.65 × (18/140), which is 17.8 per cent, not 20.6. The finding survives (roughly one invoice in six still involves a workaround), but the headline moved by nearly three points, because the sample composition was a choice, and the choice mattered.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Behaviour is not preference

Seeing a workaround tells you that something is costly or untrusted; it does not tell you that the user would value a replacement. Observation yields problems, not purchase intent.

The observer effect is real but manageable

People tidy up when watched, which is the Hawthorne effect. Long sessions, the first hour discarded, and an unobtrusive position reduce it. They never remove it, so findings of messy behaviour are more credible than findings of tidy behaviour.

Observation is not usability testing

A usability test hands a user a prepared task on your design. Contextual inquiry watches their real task on their real setup, including the parts your product never touches. The notebook was invisible to any test.

Observation is not shadowing for evaluation

The user must understand you are not judging their efficiency. Without that, they hide the very shortcuts you came to see.

Eight shops cannot give you a rate

The 20.6 per cent is a description of eight afternoons, not an estimate of the base. Observation finds the kinds of behaviour; counting how many people share them needs a survey or product data afterwards.

It cannot see the invisible

Thought, long-horizon behaviour, and rare events do not occur on demand. A shop's year-end tax filing happens once. Diary studies, the natural next method, cover what a single visit cannot.

Ask before relying on it

Who chose the sites? What did I ignore? Did anything I expected not happen? A good observer reports the absences, such as no Tally mentions, as carefully as the presences.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

SettingWhat you watchTypical difficulty
ConsumerUse in a kitchen, commute or sofa; other apps and people in the momentBehaviour is private and intermittent; sessions are short
B2BA role's full workday, including colleagues, paper, spreadsheetsThe buyer and the user differ, so watch both
MarketplaceBoth sides, separately, then the handoff between themTwo sets of visits; the seam is where friction hides

Exhibit 6. Differences by product type.

Tantu is a B2B product used by its own buyer, which is the easy case. In an early-stage company, observation is usually done by the founder or designer personally, informally, with five or six visits and no template; the risk is that the team never writes anything down. In a large company, observation is often outsourced to a research function, and the risk reverses: the findings are rigorous but never reach the engineers. The remedy in both is the same: take the engineer to the shop.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Leading while watchingNotes full of "user said she would…"Observation is a faster interviewCount lines of behaviour versus lines of opinion
Friendly sampleEvery site is a top accountAny customer will doCompare sites' engagement with the base
Fix-as-you-seePrototype built after visit twoInsight arrives per visitAsk what visit six would have to show to change your mind
Observations as statistics"20.6% of shops…" in a deckCounts from eight sites generaliseAsk what population the denominator represents

Exhibit 7. Four failures that look like rigour from a distance.

8. What good looks like

Done well, Tanishka's team would have watched before proposing, in a sample chosen by engagement and not by friendship. Each visit would end with a one-page log of behaviours, a photograph of every artefact, and a short list of things expected but not seen. Sales would have seen the notebook photographs before the roadmap review, and the proposal on the table would be sized against the observed workarounds and their frequency, not against the loudest hypothesis. Findings would then be handed to Ulrike to test against product data across the whole base.

9. Closing: what Tanishka decided

She did not fund the import module. Of the 64 workarounds, 37 (23 code lookups plus 14 WhatsApp photographs, 57.8 per cent) could be removed by two smaller changes: an HSN suggestion as the item name is typed, at ₹18 lakh, and a one-tap share of the invoice to the accountant, at ₹14 lakh. Together that is ₹32 lakh against ₹120 lakh. The tally-notebook habit needed a trust fix, a visible daily total and a printable day-book, which she scoped for a later review. She asked Ulrike to measure, across the base, how many shops use WhatsApp-share within a day of invoicing.

OptionCost (₹ lakh)Observed workarounds addressedShare of 64
Bulk import from Tally12000%
HSN suggestion182335.9%
One-tap invoice share141421.9%
Funded package (last two)323757.8%

Exhibit 8. The decision. Shares are each count divided by 64.

Learn next the diary study, in which participants log their own behaviour over weeks, because it covers what one visit cannot; then field research for physical products, where the environment is part of the product; then lightweight ethnography, for when you cannot afford a full study.

Two questions to sit with. If Uday had been right about Tally, what would Umesh have seen in the 44 hours, and how long would you have watched before concluding he was wrong? And which of the facts you rely on in your own product came from watching, and which from being told?
case20v1-res.solution.interview:
Swaadika Meals: Politeness or Purchase?

A teaching case on solution interviews and concept tests

1. Opening

On Monday 9 November 2026, with the Diwali holidays just over, Charita Hardikar sat in the glass meeting room at Swaadika Meals' head office in Baner, Pune, with two documents open. One was a board deck dated 6 November recommending that the company build a premium, dietician-guided lunch plan. The other was a spreadsheet of nine interviews she had finished on 30 October. The deck said customers loved the idea; the spreadsheet said something quieter.

Charita, the head of product, had until Friday 20 November to tell the steering committee what to do with an ₹86 lakh build request. Her chief executive wanted the product live for the January resolution season. She had to decide whether the evidence justified that spend, and if not, how to learn more cheaply.

2. Company background

Swaadika Meals was founded in 2019 by Chirantan Hajela and two classmates from Pune. It sells prepaid weekly lunch subscriptions to office workers, a home-style thali, cooked in two central kitchens and delivered to a pickup shelf in the employee's office building by 12:30. Today it has 6,200 active subscribers, 3,900 in Pune and 2,300 in Bengaluru. They eat an average of 21 meals a month at a realised price of ₹146, which makes monthly sales of about ₹1.90 crore.

The competition is crowded. Swiggy and Zomato will deliver almost anything to an office door within thirty minutes; Zepto Cafe and Box8 compete for the same lunch hour; and the corporate canteen, run by contractors, remains the default for the large IT campuses of Hinjewadi and Whitefield. Swaadika has survived by being predictable, cheap and trusted.

The new idea, called Swaadika Plan, would add a weekly menu tuned by a dietician to each subscriber's goal, such as lower blood sugar, weight loss or less oil. It would be priced at ₹189 a meal, a premium of ₹43, or about 29 per cent, over the ₹146 average.

3. The situation

The idea came from the growth team and went through two rounds of customer contact, shown on the timeline in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1. Timeline of the evidence and the decision. Dates only; the spacing is illustrative.

In August, head of sales Clement Harlalka and his team ran 22 demonstrations of the idea to existing subscribers and to HR managers. They showed the menu, described the dietician and asked whether people would use it. Nineteen said yes, and 17 signed a free interest form. The deck turned this into a forecast that 18 per cent of the 6,200 subscribers, or 1,116 people, would upgrade.

Charita was uneasy. The demonstrators were salespeople, the audience had been told the price was provisional, and a signature on a free form commits no one. In October she therefore ran nine solution interviews of a different kind. She opened by asking each person about the last time they tried to eat better at work and what it cost them, and only then showed a concept board designed by Catarina Henriques in Lisbon. At the end she asked for something real: a refundable ₹500 deposit, paid by UPI through Razorpay, to join a founding wait-list. Exhibit 2 sets the two rounds side by side.

Exhibit 2. What customers said and what they did
RoundConversationsLiked the ideaFree interest formPaid ₹500 deposit
August sales demos2219 (86%)17 (77%)not asked
October solution interviews97 (78%)not offered3 (33%)

Percentages are shares of the conversations in each round. The two rounds asked for different commitments, so the last two columns are not like-for-like. Of the nine October participants, six described the lunch problem unprompted before seeing the concept; all three who paid were among those six. Two of the nine reacted neutrally.

Liking was high in both rounds, at 86 per cent and 78 per cent. Payment was a third. The three payers were vivid, though. One had paid a private dietician ₹4,000 a month and still ate canteen food on four days out of five. The three who described the problem but did not pay all said ₹189 felt high before they had seen it work.

The global team read the evidence differently. Colette Hamel, the data scientist in Montreal, who is ten and a half hours behind Pune, warned that nine conversations cannot support a percentage and proposed a paid price test on the website. Cynthia Hinga, who leads customer success from Nairobi, noted that 63 of October's 1,480 support tickets, or 4.3 per cent, had asked for lower-oil or diabetic-friendly menus, but cautioned that a complaint is not a purchase.

4. The people

Chirantan Hajela, chief executive, Pune. He believes premium plans are the way to lift revenue per subscriber, and he wants a January launch to catch New Year resolutions.

Clement Harlalka, head of sales, Pune. Corporate HR teams have asked him for wellness benefits, and he argues that waiting loses the season.

Colette Hamel, data scientist, Montreal. She wants a measurable test of willingness to pay before any build, and distrusts the 18 per cent forecast.

Cynthia Hinga, customer success lead, Nairobi. She is 2.5 hours behind Pune and answers the tickets. She worries that a launch that disappoints diabetic customers will hurt the trust the core subscription depends on.

5. The economics

The deck's premium revenue rests on the upgrade rate, which is the shakiest number in it. Each upgrader pays ₹43 more on each of 21 meals, which is ₹903 a month. Exhibit 3 shows what the ₹86 lakh build would take to recover at three plausible rates. The recovery is measured against gross premium revenue, not profit, so true payback would be longer.

Exhibit 3. Premium revenue and recovery of the ₹86 lakh build
Upgrade rate (of 6,200)UpgradersPremium revenue, ₹ lakh a monthMonths to recover ₹86 lakh
18% (board deck)1,11610.088.5
9%5585.0417.1
5%3102.8030.7

Premium revenue is upgraders times ₹903 (₹43 premium times 21 meals). Months to recover is ₹86 lakh divided by monthly premium revenue, before any cost of food or delivery.

Exhibit 3 says that a wrong guess matters a great deal: the same build takes 8.5 months to recover at 18 per cent and more than two and a half years at 5 per cent. Exhibit 4 prices the three courses of action.

6. The options

Exhibit 4. Cost of each option, ₹ lakh
Cost headA: Build nowB: Test firstC: Hyderabad
People and contractors18.03.69.0
Product and engineering34.00.00.0
Kitchen, packaging and fit-out22.01.531.0
Research and recruitment0.03.90.0
Launch marketing12.00.015.0
Total86.09.055.0

Option A is the ₹86 lakh in the board deck. Option B costs about a tenth of Option A.

Option A: build now. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune build the plan engine, two dieticians are hired, and the product is ready by mid-January 2027. The upside is the resolution season; the cost is ₹86 lakh spent on a forecast built on a friendly audience.

Option B: test first. From Monday 23 November, Charita would spend six weeks running twelve more solution interviews with a fixed script, and deliver hand-made plans, prepared by two contract dieticians, to the 3 depositors and 20 paying volunteers, with a go/no-go on Friday 8 January 2027. The upside is evidence of repeat purchase at ₹189 for ₹9 lakh. The cost is time: if the answer is go, the build finishes in early March, seven weeks later than Option A, and the January season is lost.

Option C: shelve the plan. The money, ₹55 lakh, would open a Hyderabad kitchen for the core thali, a proven product. The upside is certain demand; the cost is that the premium question stays open.

7. Questions for discussion

1. In Exhibit 2, what separates a polite answer from a revealing one? Which finding would you trust most?

2. Why did the two rounds produce different results, and what did each ask the customer to risk?

3. Using Exhibit 3, how much of the ₹86 lakh decision depends on one assumption, and could any interview you can run before 20 November change that assumption?

4. Which option would you recommend to the steering committee, and what result in the next six weeks would change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

A solution interview asks whether a concept solves a problem the customer already feels, without selling it. The test is behaviour: did the person describe the problem before the concept, spend or risk something afterwards, and reveal price resistance honestly? Compliments, and signatures on free forms, cost the customer nothing and predict little. By that test the August round is weak evidence and the October round is thin but real. Six of nine described the problem unprompted, and a third paid.

The defensible path is Option B. Exhibit 3 shows that the build recovers its cost in 8.5 months only if the 18 per cent forecast holds, and the October evidence suggests a smaller early market. The test costs ₹9 lakh, about a tenth of the build, and replaces a guess with repeat purchases of a hand-made plan at the real price. A larger panel answers Colette's sample-size point, and volunteers protect the trust Cynthia worries about. If the pilot sustains an upgrade rate near 9 per cent, the build is still justified, at about 17 months to recover on revenue. If it sits near 5 per cent, Charita can redirect the budget toward Option C with her reputation intact.

Chirantan will resent the seven-week delay, and she should say so plainly. The delay buys the right to be wrong cheaply: the January season matters less than a ₹86 lakh decision made on a polite answer.

ISB · Discovery & Design · Case 40

Takhti Works: The Reason Box

Three rounds of customer contact, one contract clause, and a board meeting on Wednesday morning.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Tuesday 17 November 2026, Digisha Idiculla sat at the kitchen table of her flat in Thiruvanmiyur, Chennai, with three documents she could not reconcile: the board pre-read circulated that afternoon, asking for ₹168 lakh to build a rejection-traceability module called Takhti Trace; a spreadsheet of fourteen conversations finished at nine customer plants on Friday 9 October; and a coding sheet in which a colleague in Copenhagen had heard the June concept-test recordings and counted who said what first.

The pre-read said customers had asked for Takhti Trace and would pay for it. The spreadsheet said five of the fourteen she met had raised anything resembling the problem before she showed them a picture of the solution. The coding sheet said that in June the problem had mostly been raised by Takhti's own interviewers.

Digisha was vice-president of product at Takhti Works, a ten-year-old industrial software company turning over ₹2.16 crore a year. The board met at ten on Wednesday 18 November and had asked for a recommendation; she had written one line in the box and deleted it twice.

2. The company, and the clause

Takhti Works was founded in March 2016 in Coimbatore by Dhyanesh Iyyappan, a machine-tool salesman, and Dron Imchen, a firmware engineer. Their product, Takhti Shift, replaced the paper job card on mid-sized engineering floors with a tablet bolted to a pillar beside each machine group. Operators tapped start, stop, part number and, if they chose, a reason for a stoppage or a rejected piece, and plant heads got a downtime report by 7 a.m. instead of a clipboard on Saturday.

By October 2026 the product was live on 1,240 machines across 38 plants at a uniform ₹1,450 per machine per month: monthly subscription revenue of ₹17.98 lakh. A ₹22 crore Series A from Tabeer Partners in January 2025 had left ₹9.40 crore in the bank on 30 September 2026 against a ₹31 lakh monthly burn, about thirty months of runway.

The decision that constrains everything today was signed in November 2022, when Takhti had 190 machines live and no money. Tumbi Devices Group, a Rajkot maker of retrofit sensor boxes, paid a ₹3.6 crore channel advance and opened its dealer network. In exchange, clause 9.2 of the five-year agreement, which runs to 31 October 2027, says any Takhti module reading a signal directly from a machine controller may be sold only bundled with a Tumbi box. That clause bought the company its life; today it means the only version of Takhti Trace not dependent on an operator typing a reason is one Takhti cannot price on its own.

3. The industry

Takhti's customers are tier-two and tier-three component makers: forging shops, pump assemblers and fastener mills that supply Tata Motors, Mahindra, Ashok Leyland, Bajaj Auto, TVS and Bosch, and are audited against IATF 16949 by customers who send 8D reports back when a part fails. Their margins are thin, their quality cost largely unmeasured, their floors run on paper.

Exhibit 1 maps the field. Above Takhti sit the execution suites of SAP and Siemens, which tier-one plants buy and these cannot; beside it, Tehzeeb Plant Labs of Pune, with a cheaper app and an aggressive channel, and Tumbi itself, now shipping a thin analytics layer on its boxes; below it the real competitor, a spreadsheet kept by one earnest engineer. Software for small Indian manufacturers has been fashionable since Zoho and Freshworks proved what Chennai can export.

Two outside forces press on the decision. The DPDP Act makes per-operator attribution a question for counsel, since a rejection record carrying an employee number is personal data and plant unions read circulars. And four of Takhti's plants supply safety-critical parts to Tramontana Mobility of Milan, whose purchasing team circulated a draft supplier manual on Wednesday 2 September 2026 requiring digital, timestamped rejection-cause records, kept twenty-four months, from Thursday 1 April 2027. It is unsigned, and Tramontana's purchasing quality manager, Davide Innocenti, has told two suppliers the date may move.

Exhibit 1. Where Takhti Works sits

Labels and relationships only; no quantity is encoded in any position or length.

4. What happened, and what was believed

The idea is nine months old. Its evidence was gathered three times, by three methods, dated in Exhibit 2, each round believed completely until the next arrived.

Round one, February 2026. At an engineering expo in Chennai on 24–26 February, the sales team ran a stall with a ranking card: seven shop-floor problems, pick your top one, collect a ₹2,000 fuel voucher. Of the 31 who filled it in, 22 of 31 (71 per cent) put rejection and rework cost first, and the number went into the roadmap as settled fact.

Round two, June 2026. Doroteia Inacio, the designer in Lisbon, who had argued against printing a price and been overruled, drew three boards: a weekly quality dashboard; automatic capture of the rejection cause from the machine, with ₹650 per machine per month in the corner; and a mobile approval flow for scrap notes. Only the second carried a price. Dulari Ithape's team showed all three to 18 plant heads in Pune, Rajkot, Ludhiana and Coimbatore, and 14 of 18 (78 per cent) said they would buy Board 2, 9 of 18 asking for a quotation. A deck dated Tuesday 30 June 2026 turned this into a forecast and a ₹2.41 crore prize: the scrap-and-rework ledger cost, for the year ended 31 March 2026, of the eleven plants that had shared ledgers.

August 2026. Doyel Ipe, the chief financial officer, went through four of those eleven ledgers line by line. She found ₹1.12 crore of the ₹2.41 crore — about 47 per cent — was rework labour already inside standard labour cost, counted twice. Applying that share to all eleven leaves ₹1.29 crore addressable, and at the deck's own 15 per cent the saving is ₹19.35 lakh a year across those eleven plants, or ₹1.76 lakh per ledger-sharing plant per year — against the ₹4.97 lakh a year a 60-machine plant would pay at ₹690 per machine per month. Her extrapolation rests on four plants; she has said so twice in writing.

September and October 2026. Digisha ran the third round herself: fourteen conversations at nine plants between Monday 14 September and Friday 9 October, on a problem-first script that reached the concept only in the last ten minutes and ended with an ask, a ₹1.5 lakh paid pilot. Six of the fourteen were not buyers but supervisors and inspectors, who would have to touch the thing. Five of 14 (36 per cent) described a rejection-traceability problem unprompted; six of 14 (43 per cent) raised instead the end-of-shift handover, reconstructed every evening from memory and a notebook. Three of the 9 plants (33 per cent) signed a pilot letter — two of them plants where Dulari had already offered a renewal discount, which Digisha learned on 6 November from the plant head rather than from Dulari.

Exhibit 2. Timeline

Dates and labels only; horizontal spacing is illustrative and encodes no interval.

5. The people

Dhyanesh Iyyappan, chief executive, Coimbatore. He wants Trace approved on Wednesday, and his pre-read says half the revenue sits in plants that will be audited; the exposure is 372 of 1,240 machines (30 per cent), and, the price being uniform, 30 per cent of revenue. Unsaid: Tabeer Partners wants a second product line before any Series B talk.

Digisha Idiculla, vice-president product, Chennai. She believes June measured politeness and October something thinner but real. Unsaid: she wrote the June script herself, in a hurry, before going on leave.

Dulari Ithape, head of enterprise sales, Pune, whose variable pay is tied to new-module bookings. Her forecast is nine plants in two quarters: 540 machines at ₹700 each a month, or ₹3.78 lakh a month. Unsaid: three of the nine are the pilot plants, two are prospects rather than customers, and the base holds only six plants above fifty machines.

Dron Imchen, co-founder and vice-president engineering, Bengaluru. Clause 9.2, he says, permits two designs: automatic capture bundled with a Tumbi box, or manual entry by the operator. He prefers the second and dislikes what Exhibit 5 says about it. Unsaid: two of his four senior engineers are serving notice.

Doyel Ipe, chief financial officer, Chennai. She will not sign a case built on the ₹2.41 crore figure. Unsaid: she has modelled a down round at this burn and wants no ₹168 lakh in it.

Dag Isaksen, data scientist, Copenhagen, four and a half hours behind Chennai in November. He produced Exhibit 4, yet argues for the build: labelled defect causes would feed the predictive-quality model he promised the board in April. Unsaid: he chose the coding scheme after hearing the June tapes.

Dalia Izaz, customer success lead, Muscat, an hour and a half behind. Her two Gulf plants want Arabic reason codes, which no option prices. Unsaid: one has asked Tehzeeb Plant Labs for a demonstration.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 3. Three rounds of customer contact
RoundWho was in the roomWhat was shown, and asked of themHeadline result
1. Expo card, 24–26 Feb 202631 plant heads and purchase managers, self-selectedA card of seven problems; a tick, for a ₹2,000 voucherRejection and rework first for 22 of the 31 (71%)

3. Solution interviews, 14 Sep–9 Oct 202614 people at 9 plants: 8 plant heads, 6 supervisors and inspectorsProblem first, concept last; a ₹1.5 lakh paid pilot5 of the 14 (36%) named the problem unprompted; 3 of the 9 plants (33%) signed

Bases differ and are stated in each cell: rounds 1 and 2 count people, the signing figure counts plants. Round 3's 14 conversations include six non-buyers, so its 36 per cent is not comparable with round 2's 78 per cent, a share of buyers only. Two of the three signing plants had been offered a renewal discount beforehand; the third had not.

Exhibit 5 asks a different question: not what customers say about a reason field, but what they do with the one they have, Takhti Shift having carried an optional reason dropdown since 2021.

Finance, 12 November 2026.

7. Voices

“Fourteen of eighteen plant heads told us they would buy it. I have never had a clearer answer in nine years of selling. And now we ask the board for six more weeks to ask again?”

Dulari Ithape, sales channel, 10 November 2026

“In eleven of the fourteen recordings we could hear, the benefit was in the room before the customer was. That is not a finding about customers. It is a finding about us.”

Dag Isaksen, email to the leadership list, Wednesday 21 October 2026

“The reason box takes eleven minutes at the end of a shift for my section. I put Material, because Material is first in the list and the bus leaves at 8:40. If the tablet knew by itself, I would not have to lie politely.”

Diganta Ippili, shift supervisor, Tipaai Forgings, interview of 23 September 2026

“If the OEM asks for it in the audit, I will buy it that week, at your price. Until the audit asks, it is your product and not my problem. Write that down.”

Digvijay Ivalekar, plant head, Taqat Pumps, interview of 1 October 2026

“Clause 9.2 does not care about our roadmap. Automatic capture means a Tumbi box on every machine. Manual capture means selling a field Exhibit 5 says most users already ignore.”

Dron Imchen, engineering channel, 14 November 2026

8. The options as Digisha sees them

A. Build Takhti Trace. ₹168 lakh, seven months from 1 December 2026, putting a shipped module in early July 2027, three months after the Tramontana date, and assuming a clause 9.2 waiver Tumbi has no reason to grant in the last year of an agreement it is renegotiating.

B. Run the evidence loop. ₹19 lakh, six weeks from Monday 23 November to Monday 4 January 2027: sixteen problem-first interviews, half with supervisors and inspectors, then eight weeks in which Takhti's own field staff key rejection causes by hand at two plants, as a service rather than a product, to a decision on 1 March 2027. No schedule then gets a built module out before the mandate.

C. Bundle Tumbi's analytics layer now. ₹75 lakh, no clause 9.2 problem, and the only path that could put something auditable in the four Tramontana plants before April — except that Tumbi fields two crews, nine weeks per plant, putting the fourth plant live on 6 April 2027, five days late. It hands the relationship, and the pricing, to the channel partner.

D. The handover summary. ₹11 lakh, five weeks, and the one thing six of fourteen people raised unasked. Digisha's margin note calls it “not a real option”: no plant head asked for it, no audit requires it, nobody will pay a premium for it.

Each option answers “what should we build?” None answers the two questions the evidence raises: whose problem is the top problem when buyer and user name different ones, and whether the trigger is a problem at all rather than a signature in Milan. A fifth course nobody has costed is six weeks on Tramontana's purchasing team and Tumbi's contract instead of on customers.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at ten on Wednesday 18 November 2026 and will not reconvene before the third week of January. Cash is ₹9.40 crore against a ₹31 lakh monthly burn, and Doyel will not approve both A and C in one financial year. Clause 9.2 binds until 31 October 2027, and Tumbi wants renewal terms by February. The unsigned Tramontana draft names Thursday 1 April 2027, 134 days after the board meets. Two of Dron's four senior engineers are serving notice, so Option A's seven months assume two replacements hired by January. And Takhti has one product manager, who cannot run Option B's interviews and supervise Option A's build in one quarter.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. In Exhibit 3, what did each round ask the customer to risk, and what does each result license Takhti to believe? Which number would you put before a board, with what base beside it?
  2. Exhibit 4 undermines round 2, but its own base is 14 of the 18 interviews conducted, its scheme was written after the tapes were heard, and its author wants the module built. How much weight can it bear?
  3. Exhibit 5 reports behaviour, round 2 intent. If they disagree, which is better evidence that Takhti Trace solves a problem — and whose problem does each measure?
  4. Using Exhibit 6, whom can Takhti profitably serve under clause 9.2, and what does that do to the product's definition? What happens to the blended ₹100 margin if one large plant leaves?
  5. If the real trigger is the Tramontana mandate rather than any felt problem, is this a discovery question at all? Design the cheapest test that would settle it, and name the evidence that would change your mind.
  6. What should Digisha do on Monday morning, 23 November, and what should she tell the board about the ₹1.5 lakh pilot letters a renewal discount may have bought — given that her own June script is why Exhibit 4 exists?

At midnight she opened the recommendation box again, typed that the June evidence could not carry ₹168 lakh, deleted it, and typed instead that the company might have nine weeks a plant and five days too few. On her second screen was Diganta Ippili's sentence about the bus at 8:40, beside Digvijay Ivalekar's about the audit. One described a problem, the other a trigger; the pre-read treated them as one thing, and she was no longer sure which she would defend at ten o'clock.
exp40v2-res.solution.interview:
Solution Interviews and Concept Tests

Does my concept solve the problem, or am I just hearing politeness? What a commitment actually buys you, and what it cannot.

1. Two concepts, two instruments

On Monday 2 February 2026, in a mill office in Nagpur, Jaswant Kalgaonkar asked his product director to commit. He had co-founded Kshetra Land Systems in 2021 to sell collateral-file software to rural secured lenders: the workflow by which a branch officer checks the title documents behind a loan against land. Kshetra had 36 lender customers and annual recurring revenue of ₹1,440 lakh, an average of ₹40 lakh per customer. Kalgaonkar wanted the next release to be title-chain extraction — machine reading of scanned registry documents. Javiera Lagos, his engineering head in Santiago, costed it at six engineers for twenty weeks: 120 engineer-weeks at ₹0.95 lakh each, or ₹114 lakh, plus ₹26 lakh of registry licences — ₹140 lakh in all, which is 140 of the 1,440 lakh of recurring revenue, or 9.7 per cent.

Kumud Latkar, the product director, had a rival sketch costing ₹40 lakh: a dispute register, a shared queue in which the branch and the borrower's lawyer agree which document is actually missing. Three engineers for eleven weeks is 33 engineer-weeks, ₹31.35 lakh, plus ₹8.65 lakh of operations setup. Her objection was not a preference for the cheaper thing: eleven credit managers had called automatic extraction "very useful" the previous quarter, and she no longer believed the sentence. The roadmap locked on Friday 13 March, thirty-nine days away.

Six hundred kilometres away, Krupa Jhaveri faced the mirror image. Katran Tailoring Network, co-founded in Indore, ran a consumer app and a pickup network of karigar workshops for alterations; 4,20,000 users had registered and 1,80,000 had ordered in the previous ninety days. Her concept was Fit Pass: ₹499 a month, unlimited pickups, up to four garments. Rather than interview anyone she would put a card in the app and count the taps. The same method ran from opposite ends: Latkar with fourteen people and money on the table, Jhaveri with 756 she never met.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A solution interview is a structured conversation with someone who has the problem, in which a proposed answer is shown and the response measured by what the person gives up rather than by what they say. A concept test is the same exercise built on a stimulus — storyboard, mock-up, one-page description — kept rough on purpose, so the reaction attaches to the idea, not the craft. What is measured is not approval but cost borne: time, data, reputation or money.

The lineage predates software. Mid-century researchers testing packaged-goods concepts established that stated purchase intent runs ahead of purchase, and built correction factors to deflate it. Steve Blank's customer development (2005) moved the habit into start-ups; Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) supplied the craft rule, ask about the person's life and not your idea, because even your mother will lie to be kind; Alberto Savoia's pretotyping demanded skin in the game. From contextual design — Beyer and Holtzblatt — comes the contrary instinct: watch work, do not stage a transaction.

Three schools coexist and do not agree. The commitment school signs this: no qualitative signal is admissible unless the respondent surrendered something they would miss. It will not sign that a conversation without an ask can establish demand. The observation school signs that the job to be done is visible in current behaviour and workarounds, and that an ask begins selling and biases the sample toward the agreeable. It will not sign that a deposit is evidence of fit. The experiment school — Ron Kohavi's lineage, Stefan Thomke's on cheap tests — signs that fourteen conversations cannot estimate a rate, and will not sign that interviews substitute for one. Each was right about one protagonist and wrong about the other.

3. Mechanics: the price of a signal

Experts do not run a ladder of enthusiasm; they run a ledger of asks. Latkar had kept one since 2024: 80 solution interviews and the 222 commitment requests made inside them, or 2.775 asks per interview, each recorded as granted or not, and honoured within thirty days or not. Honouring is the part amateurs omit, and where the method earns its keep.

Exhibit 1. Kshetra's commitment ledger: 222 asks across 80 solution interviews, 2024–2026. Asks are not exclusive; one interview could carry four.
AskAskedGrantedGrant rateHonoured in 30 daysHonour rateHonoured per 100 asks
Verbal endorsement ("we would buy this")807290.0%912.5%11.25
