Total / blended22213159.0%5340.5%23.87

Blended grant rate = 131 / 222; blended honour rate = 53 / 131; honoured per 100 asks = honoured / asked × 100, blended 53 / 222.

Read the two rate columns against each other and the method's structure appears. The asks are listed in rising order of what they cost the respondent: an endorsement is free, a live file costs a permission, a colleague's hour spends standing with that colleague, a ₹2 lakh pilot costs money. As the price rises, the grant rate falls at every step, from 90.0 per cent to 30.0 per cent. The honour rate rises across the range, 12.5 per cent to 88.9 per cent, but not at every step: it dips from 75.0 on the live file to 66.7 on the colleague's hour, because a promise resting on a third person's diary is the one most often broken. Cheap agreement is abundant and nearly worthless: 9 of those 72 endorsements survived thirty days, which is 12.5 per cent. Expensive agreement is scarce and nearly reliable, and that inversion is why "everyone said yes" and "nobody signed" are often the same dataset.

Two second-order effects follow. First, the blended figures are not the averages of the columns: the four grant rates average 51.875 per cent, but the ask-weighted rate is 131 of 222, or 59.0 per cent, because the cheapest ask was also the most frequent. Blend from counts, never from rates. Second, the most expensive ask is not the most informative per unit of effort: yield — honoured commitments per hundred asks — peaks at 37.50 on the live-file ask, above the paid pilot's 26.67, because a pilot is refused by people who would have handed over the file. So an expert follows a refusal at a high price with a cheaper ask that still costs something.

The steps usually left implicit are these. Fix the admissible evidence and the threshold in writing first: Latkar's note of 4 February required 6 of 14 respondents to grant a costly ask and those grants to cover ₹200 lakh of the sample's contract value. Build both concepts at equal fidelity, alternate the order, and say aloud that neither has been built, so criticism is free. And code each conversation the same day, because memory is a sales instrument.

4. When the method applies, stated as testable claims

Three conditions, each falsifiable. One: the respondent can bear the cost you ask for. Every Kshetra respondent was a credit head who could commit a file and an hour; at Katran ₹499 was within reach of every user, which is why the output was weak — a trivially affordable ask discriminates poorly. Two: the problem recurs often enough to be remembered concretely. Collateral disputes arose weekly at Kshetra's lenders; an alteration need arises perhaps four times a year, so Katran's "last time" stories were thin. Three: the buyer and the payer are one person, or both are in the room. True for Latkar's NBFCs, false for the large bank's rural vertical, where nobody she reached held a budget code.

It misleads where value appears only after accumulation, so no first-day commitment represents what is bought; where social desirability makes yes cheaper than explaining no; and where willingness to commit follows the procurement cycle, so the measurement reads the calendar.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Disaggregated, Latkar's fourteen interviews, run across the twenty-five days from 9 February to 6 March, show the seam.

Exhibit 3. Kshetra: the 14 interviews, 9 February to 6 March 2026, by archetype. K1 = title-chain extraction; K2 = dispute register. A costly ask granted means a live file, a booked hour, or a signed ₹2 lakh pilot.
Lender archetypeInterviewsIndicative ACV (₹ lakh)Value in sample (₹ lakh)K1 restated correctlyK1 costly ask grantedK2 restated correctlyK2 costly ask granted
Small-ticket land and gold NBFC6221324155
Regional co-operative bank414563043
Large private bank, rural vertical4853404120
Total14—528112118

Value in sample = interviews × indicative annual contract value. Restatement was scored unprompted.

Comprehension was identical: 11 respondents restated each concept correctly. Commitment was not. K1 drew a costly grant from 2 of 14, which is 14.3 per cent; K2 from 8 of 14, or 57.1 per cent. Understanding a concept and wanting it are separate measurements, and notes recording only the first show the two as equals.

The seam is money. Weighted by contract value, K2's eight grants cover ₹110 lakh plus ₹42 lakh — ₹152 lakh of the ₹528 lakh in the sample, 28.8 per cent. K1's two grants, one from the large bank, cover ₹107 lakh of the same ₹528 lakh, or 20.3 per cent. By headcount K2 wins four times over; by revenue its lead shrinks to 1.42 times, ₹152 lakh against ₹107 lakh, because 5 of the 6 NBFCs granted, 83.3 per cent, and 3 of 4 co-operative banks, 75.0 per cent, while the large private bank granted nothing. The threshold was half met: eight grants against a bar of six, ₹152 lakh against ₹200 lakh.

Other edges behave characteristically. In two-sided products both sides must commit: Katran approached 24 karigar workshops, 9 of which reserved 42 hours a month — 378 hours, exactly the 567 alterations later delivered at 40 minutes each. Had all 756 subscribers been active at 1.5 garments, demand would have been 1,134 garments, or 756 hours, twice the reserved supply. In hardware the commitment arrives too late: Jwala Burner Works in Rajkot committed ₹46 lakh of tooling before a unit existed, against letters of intent from 3 of 9 bakery chains covering 140 units at ₹38,000 each — ₹53.2 lakh nobody had paid for. In regulated settings the costly ask is often impossible — an insurer's team cannot hand over live complaint text — so it is re-denominated into a scarce internal resource: an audit slot, a compliance sign-off. What mature firms call concept testing is usually a stage gate at which a business case is defended, the research assembled afterwards.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert

A commitment measures cost, not enthusiasm.

The question is never how warm the yes was but what it cost the person who gave it. The tell is a memo describing commitments with adjectives — "very keen", "strong buy-in" — instead of nouns: a file, an hour, an invoice. Warmth and cost seem to travel together; they do not, since warmth comes from the interviewer's presence.

Affordability destroys discrimination.

An ask the respondent barely notices separates nobody. Katran's ₹499 bought curiosity and almost no intent, which is why half the payers never used the service. The tell is a grant rate very high or very low: both mean a mispriced ask.

Restatement is the cheapest neglected instrument.

Making the respondent explain the concept back, before you clarify anything, separates confusion from rejection. Exhibit 3's equal restatement counts made Latkar's verdict credible: K1 did not lose because nobody understood it. The tell is a team revising the stimulus after every interview without recording whether comprehension bound.

Order effects are large and nearly free to remove.

The concept shown first gets the warmer hearing, so alternate and record the order. The tell is a results table with no order column. Fourteen looks too small for order to matter; in truth, the smaller the sample the more a systematic bias dominates.

A refused ask is data, not failure.

The reason for refusal is often the hour's most valuable sentence. "I can't share the file because the registry copy sits with our empanelled lawyer" told Latkar more than any grant did. The tell is a notebook with no refusals in it; Exhibit 1 counts them.

Sample size and rate answer different questions.

Small samples detect patterns well and estimate magnitudes badly. The tell is a percentage from n = 14 quoted with no interval: Latkar's 57.1 per cent carried a 95 per cent interval of roughly 31.2 to 83.1 per cent.

Segment and weight before you pool.

A pooled rate hides a split: 57.1 per cent conceals 83.3, 75.0 and 0.0, and counting heads treats a ₹14 lakh co-operative bank as an ₹85 lakh private bank's equal. Weighting by contract value turned Latkar's majority into 28.8 per cent of the money. The tell is a headline rate with no value column beside it.

The stimulus must be as good as the shipped thing, and no better.

A demo that flatters the product measures a product you will not ship — the defining hazard of AI concepts, where a curated demo can run thirty points above live. The tell is a stimulus with no failure cases in it.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products only money at a price the person feels, or a behaviour change held for a week, discriminates; the sample is cheap enough that a measured rate usually beats a conversation. In B2B the user, the budget holder and the approver differ, so one yes is not a decision, and the costly asks are real data, a colleague's booked time, a paid pilot; in enterprise, a slot in a release plan someone else owns. On marketplaces the ask must be made of both sides, the second side's yes being conditional on the first. In hardware the commitment lands after the irreversible spend. In AI products the stimulus is the problem: curated performance is not performance.

By stage the difference lies in what may be accepted, not in the method. A seed-stage team can take ₹25,000 on a handshake; a listed company often cannot invoice for an unbuilt product, so it substitutes letters, pilot slots and signed scoping documents — and needs written thresholds, because its internal audience will otherwise re-argue the result. Overstated: the craft itself, identical at eight respondents and eight thousand.

8. Three worked examples

Kshetra, where the method worked and the threshold did not. The research cost ₹6.5 lakh: two people for about 3.6 weeks each at ₹0.75 lakh per person-week, or ₹5.4 lakh, plus ₹1.1 lakh of travel and incentives. Against the ₹140 lakh K1 build that is 4.6 per cent. If those 3.6 weeks had even a two-in-five chance of averting a build that would have failed, the expected saving was 0.40 × ₹140 lakh, or ₹56 lakh, against ₹6.5 lakh spent — 8.6 to one. That calculation persuaded Kalgaonkar to allow the delay.

Katran, where a measured rate was precise and uninformative. The fake door ran from Tuesday 14 April to Tuesday 28 April 2026. Of 1,80,000 users shown the card, 27,000 tapped it (15.0 per cent); 6,750 of those reached the price screen (25.0 per cent); 1,080 entered card details (16.0 per cent); 756 completed the ₹499 charge (70.0 per cent). End to end, 756 of 1,80,000 is 0.42 per cent, against a pre-registered threshold of 0.75 per cent. Month-one revenue was 756 × ₹499 = ₹3,77,244. Then behaviour arrived: 378 of the 756, exactly 50 per cent, used the service even once in thirty days, so revenue per active subscriber was ₹998 a month. Those 378 sent 567 garments, 1.5 each, at ₹210 apiece to collect and alter — ₹1,19,070 — a gross margin of ₹2,58,174, or 68.4 per cent, and ₹157.50 of cost to serve per subscriber. On 28 May, 504 of 756 renewed, 66.7 per cent, giving ₹2,51,496. Jhelum Karkhanis's eighteen interviews, 4 to 22 May, explained what the funnel could not: subscribers hoarded the pass for a wedding season not yet arrived, the concept having been written as a volume discount when the job was a deadline.

Kautuk AI Works, where the method failed outright. Jigar Lalwani's team in Bengaluru built an assistant that drafts insurer grievance replies and tested it on a demo of 50 curated tickets, of which 47 were correct — 94 per cent. Nine of eleven respondents signed a ₹1.5 lakh pilot, 81.8 per cent, and that ₹13.5 lakh licensed a build of five engineers for twenty-six weeks: 130 engineer-weeks at ₹1.1 lakh, or ₹143 lakh, 10.6 times the revenue it rested on. In production the system got 852 of 1,200 tickets right, 71 per cent, and 2 of 9 pilots renewed — 22.2 per cent. The ask worked as designed; the stimulus measured a product that did not exist. The recovery: re-run the test with the demo degraded to 72 per cent, close to live. Of twelve new respondents 3 granted a pilot, 25 per cent, at ₹2.4 lakh — ₹7.2 lakh — and all three renewed, having bought draft-and-route with a human always sending.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Exhibit 4. Four failure modes, the first sign, the question that catches it, and the cost of catching it late.
Failure modeEarliest warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Endorsements counted as demandGrant rates near 90 per cent, no honouring columnWhich yeses survived thirty days?A release cycle; at Kshetra, ₹140 lakh
Flattering stimulusNo failure cases in the demoAt what accuracy would this still be bought?Pilots signed, not renewed; Kautuk lost 7 of 9

One-sided test of a two-sided productSupply sized from the subscriber countWhat happens to supply if every buyer is active?Service collapse at success; Katran was short by half

Each is cheap to catch in week one and expensive after a build, which is the argument for written thresholds. Concept tests fail quietly: the signal is a flat adoption curve two quarters on, when failure is blamed on execution.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the commitment ask corrupt the data? The observation school's strongest form is not squeamishness: an ask for money or data turns research into negotiation, which selects for social style rather than need. On that reading Latkar's co-operative bankers granted because refusing a guest is rude in their setting, and the 75.0 per cent is hospitality. The commitment school answers with Exhibit 1: were that so, honouring would not be seven times likelier on a paid pilot, at 88.9 per cent, than on a free endorsement, at 12.5. For the observation school to be right, honouring would need another explanation — contract cycle, say.

Can fourteen conversations decide a ₹140 lakh question? The experiment school says no: an interval from n = 14 is wider than the difference most roadmap arguments turn on, and a fake door costs less. Its evidence is Katran, where a fortnight and no interviews measured 0.42 per cent on 1,80,000 impressions. The reply is also Katran: the rate said nothing about why, and ₹499 was too cheap to discriminate. The disagreement reduces to the decision at hand: rates for go or no-go on a priced thing, conversations for choosing mechanisms.

Is intent ever predictive? The market-research tradition holds that stated intent predicts behaviour once deflated by a known factor; the start-up tradition holds the factor is unknowable in a new category. The first rests on decades of packaged-goods validation, the second on the point that such factors are calibrated on categories that already exist. No synthesis: deflate if you have a long concept-test history in a stable category; otherwise demand costly commitments.

How many interviews. The detection arithmetic is uncontroversial; the inference from it is not.

Exhibit 5. Probability of seeing a pattern at least once, 1 − (1 − p)n, for a pattern present in a share p of a population.
Share of population with the patternn = 5n = 8n = 14
30 per cent83.2%94.2%99.3%
10 per cent41.0%57.0%77.1%
5 per cent22.6%33.7%51.2%

Detection only. The same n = 14 measures a rate loosely: 8 of 14 is 57.1 per cent, with a 95 per cent interval of roughly 31.2 to 83.1 per cent, or some ±26 points.

Five conversations will nearly always reveal a common pattern and will miss a one-in-twenty pattern three times in four. Experts use small samples to find mechanisms and refuse to quote them as rates. What stays contested is whether a one-in-twenty pattern matters: in a mass consumer product it is noise; in Kshetra's few hundred lenders it may be the segment that pays.

11. What mastery looks like

One who has merely studied this runs good interviews and writes an honest memo. Someone who has internalised it changes the order of operations: threshold and admissible evidence circulated before recruiting, asks priced so the grant rate lands in the discriminating middle, a value column beside the count. They quote intervals with rates, treat a refusal as a finding, and degrade their stimulus to what engineering can ship. When a result half-clears the bar, they narrow the decision to what the evidence covers.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Tuesday 10 March 2026, three days before the roadmap locked, Latkar recommended building the ₹40 lakh dispute register for the NBFC and co-operative segments only, and explicitly not as the platform bet: 8 of 14 had granted, clearing the count bar of six, but the ₹152 lakh of covered value fell short of the ₹200 lakh written down on 4 February. For the large private bank, which granted nothing of its ₹340 lakh, she proposed a paid scoping engagement instead. Title-chain extraction was deferred, not killed: the register would show how many disputes came from missing documents rather than disputed ones, the number that would justify ₹140 lakh.

On Monday 1 June 2026, Jhaveri cancelled Fit Pass as a subscription and kept it as a deadline product: a ₹149 express-alteration promise with a named return date, priced per use. Her reasoning: 0.42 per cent against a 0.75 per cent bar was a clear miss, 50 per cent dormancy and a 66.7 per cent renewal made the economics a wasting asset, and the interviews had located the real job. Leena Kagalkar's supply plan was rebuilt around 756 hours a month rather than 378, capacity being sized for full activation.

Three questions. First: Latkar's threshold had two clauses and the result met one — defensible narrowing, or a rewritten bar in disguise? Second: if ₹499 was too cheap to discriminate, what price would have been informative, and what would Jhaveri have given up by charging it? Third: Kautuk's degraded demo produced three grants instead of nine — why should a team prefer the smaller number, and who will argue against it?

13. Going deeper

Interview fundamentals. The craft assumed here; without it an ask is a pitch.

Concept and elevator pitch. You cannot test what you cannot state in two sentences.

Usability testing. The next question, on a different instrument: competence, not desire.

Concept → feedback → iterate. Makes one test a cadence; threshold discipline compounds.

Qualitative vs quantitative research. Settles the Katran argument: mechanisms from talk, magnitudes from rates.

Designing an interview guide. Where the asks and their prices are written down.

Recruiting research participants. Decides whether Exhibit 3's segments exist at all.

How many interviews. Exhibit 5's arithmetic, and not quoting small samples as forecasts.

Cognitive biases in research. Acquiescence, order and confirmation effects, each structurally remediable.

Synthesising research. How coded conversations become a recommendation that names its fragility.
exp20v2-res.solution.interview:
Solution Interviews and Concept Tests

Does my concept solve the problem, or am I just hearing politeness?

1. The roadmap that nobody objected to

On Monday 3 August 2026, Anjali Bhadra, product manager at Ankur Receivables Network in Pune, stood at a whiteboard with a decision she disliked. Ankur sold a WhatsApp-based tool to small textile wholesalers in Surat's Ring Road markets, who sell cloth on credit and then wait, sometimes for months, to be paid. Bimal Choudhury, the founder, wanted the next quarter committed to an automatic reminder engine: a system that would message late-paying buyers on the wholesaler's behalf. Cyrus Batliwala, head of engineering, estimated four engineers for fourteen weeks.

The arithmetic was unforgiving. Fourteen weeks of four engineers is 56 engineer-weeks, which at an internal cost of ₹0.75 lakh each comes to ₹42 lakh. Ankur held ₹360 lakh in cash and burned ₹30 lakh a month, so the engine would consume 11.7 per cent of its cash and 1.4 months of its life. Everyone agreed it was a good idea. Anjali had heard that sentence in June, from fourteen traders, and she no longer trusted it. Agreement is cheap. She had eleven days before the roadmap was due on 14 August, and she meant to spend them learning whether the idea solved the problem or merely sounded as though it would.

This page follows her through that fortnight.

2. The idea

A solution interview is a structured conversation with a person who has the problem, in which you show or describe a proposed answer and measure the response by what the person is willing to give up, not by what they say. A concept test is the same exercise built around a stimulus: a storyboard, a mock-up or a one-page description of the product, rendered rough on purpose so that the customer reacts to the idea rather than the polish.

The problem it was invented to solve is older than software. Market researchers tested product concepts in the mid-twentieth century and learned that stated purchase intent overstates real purchase. Steve Blank's customer development, set out in 2005, moved the habit into start-ups. Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) taught that if you ask people about your idea, even your mother will lie to be kind, so you should ask about their lives instead. Alberto Savoia's pretotyping argued for asking the customer to put "skin in the game". From these comes the sentence Anjali could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib: a compliment costs the speaker nothing, so we weigh only what the customer will spend, in time, reputation or money, to get the concept.

Exhibit 1 is that sentence turned into a measuring instrument. Level 0 is politeness. Level 1 is stated interest, which sounds like evidence and is not. Levels 2, 3 and 4 each ask the customer to pay something real: an hour of attention and a real ledger, the credibility of an introduction to their accountant or the right to message an actual debtor, and finally rupees.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have six steps, and the ones practitioners leave implicit are the ones that go wrong. First, restate the problem you believe you are solving, in the customer's own words from earlier interviews. Anjali's was that a trader could not tell whether a buyer was late or merely disputing the amount. Second, build the stimulus. She drew two storyboards at the same fidelity: Concept A, automatic WhatsApp reminders to late buyers, and Concept B, a monthly statement reconciled line by line against the buyer's own records and sent before any reminder.

Third, recruit people who recently had the problem. Fourth, sequence the conversation: begin with the last time an invoice went unpaid, told as a story; only then show the concept, in silence, and ask the trader to explain it back. Fifth, make the commitment ask, a small and specific request, and note the response. Sixth, code the level immediately afterwards.

Three steps are usually unstated. Show the concepts in alternating order, because the first one seen gets a warmer hearing. Say aloud that you did not build either one, so criticism feels costless. And decide before the first interview which result would change the plan; otherwise every result will seem to confirm it. Anjali wrote that threshold down on 3 August: if fewer than three of eight traders reached level 3 or above on a concept, she would not recommend building it.

4. A worked example

Between 4 and 12 August she held eight conversations in Surat, each about fifty minutes, with owners whose outstanding receivables ranged from ₹28 lakh to ₹150 lakh. Exhibit 2 gives the result.

Exhibit 2. Eight conversations, 4-12 August 2026. Outstanding receivables in ₹ lakh; levels per the commitment ladder.

Read the arithmetic line by line. Concept A scored a sum of 9 across eight traders, an average of 1.125; nobody reached level 3. Concept B scored 17, an average of 2.125, and three traders reached level 3 or above: Bharat Choksi and Brijesh Agarwal each paid a refundable deposit of ₹25,000 toward a three-month pilot, which is ₹50,000 in all, and Bhavin Chokshi offered to introduce his accountant and let Ankur message one real buyer. Three of eight is 37.5 per cent, clearing her threshold for B and failing it for A.

Seven of eight traders scored at least 1 on each concept, so politeness alone would have called the two ideas equal. The separation appears only above level 2. Notice also the weighting. Those three traders carry ₹120 lakh, ₹150 lakh and ₹95 lakh, a combined ₹365 lakh of the ₹620 lakh outstanding across all eight, or 58.9 per cent. The committed minority held most of the money at stake.

Now change one input. Suppose Bhavin's accountant introduction proves to have been his accountant's idea rather than his own, and Anjali downgrades him from level 3 to level 2. The sum for B falls to 16 and its average to 2.0. Only two traders remain at level 3 or above, 25 per cent, which falls below her threshold, and their weight drops to ₹215 lakh, or 34.7 per cent of ₹620 lakh. One judgment about one conversation moves the verdict from proceed to continue testing. The coding rule must therefore be fixed in advance.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Interest is not intent, and intent is not behaviour.

"I would use that" describes a hypothetical self. Behaviour is what the person did the last time the problem arose, and the best solution interviews spend more minutes on that history than on the concept.

You are testing a concept, not a feature list.

A concept test asks whether a described outcome is wanted. It does not ask whether a button should sit on the left. Interface questions belong to usability testing, which comes later and answers a different question.

Pitching contaminates the data.

The moment you defend the concept, you are selling, and the customer begins to manage your feelings. Silence after showing the stimulus is the interviewer's best tool.

A commitment must be proportionate.

Asking a trader with ₹28 lakh outstanding to pay ₹25,000 is a larger ask than asking the one with ₹150 lakh. Compare commitments to the person's means and pain, or you will mistake the wealthy for the keen.

The sample has a size and a bias.

Five to eight conversations reveal strong patterns and weak ones poorly. They cannot estimate market share. Respondents arrive through your network, which favours the helpful.

Nothing here prices the product or proves it will be used.

A deposit shows willingness to start. It does not show retention, the right price or whether the buyer's buyers will respond. Those need a working pilot over weeks.

Confusion with a problem interview.

A problem interview asks whether a pain exists and how much it matters. A solution interview assumes that answer and tests the fix. Running them in the wrong order produces confident answers to the wrong question.

Questions to ask before relying on it.

Who was in the room? Which commitments were requested, and which were volunteered? What result would have changed the plan, and was it written down beforehand?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products

Exhibit 4. How the method bends by product type.
SettingWhat counts as costlyMain hazard
ConsumerPre-order, waitlist with a payment, a week of changed behaviourPoliteness is high and prices are small, so deposits are easy to give and prove little
B2BReal data shared, a named colleague's time, a paid pilotThe user, the buyer and the approver are different people, so one yes is not a decision
MarketplaceA first listing, a first transaction, a payment taken from one sideBoth sides must be tested, and each side's yes depends on the other showing up

Ankur is a B2B product, and Anjali's costliest signals were a real ledger and a deposit from the owner, who was both user and buyer. In a larger company the signal to hunt for is budget authority: a team lead's enthusiasm counts for little until someone with a cost centre signs. In a marketplace she would have run two parallel sets of interviews and asked each side to commit before the other existed.

A start-up can ask for a deposit on a handshake. A large company often cannot take money for an unbuilt product, so it substitutes proxies such as a signed letter of intent or a pilot slot booked in someone's own plan. Its internal audience also wants confirmation, which makes written thresholds more necessary.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 5. Four mistakes, how they show from outside, and the cheapest check.
MistakeSymptomMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Counting complimentsNotes say "loved it" and no one followed upStated interest is treated as demandAdd a level column to the notes and count only levels 3 and 4
One concept onlyEvery trader says yes, so the plan is unchangedAbsolute approval is mistaken for preferenceShow a rival concept to the same people in alternating order
Leading the witnessQuotes read like the pitch deckThe interviewer is explaining, not listeningHave a colleague review the recording for how long the interviewer talked
Moving the goalpostsThe bar is lowered after the results arriveThe decision rule was never writtenDate and share the threshold before the first call

Concept tests fail quietly: the failure arrives later as a flat adoption curve, not as a bad interview.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Anjali's fortnight has five marks. Two concepts of equal fidelity were tested against a recent story, not a hypothetical. The threshold, three of eight at level 3 or above, was written down and dated on 3 August. Every conversation was coded straight afterwards, and the memo carried raw quotes and named what the sample could not show. Finally the verdict stated its own fragility, as the Bhavin sensitivity did, so the room could argue about the right thing.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On Monday 17 August Anjali told Bimal and Cyrus that Concept B had cleared the bar and Concept A had not. Her reasoning was that the traders did not have a reminder problem; they had a disagreement problem, and a polite message about an amount the buyer disputes only restates the argument. She asked to build the reconciled statement first: three engineers for eight weeks, 24 engineer-weeks at ₹0.75 lakh, or ₹18 lakh, which is 5.0 per cent of the ₹360 lakh in cash, against ₹42 lakh for the reminder engine. The reminder engine would wait until the statements showed whether disputes were the real blockage. Bimal agreed.

The natural next topic is usability testing, which asks whether people can operate the thing you decided to build, and the loop of concept, feedback and iteration, which turns one test into a habit. Two questions to sit with. If Bharat and Brijesh had been unable to pay a deposit because of how their firms handle cash, what other level 3 or 4 commitment could have told Anjali the same thing? And what would you need to see before you trusted a result that confirmed what you already hoped?

Forty-Three Themes

Bhoopali Health Exchange and the question of enough — a case for discussion

1. Sunday night, Indiranagar

At twenty past eleven on Sunday, 18 October 2026, the north-east monsoon had settled over Bengaluru into a flat, patient drumming. Haimanti Lahiri, Senior Vice-President for Product at Bhoopali Health Exchange, had two windows open on her laptop: a one-page memo due in the chief executive's inbox by nine next morning, and a spreadsheet with forty-three rows in it.

On Thursday, 29 October, Bhoopali's investment committee would be asked to release ₹4.20 crore to build Bulava, a pre-authorisation and cashless-discharge module for hospital insurance desks. The 2 November engineering start could not move: the module promised to the Bustan Hospitals Group in Doha had to be code-complete by 27 January 2027 to clear a nine-week on-premise certification train and reach production by 31 March 2027. Twelve weeks and two days, with no slack.

The memo had to answer one question. After thirty-five interviews between June and September, did Bhoopali know enough to spend ₹4.20 crore, or did it need to go back into the field? Haimanti had two analyses from two colleagues she trusted. One said the research was eighty-three per cent complete. One said fifty-eight. Both were arithmetically correct.

2. The company, and the decision of 2023

Bhoopali Health Exchange was founded in Pune in 2018 by Hukumchand Lunawat, a hospital-finance consultant, and Hoshang Lotwala, an engineer. Bhoopali Desk follows a claim from admission through pre-authorisation, queries, discharge and settlement, telling the billing team which claims are stuck and with whom.

In 2023 the company made the choice that still shapes everything. To win Betwa Hospitals Network, a chain of large private hospitals, Bhoopali agreed to deploy inside the customer's own data centre rather than on its hosted platform. Ten more chains followed on the same terms, so by October 2026 all eleven large-chain customers ran Bhoopali Desk Onsite. It bought the revenue behind a ₹118 crore Series B in January 2025, led by the Beas Growth Trust of Mumbai.

It had two consequences nobody wrote down. Every feature now ships through a nine-week certification cycle per data centre, so a late finding costs a quarter, not a sprint. And those eleven relationships were the easiest insurance desks in India to get an hour inside; when Haimanti planned discovery in May 2026, the sample drifted towards them without anyone deciding it should.

Recurring revenue at 30 September stood at ₹44.21 crore: ₹32.27 crore from India, ₹9.60 crore from North America and ₹2.34 crore from the Gulf.

3. The industry

India's cashless health-insurance plumbing was being rebuilt while Bhoopali argued about interviews. The National Health Authority's National Health Claims Exchange had begun moving insurers, third-party administrators and hospitals onto a common messaging standard under IRDAI pressure for faster authorisation. Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY claims ran on their own rails, with their own documentation habits. The DPDP Act had made hospital legal teams cautious about who could see a discharge summary, which complicated the screen-sharing Bhoopali's designers liked to do.

Commercially the field was uneven. Apollo Hospitals, Max Healthcare and Narayana Health ran sophisticated revenue-cycle operations; Star Health, Niva Bupa, HDFC Ergo and Policybazaar shaped what a desk could ask for. Beneath them sat some twenty thousand nursing homes and day-care centres, for whom a rejected pre-authorisation was a cash-flow emergency and software budgets ran to a few thousand rupees a year. Bhoopali's platform touched ₹9,530 crore of claim value a year, 10.4 per cent of the ₹92,000 crore its four target segments held between them.

The exposure ran outwards too. Hardik Lodha sold a denials-management variant to billing outsourcers from Chicago. The Gulf contract — Bustan Hospitals Group, signed on 12 February 2026 at ₹2.34 crore a year — carried a service credit of ₹58 lakh, 24.8 per cent of the fee, if pre-authorisation was not in production by 31 March 2027.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. In March 2026, on six conversations with insurance-desk heads at three Betwa hospitals, the team believed the problem was pre-authorisation turnaround time. In May, Haimanti wrote a plan for thirty interviews across four segments, expecting saturation between the twelfth and the fifteenth conversation.

Humaira Lilani, the principal designer, ran the first track from Lisbon through Bahaar Field Services of Hyderabad on a cold-recruited list, completing nineteen interviews between 9 June and 18 September. Separately, Hazel Lotlikar's team in Manila had been running quarterly-review calls with existing customers; sixteen of those, between 24 June and 11 September, were close enough in territory to be coded against the same scheme.

In July, with nineteen themes logged after nine interviews and new ones falling away, Hukumchand told the board that discovery was “effectively done”. That belief held until September, when Heramb Lamture, a data scientist in Melbourne, noticed that the two tracks had never been reconciled and merged the codebooks. Exhibit 2 surprised everyone: the tracks shared only seventeen themes out of forty-three distinct ones.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. The theme count is soft: an October audit found three theme pairs whose boundaries are arguable, and Exhibit 2a shows what the estimate does when that assumption moves. Five of the forty-three themes were logged for the first time in September, all concerning National Health Claims Exchange message formats — the newest findings were not the tail of a converging process but the arrival of a new regime. And Hetal Luthra's team had been logging lost-deal reasons all along: between April and September it recorded forty-one losses among small hospitals, and twenty-three of them, 56.1 per cent, cited a settlement-reconciliation capability absent from the forty-three.

5. The people

Haimanti Lahiri, Senior Vice-President for Product, Bengaluru, must send the memo. Her position is that the evidence suffices for the Doha scope and not for India growth. She does not say that she wrote the May sampling plan, and that the skew everyone is arguing about is her own.

Hukumchand Lunawat, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, reads Exhibit 6 and sees ninety-three per cent coverage; his incentive is a Series C round that assumes a shipped module. He does not say that in August he told Dr Hashim Loomba, Bustan's chief operating officer, that it would be live in the fourth quarter.

Hetal Luthra, National Sales Head for India, Jaipur, carries a quota of which 60 per cent sits among small hospitals. She points at Exhibit 3: the segment that is 69.7 per cent of empanelled hospitals received 20.0 per cent of the interviews. She does not say that she would rather have a wrong feature commitment than none.

Hardik Lodha, President for North America, Chicago, argues that those fourteen engineers applied to his denials pipeline would return ₹6.4 crore of new recurring revenue next year. His bonus rides on that number. He does not say that he holds an offer from a competitor in Austin.

Humaira Lilani, principal designer, Lisbon, defends her nineteen cold-recruited interviews as the only genuinely independent evidence Bhoopali has. She does not say that she knew in August that three of her theme boundaries were arguable and chose not to re-code.

Heramb Lamture, staff data scientist, Melbourne, built the overlap estimate and will not let anyone quote it without its assumption: two independent samples let you estimate what you have not seen, two drawn from overlapping lists do not. He does not say that the estimator has never been validated against an outcome here.

Hazel Lotlikar, Head of Customer Success, Manila, can deliver twelve more small-hospital interviews inside a week at ₹9,000 each. She does not say that if her team runs discovery it becomes her function, the promotion she has wanted since March.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Two independent samples let you estimate what you have not seen. My nineteen came off a cold panel; Hazel's sixteen came off our own customer list, and eight of hers are in buildings where my recruiter also got in. That is not independence. Make the true overlap thirteen instead of seventeen and the estimate is sixty-eight themes, of which we have seen 63.2 per cent.”Heramb Lamture, 24 September review call, 11.30 a.m. in Melbourne
“I will not argue with Heramb's mathematics, I will argue with his question. Ninety-three per cent of what our customers have raised with us is already in the backlog. The marginal interview now costs more than the marginal theme.”Hukumchand Lunawat, same call
“Both of you are reading the wrong column. Fourteen interviews went into a segment with 640 hospitals. Seven went into one with 19,800. Why does the sample look like our customer list and not like the market?”Hetal Luthra, same call, from Jaipur
“That column is one of three. On claim value, A and B together are 76.0 per cent of the money and got 68.6 per cent of the interviews; on our own revenue they are 79.6 per cent. You cannot pick the base once you know which answer you want.”Hardik Lodha, by email five days later, 29 September, from Chicago
“I can get you twelve small-hospital conversations by Friday the twenty-third. They are our own customers: no recruiter, nothing to pay — ₹9,000 each, ₹1.08 lakh for the lot.”Hazel Lotlikar, internal chat, 14 October, 2.05 p.m. in Manila
“Then the overlap with your existing sixteen goes up, the estimated total comes down, and the coverage figure on Haimanti's slide improves. The number will get better. I am not sure the knowledge will.”Heramb Lamture, replying four minutes later

8. The options as Haimanti sees them

One: stop, and build. Take Exhibits 2 and 6 at face value, release the ₹4.20 crore on 29 October and make the Doha date. The segments carrying three-quarters of the claim value are the best covered — Exhibit 5 puts segment A at 92.1 per cent and B at 82.1 per cent — and the first release is scoped to a Gulf chain, not to a nursing home in Kanpur. Against it stand Exhibit 5's bottom two rows and Hetal's forty-one lost deals.

Two: twelve warm interviews, finished by 23 October. Hazel's offer costs ₹1.08 lakh, 0.3 per cent of the build, and lands inside the window. The difficulty is Heramb's: these interviewees come from the list that produced the sixteen, so the overlap rises, the estimated total falls and measured coverage improves whether or not anything is learned.

Three: nine cold interviews among small hospitals. At ₹26,000 each this is ₹2.34 lakh, 0.6 per cent of the build, and genuinely independent of everything Bhoopali holds. It cannot be done in time: 240 unworked contacts at an end-to-end rate of 3.9 per cent, and a median lead time of nineteen calendar days from a 19 October start, put the median completion at Saturday 7 November — after the committee, and in the week of Diwali on 8 November.

Four: change the evidence class. Hoshang notes that Bhoopali need not ask anybody: it holds every pre-authorisation rejection reason for its 512 customers. The trouble is the 2023 decision. Of the ₹9,530 crore of claim value on the platform, ₹6,820 crore sits inside the eleven Onsite chains, which send no telemetry, and ₹2,710 crore on the hosted side. Instrumentation would cover 501 of 512 customers, which is 97.9 per cent, but only 51.6 per cent of India ARR and 28.4 per cent of the claim value Bhoopali touches — the mirror image of the interview sample's blind spot. Nobody has noticed that all four options answer “how many more”, and none asks what decision the evidence is for.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The investment committee sits on Thursday, 29 October, with Hormazd Likhite of Beas Growth Trust attending. Hoshang Lotwala, the chief technology officer, has fourteen people committed from 2 November, two of them holding outside offers. Code-complete for the Doha scope is 27 January 2027, nine weeks ahead of the 31 March 2027 production date, with ₹58 lakh of service credit if it slips. The field window before the 29 October committee is seven working days, Dussehra on 20 October removed and Saturdays excluded. Research money is not the constraint: the largest plan on the table, both tracks together, is twenty-one interviews and ₹3.42 lakh, under one per cent of the build. Time, independence and attention are the constraints; the DPDP Act is part of why Bahaar's funnel loses more than half its qualified respondents before scheduling.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 3 reports three share columns. Which is the right denominator for the committee's decision, and what does that choice commit you to?
  2. Exhibit 2 says 82.7 per cent and Exhibit 6 says 93.1 per cent. What is each a share of, and what would make either the figure to act on?
  3. Why does the pooled row of Exhibit 5 sit above three of the four segment rows, and what does that imply about the allocation of the thirty-five interviews?
  4. Heramb argues that Hazel's twelve warm interviews would improve the coverage figure without improving the knowledge. Is he right? Design a version of her plan that would not, and price it in time.
  5. Five of the forty-three themes arrived in September with the National Health Claims Exchange. If the set of problems is itself changing, what work is the word “saturation” doing, and how would you decide to stop?
  6. It is Monday, 19 October, and the memo is due at nine. What do you write, what do you say on 29 October when Hormazd Likhite asks whether the research is finished, and what evidence would change your mind in January?

11. Sunday night, continued

Haimanti scrolled back to the forty-three rows. Against row nineteen was a sentence from a billing clerk at a sixty-bed hospital in Nagpur: we do not chase the insurer, we chase the patient, because the patient comes back. It had been raised once; it was one of the twelve singletons. On Heramb's reading there were nine more like it that nobody had heard. On Hukumchand's, a theme raised once in thirty-five conversations was noise.

She typed a first line, read it, and deleted it. Outside, the rain thickened. In eight hours Hukumchand would want a number. She had three.

How Many Interviews: Judging Saturation When the Decision Is Already Funded

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Friday 16 October 2026, Jagruti Lonkar closed the twenty-third interview of a programme begun thirty-two days earlier, on Monday 14 September. Lonkar is senior product manager for claims at Jaanch Underwriting Systems, a Pune firm selling motor-claims software to general insurers; the product was an assessor copilot that drafts damage estimates from a surveyor's photographs. On Friday 30 October, fourteen days later, Jaanch's board would vote on ₹2.4 crore of engineering over nine months.

Lalchand Satam, who runs enterprise sales, had heard enough: the design partner, Jyotirmay General Insurance, had supplied nine surveyors, eight claims managers and six people from IT and procurement. Kumkum Dharap, who coded every transcript, objected on arithmetical grounds. The surveyor codebook had stopped growing after the seventh interview; the buyer codebook was still climbing at the sixth. Twenty-three interviews is not a number but three numbers, and only one had finished.

Three days later, on Monday 19 October 2026, Keertana Bhoite faced the mirror image in Hyderabad. Bhoite heads product at Lakshan Care Network, a consumer triage and teleconsult app. Over the July–September quarter Lakshan took 3,80,000 installs, of which 95,000 completed a symptom check — 25.0 per cent. Of those, 19,000 booked a teleconsult, 20.0 per cent of the 95,000; 6,650 paid, 35.0 per cent of the 19,000; and 1,330 returned for a second paid consult within sixty days, 20.0 per cent of the 6,650. End to end, 6,650 of 3,80,000 installs paid once — 1.75 per cent — and 1,330 of 3,80,000 paid twice, 0.35 per cent.

Bhoite's team had run twenty-four interviews in the three weeks from Monday 28 September, split across four points in the funnel. On Friday 6 November the company would decide whether to narrow Lakshan to chronic-care follow-up. Jitesh Rajurkar, her growth lead, wanted the fieldwork stopped: three strata had gone quiet. The fourth — repeat payers, on whom the narrowing thesis rested — had produced two new themes on its fifth and last conversation. Both firms faced one question with real money behind it: has the picture stopped changing, or have we stopped looking where it changes?

2. The idea, and the people who disagree about it

Saturation is the point at which further interviews from a defined population stop adding to the distinct ideas that population holds. Defined population: saturation belongs to a sampling frame, never to a product. Distinct ideas: the unit is a code — a recurring concern, recorded once however many people voice it — not a quote or a person. Stop adding: a claim about a rate, judged only against a record of that rate.

The concept solved an embarrassment. Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss, writing on grounded theory in 1967, needed an answer to when a theory-building study was finished, and called it theoretical saturation: stop sampling a category when further cases teach nothing new. The literature that followed — Greg Guest and colleagues in 2006, Monique Hennink later — found most codes in a homogeneous group appear within a dozen interviews.

Those findings are the fault line. The inductive school treats saturation as a judgement about meaning: you are saturated when you can predict the next answer. It will sign that a number fixed in advance is incoherent; it will not sign that any count licenses a stop. The operational school treats it as a measurable property of a code-accrual curve with a rule written before fieldwork; it will sign that a pre-registered rule beats expert feeling because it is auditable, but not that the count generalises. The decision-theoretic school declines the question: the right sample size is where the expected value of another interview falls below its cost. Lonkar needed all three.

3. Mechanics: the parts usually left implicit

Competent practitioners define the segment, code each interview and watch the curve flatten. Experts do four further things, and these decide whether the claim survives a board.

They design cells, not totals. The population is cut, before fieldwork, into cells within which experience should be homogeneous, and each cell gets its own codebook, curve and stopping rule. Jaanch had three cells by role — nine surveyors, eight managers, six buyers; Lakshan four by funnel position, of seven, six, six and five. The totals, twenty-three and twenty-four, are accounting artefacts.

They write the rule before the data. It fixes three parameters: a base of early interviews whose code count is the denominator, a run of later interviews over which new codes are counted, and a threshold below which the run is quiet. Dharap's rule, agreed on 11 September, used a base of four, a run of two and a threshold of 5 per cent. In the surveyor cell the base gave 27 codes; interviews five and six added 4, a ratio of 14.8 per cent; six and seven added 3, 11.1 per cent; seven and eight added 2, 7.4 per cent; eight and nine added none, 0 per cent. The rule fired after the ninth. In the buyer cell the base gave 18 codes and interviews five and six added 3 — 16.7 per cent, three times the threshold. The same twenty-three interviews held one finished cell and one that was not close.

They estimate what they have not seen. A flat curve fits two states of the world: a population whose ideas you have exhausted, and a procedure that keeps returning the same people. Ecology faced this problem counting species. Let S be the codes observed, f1 those seen in exactly one interview and f2 those seen in exactly two; the Chao1 estimate of richness is S + f12 ÷ (2f2). Codes seen once are evidence that others were missed: the weaker the second-sighting rate, the more strangers remain.

Jaanch cellInterviewsCodes observedSeen once (f₁)Seen twice (f₂)Chao1 estimateCoverage of types (%)
Surveyors93312842.078.6
Claims managers8247727.587.3
IT and procurement62111436.158.1
Total2378——105.673.8

Chao1 = S + f₁² ÷ 2f₂. Surveyors: 33 + 144 ÷ 16 = 42.0. Managers: 24 + 49 ÷ 14 = 27.5. Buyers: 21 + 121 ÷ 8 = 36.125, displayed as 36.1. The total 105.6 is the sum of the exact estimates, 42.0 + 27.5 + 36.125 = 105.625, rounded for display; coverage uses the exact values. The 78 codes sum three separate codebooks: nine appear in both the surveyor and manager books, so the union of those two is 33 + 24 − 9 = 48.

The numbers are uncomfortable. The surveyors, declared finished by the rule, hold 33 of an estimated 42 codes — 78.6 per cent. The managers, with one fewer interview, are better covered at 24 of an estimated 27.5, or 87.3 per cent, because their codes repeated: seven singletons against seven doubletons. The buyers sit at 21 of an estimated 36.125, which is 58.1 per cent, and their profile shows why: eleven singletons against four doubletons. Across the three cells, 78 of an estimated 105.625 codes, 73.8 per cent.

They separate coverage of types from coverage of mentions. Across the nine surveyor interviews Dharap recorded 106 code-interview incidences: twelve codes appearing once, eight twice and thirteen between three and nine times, so 12 + 16 + 78 = 106, an average of 106 ÷ 33 = 3.21 incidences per code and 106 ÷ 9 = 11.8 codes per interview. The Good–Turing coverage estimate, 1 − f1 ÷ N, is 1 − 12 ÷ 106 = 88.7 per cent. Two defensible estimators thus disagree about the same nine interviews: 78.6 per cent of the kinds of thing surveyors say, 88.7 per cent of the next thing one will say. A board hearing only the friendlier number is being managed, not informed.

Two curves bend over and run flat against ceilings they nearly reach; the third still climbs, its ceiling drawn far above it. Satam generalised the first two curves to a chart he had not seen. Note too that the manager curve sits lowest and is the best covered: a low ceiling reached beats a high one approached.

4. The conditions, stated as claims you can test

Saturation licenses a stop only when four claims hold. One: the cell is homogeneous enough that one member's experience informs the next. True of Jaanch's surveyors, who do one job under one incentive scheme; false of Lakshan's "paid once, did not return" stratum, which held two populations — those whose problem resolved itself and those whose doctor never answered. Two: recruitment varies independently of the codes. False at Jaanch, where all twenty-three names came through one design partner; partly true at Lakshan. Three: codes are the right unit. True when the decision turns on what problems exist, false when it turns on how common. Four: rare codes do not dominate. Both were exposed: if a code held by 8 per cent of a stratum can kill the product, seven interviews give a 44.2 per cent chance of hearing it — 1 − 0.927 — and 90 per cent confidence needs 28, since 0.9228 = 0.0968. For a code held by a quarter of the stratum, seven suffice: 1 − 0.757 = 86.7 per cent.

Saturation misleads in two situations. The first is a changing population: where behaviour shifts monthly, an accrual curve photographs a moving object, and its flattening describes September, not December. The second is a choice between options nobody has articulated: a flat curve says the complaints have been heard, not which design will be adopted, since codes for an unbuilt thing cannot saturate.

5. Hard edges

Multi-product firms hit the seam first. Jaanch also sells a health pre-authorisation module whose PM wanted to reuse the surveyor findings; the two populations share an employer and nothing else. In two-sided markets cells multiply: saturation is needed per side and per role within a side, so serious marketplace programmes run six to eight cells and accept that the cheapest side saturates first and tells least.

Regulated contexts change the unit. At Jyotirmay General Insurance, claims head Kshipra Phondke described a workflow that IRDAI's turnaround-time rules make non-negotiable; a code raised once about a regulatory constraint is not rare but universal. Expert practice marks codes as constraint or preference before counting and keeps constraints out of Chao1, which assumes a frequency a legal requirement lacks.

Hardware-plus-software widens cells by installation context. Kyaari Irrigation Works, a Nashik firm selling a drip controller with an app, found soil type rather than farmer segment drove the codes: its first eleven interviews on black cotton soil saturated beautifully and transferred not at all to the laterite belt. AI-native products face the opposite distortion, since what users react to changes under them. Likhai Drafting Labs re-ran six interviews after a model upgrade and found four codes about verification habits that could not have existed a month earlier; its PM, Kunjal Terdalkar, now dates every code to a model version, turning the codebook into a time series.

At the organisational seam, maturity inverts: large firms say they interview until saturation, but mostly interview until the internal review is survivable. The honest practice is a standing panel, cells defined once, a versioned codebook, and a rule that every claim names its cell.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

A flat curve is a statement about your recruiter, not your market. The tell is uniformity of sourcing: if everyone came through one channel, the plateau is evidence about the channel. Jaanch's twenty-three names came from one relationship manager, who offered cooperative, articulate staff. The obvious reading — twenty-three is a large sample — is wrong, because independent draws are far fewer than heads.

Singletons are the signal, not the noise. Competent practitioners park a code heard once as weak; experts read the count of such codes as a measure of what is missing, which Chao1 formalises. The tell is a profile with many ones and few twos — the buyer cell's eleven and four. Rare codes look ignorable; their abundance is the evidence of incompleteness.

Coding granularity moves the stopping point more than sample size does. Two researchers given the same nine transcripts produce codebooks differing by a third if one splits where the other merges, and a finer book saturates later. The tell is a codebook growing faster than the interviews late in the run.

Saturation of codes is not saturation of relationships. You can hold every concern and still not know which one blocks the purchase. The tell is a memo listing sixteen problems in no order. Codes accrue early; the causal structure that makes one decisive accrues late, often in the interviews everyone wanted to cancel.

The cell you most need is the hardest to recruit. Repeat payers, enterprise buyers, regulators — the populations that decide the business case do not answer the phone. The tell is a plan whose per-cell counts track ease of access — every default plan. Budget cost per interview by cell; expect the important cell to cost several times the easy one.

A rule that has never said "keep going" is not a rule. The tell is an organisation whose stopping criterion has fired at exactly the planned budget for two years. Pre-registration has teeth only when someone has paid to honour it: Dharap's rule earned authority by forcing six unbudgeted interviews. A second interview with the same person, note, is not a fresh draw and stays out of the frequency counts.

Saturation is cheap to buy and expensive to fake. Six more buyer interviews cost Jaanch 6 × ₹21,000 = ₹1,26,000, which against a ₹2.4 crore build is 0.525 per cent. The tell is a team arguing about three weeks of calendar while a nine-month commitment sits on the same page. Calendar binds, not cash: run cells in parallel, hard one first.

What people say saturates long before what they do. Interview codes converge on a stable account of stated preference; behaviour under real cost may contradict it. The tell is a saturated codebook and no instrumented behaviour. This is the hinge into evidence strength — say, do, pay — and why saturation is a milestone, not a conclusion.

7. Where the differences are real, and where they are not

Across product types the mechanics do not change; the cell structure does. Consumer cells are cut by behaviour, not role, and are cheap: Lakshan's interviews cost ₹1,200 incentive, ₹600 recruiting and ₹3,600 of staff time each, ₹5,400 in all, or ₹1,29,600 for twenty-four — ₹1,29,600 ÷ 76 codes = ₹1,705 per code. B2B and enterprise split by role first, because buyer, user and approver inhabit different problems, and cost rises with seniority: Jaanch spent ₹14,000 per surveyor, ₹18,000 per manager and ₹21,000 per buyer, a total of ₹1,26,000 + ₹1,44,000 + ₹1,26,000 = ₹3,96,000, a blended ₹3,96,000 ÷ 23 = ₹17,217 per interview and ₹3,96,000 ÷ 78 = ₹5,077 per code — just under three times Lakshan's, 5,077 ÷ 1,705 = 2.98.

Cell cost = interviews × cost per interview. The blended figure in the total row is 3,96,000 ÷ 23 = ₹17,217.39, not a column sum.

Platforms and marketplaces differ only in cell count. Hardware differs because installation context is a cell dimension and error costs tooling rather than a sprint. AI products differ because the codebook decays. By stage the difference is real but mis-stated: a seed-stage company is not entitled to fewer interviews for being small, it has fewer cells that matter. The late-stage firm has the reverse problem — abundant access, abundant confirmation, a preference for the curve already flat.

8. Three programmes with numbers

Lakshan, the stratified read. Bhoite's four cells produced 23, 17, 19 and 17 codes from 7, 6, 6 and 5 interviews: 76 codes from 24 interviews across four codebooks. Under the same base-four, run-two, 5 per cent rule, the "checked but never booked" cell was quiet: its base gave 22 codes and interviews five and six added 1, a ratio of 4.5 per cent. The "paid once, did not return" cell looked quiet and was not — a base of 18 codes, interviews five and six adding 1 for 5.6 per cent, just over the line, on a code about follow-up prescriptions never arriving by SMS. The repeat-payer cell was nowhere near: a base of 15 codes, and the fifth interview alone added 2, 13.3 per cent. Its Chao1 estimate is 17 + 81 ÷ 4 = 37.25, so Lakshan holds 17 of an estimated 37.25 repeat-payer codes, 45.6 per cent, against 23 of 25.083 estimated in the easiest cell, 91.7 per cent; its five singletons and six doubletons give 23 + 25 ÷ 12 = 25.083.

Populations are the July–September quarter: 95,000 − 19,000 = 76,000 checked but never booked; 19,000 − 6,650 = 12,350 booked but never paid; 6,650 − 1,330 = 5,320 paid once only; 1,330 repeat payers. The four sum to 95,000, the activated base. The quarter's 7,980 paid consults — 6,650 first plus 1,330 second — at ₹249 each are ₹19,87,020, or ₹19.87 lakh.

Jaanch, the rule that cost money. Dharap asked not for "more research" but for six buyer interviews recruited outside Jyotirmay — two at another insurer, two at a third-party administrator, two at a broker — at ₹21,000 each, ₹1,26,000, which is 0.525 per cent of the ₹2.4 crore at stake. The frequency profile carried the room: eleven singletons against four doubletons in the cell that signs the cheque.

Khoj Field Services, where it failed. Kaivalya Tembe's Jaipur home-repair marketplace ran fourteen customer interviews before its 2 February 2026 launch, all recruited by an in-app prompt. The accrual looked textbook: 6, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1 and then six consecutive zeroes, 19 codes in all, flat from the eighth interview. The team shipped a prepaid-wallet requirement on that basis. A field study of nine customers recruited in person at housing societies, 20 to 28 April 2026, produced 11 codes absent from the original book — so the fourteen pre-launch interviews had held 19 of 30 codes, 63.3 per cent — and three of the eleven called the wallet a reason not to book at all. The in-app recruiter reached only customers comfortable enough to answer a prompt inside the app. Recovery cost ₹46 lakh of rebuilt engineering and shipped on 14 July 2026, seventy-seven days — eleven weeks — after the study closed. Two off-channel interviews, about ₹11,000, would have caught it in February.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Single-channel recruitment. Early sign: everyone describes the same workaround in the same words. Diagnostic: how was each person found, and who was not asked? Cost if caught late: Khoj's ₹46 lakh and eleven weeks.

Cell collapse. Early sign: a memo that says "users" with no qualifier. Diagnostic: which cell does this claim belong to, and what is its code count? Cost: a product built for the easiest cell, not the paying one.

Threshold drift. Early sign: the rule is restated after the data arrives. Diagnostic: show me the rule and its date. Cost: the evidentiary value of the programme.

Stopping before the hard cell starts. Early sign: the hardest-to-recruit cell is scheduled last. Diagnostic: if we stopped today, which cell has fewest interviews, and does it carry the thesis? Cost: Lakshan's exposure — a narrowing decision on 45.6 per cent coverage.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The inductive position at its strongest: codes are interpretive constructs, not countable objects, so feeding counts to an ecological estimator imports a false assumption — that codes exist independently of the coder with a fixed frequency. Its evidence is the literature on inter-coder variation, where codebooks differ by a third. It would be wrong if independent teams coding one corpus converged on richness while differing on labels, and there is some evidence.

The operational position, steelmanned: research that cannot be audited cannot be trusted with other people's capital, and a pre-registered base-run-threshold rule converts connoisseurship into a claim a sceptic can check. Its evidence is the Guest-style work and the observation that teams without rules stop when budgets end. It would be wrong if such rules systematically stopped programmes before the decisive code arrived, and Lakshan's 5.6 per cent cell is a near-miss.

The decision-theoretic position: saturation is the wrong target, since the question is never "have we heard everything" but "would another interview change what we do". Its evidence is the asymmetry in every case here — ₹1,26,000 against ₹2.4 crore. It would be wrong if the value of information could not be estimated in advance, which is the standing objection: you cannot price a surprise you have not had. Nobody holds a synthesis, so the honest practitioner picks per decision.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this quotes a number — twelve, or five to eight — and reports a total. Someone who has internalised it never states a count without a cell, lets the written rule overrule them, reads the singleton-to-doubleton ratio before the curve, and prices the next interview against the decision. Asked how many interviews they ran, they answer with a structure, not a number.

12. What each of them decided

Lonkar took Dharap's recommendation to the board on 30 October and asked for the ₹2.4 crore in two tranches: ₹38 lakh for a nine-week assessor-facing prototype, with the remaining ₹2.02 crore — ₹240 lakh less ₹38 lakh — released only once the six off-channel buyer interviews were in. Surveyor evidence at 78.6 per cent coverage was strong enough to build against; buyer evidence at 58.1 per cent could not carry a year of engineering built on one insurer's procurement story.

Bhoite did the opposite of what her growth lead wanted. She closed the three quiet cells and commissioned nine further repeat-payer interviews — recruited by telephone from the 1,330, by a researcher who had not run the first five — at ₹5,400 each, ₹48,600, reporting by 4 December. The narrowing decision moved from 6 November to mid-December. Her justification ran to one line: a thesis about repeat payers cannot rest on the cell with the fewest interviews and worst coverage.

Three questions. First: the rule fired on the surveyor cell at nine interviews, yet Chao1 put its coverage at 78.6 per cent — tighten the rule, or is that the right place to stop when the alternative is calendar time? Second: all twenty-three Jaanch interviews came through one design partner; what is the smallest change that would most improve the programme's evidentiary value? Third: Bhoite spent ₹48,600 on a 1,330-person segment while 76,000 sit in the cell she closed — defend that allocation, or argue against it.

13. Going deeper

Interview fundamentals — saturation means nothing unless interviews produce signal. Evidence strength: say, do, pay — how much hearing weighs, and the move to experiment. Qualitative versus quantitative research — why codes and prevalences are different currencies. Designing an interview guide — coding grain and guide structure are one decision made twice. Recruiting research participants — what decides whether a flat curve means anything. Cognitive biases in research — how teams declare saturation they have not reached. Synthesising research — what to do with 78 codes. AI-assisted synthesis — cheap frequency profiles, and hidden grain drift.

How Many Interviews: Knowing When More Conversations Stop Changing the Picture

1. The decision on the table

On Monday 4 May 2026, Aditi Chhabra, a product manager at Bharan Warehousing Exchange, laid twelve interview summaries across a meeting-room table in Hyderabad. Bharan is a marketplace that lets owners of idle warehouse space, typically 2,000 to 10,000 square feet along the Medchal and Shamshabad corridors, rent it by the month to small traders. Between 6 April and 1 May she had interviewed twelve warehouse owners. On Friday 15 May the board would decide whether to release ₹60 lakh for a pilot built on what those conversations had shown.

Baldev Chauhan, the head of sales, wanted a short answer. "Twelve is plenty," he said. "Every interview after the fifth sounded the same." Chitra Anand, the research lead, was less sure: the last twelve days had produced one fresh surprise, and she could not tell whether that was the tail of a curve or the first sign of a second one. Another three interviews would cost about ₹28,500 and a week. Being wrong about stopping would cost a pilot designed around a partial picture of the owners, and ₹60 lakh is the exposure.

ItemFigure
Interviews completed (owners)12
Pilot spend at stake₹60,00,000 (₹60 lakh)
Cost of three more interviews₹28,500
Extra cost as share of pilot spend (28,500 ÷ 60,00,000)0.475%

The asymmetry in the last row is why the question deserves rigour: further interviews are cheap relative to the decision. It does not, however, mean more is always better, as the next sections show.

2. The idea: saturation

Saturation is the point in a qualitative study at which additional interviews stop producing new themes. A theme here means a distinct pattern in what people say, such as "owners distrust advance payments from strangers", recorded once however many people mention it. The idea comes from grounded theory, which the sociologists Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss introduced in 1967 to build explanations from observation rather than from hypotheses, and which they called theoretical saturation. Later researchers, notably Greg Guest and colleagues in 2006, tested it empirically and found that most themes in a homogeneous group surfaced within the first twelve interviews, with the bulk visible after six.

The problem it was designed to solve is arbitrary stopping: researchers quitting when the budget ended or when a story felt familiar. A survey has a sample-size formula because it estimates how common something is. An interview programme estimates something different, namely what kinds of things exist. Counting heads is the wrong tool for that task. Chitra's sentence, the one Aditi could repeat without sounding glib, was this: "We stop when a new interview from the same kind of person no longer teaches us anything we did not already know, and we have checked that claim rather than felt it."

3. How it works, step by step

The mechanics are less mysterious than the vocabulary. First, define the segment: the group of people whose experience you are trying to understand. Saturation is only ever claimed for one segment at a time. Second, after each interview, code the notes: list the themes heard, matching them against a running master list. Third, record for each interview how many themes were new, meaning absent from every earlier interview. Fourth, plot the running total and watch its slope.

The step practitioners leave implicit is the fifth: set the stopping rule before looking at the data. Bharan's rule, agreed on 6 April, was two consecutive interviews with zero new themes, never before the eighth interview. Without a rule written in advance, a hopeful researcher finds a reason to stop at every plateau. The sixth step is a deliberate attempt to disconfirm: seek the owner least like the earlier ones, since a theme never found by the easy interviews is the likeliest to be missing.

4. A worked example

Chitra's coding log for the twelve owner interviews is below. "Cumulative" is the running sum of the "new themes" column.

InterviewNew themesCumulative themes
