Total26n/a (running column)

The new-theme column sums to 7 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 26. By interview 6 the team held 23 of 26 themes, or 88 per cent (23 ÷ 26 = 88.5 per cent, rounded down); by interview 9, 25 of 26, or 96 per cent. Interviews 11 and 12 both added nothing, so the rule was met. Baldev was right that the fifth interview onward sounded familiar: five interviews had yielded 21 of 26 themes, 81 per cent. But the tenth interview, which produced a lone theme about owners fearing tenants who store flammable goods, shows why "sounds the same" is a poor test. It matters to the product's insurance clause.

Cost is straightforward. Each interview carried ₹2,000 for the owner's time plus ₹1,500 of travel, ₹3,500 in cash, and five staff hours (two interviewing, three coding) at ₹1,200 an hour, ₹6,000. That is ₹9,500 an interview: twelve cost ₹1,14,000, and three more cost ₹28,500.

Second pass: change one input

The pilot needs renters as well as owners, and Chitra proposed three renter interviews. Saturation in one segment says nothing about another. Interview 13, with a Secunderabad e-commerce seller, produced four new themes; interview 14 two; interview 15 none. The total became 26 + 4 + 2 + 0 = 32. The first twelve interviews had therefore uncovered only 26 of 32 themes, 81 per cent, and six themes, 19 per cent, belonged to a segment nobody had sampled.

The chart repays a slow reading. The owners' curve rises steeply and bends over, the shape saturation predicts. The step at interview 13 is not a failure of the first twelve. It is the same method reporting that a new population had begun.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Saturation belongs to a segment, not to a product

The renter step above is the pattern. State the segment before you state the count: "saturated for owners with 2,000 to 10,000 square feet on the Medchal corridor" is a claim; "saturated" alone is not.

A theme is not a quote, and coding is a judgement

Two coders can split or merge the same remarks differently, and more splitting means more themes and later saturation. Fix the coding definitions in advance, and have a second person code two or three interviews independently.

Saturation is not statistical significance

Twelve interviews cannot tell you that 70 per cent of owners dislike advance payments. They tell you that the objection exists and what it sounds like. Prevalence needs a survey, which should come after interviews, since interviews supply the questions worth asking.

The chance of hearing a theme is arithmetic

If a theme is held by a fraction p of the segment and interviewees are drawn independently, the chance of hearing it at least once in n interviews is 1 − (1 − p)n. For p = 20 per cent and n = 12, that is 1 − 0.812 = 1 − 0.0687 = 93 per cent. For p = 10 per cent, 1 − 0.912 = 72 per cent, and after fifteen interviews 79 per cent. A theme held by one owner in ten still has more than a one-in-four chance of having been missed at interview 12. To be 95 per cent sure of catching a 10 per cent theme you need 29 interviews (0.929 = 0.047), and 14 for a 20 per cent theme (0.814 = 0.044).

Rare themes can be the important ones

Saturation is a statement about common themes. A once-in-ten risk, such as a flammable-goods dispute, can sink a pilot. Decide whether the stakes justify chasing rare themes; if so, the sample goes up to the 29 above.

Recruiting bias defeats the count

If all twelve owners came from Bharan's existing contacts, they share networks and opinions, and a flat curve may mean only that you keep talking to the same kind of person. Disconfirming recruits matter more than additional ones.

Diminishing returns are not zero returns

A flat curve means the marginal interview adds little to this picture. It may still add a vivid quote or a better phrasing, which is why teams sometimes continue after saturation for persuasion rather than discovery.

What it cannot tell you

Saturation says nothing about whether what people say matches what they do or will pay for. That question belongs to the next topic in this module, evidence strength: what customers say, what they do, and what they pay.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace products, early and late

ContextSegments to saturateTypical consequence
ConsumerUsually one dominant behaviour group, but several if age or city differ sharply6 to 12 per group is common
B2BBuyer, user and approver are different people in the same accountEach role needs its own run; a buyer's view does not stand in for the user's
MarketplaceAt least two sides, as Bharan found: owners and rentersSaturation counted separately per side, so the total is higher

The early-stage company has fewer people to recruit and more unknowns, so it reaches saturation slowly and gains most from each conversation. A large company usually has the opposite problem: abundant access, such as support logs and account managers, and a tendency to treat the first familiar answers as the picture. It should hold itself to the written stopping rule and the disconfirming recruit more strictly, because nobody is short of data to confirm what they already believe.

7. Common mistakes

Stopping on a number. Symptom: the plan says "five interviews" with no segment attached. Misunderstanding: that the number rather than the curve is the rule. Cheapest diagnostic: ask "what was the new-theme count for the last two?"

Declaring saturation across segments. Symptom: owners' findings used to justify renter features. Misunderstanding: that a topic, not a population, saturates. Diagnostic: ask who each interviewee was, and whether the segment label appears on the log.

Counting the same person twice. Symptom: a flat curve that came from interviewing three people from one warehouse group. Misunderstanding: that independence is automatic. Diagnostic: tabulate how each interviewee was recruited, and look for clusters.

Reading flat as true. Symptom: team confidence rises while no one has asked a sceptic. Misunderstanding: that saturation validates the themes, rather than merely exhausting them. Diagnostic: interview one person who should disagree.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Aditi's week looks different in four ways. The stopping rule was written on 6 April. The coding log is a table of interviews against themes, not a folder of notes. The segment is named in every claim. And the team has two numbers on the page, themes found and the chance that a 10 per cent theme remains unheard, so the board debates a risk it can see. A good memo ends: "Owners: 26 themes, saturated at interview 12 under the agreed rule; renters: 3 interviews, not saturated; risk of an unheard 1-in-10 owner theme about 28 per cent (1 − 0.718)."

9. What Aditi decided

She proposed to the board that the owner research be treated as complete and that renter research continue. Her reasoning was in the numbers: owners had met their rule, 26 of 26 themes found; renters had given six new themes in three interviews, so the picture was incomplete. She asked for five more renter interviews, at 5 × ₹9,500 = ₹47,500, completed by Friday 29 May, and for the pilot approval to depend on them. Baldev accepted when the figure was set beside ₹60 lakh.

The next topic, evidence strength, asks how much weight each interview's content should carry once you have it. Two questions to sit with: if the board asked what you would do were the renter curve to keep rising after ten interviews, what would your answer be? And which segment in a product you know has never been interviewed at all?

Twelve Stores Later: How Many Interviews Are Enough?

1. Opening

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Sneha Bedekar sat in a corner of the Pune office of Maitri Shelf Labs with a laptop, a cold cup of chai and a deadline. On Friday, 30 October, the board would be asked to release ₹62 lakh to build a reorder-and-credit module and take it to Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. As head of product, she had to tell the board whether the evidence behind that module was sufficient, or whether more customer interviews were needed first. Fieldwork was possible for only two more weeks. Dussehra fell on 20 October, and from the first days of November kirana owners would be too absorbed in Diwali, on 8 November, to give anyone an hour.

She had twelve interviews on file. Her chief executive thought that was plenty. Her sales head thought it was a Maharashtra sample being asked to speak for a subcontinent.

2. Company background

Maitri Shelf Labs, founded in 2019 by Saurabh Banerji and two classmates from Pune, sells a phone app to neighbourhood grocery stores. It replaces the paper khata with a digital ledger, tracks which items are running low and nudges the owner to reorder from a wholesaler. In October 2026 it had 9,200 paying stores, almost all in Maharashtra, at ₹399 a month, which is an annual revenue run-rate of roughly ₹4.40 crore.

The market is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the idea of the digital khata, while Udaan, Jumbotail and Reliance Retail's JioMart Partner pull stores towards their own wholesale catalogues. PhonePe for Business and Paytm's Soundbox sit on the counter already, and ONDC promises open networks that could, in time, route a store's orders anywhere. Maitri's edge is the narrow one of knowing a Maharashtra grocer's week well, which is precisely why its founders worried about leaving Maharashtra.

3. The situation

Sneha had run the interviews herself with a product designer and a researcher. Each lasted about 45 minutes, in Marathi or Hindi, in the shop, at the counter, while customers came and went. Interviews 1 to 5 were in Pune, 6 to 9 in Nashik and 10 to 12 in Kolhapur. Each cost ₹18,000, covering a ₹1,500 thank-you voucher, ₹4,500 for a recruiting partner, ₹6,000 for travel and translation, and ₹6,000 for transcription and synthesis, so the twelve had cost ₹2.16 lakh.

After every conversation, Shreya Bendre, the data scientist, coded the transcripts into distinct problem themes: a store owner forgetting to chase a credit customer, say, or ordering from three wholesalers because none holds every brand. Exhibit 1 shows what she found. The first interview produced seven themes, the second five, and the discoveries tapered: by interview 7 the team had 23 themes, interview 9 added the twenty-fourth, and interviews 10, 11 and 12 added nothing at all. Twelve conversations had produced 24 themes in all, and the last three were pure repetition.

That was the comfortable reading. The less comfortable one came from Lucknow, where Sailesh Bagwe had sat through forty distributor demonstrations since August. He reported that owners there kept asking about cash-on-delivery settlement and about suppliers who deliver only on alternate days, neither of which appeared anywhere in the twenty-four themes. In London, Samantha Brandt, the designer, noted that the prototype would need six weeks regardless, so every week of delay in deciding was a week of design lost.

4. The people

Saurabh Banerji, chief executive, Pune. He has promised the board a plan and believes the curve in Exhibit 1 is flat, so the question is answered. He wants the money released on 30 October.

Sailesh Bagwe, head of sales, Lucknow. He carries the expansion revenue target and does not want to launch something that a Lucknow grocer will dismiss in one demo. He wants interviews in Uttar Pradesh first.

Samantha Brandt, lead designer, London. She works from a different clock, starting when Pune is finishing lunch, and wants a firm brief this month. She is indifferent to the exact number as long as it arrives quickly.

Shreya Bendre, data scientist, Austin. She built the theme coding and is wary of the word saturation. In her view the curve shows the sample has stopped surprising her, which is a different thing from the market having stopped surprising anyone.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the per-interview theme counts. Exhibit 2 is Shreya's estimate of how likely a sample of a given size is to miss a problem entirely. Exhibit 3 prices the choices facing Sneha.

If a problem affects a share p of stores, the chance that n random interviews all miss it is (1 − p) raised to the power n. For a problem hurting one store in four, five interviews miss it with probability 0.755, which is 23.7%.

6. The options

Option A: build now. Exhibit 1 shows no new theme in the last three conversations, and Exhibit 2 says that a problem hitting one store in four would escape twelve random interviews just 3.2% of the time. The upside is speed: Samantha starts the brief next week and the board sees decisiveness. The cost is that all twelve stores sit in three Maharashtra cities, so the 3.2% applies only to Maharashtra. If Uttar Pradesh or Tamil Nadu stores hold different problems, ₹62 lakh gets spent against an incomplete picture.

Option B: eight more in Maharashtra. This reaches twenty interviews for ₹1.44 lakh and drives the miss probability for a one-in-four problem to 0.3%. Yet the last three interviews already returned zero new themes, so the likeliest harvest is more of the same, and the cost is roughly two weeks.

Option C: three each in Lucknow and Coimbatore. Six interviews, ₹1.80 lakh, eighteen in all. Three interviews cannot saturate a region; with a one-in-four problem, three miss it 42.2% of the time. But the purpose is to test whether the picture changes, and a new theme in the first conversations would be decisive. The cost is the extra expense and, with Diwali near, a tight fortnight.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Read Exhibit 1. What does it show about the sample, and what does it not show about the market? Why did Shreya hesitate over the word saturation?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, how would you explain to Saurabh what a 3.2% chance of missing a problem does and does not cover?
  3. Sailesh reports themes from forty demonstrations that no interview surfaced. How much weight should that evidence carry compared with the twelve interviews, and why?
  4. Rank Options A, B and C using Exhibit 3, and say what result from the new interviews would change your ranking.

8. A note for the learner

This topic reframes the question. How many interviews are enough is not a number to be looked up; it is a judgement about when additional conversations stop changing the picture. Two tests apply. The first is the shape of the discovery curve: new themes per interview should fall to zero and stay there for several conversations. The second is coverage: the people interviewed must resemble the people the decision will affect. A flat curve certifies the first test, and says nothing on the second.

A well-reasoned answer therefore separates what is saturated from what is untested. Maharashtra is saturated: seven, five, four, three, two, one, one, zero, one, zero, zero, zero, a curve that reached 24 and stopped. Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu are unobserved, and Sailesh’s two unmatched themes are a warning that they differ.

One defensible path is Option C with a stopping rule agreed in advance. Interview three stores in each of Lucknow and Coimbatore before 28 October. If the first three in a city produce two or more themes absent from the 24, extend that city for three more interviews and ask the board to hold the build briefly; if they produce none, release the ₹62 lakh on 30 October with the evidence stated honestly. Option B buys comfort where the evidence is strongest. Option A is the right call only if the expansion were confined to Maharashtra. The extra ₹1.80 lakh is 2.9% of the build, a modest premium against a ₹62 lakh decision the existing sample cannot yet speak for.
case20v1-res.recruiting:
Padosi Services: Finding the People Who Run Short

A teaching case on recruiting research participants

1. Opening

On the morning of Thursday 29 October 2026, Aditi Easwar, a senior product manager at Padosi Services, sat in the company's Pune office with a one-page brief and a calendar. The brief described a proposed product called Padosi Advance, a small earnings advance of ₹5,000 to ₹15,000 that a service partner (an electrician, plumber or carpenter) could draw against jobs already booked, repaid automatically from the next payouts. The calendar showed 25 days to the product council on Monday 23 November, where Aditi had to defend either a build, a pilot or a stop.

Her chief executive had been plain: the council would not fund a lending feature on a survey. It wanted twelve real conversations with partners who had actually run short of cash in recent weeks, summarised in a problem memo. Aditi had a research budget of ₹2.5 lakh and one decision to take that day: how to find those twelve people. Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November, and every partner she hoped to meet would be at full stretch until then.

2. Company background

Padosi Services, founded in 2019, lets households in 14 Indian cities book vetted home-repair professionals through an app. It keeps roughly 18 per cent of each booking and pays the partner by UPI within 48 hours. Annual booking value is about ₹640 crore, which implies net revenue near ₹115 crore. It competes with Urban Company at the premium end, with JustDial listings and neighbourhood contractors at the low end.

The company has 42,000 registered partners. Partner churn had risen through 2026, and the product team suspected cash was part of the reason. Partners buy wire, fittings and tools up front and are paid after the job, so a slow fortnight can push a skilled worker toward a competitor that pays the same day.

3. The situation

Aditi had already tested three ways of recruiting. Between Monday 12 and Sunday 25 October, her team ran a two-week pilot of each channel against the same screener: had the partner run short of cash for tools or materials in the last 30 days, and did it cost them a job? A partner who answered yes was counted as having a live problem. Exhibit 1 sets out what each channel produced.

Exhibit 1. Recruiting pilot, 12 to 25 October 2026

Cost per live-problem interview is channel cost divided by interviews in the channel with a live cash problem. The total row divides total cost by total interviews (25 and 11), not by the mean of the channel figures.

Referrals were cheapest per completed interview at ₹3,000 and the screener pass rate was 80 per cent (20 of 25), but only 2 of the 8 completed conversations involved a recent cash problem. The panel passed 18 of 60, or 30 per cent, and delivered 10 interviews, of which 3 had a live problem. Direct outreach passed only 21 of 90, about 23 per cent, and cost ₹8,000 per completed interview, yet 6 of its 7 conversations were with partners in the middle of the problem, which made it the cheapest of the three at ₹9,333 for each live-problem interview.

Exhibit 2, from the data team, splits the partner base by recent activity and counts support tickets that mentioned a cash gap in the last six months.

The team's views of the situation differed by location. In Nagpur, partner-success staff said the real pain arrived in the fortnight before festivals, when wire and switchgear prices climbed. In Lisbon, the design team wanted research that could be scheduled and recorded cleanly. In Montreal, the data scientist saw a population already identifiable in the database. Any recording needed written consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and any lending partner would follow the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions.

4. The people

Aditi Easwar, senior product manager, Pune, owns the Padosi Advance brief and must deliver the problem memo.

Alok Eapen, head of partner success, Nagpur, manages 40 relationship managers. He would rather Aditi use referrals: he can supply eight partners within a week, and he worries that cold calls to lapsed partners will annoy people the company still hopes to win back.

Ananya Edathil, lead designer, Lisbon, favours the panel vendor. Five and a half hours behind Pune, she wants fixed slots, translators and recordings she can share with her team without chasing individuals.

Aamir Ekka, data scientist, Montreal, argues that the lapsed segment is where the signal lies and offers to build a call list of 300 names from job history in two days. He cautions that lapsed partners left for many reasons.

5. Timeline

Figure 1. Dates and labels only; spacing is schematic.

6. The options

Option A: buy a panel. The vendor can fill twelve recorded, translated slots by 20 November. At Exhibit 1's ₹10,500 per completed interview, twelve interviews cost ₹1,26,000. The pilot's live-problem rate of 3 in 10 implies about four useful conversations. The upside is speed and tidy evidence. The cost is that panel members are experienced respondents who answer surveys for pay, and most were not living the problem.

Option B: use referrals from partner success. Alok's team can deliver quickly and cheaply: twelve interviews at ₹3,000 come to ₹36,000. The pilot rate of 2 in 8 implies about three live-problem conversations. The upside is trust and low cost. The cost is selection: relationship managers nominate partners they like, who are active and in good standing, and Exhibit 2 shows that segment raises a quarter of the lapsed segment's tickets per head.

Option C: go to where the pain happens. Aamir builds a list of lapsed partners with a past cash-gap ticket, and Aditi's team adds visits to the wholesaler counters in Nagpur and Indore, where partners buy wire on credit. Twelve interviews at ₹8,000 come to ₹96,000, and the pilot rate of 6 in 7 implies roughly ten live-problem conversations. The upside is relevance. The cost is effort, a pass rate near 23 per cent, and the risk of upsetting partners who left unhappy.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Which segment of Padosi's partner base is most likely to hold the problem Padosi Advance would solve, and what in Exhibit 2 supports your answer?

2. Using Exhibit 1, compare the three channels by cost per completed interview and by cost per live-problem interview. Why do the rankings differ, and which measure should Aditi trust?

3. What biases does each option carry, and what would you do in the screener and the interview guide to reduce them?

4. Which option, or combination, would you recommend to the council, and what evidence would make you change your mind?

8. A note for the learner

This topic reframes the question. The decision is not how many people to interview but where to find those who have the problem now. A channel should be judged by how much of what it delivers is relevant, not by how cheaply it delivers bodies. Exhibit 1 shows this: referrals are cheapest per completed interview, yet direct outreach is cheapest per live-problem interview, and the panel, which looks efficient, is the costliest on that measure. Exhibit 2 tells you where to look, because moments of pain leave traces in the data.

A well-reasoned answer picks a channel by the likelihood that its people are in the moment of pain, names the bias that remains, and sets a screener that enforces it. One defensible path is Option C as the main route, with the screener of Exhibit 1 unchanged. Twelve interviews would cost about ₹96,000, leaving roughly ₹1.54 lakh of the ₹2.5 lakh budget for incentives, translators and a second wave. Aditi should use Aamir's list for the lapsed segment, work the Nagpur and Indore counters in the week after Diwali, and ask Alok for two or three referrals as a deliberate contrast group. She should start calling on Monday 9 November, once the festival rush has ended, and finish by Friday 20 November, three days before the council meets.

The risks are real. Seven interviews is a thin basis for a rate, so the memo should speak of patterns, not percentages. Lapsed partners may have left for reasons unconnected to cash, so the guide should ask about the last time work stopped before it mentions money. Consent for recording must be taken in writing in the partner's own language. If those conversations show that partners borrow informally and cheaply from wholesalers, the right recommendation could be a stop.
exp40v2-res.recruiting:
Recruiting Research Participants

Discovery & Design › Qualitative Research. Where do I find the people who actually have this problem?

1. Two companies, six weeks, one sampling problem

On Monday 5 October 2026, Roopal Ramaswamy, head of product at Rivaaj Field Systems in Chennai, had thirty-nine days to settle an eight-month argument. Rivaaj sells maintenance and compliance software to hospital chains: equipment servicing, the paperwork NABH accreditation demands, and the engineers who do the work. Sixteen accounts at an average contract value of ₹55 lakh gave it ₹8.80 crore of recurring revenue, and five — ₹48, ₹52, ₹60, ₹65 and ₹75 lakh, ₹3.00 crore — came up for renewal before the board review of Friday 13 November.

The argument was about whom the next two quarters belonged to. Rathin Ojha, Rivaaj's founder, wanted an analytics dashboard for the quality heads who sign and who answer email. Roopal suspected the renewals turned on something less visible — that of 1,240 licensed users only 434 were weekly active (35.0 per cent), because ward engineers wrote readings on paper and keyed them in later, if at all. Nine engineers at ₹1.80 lakh a month cost ₹16.20 lakh a month, so two quarters came to ₹97.20 lakh, and the people who could answer sat behind their own managers.

Three days later Ruchira Rajwade met the same problem from the other side. She is VP product at Riyaaz Hearing Labs in Ahmedabad, which makes a behind-the-ear hearing aid and an app that tunes it. Riyaaz shipped 18,400 devices in FY26 at an average realised price of ₹14,500 — ₹26.68 crore — and took back 1,490 of those 18,400 within ninety days, a return rate of 8.1 per cent. A tooling decision fell due on Friday 20 November: ₹62 lakh of mould, fourteen weeks of lead time, for a rechargeable battery and cradle or a directional two-microphone array. Her researcher Rudrani Rohra and a contract audiologist in Zagreb, Renata Oreskovic, agreed on the diagnosis. Riyaaz's database held buyers, mostly the adult children who paid; whoever could settle the question had bought a device and stopped using it, and nobody had their number.

The decision at stakeRivaaj Field SystemsRiyaaz Hearing Labs
Product typeEnterprise B2B softwareHardware plus app
Scene dateMon 5 Oct 2026Thu 8 Oct 2026
Hard deadlineFri 13 Nov 2026Fri 20 Nov 2026
Days available3943
Money committed by the decision₹97.20 lakh (two quarters, nine-person squad)₹62.00 lakh (mould tooling)
Revenue exposed if wrong₹3.00 crore of renewals₹26.68 crore run-rate
Research budget approved₹4.00 lakh₹3.50 lakh

Exhibit 1. Each firm spends about one per cent of the committed sum on finding out whom to ask. The asymmetry is not the interesting part; the sample's composition is.

2. The idea, and the five schools that disagree about it

Participant recruitment is the joint design of four things: the qualifying event that defines eligibility, the frame from which candidates are drawn, the screening instrument that sorts them, and the incentive and consent regime under which they agree — chosen so that variation in the sample spans the variation that could change the decision. That last clause is the whole discipline: recruiting is not a search for typical people but the deliberate construction of disagreement.

It was invented against a failure hard to see from inside: teams talked to whoever was reachable, then could not tell whether a pattern came from the world or from the frame. Glaser and Strauss, in The Discovery of Grounded Theory (1967), proposed theoretical sampling — choose the next participant from what the last taught you, and stop when interviews stop changing the categories. Market research, chastened by the quota-sampling failures of the 1948 American election polls, fixed composition in advance against a known population. Human factors, formalised by Nielsen and Landauer's 1993 discovery curve, held that a handful of participants finds most usability defects — a claim about tasks over-applied to problem discovery ever since. Customer development — Blank in 2005, Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test in 2013, Moesta's switch interviews — made eligibility an event: whoever changed something in the last ninety days still holds the memory. Research operations has since added a fifth position: recruitment is infrastructure.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
Theoretical samplingComposition is decided interview by interviewFix the quota before fieldwork begins
Quota and representativenessComposition must be fixed in advance against the populationTwenty interviews can settle a problem question
Discount usabilityFive participants surface most defects in a known taskFive participants tell you which problem to solve
Switch interviewingOnly a recent decision can be reconstructed reliablyNon-adopters are the best informants about demand
Research operationsA firm should own a consented participant poolConvenience inside your own pool is harmless

Exhibit 2. The five positions do not reconcile. Section 10 returns to the two that bite hardest.

3. Mechanics: the funnel is a rate chain, and the cell is the constraint

Expert practice runs six stages: people reached, people who replied, people who qualified, people scheduled, people who showed up, interviews completed. Each rate is the count divided by the stage above it. Over the three weeks from Monday 12 October to Friday 30 October, Rudrani ran five channels: intercepts at two partner ENT clinics; six WhatsApp groups of senior-citizen associations; a panel from Rozmarra Panel Network at ₹6,800 per interview; a two-ward sweep by Rubaru Fieldwork Services at ₹1.10 lakh fixed; and Riyaaz's buyer database. Every channel but the panel paid ₹1,200.

Senior associations600483620161536,0002,400

Exhibit 3. Riyaaz pilot, 12–30 October 2026. ENT = ₹40,000 + 12 × ₹1,200; associations = ₹18,000 + 15 × ₹1,200; sweep = ₹1,10,000 + 11 × ₹1,200; panel = 9 × ₹6,800; database = 9 × ₹1,200; blended = ₹2,85,600 ÷ 56.

The rates repay slow reading. The clinic qualified 48 of 120 repliers (40.0 per cent): a hearing clinic's waiting room is pre-filtered by the event Riyaaz cares about. The associations replied at 48 of 600 (8.0 per cent) yet qualified 36 of 48 (75.0 per cent) — self-selection, since in a cold channel replying is itself a screening step. The panel inverted this: 100 of 200 replied, but 20 of 100 qualified (20.0 per cent), the mark of respondents who answer everything.

Two steps are usually left implicit, and both matter more than the channel mix. The first is the disqualifier list: Rudrani excluded profound loss, which needs a different device class, and purchases inside thirty days, which have no abandonment story yet. The second is scheduling discipline: 166 qualified and 74 were scheduled, a gap that is not leakage but Rudrani closing cells as they filled. Keeping the list of the 92 qualified-but-not-scheduled is the only record of your own selection rule.

The formal treatment is an inversion. If a channel's stage rates multiply to p, the reach required for n completions is n ÷ p. But a decision rarely needs total completions; it needs completions in one cell. Define the cell yield as completions in the target segment divided by people reached. Riyaaz's cell was people who had bought a hearing aid and abandoned it. The clinic produced 2 from 240 reached — 1 in 120, so twelve abandoner interviews would need 1,440 approaches.

This is the central arithmetic of the topic. Riyaaz's blended cost per interview was ₹5,100, defensible in any budget meeting; its cost per decision-relevant interview was ₹31,733, six times higher. Every channel ranking built on cost per interview answers a question nobody asked.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be put as testable claims. First, the decision must be sensitive to composition: Riyaaz's tooling choice turns on abandoners, 9 of 56 interviews (16.1 per cent). Second, the event must be recent enough to remember and rare enough to screen for: abandonment within the last year qualifies, "finds conversation difficult" does not. Third, a frame must exist in which the event is denser than in the population: the clinic waiting room is one, while no frame of ward engineers exists outside Rivaaj's customers' employment records. Fourth, a wrong decision must cost far more than recruiting: ₹62 lakh against ₹3.50 lakh.

The idea actively misleads in three situations. When the question is about a task — can a user complete the tuning flow — five participants from almost any frame will do, and ₹31,733 a head on composition is waste. When it is about prevalence, interviews cannot answer at all: Rivaaj has a telemetry log, and should count rather than ask. And when a product has no users and no analogue, the event has not happened, so nobody is at the moment of pain; the honest move is to recruit for the surrounding event, such as a recent purchase of a substitute.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Enterprise is hardest, because recruiting runs through a gatekeeper with a stake in the answer. Rivaaj's funnel had a stage Riyaaz's did not: access. Omana Ruikar, Rivaaj's researcher in Kochi, asked all sixteen account owners in customer success for introductions. Eleven replied (68.8 per cent of 16), seven obtained a sponsor's agreement, and those seven accounts nominated twelve engineers each — 84 names, of whom 48 replied, 36 qualified and 28 were interviewed. A cold route through two technicians' WhatsApp groups and a biomedical-engineering association reached 700 people, of whom 84 replied (12.0 per cent), 30 qualified and 18 were interviewed: 46 in all.

StageNominated routeCold route
Frame16 accounts asked700 engineers reached
Replied11 accounts84 engineers

Candidates available84 nominated84 replied

In top usage quartile234

Exhibit 5. Rivaaj, 7–30 October 2026. Procurement rules barred honoraria to staff, so the nominated route paid ₹2,000 per interview into each hospital's welfare fund; the cold route paid ₹2,500 each plus ₹60,000 of sponsorship. Top quartile = the 310 heaviest of 1,240 users.

The penultimate row holds the most useful number here. Were managers nominating at random, a quarter of the 28 would sit in the top usage quartile — about seven. In fact 23 of 28 did (82.1 per cent), while on the cold route 4 of 18 (22.2 per cent) were top-quartile, as chance predicts. Nomination bias is a measurable quantity, not a worry to manage.

The other seams behave characteristically. In two-sided markets the scarce side is hardest to reach and most wary of being reported on: Odhani Apparel Exchange, a Surat fabric marketplace, found weaver-suppliers spoke freely at a trade fair and not at all through platform messaging, which the platform controls. Regulated categories constrain recruiting itself — hearing aids are medical devices under CDSCO rules, so Riyaaz's screener could not imply diagnosis. In hardware the frame is often a service record. In AI-native products the qualifying event is usually an unreported failure, so the only honest frame is the log, and log-triggered invitation raises its own question under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Mature companies say they run panels and quotas; mostly they run consent records, a participant bank, an agency contract for hard segments, and a habit of phoning friendly accounts when the quarter is short.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The binding constraint is the scarcest cell, not the sample size.

The tell-tale sign is a researcher who reports the headline count before the cell counts — "we spoke to 56 people" rather than "nine abandoners from five channels". Confidence is per cell: Riyaaz's 25 never-tested participants said nothing about abandonment.

Incidence is a property of the channel, not of the population.

The expert's signal is a qualification rate that rises as the channel gets colder — 40.0 per cent at the clinic, 75.0 per cent in the associations. The naive reading is that associations hold more sufferers. In fact a high rate in a cold channel measures self-selection, not prevalence.

No-shows are not random, and they lean the wrong way.

Of the 13 people scheduled who did not appear, 9 (69.2 per cent) were in shift work or were sole caregivers: the people whose problem is worst and whose time is least their own. Over-booking preserves that bias at scale; flexible hours, home visits and a second attempt are the fix.

Managers nominate stars, and the bias is measurable.

Rivaaj's 23 of 28 against an expected seven is the generic shape. The expert computes a usage percentile for every participant before the first interview, and reads the distribution as data about the gatekeeper. Nominated participants are more articulate — backwards for discovery, since the product already works for them.

Incentives are a filter, and in India the dangerous direction is downward.

Too large an honorarium draws professional respondents; too small a one draws the under-occupied. The tell-tale sign is a participant who knows what the first question will be. In B2B it is often barred outright, as at Rivaaj, so the price is paid in relationship capital, which no budget tracks.

A screener has two error rates and only one is visible.

False positives announce themselves by minute four; false negatives are silent. Rudrani therefore interviewed 24 candidates her screener had rejected and found 7 of 24 (29.2 per cent) squarely in the target — people who described their trouble not as "difficulty in groups" but as relatives speaking too fast. A clean screener reads as precision; the expert reads a failed vocabulary test.

Cash cost understates enterprise recruiting by a factor of two.

Rivaaj's cash outlay was ₹1,61,000 across 46 interviews, or ₹3,500 each. Adding Omana at 0.6 FTE for four weeks (₹1.68 lakh of her ₹2.80 lakh monthly loaded cost) and fourteen hours of customer-success time at ₹2,000 an hour gives ₹3,57,000, or ₹7,761 per interview — 2.2 times the cash figure. Benchmarking against a panel's price list compares an invoice with a subsidy.

Warm channels borrow against the future.

Referrals and your own database are fast, cheap and agreeable. Riyaaz's database cost ₹1,200 an interview and supplied 6 of the 8 current users. The cost arrives a quarter later, as a roadmap that tests nothing, because the confirming quotes came from people who had already chosen you.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

The craft of writing a behavioural screener does not change between consumer, B2B and AI products; saying otherwise is a consultant's flourish. What changes is the frame, the gatekeeper and the quota unit.

ContextScarce thingWhere the frame comes fromQuota unit
ConsumerThe moment, not the personCommunities, in-product intercepts, panelsEvent recency
B2B and enterprisePermission to reach the userAccount teams, trade bodies, eventsRole, plus usage percentile
Platform and marketplaceThe scarce side's trustField visits, trade fairs, local leadersSide, and position in the chain
Hardware and physical goodsPost-purchase contactService records, dealers, returnsLifecycle stage
AI productsThe unreported failureLogs and triggered invitationsFailure type

Exhibit 6. The quota unit is the practical difference: in enterprise it is two-dimensional, which is why Rivaaj needed a percentile as well as a title.

Stage changes the failure, not the method. A seed-stage team recruits by hand through founders' networks, knows the sample is biased, and proceeds anyway. At Riyaaz's scale the error is the one in Exhibit 4: a channel chosen on cost per interview rather than cost per cell. At Rivaaj's it is nomination bias dressed as access. In large firms procurement makes recruiting cheap, and the same professional respondents answer every study in the category.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Riyaaz, and the chart nobody wanted. The composition of the 56 interviews, not their number, decided what the pilot could support.

Never-tested people were 25 of 56 (44.6 per cent) and the cheapest to find; abandoners were 9 of 56 (16.1 per cent), and 3 of those 9 came from the one channel that cannot hold anyone who abandoned a rival device.

Rivaaj, and the quartile test. The second example worked because it was audited. The nominated route was cheap, and 23 of 28 participants sat in the top usage quartile; the cold route was expensive, and of its 18 participants 14 (77.8 per cent) described recording readings on paper and keying them in later. Had Omana run only the nominated route, the dashboard would have won on evidence that excluded the behaviour at issue.

Ropan Credit House, and the panel that was not there. The failure is instructive because nothing looked careless. Ropan, a Jaipur lender to agri-input shops, bought 40 interviews at ₹7,500 each, ₹3,00,000 in all, screened for owners with ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore of turnover who had borrowed working capital within six months. Afterwards the product manager asked for evidence: a GST registration and a photograph of the shopfront. Thirteen of 40 (32.5 per cent) could not produce a shop; 9 of 40 (22.5 per cent) had taken no loan; four failed both, so 18 of 40 (45.0 per cent) were unusable and 22 remained. Effective cost rose from ₹7,500 to ₹13,636 per usable interview, 81.8 per cent higher, and the study was already presented. The recovery was not more panel: the team attended six dealer meets and completed 11 interviews in nine days for ₹45,100 — ₹4,100 each — eligibility verified on the spot. The proposed fourteen-day grace period was dropped: the real friction was the documentation demanded at sanction, which nine of the eleven verified interviews raised and none of the fabricated ones had.

9. Failure modes, with their early warning signs

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Convenience sample as discoveryEvery interview ends in encouragementHow many knew someone here?₹48.60 lakh, a quarter at Rivaaj's squad rate
Single-channel concentrationSame phrases in eight of ten interviewsAny channel above half a cell?A finding undefendable at a board review
Nomination biasParticipants unusually fluentWhat usage percentile is each in?Building for users who succeed already

Screener false negativesCandidates reject your termsInterviewed anyone it rejected?A segment that never appears

Recruiting after the guide is frozenQuestions suit nobody foundWas the screener drafted first?Fieldwork repeated inside a deadline

Exhibit 7. Every warning sign is observable before analysis.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first live disagreement is recency against breadth. The switch-interview position holds that only someone who decided recently can reconstruct the decision, so the scarce slots belong to switchers and abandoners; its evidence is the decay of recall. Ruchira's nine abandoners are that prescription. The breadth position holds that recent switchers are the people the category already reached, so a firm interviewing only them optimises inside its current market while the larger non-adopting population stays invisible; its evidence is India's treatment gap in hearing. For recency to be wrong, abandonment stories would have to mislead about the next purchase — which Riyaaz's 8.1 per cent return rate hints at, a returned device saying more about the retailer than the product. For breadth to be wrong, never-tested people would have to be unable to forecast their own behaviour, which the stated-preference literature suggests.

The second is panels against fieldwork. The panel position, steelmanned, is that composition is all that matters and panels alone deliver it on a deadline; professional respondents are a screener problem, solvable with behavioural screeners and verification. The fieldwork position is that eligibility you cannot verify is not eligibility, and that Ropan's 18 of 40 is the equilibrium of a market paying per completed interview. It would be wrong if verification became routine — the bet research operations is making.

The third disagreement is about who should recruit. One camp holds that a product manager who has never recruited her own participants does not know what her evidence is made of; the other that recruiting is a specialist craft with legal exposure, and a PM doing it badly is worse than a vendor doing it adequately.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four ways. She writes the cell quotas before the interview guide, as a composition rather than a count: twelve abandoners, no more than four from one channel. She audits her own sample while fieldwork runs — usage percentile, source column, the qualified-but-not-scheduled list — since the only cheap time to fix composition is before the calendar fills. She distrusts her easiest channel most. And she routes prevalence questions to the telemetry log without apology.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Friday 6 November, Roopal took the offline-first engineer app to the board for the first quarter — ₹48.60 lakh — and made the dashboard contingent on a second study. Her reasoning was not that the engineer evidence was larger, it was that the nominated evidence was measurably about the wrong engineers, 23 of 28 from the top usage quartile against an expected seven, while the cold route, whose distribution looked like chance, was where the paper fallback appeared. She also asked Rathin for an unchaperoned-access clause in the next four renewals.

On Monday 16 November, Ruchira committed the ₹62 lakh mould to the rechargeable cradle. Six of the nine abandoners (66.7 per cent) had stopped over batteries — zinc-air cells bought loose from a neighbourhood shop, of uncertain age — while the group-conversation complaint that argued for the microphone array came from the never-tested cell, which has no purchase behaviour to evidence. One rule went into the next study: twelve abandoner interviews from three channels, none above four, with ₹1.20 lakh for verification.

Questions for discussion. First: Riyaaz's cheapest route to the scarce cell was its own buyer list, ₹3,600 against a blended ₹31,733 — on what evidence would you use it, and what would you collect alongside? Second: Rivaaj could measure nomination bias because it held a usage percentile for every participant; what is the equivalent in a consumer product? Third: if verification costs more than the panel discount it protects, at what study size does it stop paying for itself?

13. Going deeper

  • Interview fundamentals — what you will ask tells you whom to find.
  • Designing an interview guide — guide and quota are one artefact; apart, they produce Exhibit 7's last row.
  • How many interviews — Exhibit 4's cell arithmetic is the honest version of that question.
  • Research operations — consent records, incentive rails, a participant bank.
  • Research in unfamiliar markets — where Exhibit 6's frames may be absent.
  • Qualitative vs quantitative research — routing prevalence away from interviews.
  • Cognitive biases in research — biases entering during the conversation, not before.
  • Synthesising research — the source column weights a pattern by where it came from.
  • AI-assisted synthesis — a model reads a bad sample as confidently as a good one.
case40v1-res.recruiting:
Rabta Works: Six Operators

A case on finding the people who have the problem — Pune, December 2026

1. The night before

At nine on the evening of Tuesday 8 December 2026, the Rabta Works office on Baner Road in Pune had emptied except for Basanti Gupte, vice-president of product, and a whiteboard on which an engineer had written one number in blue marker: six. Six line operators, out of thirty-one research conversations, three weeks of field work and ₹5.23 lakh.

At half past nine the next morning she had to tell the product review, with Brijesh Goswami, the chief executive, two function heads on video and a board observer in Mumbai, how Rabta would recruit the second wave of research for Rabta Line Voice, the operator-facing defect-logging module funded in July. She also had to say what the company would do about two interviews it had already conducted, which its own counsel believed it should not have conducted at all.

The deadline behind the deadline was commercial. Rabta's master services agreement with Rokkaku Mobility Group, the Osaka tier-one supplier whose Indian arm ran nine plants on Rabta Line, expired on Wednesday 31 March 2027, and renewal terms were due by Friday 15 January 2027, thirty-seven days after the review. Rokkaku was ₹3.20 crore of Rabta's ₹7.44 crore of annual recurring revenue on 30 September 2026: 43.0 per cent of the company, in one signature.

She had a folder of exhibits and no way to make them agree.

2. How Rabta got here

Rabta Works was founded in Pune in 2018 by Brijesh Goswami and two classmates from foundry automation. Its product, Rabta Line, replaced the paper defect register on an auto-component shop floor: a supervisor logged rejections, downtime and rework on a tablet, and the quality manager got a first-pass-yield dashboard instead of a Monday reconciliation. By November 2026 it ran in 41 plants on 1,284 licensed supervisor seats, with 86 employees in Pune, Bengaluru and four other cities.

One decision from 2023 shaped everything Basanti could now do. To win Rokkaku's nine-plant rollout, signed on Tuesday 14 March 2023, Rabta conceded three things. It cut the seat price: Rokkaku paid ₹40,353 a seat a year against ₹86,354 for everyone else, 46.7 per cent of what other customers paid. It accepted clause 14.3, under which all contact with Rokkaku personnel, permanent or contract, ran through a single plant point of contact, with no recording inside the plant. And it built Rabta Line with no operator accounts: a login per line per shift, held by the supervisor, because worker accounts would have meant tracking a contract workforce Rokkaku's industrial-relations team would not touch.

That architecture made the company, and it meant that in December 2026 Rabta had no list, anywhere, of the people whose problem Line Voice existed to solve.

3. The industry around it

Indian auto-component manufacturing was in a measurement decade. Tier-one suppliers to Tata Motors, Bajaj Auto, TVS Motor and Mahindra were being asked for traceability they had never kept: which line, which shift, which operation produced a defect. The production-linked incentive schemes rewarded capacity; the customers rewarded parts per million. Bharat Forge and Sona Comstar built their own systems; below them, plants bought software from SAP or Siemens at the top and from Pune and Coimbatore startups at the bottom. Rabta sat in the middle, where a customer could leave over ₹6 lakh a year.

Two rules mattered. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act made recorded research with a worker a consent transaction, revocable, with deletion on withdrawal. And Rokkaku's supplier-quality directive, issued from Osaka on Monday 8 June 2026, required defect traceability to line and shift from 1 April 2027: a date in the next financial year, beyond the one ending 31 March 2027, and so beyond every number in Rabta's plan. It was why the board funded Line Voice on Friday 24 July 2026, with ₹18 lakh of research budget for FY2026-27 and an instruction not to design an operator product without talking to operators.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In August the team believed recruitment was a scheduling problem: Rabta had 41 plants, friendly quality managers and a customer-success function, so it would ask and people would come. Bridget Gaskell, in Melbourne, argued that the company had never spoken to an operator, and that the supervisors it had spoken to for six years were the people whose work the new module would redistribute.

So Basanti ran three recruiting channels in parallel for the three weeks from Monday 2 November to Sunday 22 November 2026, against one screener: had the person tried to report a defect in the previous seven days and failed to get it into any system? A yes was recorded as in-moment. Exhibit 1 is what the channels returned.

Three beliefs held in early November were wrong by the end of it. First, that the plant-nominated route would reach operators: it produced one in fourteen conversations, because points of contact nominate people who present well. Second, that a panel could be bought: on Monday 16 November Ropan Research Collective flagged 11 of its own 44 screener passes as sharing device identities with earlier studies, and its nine completed interviews were managers, engineers and supervisors, with no operator. Third, that the festival calendar was noise: the Rokkaku plants shut for maintenance in the week around Diwali, Sunday 8 November, and fifteen of twenty-nine nominations never converted.

Then, on 25 November, a researcher coding transcripts noticed that two of the five operators recruited at the tooling markets in Bhosari and Rajkot were apprentices on contract at Rokkaku Bharat's Chakan plant. They had come through a route chosen precisely because it did not run through a plant gate. On Friday 27 November, Birva Gaitonde, Rabta's part-time general counsel in Mumbai, wrote a memo on clause 14.3 and on consent taken in Marathi from an apprentice without his employer's knowledge. On Tuesday 1 December, Bimal Gondkar offered a way out.

5. The people

Basanti Gupte, vice-president of product, Pune, owns Line Voice and the research budget, and wants the second wave to reach operators failing to report defects now. Her incentive is a module already staffed with nine engineers. What she does not say: she authorised the tooling-market intercepts herself, verbally, without asking counsel.

Brijesh Goswami, co-founder and chief executive, Pune, wants the renewal signed before anyone litigates research method, and has told two investors that Line Voice is why Rokkaku will renew at a better seat price. What he does not say: Rokkaku's procurement has asked why it pays for 793 seats when it employs 468 supervisors.

Bibhas Ganguly, head of customer success, Osaka, three and a half hours ahead, holds the Rokkaku relationship and backs Bimal's offer, because an audit finding lands on his desk. What he does not say: he has not told Osaka about the apprentices.

Bridget Gaskell, director of design research, Melbourne, five and a half hours ahead, wants the intercept route scaled and the panel dropped, and has read all thirty-one transcripts. What she does not say: she thinks the module itself is wrong, and the problem lives in the shift-end handover.

Bageshri Gumaste, lead data scientist, Amsterdam, four and a half hours behind, built Exhibit 4 and will not let it be read as evidence about operators. What she does not say: her own model of reporting health is fitted on supervisor behaviour, the only behaviour the product records.

Baishali Gokani, head of enterprise sales, Milan, has a European prospect asking for vernacular voice capture by June 2027 and wants a dated roadmap, not more discovery. What she does not say: the prospect's plants are in Portugal and Poland, where none of this research would transfer.

Bimal Gondkar, manager of plant quality systems at Rokkaku Bharat, Chakan, is the clause 14.3 point of contact for all nine plants and has offered to let Rokkaku's improvement team run the eighteen conversations and hand over notes. His incentive is a clean traceability story for April 2027. What he does not say: his plant head has refused outside interviewers twice, and that the three sample notes were written by a supervisor.

Birva Gaitonde, general counsel, Mumbai, two days a week, will not approve recruiting Rokkaku's contract workers by any route that bypasses the plant, and will not say the two interviews must be destroyed, because deletion may itself be wrong under the consent the apprentices gave. What she does not say: she has never advised on industrial research.

7. Voices

“Six operators is not a finding, it is a rounding error. Get me eighteen conversations I can put in front of Osaka by early January, and I do not much care which door they come through, so long as it is legal.” Brijesh Goswami, review pre-read, 7 December 2026

“Of the six operators, five came through the one door Birva wants shut. That is not a coincidence we can design around. It is the finding.” Bridget Gaskell, in the research channel, 30 November 2026

“Exhibit 4 says the Rokkaku plants log 7.5 events per line per day and others log less. It does not say operators report more there: 71 per cent of those events arrive in bursts after the shift ends. I can measure supervisors. I cannot measure the man who told the supervisor something and watched it not get written.” Bageshri Gumaste, data note to Exhibit 4

“I tell supervisor sir the fixture is cutting oversize, he says note kar lenge, and at shift end sometimes he writes it and sometimes he forgets. I don't have the app. Only sir has the tablet.” Badal Gavit, contract apprentice, Chakan, 19 November 2026

“My plant head has twice said no to outside interviewers on the floor. If our improvement team runs the conversations, you get your eighteen, properly translated, and nobody reads clause 14.3 to anybody. I am offering cooperation.” Bimal Gondkar, call with Bibhas Ganguly, 1 December 2026

“Two participants are my customer's contract workers, spoken to outside the plant about conditions inside it, with consent taken verbally in a tool market. I am not telling you to delete the transcripts. I am telling you I do not know what they consented to, and nor do they.” Birva Gaitonde, memo, 27 November 2026

“Our verified tier is ₹52,000 a conversation and converts at about 60 per cent on screeners like yours. But verification means a payslip and a plant email, and an apprentice on a contractor's roll has neither.” Bhishma Golatkar, Ropan Research Collective, 3 December 2026

8. The options as Basanti sees them

She has four lines on a page, priced in Exhibit 6 against what the pilot paid per in-moment conversation in Exhibit 5, and suspects the page itself is the problem.

Accept Bimal's offer. Eighteen conversations, ₹1,10,000 of coordination and translation, no contractual exposure, a better renewal conversation. But Rokkaku writes the screener, picks the operators and takes the notes, and its three samples are in a supervisor's voice, with no instance of a defect going unreported. Rabta would be buying agreement.

Scale the intercept route, outside Rokkaku plants. Exhibit 1 says this is where the in-moment people are: seven of eight conversations, at ₹13,714 each. It also produced the two apprentices, and confining it to the other 32 plants confines it to 491 of 1,284 seats and to simpler lines than the directive concerns. Bageshri calls that designing for small plants and selling to large ones.

Buy the verified panel. ₹9,36,000 for eighteen conversations leaves ₹3,41,000 and yields, on the pilot's conversion, four in-moment conversations; on Ropan's claim, ten or eleven. Verification excludes precisely the contract workforce Line Voice is for.

Stop recruiting and instrument. Ship the module to two friendly plants as a beta, nine person-weeks of engineering, and learn from use rather than conversation. No consent problem, no gatekeeper, and no answer to why a defect goes unreported: only how often the new button is pressed by people who already have a tablet.

Bridget's note of 30 November fits none of the four lines: we keep recruiting individuals, and every transcript describes a handover between two people at the end of a shift. If the unit of study is the handover, the right recruitment is a pair, a supervisor and the operator who reports to him, consented together inside a plant: the thing clause 14.3 makes hardest and the thing Bimal's offer could deliver.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The review is at half past nine on Wednesday 9 December 2026. Renewal terms are due on Friday 15 January 2027, thirty-seven days later; the agreement ends on 31 March 2027. ₹12,77,000 of the ₹18 lakh budget remains, and Brijesh will not go back to the board for more this financial year. Clause 14.3 permits no contact with Rokkaku personnel or contract workers without the point of contact's written approval, and no recording inside the plant; breach is grounds for termination on thirty days' notice. The DPDP Act requires consent that is specific, recorded and revocable, with deletion on withdrawal, and two transcripts sit in a state Birva will not characterise. The traceability directive begins on 1 April 2027, in the next financial year. And Rabta has no list of operators anywhere in its systems, because in March 2023 it agreed not to have one.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, rank the channels on cost per completed interview and on cost per in-moment interview. Why do the rankings disagree, and which denominator should Basanti take to the review?
  2. Exhibit 2 offers several counts of a population and none of the people Line Voice is for. What population should Rabta sample, and what would it take to define it?
  3. Exhibit 4 shows the Rokkaku plants logging the most events per line per day; Exhibit 3 shows them yielding one operator in fourteen conversations. Reconcile the two, and say what you would measure to know which exhibit misleads you.
  4. What is wrong with Bimal's offer, and what would have to be true of its screener, selection and note-taking for it to be acceptable?
  5. Should Rabta disclose the two apprentice interviews to Rokkaku before 15 January? Work through disclosing, deleting and doing neither: for the renewal, the research and the apprentices.
  6. All four options assume the unit of research is an individual. If Bridget is right that the subject is the shift-end handover, what recruitment design follows, what does it cost against the ₹12,77,000 remaining, and what does Basanti do on Wednesday morning, and then on Monday 14 December once the review is over? What, in three sentences, would she say to the board?

At a quarter to eleven Basanti erased the six, wrote who has this problem, and who is allowed to tell me, and looked at it. Osaka would be awake in four and a half hours; Bimal's offer was open until Friday. The whiteboard did not help.
exp20v2-res.recruiting:
Recruiting Research Participants

Discovery & Design, Qualitative Research. Where do I find the people who actually have this problem?

1. Twelve days in September

On Tuesday 1 September 2026, Vasundhara Vyas, head of product at Vishram Sleep Labs in Pune, was handed an ultimatum disguised as a calendar invitation. The board review was fixed for Friday 16 October. Before it, the company had to say which of two problems its engineering squad of six would spend the next quarter solving. The squad cost ₹14 lakh a month, so a quarter spent on the wrong problem would burn ₹42 lakh.

Vishram's app coaches shift workers to sleep better: call-centre agents, hospital nurses, warehouse pickers on night rotations. Vivek Vohra, the founder, believed the problem was biological, and wanted the quarter spent on wearable integrations that measure sleep and adjust advice. Vasundhara suspected something more domestic: that her users failed to sleep not because their bodies were unmeasured but because their daytime homes were loud, bright and full of other people's expectations.

Waheeda Wagle, the company's lone researcher, working remotely from Lisbon, put the issue plainly. Interviews could settle the argument, but only if the right people were in the room. Vishram's own user base, people who had downloaded a sleep app, were by definition the people who had already decided their problem was sleep. People who had solved the problem in some way the company had not imagined were nowhere in the database. Whom to talk to, and how to find them within the time, was the decision on which the other decision depended.

FactFigure
Squad cost per month₹14 lakh
Months at stake3
Cost of a wrong quarter (₹14 lakh × 3)₹42 lakh
Pilot recruiting budget₹1,00,000

Exhibit 1. The asymmetry that justified spending on recruiting: the pilot budget is a small fraction of the cost of one wrong quarter.

2. The idea

Participant recruitment is the deliberate search for, and screening of, people who currently have the problem under study, so that what they say reflects lived experience rather than opinion. It was invented to solve a quiet failure of early customer research: teams talked to whoever was easy to reach, typically friends, colleagues and existing users, and then mistook politeness for evidence. Steve Blank's customer-development method, set out in 2005, sent founders "out of the building"; Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013) taught what to ask once there; and the jobs-to-be-done practitioners around Bob Moesta insisted that you recruit people who recently switched something, because a recent decision leaves a memory that can be interrogated.

The practical consequence is a shift in what is being sampled. A persona describes a type of person. A moment of pain describes an occasion: the last time the problem bit hard enough that the person did something about it. Recruiting is the craft of locating people close to such an occasion. Vasundhara could repeat the idea in a meeting without sounding glib: "We are not looking for people who fit our customer profile; we are looking for people who had a bad day recently, and who will tell us what they did about it."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, two of which practitioners usually leave implicit. The first is to define the qualifying event, not the person. Vasundhara and Waheeda wrote: "In the last 60 days, worked at least three night shifts in a week, and tried to sleep by day." The second, the one rarely written down, is to name the disqualifiers: people who work nights by choice, or who had already bought a wearable, were set aside for this round because they would answer a different question.

The third step is to write the screener, a short questionnaire of factual questions that sorts respondents without revealing the "right" answers. "Do you have trouble sleeping?" leaks its own purpose and invites everyone to say yes. "What time did you last go to bed, and where?" does not. The fourth step is to choose channels and send invitations, at a volume set by the funnel arithmetic of the next section. The fifth, and the other implicit one, is to log how every participant arrived. Without the source column, the team cannot later tell whether the confident pattern in its notes came from the world or from a single WhatsApp group.

4. A worked example

From Monday 7 September to Friday 18 September, twelve days, Waheeda ran a pilot through four channels. Referrals came from twenty Vishram users, each asked to introduce someone who worked nights. The community channel meant posting the screener in night-shift groups on WhatsApp and Facebook, with a ₹1,000 voucher for each completed interview. The panel was supplied by Vartul Research Services, an agency charging ₹5,000 per completed interview. Cold outreach used LinkedIn messages to nurses and operations staff, with a ₹12,000 tool subscription plus ₹1,000 per interview.

Each channel is a funnel of four stages: people reached, people who replied, people who qualified on the screener, and people who completed an interview. The rate at each stage is the count divided by the stage before it, and the end-to-end rate is completed divided by reached.

ChannelReachedRepliedQualifiedCompletedSpend (₹)Cost per interview (₹)
Panel (Vartul)2006012945,0005,000
Community groups64032161212,0001,000
Referral2012966,0001,000
Cold outreach400208416,0004,000
Total / average1,260124453179,0002,548

Exhibit 2. Pilot funnel, 7 to 18 September 2026. Average cost = ₹79,000 ÷ 31 interviews = ₹2,548 (rounded). Cold outreach spend = ₹12,000 subscription + 4 × ₹1,000.

The rates repay slow reading. Vartul's panel replied at 30 per cent (60 of 200) but only 20 per cent of repliers qualified (12 of 60), because panels hold professional respondents who answer everything. Community groups replied at 5 per cent (32 of 640), yet half qualified (16 of 32), since a night-shift group is already filtered by the very event Vishram cares about. Three-quarters of qualifiers in both channels completed (9 of 12; 12 of 16). Referral held 30 per cent end-to-end (6 of 20), cold outreach only 1 per cent (4 of 400).

Now the second pass. Community was cheap in money but not in effort, and Waheeda wondered whether a higher voucher would lift replies. Suppose the voucher rises from ₹1,000 to ₹1,500 and replies rise from 5 to 8 per cent. Contacts needed for 12 interviews equal 12 divided by the product of the three stage rates. At 5, 50 and 75 per cent that product is 0.01875, giving 640 contacts. At 8 per cent it is 0.03, giving 400. But a richer voucher also draws people who are there for the money, so suppose the qualifying share falls to 40 per cent. The product becomes 0.024 and the contacts needed 500.

The answer changed in a direction the intuition missed. A 50 per cent bigger voucher (₹6,000 more across twelve interviews) saves 240 contacts if quality holds, but only 140 if it slips, and the interviews are worth less. Money moves one stage of the funnel and can damage another.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

Reach is not representation.

Referral looked best in Exhibit 2 and was the least trustworthy. All six referred participants worked at one Pune hospital. A funnel measures efficiency, not coverage.

Recruiting for the event, not the demographic.

"Women aged 25 to 40 in tier-1 cities" predicts little about a bad night. A recent bad night predicts a great deal.

Panels sell speed and sell professionals.

The 20 per cent qualify rate at Vartul was the signature of respondents who had learned to pass screeners. Ask for a behaviour-based screener.

Incentives shape who comes.

A voucher is a filter as well as a thank-you. Too small and only the unusually keen attend; too large and Exhibit 3 shows what follows.

Existing users are the wrong people for some questions.

They answer questions about the product well and about the problem badly, since they have already chosen a solution. Lapsed users and non-users are better for discovery.

Recruiting is not sampling in the statistical sense.

Thirty interviews do not estimate how common a problem is. They show what shapes the problem takes. A survey must still measure prevalence.

Consent and data protection are part of recruiting.

Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, collecting names, phone numbers and sleep patterns requires clear notice and purpose. Scraping contacts from a group is a legal and trust risk.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products the difficulty is volume and incentives: people are plentiful but the right moment is hard to catch. In B2B the difficulty is access: the buyer, the user and the person who pays differ, and each needs recruiting separately, usually through account managers or an introduction. In marketplaces there are at least two sides, and the scarce side, such as drivers or sellers, is often hardest to reach and most distrustful of researchers who might report on them.

ContextScarce resourceUsual best channel
ConsumerThe moment of painCommunities, in-product intercepts
B2BAccess to rolesReferrals, customer success, events
MarketplaceThe scarce side's trustField visits, local leaders, referrals

Exhibit 4. Where the difficulty concentrates in each product type.

An early-stage company recruits by hand, uses founders' networks and accepts bias. A large one has panels and research operations, but also legal review, agency contracts and a temptation to treat recruitment as procurement; in that setting the risk shifts from too few participants to the same professional respondents again and again.

7. Common mistakes

Interviewing friends and colleagues.

Symptom: every interview ends with encouragement and no story of a bad night. Misunderstanding: that goodwill is data. Cheapest diagnostic: count how many participants knew someone at the company before the call.

A vague screener.

Symptom: participants who cannot recall the last time the problem occurred. Misunderstanding: that the problem is the same as the demographic. Diagnostic: ask the first question, "tell me about the last time," and see whether anyone can answer.

A single channel.

Symptom: the same phrases recur in eight of ten interviews. Misunderstanding: that agreement means truth. Diagnostic: tabulate the source column and check no channel exceeds half the sample.

Recruiting after the guide is fixed.

Symptom: the team discovers mid-study that its questions suit nobody it has found. Misunderstanding: that the guide and the sample are independent. Diagnostic: draft the screener first, since the interview guide only tells you whom to look for.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, the pilot of Exhibit 2 would have been designed to find disagreement. Waheeda would have set a quota before the first invitation: no channel above half the sample, at least four people who had never used a sleep app, and at least three who had abandoned one. Screener questions would have been factual and behavioural. Every participant's source would sit in one column of the notes, and the first three interviews would be reviewed by two people so the guide could be repaired before the rest.

9. The decision

On Monday 21 September, Vasundhara chose a mixed plan of 24 interviews: 12 from community groups, 6 from referrals and 6 from the panel, with cold outreach dropped as the costliest per interview after the panel and the lowest yield. The cost was 12 × ₹1,000, plus 6 × ₹1,000, plus 6 × ₹5,000, which is ₹48,000, or ₹2,000 per interview on average. She capped referrals at a quarter of the sample precisely because of the hospital problem, and asked Vartul to rebuild its screener around the last night shift worked. The reasoning was not that the cheapest channel won. It was that no single channel could be trusted alone, and the board would ask where each voice came from.

To go further, study research operations, which turns this craft into a repeatable system with consent templates, incentive payments and a participant bank, and research in unfamiliar markets, where the usual channels may not exist at all.

Two questions to sit with. If Vishram's wearable-first hypothesis were true, which participants in your recruiting plan would be most likely to hide it from you? And if the interviews you most wanted could only come from one channel, what would you do to know how far to trust them?
case40v1-res.continuous:
Avinya Taana Works: Whose Week Is It?

An ambiguous case on continuous discovery habits

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Greeshma Karnad was still at the dining table of her flat in Jayanagar, Bengaluru, with three documents open: a proposal titled Weekly customer contact: every triad, every week, from 4 January; a cost sheet her team had built; and a forwarded email she had not been meant to see, in which the plant head of Avinya Taana Works' third-largest customer explained politely why his line supervisors had switched off the feature the company had spent six months building.

At ten next morning she was to take fifteen minutes of the board's product committee. The agenda item said only "Discovery operating model, FY28 planning input". What the committee wanted, she suspected, was reassurance that the ₹1.87 crore of engineering time spent on Autoline would not be spent that way again. What she had was three options she did not believe in, six exhibits that disagreed with one another, and a suspicion that the question she had been asked was not the one that mattered.

2. The company, and the decision that still binds it

Avinya Taana Works was founded in Bengaluru in March 2017 by Gorakh Kanvinde, nine years at Infosys and two running IT for a knitwear exporter, and Ghanshyam Kibe, an engineer from Pune. It sells a factory operating system to Indian apparel exporters. Two products carry almost all the revenue: Awaaz Floor, a tablet application in Hindi, Tamil and Kannada in which line supervisors record hourly output, downtime and rejections; and Aarohi Plan, where merchandisers turn a buyer's order into daily line targets.

In November 2023 the founders made the decision that defines Avinya today. Allegra Fashion Group, a Milan fast-fashion buyer, agreed to require its Indian vendors to run Avinya for order tracking. In exchange Avinya signed a master agreement with two features that have outlived everyone's enthusiasm: Annexure C, a committed feature schedule to 31 March 2027 fixing what Avinya's engineers build and when; and Clause 11.4, added by Allegra's compliance team after an audit controversy elsewhere in its supply chain, under which Avinya may not interview vendor floor employees on any matter "relating to or capable of disclosing working conditions" without Allegra's written consent.

Clause 11.4 was read in 2023 as a formality about labour audits. It is now the largest obstacle to putting an engineer in front of a supervisor, because the vendors it covers are Exhibit 1's six Tier 1 accounts — 31 of Avinya's 68 plants, or 45.6 per cent, and 58.4 per cent of the ₹42.1 crore of vendor annual recurring revenue. Gurveer Kabra's board slide calls the same exposure 56.8 per cent, dividing by the ₹43.3 crore that includes Allegra's own dashboard fee; counting that fee as at risk too makes it 59.6 per cent.

A second legacy decision compounds it. When the hosted release shipped in June 2024, migrating existing installations was deferred to keep the Annexure C dates. Twenty-four plants therefore still run Awaaz Floor 2.2 on their own servers and send no telemetry. Everything Avinya knows about how its software is used, it knows about the other 44.

3. The industry

Indian apparel exports run on a shortening clock. Vendors in Tiruppur, Noida, Bengaluru and Hindupur bid against Bangladesh and Vietnam on price and each other on lead time, and buyers — Allegra, and houses such as H&M, Inditex and Marks & Spencer — have compressed order-to-ship windows that once ran twelve weeks into six. Reliance Retail and Myntra expect domestic replenishment in days, and Apparel Export Promotion Council members complain that the schemes they rely on reward capacity, not responsiveness.

In software, Avinya sits in a gap: above it SAP and Infor, which exporters the size of Shahi Exports and Gokaldas Exports can afford; below it spreadsheets and Zoho. Its claim is that it alone reaches the line rather than stopping at the merchandising desk — a claim Exhibit 3 makes uncomfortable reading for. Two regulatory facts bear on discovery: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs any recording of an identified worker, and GST e-invoicing reaches vendors small enough that compliance competes for the same engineers. Avinya earns rupees from Indian factories; its specifications are written in Milan.
