Greeshma Karnad joined in February 2024 and inherited five triads — a product manager, a designer and an engineering lead each, except that three designers cover five triads. Discovery was a customer-success activity: Gomati Kuttappan's team ran plant visits and wrote them up for product.

Between January and June 2026 the planning triad built Autoline, an automatic line-balancing engine inside Aarohi Plan. It consumed 110 engineer-weeks, which at a fully loaded ₹1.70 lakh per engineer-week is ₹1.87 crore. The belief rested on the only evidence anyone had: merchandisers in four accounts had asked for it in writing, and one's pilot spreadsheet showed Autoline beating manual plans.

Autoline shipped on 1 July 2026. By 30 September it had been enabled at 9 of the 44 telemetry-bearing plants, or 20.5 per cent, and at 6 of those 9 — two-thirds — supervisors had reverted to manual planning within three weeks. Three plants, 6.8 per cent of the measurable base, still use it. The reason surfaced on 22 September, when Gnanavel Kathiresan, plant head at Aadhavan Knitwear Industries in Tiruppur, wrote to his account manager. Autoline assumed a 4 per cent absentee rate when allocating operators; the figure came from the merchandiser's spreadsheet. Across the three plants where Gulzar Kashelkar later sat with supervisors, Monday absenteeism averaged 11 per cent, worse after a festival weekend. A plan built on 4 per cent collapses by the second hour of the shift, and a supervisor who re-plans by hand at 9:40 does not return to the software at 11.

Gulzar had been hired in August 2026 as Avinya's first and only research-operations manager; of her six interviews that quarter, four were with the same two accounts, those being the owners who said yes. On 6 October Gitonga Kinuthia circulated the analysis that became Exhibit 4. On 9 October Ashray Garment Works in Noida declined floor access outright, citing works-committee sensitivities. On 12 November Gorakh Kanvinde learned from a contact on Allegra's sourcing side that Allegra had quietly issued a request for proposals. He has told no one on the product side.

Exhibit 6 puts the direct cost at ₹7.00 lakh, or ₹87,500 for each of the eight floor conversations. Clause 11.4 is never tested, Annexure C never disturbed, and the triads keep reading other people's notes. This produced Autoline.

Option 2: all five triads, one conversation a week, from 4 January. Fifty-five conversations, each with a triad member in the room, against Exhibit 2's 14 such conversations — nearly four times as many — and 33 with a floor user against 16, twice as many. At ₹12.41 lakh it is 1.77 times Option 1. Gurveer's slide divides that total by all 55 and gets ₹22,564 each, a quarter of today's unit cost; the comparable base is the 33 floor sessions, which gives ₹37,606, so Avinya would pay 43 per cent of today's price for four times the floor contact.

Option 3: a standing floor panel. Forty supervisors across twelve plants, paid ₹2,000 a month, reachable on WhatsApp outside shift hours, four conversations a week — 44 in all for ₹5.30 lakh, or ₹12,045 each: the cheapest floor contact on the page, at 76 per cent of Option 1's cost. It is also likeliest to breed professional respondents, and most plainly engages DPDP consent and Clause 11.4: a supervisor explaining a failed plan will talk about absenteeism, and absenteeism is a working condition.

Greeshma has written all three as a choice about interviews: how many, by whom, at what price. Guneet Khaire's resignation note said something else — that the planning triad owned no outcome, only a feature list, and that Autoline had been approved by four people who each believed someone else had checked it with the floor. The committee wants a recommendation, not a paper. Whatever is chosen must start on 4 January 2027: the FY28 budget closes in late December, and Gulzar cannot build a channel in a fortnight.

The constraints are these. Clause 11.4 requires Allegra's written consent for floor interviews at 31 of the 68 plants; the master agreement expires on 31 March 2027 and its renewal notice window opens on 1 January, three days before the cadence would begin — asking for consent is itself a signal, and Gorakh knows what he has not said. Gomati will grant access to 12 plants, no plant twice. The quarter has 13 weeks, 11 usable (Figure 1). There are three designers for five triads and 26 unallocated engineer-weeks out of 494. The board has approved no FY27 headcount, so Option 2's research lead must be funded by leaving Guneet Khaire's vacancy unfilled. And whatever the cadence learns, the 24 dark plants stay invisible to the next review.

Continuous discovery habits

Weekly customer contact for the whole product trio, and the two quantities that decide whether the habit pays.

1. Two decisions, two product types

On Monday 13 April 2026, Jaishree Komarraju, vice-president of product at Jugnu Learning Network in Bengaluru, had a roadmap she did not believe. Jugnu sold a mobile learning app to parents of Class 6 to Class 8 students on the CBSE and state-board syllabi; 38 lakh learners opened it in a month. The proposal on her desk was a live doubt-clearing marketplace — a student photographs a maths problem at nine at night, a tutor answers within four minutes — costed at ₹3.6 crore across two quarters. Its evidence was a research round completed on Friday 13 February 2026, fifty-nine days earlier, which Ojal Vazirani in design and Jatin Chaphekar in platform engineering had never seen in raw form.

The problem was not a shortage of research but that research arrived as a document, and that by the time a decision needed it, nobody who had to act had heard a parent speak. So Jaishree proposed something faintly embarrassing to say out loud: for the twelve weeks from Monday 13 April to Friday 3 July, the three of them would sit in on three customer conversations a week and settle it on Monday 13 July with whatever they had heard.

In Ahmedabad, Omisha Hublikar faced a harder version. She was product lead at Ooshma Thermal Industries, which made temperature loggers and the cloud service that read them, fitted to refrigerated vans carrying vaccines for pharmaceutical distributors: 214 accounts, 1,870 instrumented vans. Her decision was a new logger board, budgeted at ₹5.60 crore in Exhibit 5, with tooling lead times that made it irreversible the day it was signed. She could not message 6,000 customers; she had 214, each known by name to her sales colleagues and several able to escalate an unwelcome request to her chief executive.

2. The idea, its history, and who refuses to sign it

Continuous discovery, in Teresa Torres's formulation, is the practice of a product trio — product manager, designer, engineer — making contact with customers at a minimum weekly cadence, in decision-sized doses, while building. Torres set it out in Continuous Discovery Habits (2021) with the opportunity solution tree: a measurable outcome above the customer needs, pains and desires (opportunities) that might move it, and each opportunity above its candidate solutions.

The definition matters less than the thing it replaces. Steve Blank's customer development (2005) and Eric Ries's build-measure-learn loop (2011) had told teams to leave the building, but both were read as phase structures: discovery, then build. Marty Cagan's work from 2008 onward insisted the two run in parallel, and Jared Spool's "exposure hours" research supplied the field's only hard number — two hours of direct customer exposure per team member every six weeks, below which design quality measurably degrades. Torres's contribution was to change the unit of account: the project model counts research in rounds, continuous discovery counts it as a rate and asks whether the rate has lapsed.

Four schools can be named, and each signs a different sentence. The habit school (Torres; much of the product-coaching field) signs: a team that has not spoken to a customer this week is deciding on stale evidence, and the trio's shared presence is the point, not the transcript. It will not sign that interviews can size a market or replace an experiment.

The immersion school, from design ethnography and Indi Young's listening sessions, signs: problem-space understanding comes from depth and duration, and a 45-minute call every Wednesday produces a thin, convenience-sampled picture. It signs the exposure claim but not the cadence claim, preferring three days in a warehouse each quarter to twelve calls.

The quantitative school — outcome-driven innovation after Anthony Ulwick, experimentation after Ron Kohavi — signs: stated needs are unweighted, and roadmaps should follow a measured importance-and-satisfaction gap across an adequate sample, or a controlled experiment. It will not sign that a dozen conversations should defer a ₹3.6 crore build.

The operations school (the ResearchOps community; Erika Hall on ritual) signs: cadence is a function of plumbing — consent, recruiting, scheduling, incentives, storage — and a team instituting the habit without it is scheduling its own failure. It is agnostic about weekliness and hostile to enthusiasm as a substitute for infrastructure.

The habit school is right about the mechanism and vague about the economics, which turn on two measurable quantities: the age of the evidence at the moment of decision and the marginal yield of the next conversation. Teams that fail optimise a third — the interview count — which matters least.

3. Mechanics in depth: the two quantities

Start with evidence age. If a team refreshes evidence in rounds of period P and decisions arrive roughly uniformly through the year, the expected age of the newest evidence at a decision is P/2. Jugnu ran two rounds a year: P of 26 weeks, expected age 13 weeks. Weekly contact makes P one week and the expected age half a week. The ratio, 13 ÷ 0.5, is 26 — a twenty-six-fold reduction with no increase in annual volume, purely by rescheduling the same conversations.

The second quantity needs a recruiting chain, where the operations school's plumbing becomes visible. Juhi Daithankar, Jugnu's research operations lead, built a standing weekly pipeline rather than a per-study one. Each Monday an in-app card went to 6,000 parents in the eligible segment — a child in Class 6 to Class 8, four or more sessions in the past fortnight, no contact in the past twelve months. Two per cent, 120, tapped it; 30 per cent of those 120, that is 36, finished the screener; a quarter of the 36, nine, matched the week's criteria; two-thirds of the nine, six, picked a slot; half of the six, three, appeared.

Three a week then governs everything: 36 conversations over twelve weeks, and annually, at 48 working weeks, 144 conversations from 2,88,000 invitations — 7.6 per cent of Jugnu's 38 lakh monthly actives, low enough that no parent is contacted twice. Jugnu logged, per conversation, whether the opportunities raised were new to the tree. Loaded at ₹4,500 an interview (a ₹500 voucher plus allocated team and operations cost), six conversations cost ₹27,000.

Because saturation is outcome-specific, a team that never changes its outcome shows a flat curve and concludes, wrongly, that discovery has stopped working. 4. When it applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions can be written as claims checkable in an afternoon.

One: a measurable outcome exists that conversations can bear on. Jugnu's was "chapters completed per learner per week", then 1.4. Ooshma's was "temperature excursions detected before dispatch", which also passes, with a wrinkle: the person who can describe an excursion is a loading-bay supervisor, not the quality manager who signs the contract.

Two: customers are reachable weekly at a cost well below the decision's value. Jugnu passes on volume; Ooshma only on value. At ₹11,000 a conversation, loaded with travel to a cold store, 96 a year cost ₹10.56 lakh against a ₹5.60 crore decision — 1.9 per cent, four times Jugnu's ratio and still trivial.

Three: the trio has decision authority. This fails most often and is checked least. Jaishree could defer the marketplace; Omisha could not unilaterally stop a revision her manufacturing head had budgeted. Weekly contact without authority produces attrition, not products.

Four: the artefact can change at the cadence of the evidence. Jugnu's app shipped weekly; Ooshma's hardware froze at tooling release for eighteen months. Here the idea becomes actively misleading: a trio collecting weekly evidence about something it cannot alter for a year and a half is keeping a grievance log. Omisha split the outcome — firmware and cloud, changeable fortnightly, from board geometry, which was not — and ran weekly contact only against the first.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

Two-sided. Jhoola Furniture Exchange, a rental marketplace, held two conversations a week with the sides alternating: over the 26 weeks to June 2026, 13 renter weeks and 13 dealer weeks, so 26 renters and 26 dealers. A renter-side opportunity, "I cannot cancel without losing the deposit", produced a free-cancellation window that lifted cancellations from 7.0 per cent to 11.0 per cent of 4,400 weekly bookings — 308 to 484, leaving 176 extra idle delivery slots a week on the dealer side. The lesson is not that alternation finds the harm but that a one-outcome tree cannot represent it.

Multi-product and the organisational seam. Across Ooshma's 214 accounts with roughly three named contacts each — 642 individuals — 96 interviews a year is a 15.0 per cent contact rate, which sounds safe. The 96 landed on 31 distinct accounts (14.5 per cent of 214), and nine accounts absorbed 54 of the 96, or 56.3 per cent, averaging six conversations each: the friendly ones, close by, mature and systematically unrepresentative of the 183 nobody called.

Mature companies say they "coordinate across teams"; what works is a shared contact ledger with a cooling-off period and a first-time quota — Ooshma required one conversation in four with an account untouched for twelve months.

Regulated. A conversation inside a customer's cold store touches batch data and sometimes patient-linked consignment records. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, consent must be purpose-specific, which rules out a blanket research opt-in at signup. Regulated teams that manage it keep a narrowly scoped consent, renewed annually per individual, in research operations rather than with the trio.

AI-native. Jigyasa AI Labs, whose assistant served chartered accountants, met the sharpest form of evidence decay: its model changed seven times in twelve weeks, and of 24 opportunities logged in that window, 9 — 37.5 per cent — were obsolete by week 12 because an upgrade had dissolved the complaint. AI products need an expiry convention: an opportunity attached to model behaviour carries the version it was heard against and is re-tested, not assumed.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Cadence is a floor, not a target

"Weekly" names the interval at which evidence may not lapse. The competent practitioner reads it as a quota and books three interviews on one Thursday to "cover" three weeks; the tell is a calendar of clusters and gaps. It fails because Exhibit 1's sawtooth is about the interval between refreshes, which a cluster leaves untouched.

Shared presence is the mechanism, not the transcript

The habit works because Jatin heard a parent say it, not because he read that a parent said it. The tell is vocabulary in sprint planning: those who were in the room use customers' phrases and names, those who read a summary say "research shows". The obvious reading, that a good write-up substitutes, is wrong: the value is the engineer's own unrecorded noticing.

Saturation is a property of the outcome, not of the customers

When yield falls to zero, as in Jugnu's sixth block, the inexperienced conclusion is that customers have nothing left to say; the expert conclusion is that the tree now covers the current outcome, so change the outcome. The tell is a tree that gained no branch in a month while the interview count held. A node phrased as a solution — "wants a reminder message" rather than "forgets that homework is due" — is the related tell.

The recruiting funnel is the product's selection bias

Three interviews a week from 6,000 invitations is a 0.05 per cent yield, and everyone who appears has chosen three times over: to tap, to screen, to show up. Juhi compensated deliberately, reserving one slot a month for a churned parent recruited by telephone — an in-app card can never reach someone who has stopped opening the app.

Counting is not sampling, and the failure is asymmetric

If 14 of 36 conversations raise the same friction, that ordering is strong evidence about what to explore, not an estimate of prevalence across 38 lakh learners. Qualitative contact reliably establishes that a problem exists and is nearly worthless for establishing that one does not: absence from 36 conversations says little about a tail.

Interviews describe the past; demand must be tested separately

A parent asked whether she would pay ₹299 a month for live doubt-clearing says yes, because yes is free. Asked about the last time her son was stuck at night, she reveals whether the obstacle was a missing tutor or a parent defeated by trigonometry. The tell is a snapshot library of reactions to mock-ups; no conversation substitutes for a demand test.

Synthesis within the hour, or not at all

The step most often left implicit is the write-up, and its deadline is the point: Jugnu filed a one-page snapshot — customer, date, one verbatim quote, opportunities heard, expected ones not heard — within sixty minutes. The tell of failure is a drive of recordings nobody has opened; a snapshot written on Friday about Tuesday's call is reconstructed from prior beliefs — the bias the habit exists to break.

Exposure hours, not interviews, is the auditable quantity

Three 45-minute interviews a week with all three present is 2.25 hours each per week, or 13.5 hours per six-week window — 6.75 times Spool's two-hour minimum. Ooshma's two hour-long conversations a week give 12 hours per window, six times the minimum. Exposure hours make under-attendance visible in a way "we do weekly interviews" never does; and the slot must sit on research operations' calendar, or the habit dies in the first incident.

7. How it differs across product types and company stages

Across types the differences are real in two places and overstated everywhere else. Recruiting differs: consumer teams have abundance and a selection problem, enterprise teams scarcity and a political problem, hardware teams the added need for site access. Decision latency differs: Jugnu could act on week 3's evidence in week 4, Ooshma's board not for eighteen months. Those two explain almost everything attributed to product type.

What does not differ is the interview itself, the trio requirement, or the structure of the tree. A loading-bay supervisor describing last Thursday's excursion and a parent describing last Tuesday's homework are the same conversation with different nouns. Practitioners who call enterprise discovery categorically different usually mean their customers are hard to book — research operations in a strategy costume.

Stage changes the binding constraint, not the practice. At seed stage the founders are the trio and contact is abundant; the failure is that nothing is written down, so the hundredth conversation cannot be compared with the tenth. At growth stage — Jugnu, eleven product teams — it is duplication and contact fatigue. At enterprise scale it is intermediation: account managers who treat direct contact as a threat to the relationship, which is why Ooshma settled on sales colleagues co-present for a new account's first conversation and absent thereafter.

8. Three worked examples, including one failure

Jugnu, consumer, twelve weeks. 36 interviews, ₹1,62,000, 20 distinct opportunities (Exhibit 2). The ₹3.6 crore proposal attached to one of the 20 — and in 9 of the 14 conversations where night-time difficulty arose, the obstacle was not an unanswerable question but a child who had stopped before reaching one.

Ooshma, enterprise hardware plus software, twelve months. Two conversations a week, 96 a year, ₹10.56 lakh, against a revision Omisha rebuilt line by line.

Exhibit 5. Ooshma logger revision, budget as signed, ₹ lakh.

₹560.00 lakh is ₹5.60 crore; the retrofit line is 1,870 × ₹9,600 = ₹1,79,52,000.

Twelve months of conversation — 96 interviews, two a week over 48 working weeks — did not stop the revision; it moved ₹179.52 lakh of it. Loading supervisors called the retrofit, not the board, the painful part — a van off the road for a day in a fleet at capacity. Ooshma kept the board and staged the retrofit against each fleet's maintenance calendar: no change in cost, six months of resequencing.

Jalaj Health Services, and what failure looks like. Jalaj, a diagnostics-booking platform, instituted weekly discovery in January 2026 and held it faithfully: 36 interviews in twelve weeks, never one missed. On that record it green-lit a ₹1.95 crore home-collection scheduling rebuild, abandoned eleven weeks later with ₹84 lakh spent. The post-mortem by its product lead, Jaymala Kelusker, is the most useful document here.

Exhibit 6. Jalaj Health Services: the failed habit and the recovered one.

The cadence was never the problem. Jalaj's product lead attended all 36, the designer 11, the engineer 4 — 11.1 per cent of them. The tree grew to 31 nodes, of which 24 (31 − 7) had fewer than two snapshots. The recovery halved the interview count and the cost, cut the tree to 16 nodes, and raised every quantity that mattered.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs and the cost of late detection

Solo interviewing. Early sign: the trio's exposure hours diverge more than twofold. Diagnostic: ask the engineer to name a customer heard this month. It cost Jalaj ₹84 lakh.

Collection without synthesis. Early sign: the tree unchanged for four weeks while interviews continue. Diagnostic: count opportunities with two or more snapshot citations — below half is a warning, Jalaj's 22.6 per cent damning. Caught late, the spend is unrecoverable: the memories have gone.

Convenience concentration. Early sign: distinct accounts in the ledger grow more slowly than interviews. Diagnostic: Exhibit 4's second bar — what share went to the top handful? Caught late, the roadmap serves the most mature customers and renewal risk sits elsewhere.

Cadence without an outcome. Early sign: team members, asked separately, state the outcome differently. Diagnostic: read it aloud before each session; if it feels unrelated to the questions, it is. Caught late, a quarter of real conversations bears on nothing anyone is accountable for.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Cadence versus immersion. The habit school rests on Spool's exposure-hours finding and Exhibit 1's latency argument: regularity beats intensity because decisions arrive continuously. The immersion school rests on its canon's deepest insights having come from extended presence, and on a 45-minute call selecting for articulate, available customers. For the habit school to be wrong, opportunities would have to differ in kind between short and long contact — needs no sequence of brief conversations will surface. That is plausible for latent needs and implausible for operational friction. Both are partly right, and no synthesis anyone holds resolves it.

Must the trio attend, or will exposure hours do? Torres holds that joint presence builds the shared mental model that makes later decisions fast. The specialist position, common in strong research shops, is that interviewing is a skill, that bad interviewing produces confidently wrong evidence, and that three amateurs doing it badly is worse than one expert doing it well with the team watching. For trio-mandatory to be wrong, observation would have to transmit as much as participation — and the evidence is mixed.

Can small-n evidence defer a large commitment? Jaishree used 36 conversations to reconsider ₹3.6 crore. The quantitative objection is precise: 36 self-selected parents cannot establish prevalence. The reply is equally precise: those conversations did not estimate demand, they changed the question — from "build a tutor marketplace?" to "why do learners stop before they get stuck?" — and reframing is what small-n evidence does well. For the reply to fail, the original framing would have to have been right, which no sampling rigour can establish.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this reports interview counts and shows a large tree. Someone who has internalised it reports three numbers: the age of the evidence behind the last decision, the exposure hours of the least-exposed member of the trio, and the marginal yield of the most recent block. They change the outcome when yield collapses rather than doubling the cadence; they prune the tree faster than they grow it; they concede that a conversation cannot size a market, and schedule the experiment that can; and they treat the standing invitation, the consent record and the booked slot as infrastructure.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Monday 13 July 2026, Jaishree Komarraju deferred the live doubt-clearing marketplace. Her reasoning had three parts: the proposal attached to one opportunity of 20; the obstacle described was abandonment before the hard question, not the hard question; and Jatin had heard those nine himself, so the engineering objection came from inside the room. Jugnu took two sprints against session abandonment, held the cadence at three a week, and changed the outcome from chapters completed to sessions resumed — restarting the saturation curve on purpose.

Omisha Hublikar signed the ₹5.60 crore revision unchanged in cost and restaged the ₹179.52 lakh retrofit against customers' maintenance calendars. The more consequential move was splitting her outcome: weekly contact against firmware and cloud, quarterly site immersions for anything touching hardware. The habit, in her hands, was not weekly everywhere.

Three questions. Jugnu's sixth block produced no new opportunities and cost ₹27,000: was it wasted, and if not, what did it buy? Jalaj halved its interviews and improved every other measure — when would halving the cadence be the wrong response to low trio attendance? And if Omisha cannot change hardware for eighteen months, what is the defensible cadence for the hardware outcome, and who should be in the room?

13. Going deeper

Research operations — the plumbing that sends 6,000 invitations on a Monday unbidden. Interview fundamentals — interviewing made a habit, and bad interviewing compounds. Calibrating interviewers across a team — the trio-versus-specialist disagreement above. Discovery at organisational scale — Exhibit 4 when eleven teams share 214 accounts. Qualitative versus quantitative research — where the small-n objection is adjudicated. Designing an interview guide — keeping a conversation about last Tuesday. Recruiting research participants — the bias inside every in-app invitation. How many interviews — the formal treatment of Exhibit 3's curve. Cognitive biases in research — why the snapshot deadline is sixty minutes. Synthesising research — how twenty opportunities become one decision.
case20v1-res.continuous:
Lenden Ledger Works: Before the Diwali Quarter

A decision case on continuous discovery habits

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Ruchika Annigeri sat in the Indiranagar office in Bengaluru, long after the squads had gone home, with a single sentence from her chief executive on her phone: "We cannot spend another quarter building things merchants do not want." Rehaan Alavi had sent it from Mumbai after the weekly business review. Ruchika, vice president of product at Lenden Ledger Works, had until Friday, 30 October to tell the leadership team how the company's four product squads would learn about their customers through the busy quarter that began on Monday, 2 November. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, and no merchant would give anyone an hour in the days around it.

She had three ways to answer him, and she did not yet trust any of them.

2. Company background

Lenden sells a bookkeeping and payment-collection app to small retailers: kirana owners, pharmacies, mobile shops and wholesalers in the cloth markets of Surat and Coimbatore. Merchants record credit sales, send payment reminders and collect through UPI links built on NPCI's rails. Founded in 2019, the company now has 9,60,000 monthly active merchants. Of these, 1,92,000, or 20 per cent, pay ₹299 a month for the subscription tier, which works out to ₹3,588 a year each and an annualised subscription run-rate of about ₹69 crore.

The market is crowded. Khatabook and OkCredit own the idea of the digital ledger, Vyapar sells billing software, and PhonePe for Business and Paytm bundle ledgers with their payment devices. Lenden's edge has been speed: four squads, each a "triad" of one product manager, one designer and one engineering lead, ship every two weeks. Speed, however, had begun to cost the company something.

3. The situation

In August the collections squad spent eleven weeks building an audio payment-confirmation feature that synchronised with the speaker devices merchants already owned. The assumption came from a hallway comment. When it launched, fewer than one merchant in twenty switched it on. Merchants, it turned out, already trusted the speakers from PhonePe and Paytm and saw no reason to route confirmations through Lenden.

Lenden does talk to customers, but only in projects. Each quarter Ruchika commissions a Mumbai research agency to run one or two studies, with interviews in Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Kannada. Exhibit 1 shows the four most recent quarters. The studies are good, but each one takes six to nine weeks from kickoff to read-out, and the squads receive a slide deck rather than a conversation. No engineer attended any of the 88 interviews.

Dividing the total by the interviews, Exhibit 1 implies ₹37,500 for each conversation, and an average of 22 conversations a quarter for the whole company. Shared among four squads, that is barely five or six conversations per squad per quarter.

The team's view of this depends on where each member sits. Rashmi Aranha, the principal designer, works from London and has argued for months that designers should hear merchants directly, yet her mornings overlap with Indian afternoons only from about 2:30 p.m. IST. Ratna Athavale in Sydney leads customer success and holds the merchant relationships, and she warns that merchants are tired of being asked for favours. From Pune, Rudra Akolkar, the engineering lead, says his engineers would join conversations only if it did not threaten a sprint.

4. The people

  • Rehaan Alavi, co-founder and chief executive, Mumbai. He wants fewer wasted builds, but he equates talking to customers with delay. He has asked for a plan that costs "no more than the agency does now".
  • Rashmi Aranha, principal designer, London. She wants every designer in conversations weekly, and she has hinted she will look elsewhere if discovery stays a deck handed over by the agency.
  • Rudra Akolkar, engineering lead, Pune. He wants protected build time. He will support engineers joining calls if they are short, scheduled and rare enough to be predictable.
  • Ratna Athavale, customer success lead, Sydney. She controls merchant access. She wants a single recruiting channel, consent handled under the DPDP Act, and a promise that no merchant is contacted twice in a month.

5. The options

Ruchika's staff have costed three courses. Exhibit 2 compares them over the 13 weeks from Monday, 2 November 2026 to Friday, 29 January 2027. The week beginning 9 November, which contains Bhai Dooj on the 11th, is treated as a no-interview week, leaving 12 interview weeks, as the timeline in Figure 1 shows.

Option A: keep the agency. Lenden would continue buying studies. The advantage is rigour and zero distraction for the squads. The cost, shown in Exhibit 2, is ₹8.25 lakh a quarter for about 22 interviews, plus the six-to-nine-week lag that produced the speaker feature.

Option B: all four triads, every week, from 2 November. Each triad would hold one merchant conversation weekly, attended by the product manager, the designer and the engineering lead. Exhibit 3 shows a quarterly cost of ₹3.23 lakh for 48 conversations. The upside is the cheapest evidence and the broadest habit. The risk is that a single coordinator must recruit 48 merchants in a festival season, and a missed week in the first month could discredit the practice.

Option C: two triads for one quarter. The collections and payments squads would begin weekly contact, supported by a part-time contractor, while the other two squads continue as they are. It yields 24 conversations at ₹1.82 lakh, and a review on 29 January 2027. The cost is that half of the company stays blind for another quarter, and Rehaan may read a pilot as hedging.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What exactly went wrong with the audio-confirmation feature, and which part of that failure would more agency studies have prevented?
  2. Read Exhibits 1 and 2 together. Is Lenden's problem the cost per interview, the lag between interview and decision, or who is in the room?
  3. Why does Ratna's demand for a single recruiting channel matter more to the habit than the number of triads taking part?
  4. Which option would you take to the leadership team on 30 October, and what evidence on 29 January would make you scale, hold or stop?

7. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. Continuous discovery, as Teresa Torres describes it, asks the whole product trio to talk to customers every week, in small conversations tied to the outcome the team is pursuing. Its force comes from two ideas. First, discovery is a habit, not a project, so the unit of design is the weekly cadence rather than the study. Second, the habit survives only when an operations backbone makes it easy: recruitment, scheduling, consent and a place to keep what was learned. A team that skips the backbone gets one enthusiastic fortnight and then silence.

What a good answer looks like. It separates the lever from the budget. Option A is not wrong; it is slow and detached, and it cannot put an engineer in front of a merchant. Option B is right in direction, but it attempts to build the habit and the backbone together in the hardest quarter of the year. A strong answer also checks the arithmetic of the calendar: thirteen weeks, less the Diwali week, is twelve interview weeks, which gives 24 conversations for two triads and 48 for four.

One defensible path. Choose Option C, with commitments. Start on 2 November with the collections and payments squads. Hire the coordinator first, because Ratna's single channel and consent process is the backbone. Make every interview a triad event, with engineers attending two of every three, which answers Rudra. Ask Rashmi's designers to keep interview snapshots in one shared repository. Tell Rehaan the pilot costs ₹1.82 lakh against the ₹8.25 lakh he spends today, and that the review on 29 January will test one thing: whether a squad changed a build decision because of something heard in the past fortnight. If two squads manage 12 weeks at one conversation each, extend the practice to all four in the following quarter, with a full-time coordinator. The reasoning is that a visible habit from two squads is more persuasive than a plan for four, and it lets the backbone be tested before the load doubles.
exp20v2-res.continuous:
Continuous discovery habits

How a whole product team can talk to customers every week without turning it into a project.

1. The decision on a Monday morning

On Monday 6 July 2026, Priyamvada Gokhale, head of product at Parivartan Clinic Systems in Pune, opened a planning document with one line at the top: "Do we start the billing module on 3 August?" Parivartan sold appointment and records software to small clinics, and about 1,200 of them used it daily. The billing module was a proposed build of ₹1.8 crore, two quarters of engineering time, justified by a sales-team belief that clinics wanted integrated invoicing. Priyamvada doubted it.

The company did talk to customers. Between Monday 12 January and Friday 20 February, Gitika Pandit, the team's researcher, had run a discovery round of 14 interviews, written a forty-page report and presented it to the leadership team. By July it was five months old, and the engineers who now needed it had never heard a single interview. Gaurav Pendharkar, the design lead, put the problem plainly: "We keep deciding in July what customers told Gitika in February."

Priyamvada proposed a different arrangement. For the thirteen weeks of the quarter, she, Gaurav and Prakash Gaikwad, the engineering lead, would each take part in customer conversations every week. Gitika would build the recruiting plumbing. The trio had about 1,560 working hours in the quarter, and a habit that swallowed too many would delay the roadmap; the other risk was a ₹1.8 crore build aimed at the wrong problem.

2. The idea

Continuous discovery is the practice of a small cross-functional team, the product manager, a designer and an engineer, collecting evidence from customers in at least one conversation every week, in the course of building the product rather than before it. Teresa Torres, a product coach, set the approach out in her 2021 book Continuous Discovery Habits. She calls the three roles the "product trio". Discovery means finding out which customer problems are worth solving and which solutions might solve them; delivery means building and shipping the chosen solution.

The idea was invented to repair a specific failure. In the project model, discovery is a phase with a start and an end, run by a specialist and handed over as a document. Evidence decays, and the people who must act on it did not hear it. Torres's answer is to change the unit of work from a project to a habit, so that the marginal cost of one more conversation is small and the evidence never goes out of date.

The sentence Priyamvada could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: "We are not doing more research; we are making sure the three people who decide have heard a customer this week."

3. How it works

The mechanics have four moving parts, and the first is not interviewing at all. A team needs a desired outcome, a measurable change in customer behaviour that the business cares about. Priyamvada chose "fewer missed appointments per clinic", because a missed appointment is lost revenue for the clinic and lost usage for Parivartan.

The second part is a recurring recruiting mechanism. Waiting until the week of the interview to find a customer is what makes research feel like a project, so recruiting is automated: an in-product message invites a fixed number of clinic owners each week to book a thirty-minute slot. The third part is the conversation itself, in which customers recount specific recent events rather than predict future behaviour. At least two of the trio attend. The fourth part is synthesis, and it is the step practitioners usually leave implicit. After each interview, the attendees write a one-page "interview snapshot" within an hour, naming the customer, a single quote and the unmet needs they heard, so that a conversation becomes a durable record rather than a memory.

Those snapshots feed an opportunity solution tree, a diagram that links the outcome to the customer needs, pains and desires (called opportunities) that might affect it, and each opportunity to several candidate solutions. It keeps weekly contact from degenerating into reacting to the last person spoken to.

Beneath the outcome sit three opportunities, each a need phrased from the customer's side, not a feature; beneath the first sit two candidate solutions. The billing module does not appear. A solution earns a place only by attaching to an opportunity the team has heard.

4. A worked example

Priyamvada's first question was whether the habit was affordable. The recruiting funnel is a chain of rates, and each stage applies to the output of the one before it. Parivartan would send 40 invitations a week. From earlier in-product campaigns, 20 per cent of invited clinic owners booked a slot. Of those booked, 50 per cent actually appeared, because a doctor with a waiting room often cancels at the last minute.

StageRate appliedPer week13 weeks

Four interviews a week over thirteen weeks gives 52 conversations. Each costs three people one hour: a 30-minute call, a 15-minute debrief and 15 minutes writing the snapshot. That is 3 person-hours an interview, so the quarter costs 52 × 3 = 156 person-hours. Against the trio's 1,560 hours (3 people × 40 hours × 13 weeks) that is exactly 10 per cent. Priced at an internal ₹2,000 an hour, 156 hours is ₹3,12,000, or ₹3.12 lakh. The proposed billing build is ₹1.8 crore, which is 180 lakh, so the whole habit costs 3.12 ÷ 180 = 1.7 per cent of the bet it informs.

The second pass changes one input. Suppose automated reminders lift attendance from 50 to 75 per cent while invitations stay at 40. Booked slots remain 8, and interviews rise to 6 a week, or 78 in the quarter. The habit now consumes 234 hours, which is 15 per cent of the trio's time. Better attendance is not free.

With 20 invitations, 4 slots are booked and 2 interviews are held, giving 26 in the quarter. Every scenario costs ₹6,000 an interview (3 hours at ₹2,000). Priyamvada chose the base case. The test was whether four weeks, 16 interviews, would show if the billing hypothesis had any foothold before 3 August.

5. Nuances a learner must understand

Continuous does not mean constant

The habit is a minimum frequency, one conversation a week, held reliably. Teams that read it as "always researching" burn out within a quarter.

It is not the same as feedback collection

Surveys and support tickets measure what customers say about the product as it is. Discovery interviews ask about the customer's life, the specific last time something went wrong, to find needs the product has never addressed.

The whole trio must be present

The point is shared exposure. If only the product manager attends and relays the findings, the team has recreated the hand-off document with a faster cadence.

Interviews describe the past, not the future

A clinic owner asked "would you use billing?" says yes, because yes costs nothing. Asked "tell me about the last time you sent a patient an invoice", the same owner reveals whether the task is painful. No interview can serve as a demand test.

Counting is not sampling

If 11 of the first 16 interviews raise no-shows and 3 raise billing, that ordering is strong evidence about what to explore next. It is not an estimate of the share of 1,200 clinics holding each view. Qualitative contact finds what exists; it cannot size it. Sizing needs a survey or product analytics once the team knows what to measure.

It tells you what to explore, not what to build

Weekly conversations generate opportunities. The decision about which to pursue still requires an assessment of impact on the outcome, effort, and strategy.

The habit needs a backbone

Weekly contact only stays weekly if someone owns recruiting, consent, scheduling and storing of recordings. Otherwise the whole thing relapses into a project the first time a sprint gets busy. This is research operations, and it is why Gitika's job changed.

Ask before relying on it

A thoughtful newcomer should ask three things. Do we have an outcome narrow enough that conversations can bear on it? Can our customers actually be reached weekly? And are we prepared to change our plans when the evidence says so? If the third answer is no, the habit is theatre.

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

Figure 2 shows the base case as a calendar, and the calendar is where product types diverge. In a consumer product with millions of users, recruiting is easy and the hard part is selecting people who face the problem. Invitations go out by push notification in an afternoon; the bottleneck is the team's attention.

In B2B, the reverse holds. Parivartan's buyer, the clinic owner, is a time-poor professional, and the user, the receptionist, is a different person with a different view. Weekly contact requires both, and a vendor with few accounts may need its customer-success team to keep a slot filled. In a marketplace, there are two sides, and the cadence has to cover both, usually alternating weeks, because a fix that pleases buyers can quietly harm sellers.

Company stage matters too. An early-stage team of six has no research function, and the founder often is the trio; the danger is not too little contact but contact that never reaches a written record. A large company has the opposite problem: many trios, each recruiting from the same customers, and a research team worried about over-contact.

7. Common mistakes

Interviewing to validate. The symptom, visible from outside, is that every interview ends with a demonstration of a mock-up and a question about whether the customer likes it. The misunderstanding is that discovery confirms a solution already chosen. The cheapest diagnostic is to read three snapshots and count how many record a customer story versus a reaction to a design.

The product manager as the sole interviewer. The symptom is that engineers and designers quote the product manager's summaries, not customers. The diagnostic is to ask each member of the trio, unprompted, to name a customer they heard this month.

Collecting without synthesising. The symptom is a folder of recordings and no tree. The misunderstanding is that exposure produces insight. The diagnostic is to check whether the tree changed on the last four Fridays; if not, the snapshots are not being used.

Treating the cadence as sacred and the content as optional. The symptom is a team that holds its interview every week but whose conversations never touch the outcome. The diagnostic: read the outcome aloud before each session.

8. What good looks like

By Friday 31 July, the end of the fourth week, the picture at Parivartan was clear. The trio had completed 16 interviews, four a week as planned. Eleven of them had volunteered no-shows without prompting; three had mentioned billing, and in two of those three, the clinic already used a separate accounting package and wanted only a simple export. Prakash had been on 11 of the calls. When Priyamvada showed the tree to the leadership team, he explained the double-booking opportunity himself, in the receptionist's words, and nobody asked for the forty-page report. The tree held three opportunities with a snapshot trail for each.

9. The decision, and what comes next

On Monday 3 August, Priyamvada deferred the billing module and told the leadership team why: the evidence did not contradict the sales belief so much as fail to support it, and ₹1.8 crore should not be committed on that. Instead, the team would spend two sprints on a reminder and a reschedule link, measure missed appointments per clinic, and reopen billing if the next eight weeks of interviews turned up the need independently. She kept the weekly cadence at four interviews, the 10 per cent case, and not the 15 per cent case.

The reasoning rested on three claims: the whole trio had heard the evidence, the evidence was recent, and the decision was cheap to reverse.

To go further, read about how a team calibrates interviewers, because the habit multiplies conversations and therefore multiplies variation in interviewing quality; and about discovery at organisational scale, where many trios share one customer base.

Two questions to sit with. First, if Priyamvada's first four weeks had produced 11 mentions of billing and 3 of no-shows, what would she have needed to see before committing ₹1.8 crore? Second, in your own team, who was the last person on the trio to hear a customer speak, and when?
exp40v2-res.bias:
Cognitive Biases in Research

Which of my own biases are corrupting what I hear?

1. Two instruments nobody had calibrated

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Feroza Engineer, vice-president of product at Eshana Clinic Systems in Pune, read a deck she had commissioned six weeks earlier. Eshana sells hospital information and billing software to 460 mid-sized private hospitals. Should it build a module filing cashless-claim pre-authorisations with insurers automatically? Engineering had costed it at ₹3.60 crore, that is ₹360 lakh, against a blunt rule: repay the build cost from gross contribution within two years. The committee would decide on Thursday 1 October, twenty-three days later.

The deck reported that 38 of 60 hospital administrators interviewed between 10 August and 4 September wanted the module — 63.3 per cent. Fariyal Khambatta, the founder, read a mandate; Feroza read an uncalibrated measurement. Three facts were absent: five people had run those sixty conversations; nobody had spoken to the 118 hospitals Eshana had lost in three years; and past features had tested well and shipped to indifference.

Eknath Fadnis had the problem inverted. He heads product at Falak Aero Works in Nashik, which leases 480 agricultural spray drones to farmer producer organisations in Maharashtra and Telangana. Each drone flies about 900 sorties a year at roughly five acres a sortie: 432,000 sorties, 2,160,000 acres, billed at an average ₹156 per acre, or ₹33.70 crore a year. He had two features costed at ₹95 lakh each and room for one: an automatic no-spray geofence, or a variable-dose controller. On 2 September he asked 44 FPO managers to rank them, and 39 of 44 — 88.6 per cent — chose the geofence. His council met on Friday 16 October. His respondents were sincere, consistent and probably wrong.

2. The idea, and the camps that disagree about it

A cognitive bias in research is a systematic, directional distortion in how evidence is generated, recorded or weighed, as against random error, which scatters both ways and shrinks with sample size. That distinction is the argument: random error is cured by more interviews, while more interviews of the same biased kind only buy a narrower interval around the wrong number.

Five biases carry most of the damage. Confirmation bias is asymmetric treatment of agreeing evidence. Anchoring is the pull of a first figure or framing on later judgements. Survivorship bias is inference from the units still visible once the informative ones have left. Social desirability is drift toward the answer the asker wants. Zero-risk bias prefers eliminating one hazard to reducing a larger one.

Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman established from 1971 that reasoning under uncertainty uses shortcuts failing in patterned ways. Allen Edwards had shown in the 1950s that respondents shade answers toward social approval; by the 1980s Robert Groves and colleagues had built survey methodology's total survey error framework, splitting the gap between estimate and truth into coverage, sampling, non-response and measurement error.

Four positions are live. Heuristics-and-biases signs that judgement is reliably distorted and exhortation fails, so change the decision environment; it will not sign that the distortions are adaptive. Ecological rationality, after Gerd Gigerenzer, signs that many so-called biases are sensible responses judged against an artificial norm and will not sign that respondents are irrational. Total survey error signs that bias is a quantity with a sign and magnitude, to be estimated and subtracted; it will not sign that a dozen conversations support a population estimate. The behavioural-evidence school, from Steve Blank and Rob Fitzpatrick, signs that a stated answer should be replaced by a costly action rather than debiased. Contextual inquiry, after Hugh Beyer and Karen Holtzblatt, declines the frame entirely: an interview is interpretation, not measurement.

3. Mechanics: making the instrument's error legible

Expert practice starts upstream of the interview. Feroza asked Erum Jafri, Eshana's research operations lead, for what the deck lacked: what past research had predicted and what happened. Across six paid modules shipped between 2023 and 2026, Eshana held 600 pre-launch records in which a named administrator was asked whether their hospital would turn the module on, matched to whether it did.

Exhibit 1. What a stated “yes” has been worth at Eshana (600 records, six modules)

Share adopting = adopters ÷ records in that row: 135÷405, 15÷195, 150÷600.

Read it as a calibration. The base rate of adoption is 150 of 600, or 25.0 per cent. The probability an administrator said yes given that the hospital adopted is 135 of 150, or 90.0 per cent; given that it did not, 270 of 450, or 60.0 per cent. The ratio of those conditionals, 0.90 ÷ 0.60 = 1.50, is the diagnostic likelihood ratio of a yes: the multiplier on the odds held before asking. Prior odds are 150 to 450, or 0.3333; times 1.50 they become 0.5000, a probability of 0.5 ÷ 1.5 = 33.3 per cent, the first row. A no does more work: its likelihood ratio is 0.10 ÷ 0.40 = 0.25.

Hence a second-order effect practitioners miss. Because a yes is weakly diagnostic and a no strongly so, any design that suppresses noes — leading questions, warmth, interviewing only friends of the company — destroys most of the available information. Social desirability does not merely inflate the yes count; it deletes the signal. Erum's second field recorded whether the hospital had put a named owner and go-live date in writing.

4. When the correction applies, and when it misleads

The discipline rests on three testable claims. The incentive to please is non-zero and correlated with the answer you want. True at Eshana, where administrators depend on its support desk, and at Falak, where managers negotiate lease rates with the interviewer. You hold a record linking past stated answers to past behaviour. True at Eshana with 600 records; false at Falak, with 61 matched records, too few to stake ₹95 lakh on. The decision is an estimation problem with a numeric threshold. True for Eshana's 143 adopters; only half true at Falak, where one feature bears on safety. On expected value, Eknath's preference is textbook zero-risk bias.

The geofence removes ₹71.28 lakh a year and repays ₹95 lakh in 1.33 years; the dose controller removes ₹112.86 lakh and repays in 0.84 years, a difference of ₹41.58 lakh. The geofence bar stops short of the dashed build-cost line; the dose-controller bar crosses it.

And yet the correction may be what misleads. Under DGCA rules a single drift event onto habitation is not priced in rupees: it can suspend a remote pilot certificate and, badly handled, a type approval. The regulator's loss function is lexicographic, not linear. If one boundary event in a monsoon season carries a real chance of grounding the fleet, the geofence is worth nearer the option value of continuing to operate than ₹71.28 lakh — and the managers, who have lived through a district spray ban, may read that better.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulation, hardware, two-sidedness, AI

Falak is a two-sided arrangement masquerading as a lease: the manager buys, the neighbouring farmer bears the drift. Falak interviewed 44 managers and no farmers: the injured party was never in the frame. Felipe Quintero, Eknath's analytics contractor in Bogotá, showed that 198 of the 324 drift events sat in three districts.

Regulation creates a structural bias technique cannot remove. Eshana cannot speak to patients about claim rejections without consent machinery, so its base skews toward staff whom compliance has cleared, and a billing head answers as the hospital. The defence is the 460 customers' own claim-rejection logs.

Hardware and software fail differently. Falak's geofence needs a firmware change and a re-flight of the DGCA compliance matrix, so a false positive costs recertification rather than a sprint. AI-native products invert it: respondents cannot report on capability they have not experienced, so demonstrations become powerful anchors, and a model synthesising transcripts inherits its prompt's confirmation bias.

At the organisational seam, mature companies differ most from their own descriptions. Fateh Virdi's 83.3 per cent was not misconduct; he is paid on pipeline and has learned a style that produces enthusiasm. Firms say they separate research from sales. The good ones do something cheaper: adjust for the interviewer.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Bias has a sign; noise does not. The tell is a practitioner who answers a worrying result by adding interviews. An expert asks which way the error points, because a directional error converts volume into false confidence. More data is better only where the generating process is untilted.

The guide encodes the hypothesis before anyone speaks. The tell is a discussion guide naming the proposed feature. Experts write the kill criterion first: “we abandon this if fewer than a third of administrators can name who files pre-authorisations today” outperforms any post-hoc rigour.

Anchors are usually social, not numeric. The tell is findings clustering near a figure that circulated internally. Feroza found Fariyal's enthusiasm had reached the interviewers, in a thread dated 7 August. Context appears to help respondents orient; it contaminates them instead, most strongly the most cooperative.

Survivorship is a framing problem, not a weighting adjustment. The tell is a recruitment screen whose every criterion describes current engagement. No weight recovers a problem nobody in the sample has. The expert asks who would have to exist for this finding to be wrong.

Social desirability scales with dependence, not politeness. The tell is that the warmest interviews yield the highest yes rates. The defence is not coldness but completed behaviour — what the administrator did the last time a claim was rejected — because the past is costlier to flatter.

A likelihood ratio, not a discount, is the right object. The tell is one stated-intent haircut applied everywhere. A haircut assumes the distortion is proportional and stable; a likelihood ratio is specific to a question and says what a haircut cannot — that the question itself can be improved.

Zero-risk bias is rational against a step function. The tell is a regulator, a certification or a contractual cliff in the loss function. Experts look for the threshold before naming the preference a bias. Falak shows expected value failing because consequence is not continuous.

Over-correction is the signature failure of the newly converted. The tell is a corrected estimate quoted to three decimals. Corrections carry standard errors; Falak's 61 records support no useful likelihood ratio, and pretending otherwise is a fresh bias in the costume of rigour.

7. Across product types and company stages

Stage changes which defences are affordable, not which biases exist. A company with 40 customers cannot run Exhibit 1, having no calibration history; its only honest instrument is a costly signal. At Eshana's scale calibration is cheap and exposure shifts to institutional anchoring — a roadmap, a forecast, an executive's number — managed only by sequencing research ahead of forecast.

8. Three worked cases, including one that failed

Eshana. Calibration moved the estimate from 291 adopters to 110 and the payback from 0.98 to 2.60 years against a threshold of 143 — eleven days of work on a ₹360 lakh decision.

Falak: anchoring measured rather than argued. Eknath split 60 managers into two arms of 30 between 24 August and 9 September 2026. Arm A was asked what it expected to pay per acre; Arm B was first told, truthfully, that some Maharashtra operators charge around ₹250 per acre.

The unanchored arm sat 7.1 per cent below that, the anchored arm 38.9 per cent above: both biased.

Faayda Rewards Network, where the correction did the damage. Faayda, a retail loyalty network in Kochi with 20,00,000 monthly actives, had been embarrassed in 2025 by two features that tested well and failed. Its research lead, Farzana Edulji, imposed a flat 0.45 stated-intent discount on all findings. In January 2026 a referral feature tested at 52 of 80 users saying they would invite a friend — 65.0 per cent. Discounted to 29.25 per cent it implied 5,85,000 inviters against a bar of 7,00,000, and died on 14 January.

A competitor shipped something similar in the spring. At launch the realised invite rate in the equivalent cohort was 41.0 per cent — a said-versus-did ratio of 41.0 ÷ 65.0 = 63.1 per cent, not 45 per cent. 9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

Each diagnostic costs an afternoon to two weeks, against decisions of ₹95 lakh to ₹360 lakh. The only explanation for neglect is that nobody owns the question.

10. Where expert opinion genuinely divides

Can stated preference be rehabilitated? The behavioural-evidence camp says no: replace talk with a costly action, because correlations between stated intention and later behaviour are modest and unstable. Its strongest evidence is Faayda's range, 38 to 81 per cent, showing no stable conversion factor exists. Calibration replies that a likelihood ratio of 1.50 is small but real, and beats no test when the alternative costs money.

Debias the person or redesign the environment? Training studies show weak transfer, which is the structural camp's case for blind coding, pre-registered kill criteria and lapsed-user quotas. Ecological rationality counters that Firdaus Elavia's rate falling once it was visible is a representation effect, not a structural one.

Does qualitative research estimate anything? Total survey error holds that sixty purposively recruited interviews support no population estimate and that Feroza's 110 is false rigour. Interpretivists agree on the arithmetic for the opposite reason: the interviews were never for estimating, and dressing them as a forecast wastes their real yield, the complaint about implementation time.

Do costly signals contaminate the sample? Asking for a deposit selects for respondents willing to commit, lifting measured conversion for reasons unrelated to the feature. Falak's paid-pilot experience suggests the effect is real but smaller than the information gained. Nobody has published a clean decomposition in a product setting.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this names five biases and says the team should watch for confirmation bias. Someone who has internalised it writes the decision, the threshold and the kill criterion before the first interview, so research cannot be retrofitted to a conclusion; keeps a calibration record, so the organisation argues about a number rather than a vibe; and reports ranges, naming the dominant source of error rather than a point estimate.

12. The decisions, and three questions

On Thursday 1 October 2026, Feroza Engineer told the executive committee that the interviews supported roughly 107 to 110 adopters against the 143 needed for a two-year payback, and that she would not request ₹3.60 crore. She proposed a design-partner round aimed at one number: the share of customers willing to name an internal owner and a go-live date in writing. To reach 143 of 460 adopters, or 31.1 per cent, the costly-signal model needs 37.4 per cent to clear that commitment, because 0.374 × 0.6604 + 0.626 × 0.1020 = 0.3108. Today 14 of 60 clear it; 23 of 60 would imply 145 adopters. Fariyal accepted: her mandate had been priced, not refuted.

On Friday 16 October, Eknath Fadnis did what his expected-value table did not recommend. He built the geofence, saying plainly that he was overruling a ₹41.58 lakh annual advantage because the dose controller's benefit was continuous while the drift risk sat behind a regulatory step function that could stop the business. He committed to the dose controller next quarter, and to farmer-side interviews in those three districts.

Three questions. First, if Eshana's likelihood ratio for a stated yes is 1.50, is there any interview volume at which Feroza should have approved ₹360 lakh on stated preference alone? Second, Eknath overrode his own arithmetic on the grounds of a step function; what evidence would show he was rationalising a bias he had just been shown? Third, which single column added to Exhibit 8 would make it predictive for a seventh feature, and why that rather than a larger sample?

13. Going deeper

Interview fundamentals is the constraint beneath all of this: biases are how a well-formed interview still goes wrong. Calibrating interviewers across a team turns Exhibit 3 into a routine. False positives in discovery prices the hollow yes. Qualitative versus quantitative research frames section 10. Designing an interview guide implements kill criteria and anchor hygiene. Recruiting research participants is the remedy for survivorship. How many interviews depends on whether your error is random or directional. Synthesising research is where confirmatory coding happens. AI-assisted synthesis raises the stakes, because a model reproduces your prompt's prior.
case20v1-res.bias:
Fifteen Yeses at Kolam Works

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Parinita Varadarajan sat in a glass meeting room at Kolam Works in Bengaluru with a spreadsheet that looked like good news. Twenty customer interviews, run over the second half of September, had produced a headline her chief executive had already repeated twice: fifteen of twenty customers, or 75 per cent, said they would pay ₹3,500 a week for a new Premium meal plan. The company's investment committee would meet on Friday, 16 October, to release ₹1.8 crore for the build. Launch was pencilled in for Monday, 2 November, a week before Diwali on 8 November, when household food spending peaks.

Parinita, Head of Product, had designed the interview guide. She could not shake a feeling about the people who had not been in the room. She had until Friday morning to recommend whether to release the money, delay it, or change the shape of the bet.

2. Company background

Kolam Works sells weekly home-style meal subscriptions to working professionals in Bengaluru and Pune. Customers choose a plan on the app; central kitchens in Whitefield and Hinjewadi cook, pack and dispatch lunches and dinners through a rider fleet. Founded in 2021 by Pritam Vyas, a former consultant, the company has signed up 6,200 households since launch and has 1,860 of them paying today. Their average spend is ₹2,100 a week.

The market around it is crowded. Swiggy and Zomato deliver restaurant food on demand, and Zepto Cafe has pushed into ten-minute snacks and meals. Kolam's pitch is predictability: the same cook, the same kitchen, a weekly menu that tastes like a home in Coimbatore or Pune. Its challenge is retention. Roughly seven in ten households that ever signed up have since stopped paying.

3. The situation

The Premium plan, with a larger menu, a dedicated dietitian call and chef-cooked weekend specials, was Pritam's idea. In August he told the product team he was "already hearing it from customers". Parinita proposed discovery before build. Over two weeks in September, the team invited 180 customers by WhatsApp and email, offering a ₹500 Kolam credit for a 40-minute call. Sixty replied, and twenty were interviewed. Her guide opened each call by stating the price, ₹3,500 a week, and asking if it sounded fair.

Exhibit 1 shows who was heard. Eighteen of the twenty interviewees were currently paying subscribers, although paying subscribers are 30.0 per cent of everyone who ever signed up. Only two lapsed customers were interviewed, because only six of the sixty lapsed customers invited answered at all, a reply rate of 10.0 per cent against 45.0 per cent among active customers. Nobody who only downloaded the app was invited.

The interviews themselves were warm. One customer said, "Honestly, I would pay anything to stop thinking about dinner." Yet Parinita noticed that her own follow-up questions, such as "Is that because the plan helps you?", tended to draw agreement, and that the three customers who hesitated were the ones the team had quietly weighted down in its summary as "price-sensitive outliers".

On 1 October, without telling anyone, she sent each of the fifteen yeses a link to reserve a Premium slot with a refundable ₹500 deposit, open for seven days. By 7 October, three had paid. The global team read the evidence differently. Pavithra Viswanathan, a data analyst working from Lisbon, pointed out that the sample was drawn almost entirely from people still buying, and she wanted lapsed customers heard first. 4. The people

Parinita Varadarajan, Head of Product, Bengaluru, owns the recommendation. She wants a decision she can defend if either enthusiasm or doubt turns out to be wrong.

Pritam Vyas, founder and chief executive, Bengaluru, wants Premium live before Diwali. He argues that Kolam's rivals are moving and that interviews always understate delight.

Pavithra Viswanathan, data analyst, Lisbon, wants the lapsed 4,340 heard.

Parmeet Vohra, head of kitchen operations, Pune, wants a clear forecast. He needs weeks of notice to hire and train chefs, and he is wary of both over-building and missing the festive peak.

Exhibits 1 and 2 are above. Exhibit 3 translates the two readings of demand into money. It assumes the active base of 1,860 is the market for upgrades, that each upgrader adds ₹1,400 a week (₹3,500 less the current average of ₹2,100), and that the build cost is ₹180 lakh. Revenue, not margin, is shown. The stated reading is 75.0 per cent, the headline; the paid reading is 15.0 per cent, the share of interviewees who put down a deposit.
