Kargha Works: Ten Field Days

Four weeks, ten usable field days and one contested page of questions.

1. The night before

At a quarter past ten on the night of Sunday, 25 October 2026, Prachi Vanarase was still at the long table in Kargha Works' office on Avinashi Road, Coimbatore, with three stapled documents. The first was the interview guide her field team had used in August. The second was a rewrite, twenty-one questions long, sent from Bengaluru on Friday by Piyali Veeramani under the subject line "please read the coding sheet first". The third was a note from Punit Volvoikar in Surat: both were a waste of a fortnight the company did not have.

Prachi was head of product. On Monday morning, 26 October, she had to release a discovery plan: recruiters needed two days to book shop-floor appointments, and the board met on Monday, 23 November, four weeks to the day. It had asked for one thing: evidence that the company's second revenue line, a yarn-purchase advance underwritten on verified loom output, was wanted by the people who would sign for it. What she had was three sets of numbers that disagreed, ₹1,20,000 left on a research budget and a Diwali shutdown in the middle of her field window.

She had written on the top sheet, in pencil, the sentence she could not yet finish: the question is not which guide, it is…

2. How Kargha Works came to be constrained

Kargha Works was founded in 2017 by Pulkit Vasireddy, an instrumentation engineer, and two classmates. The product was unglamorous and well judged: a retrofit sensor box, clamped to a loom of any vintage, that counted picks, logged warp breaks and reported shift-level efficiency. Where owners had judged utilisation by the weight of cloth off the beam, a measured number was worth paying for.

By September 2026 the company had 310 weaving units on subscription, covering 9,400 looms at ₹450 per loom per month: annual recurring revenue of ₹5.08 crore. It employed 148 people: 46 in Bengaluru, 39 in Coimbatore, 44 in the Surat and Ichalkaranji field offices, 16 in Pune, three outside India.

Two earlier decisions shaped the night of 25 October. In June 2023 Kargha raised ₹18 crore from Khanak Growth Partners, on covenants requiring annual recurring revenue of ₹12 crore by 31 March 2028 and a board-approved second revenue line by 30 November 2026. And in 2021, short of cash and field staff, Kargha gave Kapas Agencies, a yarn trading house in Surat, exclusive resale rights there until 31 March 2027. Clause 9 barred Kargha from offering credit or advances to units Kapas introduced without the trading house's written consent. Those units were 127 of the 310, carrying 3,854 looms, or 41.0 per cent of the installed loom base.

3. The industry around the loom

India's decentralised weaving sector runs on thin, borrowed money. In Ichalkaranji, Surat and the Coimbatore belt, a unit of twenty to three hundred looms buys yarn on 30 or 45 days' credit from a commission agent, weaves grey cloth against a trader's order and is paid when the trader is paid. Machinery comes from Lakshmi Machine Works and imported rapier looms; polyester yarn, at one remove, from Reliance Industries; downstream, sellers on Flipkart and Meesho set the tempo. GST returns, Udyam registration and Technology Upgradation Fund borrowings have made unit-level data legible; the account aggregator framework has made it shareable. Reserve Bank of India lending rules require the lender of record to be a regulated entity, which is why the advance had to be built with Kist Finance Partners, an NBFC.

Competition arrived quickly: Kirmich Devices, of Ahmedabad, sold a sensor at ₹260 per loom per month bundled into a yarn marketplace. Kargha's exposure also ran outward. Kostanza Tessile, a home-textile buyer in Milan, had begun asking Indian suppliers for machine-level production records, giving the data a second buyer.

4. What happened, and what it was thought to mean

The advance idea was written down in May 2026: Kargha knew, loom by loom, what a unit produced, and a lender who could see production could lend against a yarn purchase on less collateral than a bank. Pulkit showed the sketch to Phiroza Vakil in June, and the board asked for customer evidence.

Between Monday, 10 August and Friday, 28 August the field team ran 48 conversations across 29 weaving units in Ichalkaranji and Surat, using a guide written in a week by Punit's team and Prachi's. It opened with twelve minutes of introduction and the concept, moved to a fourteen-minute walkthrough of a mocked-up screen, then asked whether the owner would use the facility and at what fee. Thirty-one of the 48 conversations ended in a stated willingness to pay within ninety days (64.6 per cent of conversations). Exhibit 1 sets out who was in the room, and Figure 1 the dates.

Read in early September this looked decisive. Prachi then did two things that unsettled it: she asked Punit to convert the interest into a paid trial at a discounted ₹240 per loom per month, and asked Piyali to code the guide's questions for leading construction. Exhibit 4 reports the trial; Exhibits 2 and 3 the coding.

In parallel, before either result landed, Pulkit commissioned Keemat Research Partners to run a vernacular telephone survey in Ichalkaranji. It was fielded from Monday, 14 September to Tuesday, 22 September and reported on Wednesday, 30 September: 1,240 completed interviews, 884 of them (71.3 per cent) calling the advance "very useful". That figure went into a slide Khanak has seen; Exhibit 5 reproduces it.

By mid-October the three sources had stopped pointing the same way. Prachi's memo of Friday, 16 October said so in one line — "we have measured three different things and are calling them one" — and asked for a second round. Paz Villanueva's note of Thursday, 22 October added a complication: 19 of the 310 subscribing units had given notice, and nobody had interviewed a leaver.

5. The people

Prachi Vanarase, head of product, Coimbatore. She releases the plan on Monday and defends what it produces. She wrote the 2024 memo that bundled the sensor hardware free into a 36-month contract, so she is slow to call an earlier method wrong. She has not told the others that two of the four trial signatures came from units run by men she studied with.

Pulkit Vasireddy, co-founder and chief executive. He wants the advance approved in November and the fieldwork sized to fit; his incentive is the covenant and the next round. He has not said that the 71.3 per cent is already in a deck at Khanak, and that withdrawing it would cost him more than being wrong.

Punit Volvoikar, vice-president, sales, Surat. The August guide worked, he argues, and a rewrite is an insult dressed as rigour. His team earned ₹1,500 per trial signature, ₹6,000 in all, and recruited all 48 conversations. He has not mentioned that three were with units he had sold to twice, nor that Kapas Agencies' consent under clause 9 has not been sought.

Piyali Veeramani, research lead, Bengaluru. She built the coding in Exhibits 2 and 3 and holds that the sample, not the wording, is the deeper defect: five operators and two agents cannot tell you how a unit decides. She wants a research function. She revised her definitions after the first twenty questions, one reason the coders agree less than she would like.

Pieter Visser, data scientist, Amsterdam. He distrusts agreement statistics on small question sets and wants a discrete-choice experiment with a proper frame. He has not said that the only usable frame, the weavers' association list, is not his to get.

Paola Venturi, design lead, Milan. She wants two shifts of observation per unit before anyone asks a question, and the concept withheld. Her contract runs to 31 December, and she has six working days free before 20 November, a fact she has mentioned only to Prachi.

Paz Villanueva, customer-success lead, Manila. The 19 units giving notice are the most honest interviews available, she argues, and her bonus is tied to renewals. She has not said that four of the 19 cited the hardware bundle — Prachi's memo — as the reason they feel trapped.

Phiroza Vakil, partner at Khanak Growth Partners, Mumbai, and a director. She has asked for "evidence of demand, not enthusiasm". She also sits on the committee that decides by March whether to lead Kargha's next round, and a thin November paper is easier to defend than a reversed thesis.

7. Voices

8. The options as Prachi sees them

She has written the choice as four designs (Exhibit 6).

Option A reuses the August guide for sixteen more conversations, keeps Punit inside the tent and delivers a memo on Monday, 16 November. It also reproduces the instrument that produced the gap between Exhibits 1 and 4.

Option B runs Piyali's 55-minute guide with a re-sampled roster: four owners, four supervisors or operators, two agents, two units that have given notice. It would surface what a unit does when yarn money is short, and finishes on 18 November with no slack.

Option C puts Paola on two back-to-back shifts in each of five units, one unit a day, and asks nothing until the second. It is the one design that would see the agent's Thursday visit rather than hear about it, and the one most exposed to a single calendar.

Option D buys a discrete-choice survey Pieter can model, and would arrive before Diwali — if a frame exists, which it does not.

The framing has a hole, and Piyali's email names part of it (Figure 3). Every option is a decision about how to ask; none is about who is asked, who recruits them, or what the answer is for. The board asked for a revenue line, and a problem memo is not one. Clause 9 sits across the Surat half of the question, and the ₹1,500 per signature across the recruitment of any design the sales team touches.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The calendar is unforgiving. Recruiters need the plan on Monday, 26 October; fieldwork can begin Wednesday, 28 October; the clusters close for Diwali from Friday, 6 November to Wednesday, 11 November, the festival falling on Sunday, 8 November; interviewing stops on Friday, 13 November. On the six-day week the units keep, that is ten field days. Papers close Wednesday, 18 November; the board sits Monday, 23 November.

Money is tighter. The FY27 discovery line, for the year ending 31 March 2027, was ₹4,00,000; ₹2,80,000 is spent — ₹93,600 on round one, ₹1,86,400 on Keemat — leaving ₹1,20,000. A and B together cost ₹84,000 and fit; B and C cost ₹1,20,600 and do not; D alone costs ₹96,000.

Three constraints are not financial. Clause 9 bars any advance to the 127 Kapas units until 31 March 2027 without the trading house's consent, and nobody has asked. Recording an interview, and sharing loom data with Kist Finance Partners, needs consent under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; the script is in draft. Paola has six working days before 20 November, the whole of Option C.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of Exhibits 1, 4 and 5 measure, and on what base? Which of Figure 2's five percentages may legitimately be compared with which?
  2. Exhibit 2 reports flagged shares of 42.3, 14.3 and 42.9 per cent. What would you need to know about Exhibit 3's coding before letting them carry an argument?
  3. Rewrite the first four questions of the August guide so that they test the assumption behind the advance without proposing it. What, in Prahlad Valvi's words, is it?
  4. Piyali says the roster matters more than the wording. Design it for ten field days: who is interviewed, who recruits them, and what you give up.
  5. Suppose the second round produces the same split, warm words and few signatures. What should Kargha want to learn, and can any Exhibit 6 design teach it?
  6. What does Prachi release on Monday morning, 26 October, inside ₹1,20,000 and ten field days — and what does she tell the board on 23 November about the 71.3 per cent already in its deck?

At twenty past eleven Prachi turned the sheet over and wrote two columns, what we know and what we only have a number for. The second filled first: Prahlad Valvi's Thursday tea, four signatures of which two were favours, the unsourceable figure. The first calls were nine hours away; the pencil line was unfinished.
case20v1-res.interview.basics:
Twelve Yeses at Heerasutra Bazaar

A teaching case on interview fundamentals

1. Opening

On the evening of Thursday, 22 October 2026, Manvi Ruparel sat in the Pune office of Heerasutra Bazaar with her laptop open to a spreadsheet she had been proud of for a week. It held notes from twelve interviews with boutique owners. Ten of them had said they would use a 45-day credit facility on their wholesale orders. Her chief executive, Mukul Rajhans, had read the summary and replied: "Ten out of twelve. Why are we still talking?"

Sprint planning was on Monday, 26 October. Mrunal Rajurkar, the chief technology officer, needed to know by Friday whether six engineers would spend ten weeks building the credit product, at a fully loaded cost of ₹60 lakh. Manvi, as head of product, owned the recommendation. That afternoon she had replayed her seventh interview and felt uneasy.

2. Company background

Heerasutra Bazaar is a business-to-business marketplace that connects handloom weaver cooperatives, mainly in Maharashtra, Rajasthan, Odisha and Tamil Nadu, with independent boutique retailers across India. It was founded in Pune in 2019 and now lists 410 cooperatives and sells to about 3,400 active retailers. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it moved ₹186 crore of goods and kept a commission of 6 per cent, which gives revenue of ₹11.16 crore.

Its rivals are larger pools of supply. Udaan and IndiaMART serve wholesale buyers broadly, Meesho carries low-priced ethnic wear, and Fabindia and Jaypore shape what boutique customers expect to see on a rack. Heerasutra's pitch is verified provenance and small minimum orders.

Heerasutra's plan was to partner with a licensed NBFC, under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending rules, which would fund the 45-day terms while Heerasutra paid weavers promptly and earned a fee.

3. The situation

The idea came from a pattern in the data. Orders from retailers spike before Diwali, which falls on Sunday, 8 November this year. The board had asked for a credit product in the first quarter of 2027.

Manvi and two colleagues ran the twelve interviews between Monday, 5 October and Friday, 16 October, each lasting about 40 minutes. The guide had been written in a hurry. When Manvi listened again she counted what she had actually asked. Three questions recurred in every call, and all three invited agreement: whether the retailer would use 45-day credit, whether cash flow was a problem, and whether she would order more if credit existed. Exhibit 1 sets out the pattern.

Exhibit 1. The three questions asked in all twelve interviews, and one asked rarely
Question as askedKind of questionInterviews in which askedPositive answers
"Would you use 45-day credit from us?"Hypothetical, closed1210
"Is cash flow a problem for you?"Leading, closed1211
"Would you order more if we offered it?"Hypothetical, closed129
"Tell me about the last time you could not afford an order."Past story, open22 specific episodes

Source: Heerasutra interview recordings and notes, 5 to 16 October 2026. The open question was dropped from ten interviews because the 40 minutes ran out.

Mylene Ramos, who leads customer success from Manila, was the first to question the result. She told Manvi that "nobody says no to free money in an interview". Mahrukh Rustomji, the designer in Lisbon, had watched four recordings and noticed that Manvi often filled a pause within two seconds by offering an answer: "I mean, most shops struggle with cash, right?"

Mathew Rozario, the data scientist in Montreal, matched the ten retailers who said yes against six months of orders, invoices and support tickets, to ask what they had done rather than what they had said. Exhibit 2 shows what he found.

Exhibit 2. What the records show for the ten retailers who said yes (April to September 2026)
Observed behaviourRetailersShare of the ten
Asked Heerasutra or a weaver for extra time to pay330%
Paid an existing 15-day invoice late, but never asked for more time220%
No sign of payment strain550%
Total who said yes10100%

Source: Heerasutra order, invoice and support-ticket records, matched by Mathew Rozario. The two retailers who said no are excluded. Shares are of the ten, not of the twelve.

The two interviews with the open question were far richer. In the seventh, Manvi asked about the last time an order had been out of reach, then stayed silent for what the recording timestamps as eleven seconds. Malti Rekhi, who owns a boutique in Jaipur, described turning down a large lot of Kota Doria sarees in August because she had no cash, and then borrowing from her cousin to buy half of it. She had not mentioned credit. She would have welcomed "somebody just holding the bill for a month", which is a related but different need.

4. The people

Mukul Rajhans, chief executive in Pune, wants speed. The board has asked for a visible new revenue line, and ten out of twelve sounds like proof.

Mrunal Rajurkar, chief technology officer in Pune, wants a stable plan. The six engineers on this build would otherwise rebuild catalogue search, and he will not shift them twice.

Mahrukh Rustomji, designer in Lisbon, wants the team to hear retailers in their own words. She relies on recordings, so she has seen exactly how the questions were put.

Mylene Ramos, customer success lead in Manila, wants to protect the retailers. A failed credit product means collections calls, and her team would make them. She also sees best who actually struggles to pay.

Figure 1 carries dates and labels only. The ten-week build ends well after Diwali.

5. The options

Manvi saw three courses, set out in Exhibit 3. Option A was to approve the build on Monday as planned. The upside is speed: the product would be ready on Monday, 4 January 2027. The cost is ₹60 lakh, six engineers for ten weeks at roughly ₹1 lakh per engineer-week, on evidence that Exhibit 2 puts in doubt.

Option B was to pause engineering for two weeks and run eight new interviews from 26 October to 6 November, using a revised guide built on past events: the last time you ordered, what happened to the money, who you asked, what you did instead. She estimated ₹1.2 lakh for incentives and travel and ₹2.0 lakh of analyst time, a total of ₹3.2 lakh. The upside is a decision built on stories. The cost is a two-week delay, which would move the end of any build to Monday, 18 January 2027 if she then approved it.

Option C was a concierge pilot: offer 45-day terms by hand to 30 retailers through the NBFC partner, with manual reconciliation and a first-loss reserve, at an estimated ₹9 lakh over five weeks to Monday, 30 November. The upside is real behaviour with real money. The cost is more time than Option B, dependence on the NBFC, and exposure to actual defaults.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared
OptionCost (₹ lakh)Time to evidence or launchWhat it tells Manvi
A. Build now60.010 weeks, to 4 Jan 2027Nothing before launch
B. Eight story-based interviews3.22 weeks, to 6 Nov 2026Whether the need is credit, and for whom
C. Concierge pilot, 30 retailers9.05 weeks, to 30 Nov 2026Whether retailers take and repay credit

Costs are Manvi's estimates of 22 October 2026. Option A is a fully loaded engineering cost; B and C are cash and analyst time.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which questions in the first twelve interviews could produce a "yes" regardless of what the retailer actually does? How would each change to reveal behaviour?

2. Exhibit 2 shows that five of the ten who said yes showed no payment strain. What does that suggest about "ten out of twelve"?

3. Why did the seventh interview surface a need the guide never anticipated? What did Manvi do, and not do?

4. Which option would you choose, and what result in the next two to five weeks would make you change your mind?

7. A note for the learner

This case turns on one idea: an interview should reveal what people do rather than what they say. Hypothetical and leading questions measure politeness and imagination. Stories about specific past events measure behaviour, because the respondent cannot easily invent the date, the amount and the person they asked. The habits are: ask for stories, keep questions open, probe why, and let silence work. Manvi's seventh interview used all four, and it produced the one real surprise.

A well-reasoned answer starts by separating evidence from agreement. Ten yeses to three suggestible questions are weak evidence. Exhibit 2 is stronger because it records conduct: only three of the ten had sought more time to pay, though Heerasutra sees only its own invoices. Diwali is also no reason to hurry, since no option delivers a product before 8 November.

One defensible path is Option B, with Option C as the sequel if the stories support credit. Eight interviews cost ₹3.2 lakh, about 5 per cent of the ₹60 lakh build, and take two weeks. If retailers describe cash gaps and workarounds like Malti Rekhi's, Manvi should approve a pilot before a full build, because only Option C tests repayment. If the stories point to something else, such as holding the bill, shared lots or smaller minimum orders, she will have avoided spending ₹60 lakh on the wrong product.

A two-week pause tests Mukul's patience, so Manvi should bring him a dated plan: interviews by 6 November, a decision at sprint planning on 9 November. Mahrukh can review recordings for filled silences and Mylene can nominate retailers who really struggled to pay.
case40v1-res.interview.basics:
Itminaan Care Network: The Pendant and the Payer

A case for discussion. Hyderabad, November 2026.

1. The night before

On the evening of Sunday, 15 November 2026, Naomi Sivaraman sat at her dining table in Kondapur, Hyderabad, the Diwali lights still up from the previous Sunday. She was head of product at Itminaan Care Network, and at half past nine the next morning she had to put one option before the product council.

The first file was a telephone survey delivered nine days earlier by Inayat Research Partners: eighty-two per cent of respondents said they were likely to pay an extra ₹499 a month for round-the-clock emergency response for their parent. The second was Nabanita Srinath's spreadsheet of a ninety-day trial in which Itminaan had put an emergency pendant into a hundred and twenty homes. Of the 519 times the button had been pressed, the clinical desk in Chennai had classified thirteen as emergencies.

Between the two files sat a contract. On 14 July, Itminaan had signed with Ichimura Sensor Industries of Osaka for six thousand pendants at ₹7,400 a unit landed in Hyderabad, a commitment of ₹444.0 lakh; walking away after Monday, 30 November cost thirty-five per cent of that, ₹155.4 lakh. The council sat fourteen days before that date, the board on Friday, 27 November, three days before it.

What unsettled her was not the contradiction between the files, but a recording she had played twice that afternoon: an August call she had run herself, with a son in Bengaluru and his father on the line, in which the eighty-one-year-old in Secunderabad talked for nine minutes about a night in May without saying the word "emergency".

2. How Itminaan came to be shaped this way

Itminaan was founded in Hyderabad in 2018 by Nitara Sukhija and Noel Sridharan. It sells a monthly subscription for care at home: an attendant on a fixed roster, nurse visits and teleconsultation. At 30 September 2026 it had 11,400 active subscriptions across Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Pune, Chennai and Kochi, and 2,900 attendants. In the year ended 31 March 2026 revenue was ₹103.7 crore, from an average of 9,100 active subscriptions at an average realised ₹9,500 a month. Cash stood at ₹61 crore against a burn of ₹3.4 crore a month, which is 17.9 months.

One decision from 2019 shapes what is possible today. Itminaan built the product around the adult child as the account holder: the child installs the app, reads the attendant's daily report, approves the care plan and pays. The parent has no login, no device and usually no contact record — Itminaan holds a verified mobile number for the elder in only 3,250 of 11,400 homes, or 28.5 per cent. That was commercially shrewd, since children abroad churn slowly and 4,674 of 11,400 accounts, or 41.0 per cent, are billed outside India. It also means every sample drawn from the account table is a sample of payers, and that fitting a device needs the elder's own consent as a data principal under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

3. The industry

Organised elder care in India is young. Portea Medical and HealthCare atHome built home nursing; Emoha Elder Care and Antara Senior Care sell membership; Tata 1mg and Practo own medicines. None has made emergency response a mass product, and all face the same arithmetic: more than 150 million people over sixty, in households where the decision-maker often lives abroad.

Hardware sets expectations: boAt and Noise have taught Indian buyers that a wrist device costs a few thousand rupees, so a ₹7,400 pendant has to be sold as a service. Counsel advises that a non-diagnostic alarm pendant is not a medical device, though claims about detecting falls would invite scrutiny. Bundling Imroz Assurance's cover needs a corporate agency arrangement under the insurance regulator's rules, and the ₹499 price includes eighteen per cent GST, leaving a net realisation of ₹423.

Itminaan is also exposed to markets it does not operate in: Naushad Shamsi sells through Ibtida Trading LLC in Muscat, and a smaller channel reaches families in Melbourne. Those buyers ask about response times in minutes, and are why the pendant was costed as a premium add-on.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 the board asked for a second revenue line by the end of the following financial year. By April the pendant led the field, and Natasha Sanzgiri's team in Amsterdam was asked to validate it. Twenty-two interviews ran between Monday, 13 July and Friday, 28 August (Figure 1); Exhibit 1 shows who was in the room and Exhibit 2 how the questions were put. Her 2 September summary reported nineteen of the twenty-two calling the pendant "reassuring" and fourteen volunteering a price at or above ₹400 a month. The Ichimura agreement was signed on Tuesday, 14 July — the second day of fieldwork — after Nitara negotiated the unit price down from ₹9,200 by committing to six thousand units.

From Saturday, 1 August to Thursday, 29 October, ninety days, Itminaan placed a hundred and twenty loaner pendants in Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Pune (Exhibit 4A). Adherence fell from 92 of 120 homes in week one, or 76.7 per cent, to 26 of 120 in week twelve, or 21.7 per cent (Figure 2). The desk judged 13 of 519 presses to be emergencies, which is 2.5 per cent, and logged 34 further emergencies in the same homes that surfaced through an attendant, a neighbour or a review.

The Inayat survey was in the field from 14 to 24 October and reported on 6 November (Exhibit 3). From 2 to 9 November the trial homes were offered the pendant at ₹499 a month: 23 of 120 accepted, or 19.2 per cent (Exhibit 4B).

Then on 11 November the reliability audit landed (Exhibit 5). Two reviewers relabelled 180 of the 519 presses independently and agreed on 142 of 180, or 78.9 per cent — but on the label that mattered they agreed on only 14 of the 30 events reviewer one called emergencies, which is 46.7 per cent, and both found emergencies among presses the desk had dismissed live. The thirteen is no longer a number anyone will defend, in either direction.

5. The people

Naomi Sivaraman, head of product, Hyderabad, owns Monday's recommendation and thinks the discovery work was poor. She also wrote the September deck that told the board demand was proven, and has not said that the ₹423 net realisation puts payback at 17.5 months, not the 14.8 in the plan.

Nitara Sukhija, co-founder and chief executive, wants the order confirmed; the new revenue line is the spine of her Series C story. She has not said that two investors asked about the Imroz arrangement by name.

Noel Sridharan, co-founder, head of care operations, Chennai, thinks the attendants are the emergency system, and the 34 other-channel events are his evidence. He has not said that an ₹800 allowance across 2,900 attendants costs ₹23.2 lakh a month, ₹2.78 crore a year, from his budget.

Neville Sorabjee, chief technology officer, Bengaluru, has eight engineers off a rostering rebuild overdue since June and needs a decision before Ichimura freezes firmware on 7 December. He has not said that the cellular fallback is untested in Kochi.

Natasha Sanzgiri, research lead, Amsterdam, coded all 22 transcripts after the fact and brought Exhibit 2 to the team unprompted. Her position is that nothing has been learned from an elder; her contract ends in January.

Nabanita Srinath, data scientist, Melbourne, built the trial file and the audit, trusts behaviour over stated intent, and knows her adherence series cannot tell a pendant in a drawer from one on charge.

Nimai Shanbhag, chief financial officer, Mumbai, has put ₹2.2 crore of Imroz fees into the plan for the year ending 31 March 2027, being 4,000 covered homes at ₹5,500 each. He quotes the survey as "eighty-two per cent of our subscribers" and the trial as proof that "Pune is the weakest arm on every count", and has not circulated the clause making the fee payable a quarter after certification.

Naushad Shamsi, Gulf accounts lead, Muscat, needs the pendant in Ibtida's January catalogue, which closes on 28 November. He has not mentioned that his best families keep asking for a weekly video call with the attendant, which Itminaan does not sell.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"Precision on the button is 13 of 519, which is 2.5 per cent. If an alarm is wrong ninety-seven times in a hundred, the desk learns to ignore it, and the real call with it."

Nabanita Srinath, team chat, Thursday 5 November 2026

"Eighty-two per cent of our subscribers will pay ₹499. That is ₹2.2 crore of Imroz fees and ₹2.40 crore of add-on revenue at four thousand homes, both now in the plan."

Nimai Shanbhag, email to the executive team, Monday 9 November 2026

"Read Exhibit 2 before my September summary. I asked 71 hypothetical questions and 31 about something that actually happened; Namrata's eleven interviews are 141 hypotheticals and 12 past episodes, with a median silence of nine-tenths of a second. And twenty of the twenty-two rooms had the payer in it, because the payer is the only person our database knows how to reach."

Natasha Sanzgiri, memo, Tuesday 10 November 2026

"Thirty-four of those emergencies came through my attendants, not the button. Give me the ₹800 allowance and a two-tap escalation in the app and I cover eleven thousand homes in March, not four thousand."

Noel Sridharan, voice note from Chennai, Wednesday 11 November 2026

In the one interview with an elder alone, on 18 August, Naomi had asked Nutan Shirodkar, seventy-six, of Pune, when she had last been frightened at home. There were nineteen seconds of silence. Then: "The night the lift was shut. I did not want to wake my daughter-in-law, so I sat on the stairs till six. Who would I have called? She is the one who would have to come."

8. The options as Naomi sees them

Exhibit 6 sets out the four courses on her slide: confirm the order, let the window lapse and spend six weeks interviewing elders at home, shrink the order, or abandon the pendant for Noel's attendant-side escalation.

A is the only course that can satisfy Imroz, and it probably cannot. Four thousand live homes is 35.1 per cent of the 11,400-home base against a trial acceptance of 19.2 per cent; at that rate the whole base yields 2,185 homes, all of which would have to be canvassed by 31 March. Naomi's own deck says "65 per cent conversion", which is the 17 of 26 homes still wearing the device, not the 23 of 120 offered. B costs ₹18.2 lakh on top of the fee, or ₹1.01 lakh a conversation, about sixty times Inayat's price for a completed call. C depends on a settlement Ichimura has only said it would "look at". D forfeits the Imroz line and adds ₹2.78 crore a year of allowance for a service it cannot price.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The council meets on Monday, 16 November and the board on Friday, 27 November; the cancellation right expires on Monday, 30 November and firmware freezes on 7 December. Cash is ₹61 crore against a burn of ₹3.4 crore a month, and eight engineers are committed either way. The Imroz fee of ₹2.2 crore requires four thousand covered homes certified by 31 March 2027 and is payable only in the quarter after certification, which cannot fall inside the year ending 31 March 2027. The elder must consent in person under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. And no one has interviewed, in a home, the person who would wear the device.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, what can the twenty-two interviews establish and what can they not? Rewrite the three questions you think did most damage.
  2. Exhibit 3 reports 412 of 503 and 412 of 604. Which denominator belongs in Nimai's sentence, and what would have to be collected to answer the question he thinks he answered?
  3. Exhibits 4A and 4B conflict with Exhibit 3, and Exhibit 5 with Exhibit 4A. Rank them by the weight you would give them on Monday, and say what would change that ranking.
  4. Nutan Shirodkar's nineteen seconds produced the only statement in the file about who an elder would actually call. Design the research that would show whether that is one woman's story or the market's shape, with its cost and delay.
  5. The 2019 decision to make the adult child the account holder is why every sample is a sample of payers. Is that a research, product or consent problem, and who should own it?
  6. What should Naomi table at half past nine on Monday, and what should she tell the board on 27 November about what Itminaan knows, what it does not, and what it spent finding out?

At a quarter past eleven she closed the survey file and opened the recording again. The old man in Secunderabad had taken nine minutes to reach the thing that mattered, and reached it after a pause Naomi could hear herself resisting the urge to fill. There were fifteen days left on the Ichimura clause, and no interview in the file conducted in a home with anyone who would wear the pendant.
exp20v2-res.interview.basics:
Interview fundamentals: how to learn what people do, not what they say

1. The Friday before the rider budget

On Friday 6 March 2026, Dhatri Pimpale, the lead product manager at Ekagra Pharmacy Exchange in Hyderabad, was handed a decision that looked already made. Ekagra is a marketplace on which 1,800 independent retail chemists in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh order medicines from 46 licensed distributors. Falgun Shirodkar, the founder, had a slide open: of 400 chemists surveyed the previous month, 248 had ticked "I would definitely use a same-day delivery guarantee". That is 62 per cent (248 divided by 400). Falgun wanted to spend ₹1.2 crore, which is 120 lakh, on a dark-store and rider network before the monsoon.

Dhatri did not think the survey dishonest, only that it measured agreeableness: asked whether they would "definitely use" something, most people say yes. The company needed to know something else: when a chemist loses a sale because a medicine is missing from the shelf, what actually happened in the hours before? She asked for ten days and eight conversations before any rider was hired. Falgun agreed on one condition: she would bring him a number, not an impression.

If the rider network solved a problem chemists described but rarely experienced, ₹120 lakh would answer the wrong question and the real cause of lost sales would stay untouched through the busiest quarter.

2. The idea

A discovery interview is a structured conversation, usually thirty to forty-five minutes, whose purpose is to reconstruct specific past behaviour so that a team can understand a problem before it designs a solution. The key word is past. An account of what someone did last Tuesday is a memory; an account of what they would do if you built something is a forecast, and people forecast themselves badly. They are polite, and they cannot know how a product will fit a day they have not yet lived.

The method exists because stated preference and revealed preference diverge. Its modern form descends from several streams: ethnographers' distinction between observation and opinion; Steve Blank's customer-development work in the mid-2000s, which told start-ups to leave the building; Clayton Christensen and later Bob Moesta, who framed demand as a "job" a customer hires a product to do, making a recent decision the unit of study; and Rob Fitzpatrick's 2013 book The Mom Test, which reduced the craft to rules for non-researchers, chiefly that you talk about the person's life, not your idea.

The sentence Dhatri could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "We will not ask chemists what they want; we will ask them to walk us through the last time it went wrong, and count what we hear."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and the usually unspoken ones matter most. Table 1 sets them beside what Dhatri did at Ekagra.

Table 1. The five steps, with the Ekagra example
StepEkagra, 9 to 18 March
1. Frame a question about behaviour"What causes a chemist to miss a sale for lack of stock?"
2. Anchor on a recent specific event"Tell me about the last medicine you could not supply."
3. Follow the story with open questions"What did you do the minute you saw the empty shelf?"
4. Probe why, then stay silent"What stopped you ordering?" then ten seconds of quiet.
5. Record and code within the hourOne line per interview: cause category and a quoted sentence.

The first step is the one practitioners leave implicit. Before a single call, Dhatri wrote the decision at the top of her page, with three rival causes of stockouts: a slow delivery, an exhausted credit limit with the distributor, and a wrong substitute. A list of rivals leaves room for the answer to be none of them.

Step two does most of the work: "usually" invites a summary invented on the spot, "the last time" invites retrieval. Step three keeps questions open, meaning not answerable by yes or no, and avoids leading questions, which smuggle in the answer ("Wouldn't faster delivery help?"). Step four is the why probe plus silence: in the pause the person usually adds the sentence that matters. Step five matters because memory drifts within hours towards what you hoped to hear.

4. A worked example, line by line

Dhatri completed eight interviews, one per chemist, across town and village shops. Near the end she asked the survey question directly: would same-day delivery matter? Separately, she classified the cause of the most recent stockout from the story told earlier. Table 2 shows both.

Table 2. Eight interviews: what chemists said, and what their last stockout story showed
#Chemist (pseudonym)"Same-day delivery would matter"Cause of last stockout, from the story
1Dinesh TandelYesCredit limit exhausted
2Esther PintoYesCredit limit exhausted
3Farooq HussainiYesDelivery wait
4Dwarkanath ReddyYesCredit limit exhausted
5Eswari NayakYesCredit limit exhausted
6Firoz QuraishiNoWrong substitute supplied
7Dhiraj PatwardhanYesDelivery wait
8Elamathi KrishnanYesCredit limit exhausted

Seven of eight said yes, which is 87.5 per cent (7 divided by 8), higher even than the survey's 62 per cent. Stopping there would have confirmed the rider plan. But credit limit exhausted appears five times (interviews 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8), delivery wait twice (3 and 7), and a wrong substitute once (6). The shares are 5/8 = 62.5 per cent, 2/8 = 25 per cent and 1/8 = 12.5 per cent, which sum to 100 per cent. In Eswari Nayak's words: "The distributor's screen simply would not let me order."

The orange bar is what chemists said; the green bars are what their stories showed. Delivery is the cause in only a quarter of them. Dhatri then converted shares into scale. Ekagra's records suggested 3 stockout events per chemist per month, so 1,800 chemists give 5,400 events a month (1,800 times 3). Applying the shares: credit 62.5 per cent of 5,400 is 3,375; delivery 25 per cent is 1,350; substitute 12.5 per cent is 675. The three sum to 5,400 (3,375 + 1,350 + 675).

Next, cost. Spread over twelve months, the rider network costs ₹120 lakh divided by 12, or ₹10 lakh a month, which is ₹10,00,000. Divided by 1,350 delivery-caused events, that is about ₹741 per event addressed (1,000,000 divided by 1,350 is 740.74). A credit programme, with Ekagra guaranteeing a short-term top-up of distributor limits, was estimated at ₹36 lakh a year including a loss reserve, or ₹3 lakh a month, which is ₹3,00,000. Divided by 3,375 events, that is about ₹89 per event (300,000 divided by 3,375 is 88.89). Credit is therefore about 8.3 times cheaper per event addressed (740.74 divided by 88.89).

Second pass: change one input. Suppose Falgun asks whether the answer survives if one story is read differently. Reclassify interview 8 from credit to delivery wait. Credit falls to 4 of 8, or 50 per cent, which is 2,700 events; delivery rises to 3 of 8, or 37.5 per cent, which is 2,025 events; substitute stays at 675. The total remains 5,400 (2,700 + 2,025 + 675). Per event, riders cost 1,000,000 divided by 2,025, about ₹494, and credit costs 300,000 divided by 2,700, about ₹111. Credit is still cheaper, now by about 4.4 times (493.83 divided by 111.11): the ranking survived and the gap narrowed. Eight interviews yield a ranking, not a precise share.

5. The nuances a learner must become aware of

Stories versus opinions

A story reports an event with a time, a place and other people. An opinion reports a belief. Only the first is evidence of behaviour. Test: could a stranger have filmed the sentence? "Last Thursday I called the distributor at five and was told my limit was used up" could be filmed; "delivery is slow here" could not.

Compliments, fluff and hypotheticals

Compliments ("great idea"), generalities ("I always check stock on Mondays") and promises ("I would definitely use that") feel like data and are not. Each should prompt a return to a specific past event.

Behaviour is not motive

The interview showed five chemists hitting a credit wall. It could not show why the wall exists on the distributor side, or whether chemists would game an Ekagra-backed top-up. The why probe reaches only the interviewee's reasons.

Recall decays and flatters

People remember the last event better than the one before, and vivid failures over dull routines. Dhatri limited her anchor to the previous thirty days.

Eight is not a sample

Eight interviews are a search for patterns, not an estimate of a population share. Treat 62.5 per cent as "most of what we heard", not a forecasting input. Enough interviews have been done when new ones begin repeating old causes.

The interviewer shapes the answer

Tone, a nod, a rewording and the order of topics change what people say. Reviewing her recordings, Dhatri found that in interview 2 she had asked "Was it the delivery?" before the chemist finished; that answer stayed in the table, marked contaminated.

Interviews versus surveys

Interviews discover which causes exist; surveys and platform logs then measure how large each is. Confusing them means treating a handful of conversations as a census, or a survey of opinions as evidence of behaviour.

What it cannot tell you

An interview cannot say whether a specific solution will work, what price will be accepted, or how people you did not reach differ. Those need concept tests and observation. Before relying on a finding, ask who was not in the room.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

Table 3. Where the same method changes shape
ContextWhat changes
ConsumerLarge pool, cheap to recruit, but weak memory for routine acts. Anchor on a recent purchase and use a receipt as a memory aid.
B2BBuyer, user and payer differ; interview each, and ask who else was in the room and who signed.
MarketplaceTwo sides with opposing interests. The credit wall is invisible from the chemist side alone, so Dhatri added three distributor calls.
Early-stageThe founder interviews and has a strong prior. The remedy for enthusiasm is a second note-taker.
Large companyResearchers, product managers and sales all talk to customers. The remedy for fragmentation is a shared repository of coded stories.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Symptoms, misunderstandings and cheap diagnostics
MistakeSymptom from outsideMisunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Pitching instead of askingInterviewer talks most; everyone is "excited".It is a sales call in disguise.Time the talk split on the recording.
Counting claimsReport says "87.5 per cent want it".Opinions equal behaviour.Ask which dated event supports each finding.
Leading questionsAnswers echo the question's wording.Questions may suggest answers.Flag any question containing a proposed cause.
Filling silenceShort answers, no surprises.Silence means failure.Count pauses over five seconds.

Each mistake lets the interviewer's expectations replace the respondent's experience; the diagnostics need only a recording and a pen.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version of Ekagra's decision has a written question, eight to ten recent-event stories, and a table in which every finding carries a date and a quote. The interviewer speaks little, records within the hour, and shows the founder the contradicting evidence, an 87.5 per cent claim set against a 25 per cent behavioural cause, without drama. The product manager reports a ranking and its sensitivity, and names what remains unknown.

9. Closing: what Dhatri decided

On Monday 23 March, Dhatri took the two tables to Falgun. She proposed holding the rider budget, piloting a credit top-up with 40 chemists for about six weeks, and running three distributor interviews to understand why the limits exist. The rider network, she said, was deferred, not dead: delivery caused 1,350 events a month in her base case and up to 2,025 in the stressed one, and a pilot would show whether that share grows once credit stops blocking orders. She chose the cheaper, reversible step because interviews rank causes but cannot show that a solution works.

To go further, study interview-guide design, so the five steps become a repeatable script; then how many interviews are enough; then cognitive biases in research, which explain why contamination like that in interview 2 is so persistent.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of the last decision you made on the strength of a survey or a customer's stated enthusiasm: what specific past event, if any, supported it? Second, if Dhatri's eight chemists had all been recruited from the 248 who ticked yes, would her tallies have been trustworthy, and what would you ask to find out?
exp40v2-res.interview.basics:
Interview fundamentals: reconstructing behaviour when every incentive points at opinion

1. Two decisions, thirty days apart

On Wednesday 28 January 2026, Nupur Sathaye sat in a windowless room at an insurer's office in Pune with a claims handler and a voice recorder. Nupur is director of product at Nirnay Underwriting Systems, which sells cashless-claims adjudication software to four Indian insurers. Her sponsor, Onkar Dhavale, had committed in a board pack to a "medical-opinion workbench" after an advisory council in which seven of nine insurer executives named medical-opinion turnaround the worst bottleneck.

Nupur doubted that executives in a council meeting could measure where days go. Over the fourteen days to Wednesday 11 February she ran twelve interviews with handlers, two medical officers, a billing clerk and a grievance officer under one rule: nothing about the workbench or the future, only a walk through one slow claim.

Nineteen days after that last interview, on Monday 2 March 2026, Manjiri Oak began fieldwork in the grape belt outside Nashik. Mausam Irrigation Works, where she is head of product, sells a soil-moisture sensor with a mobile app: 3,250 units across 410 farms, an average of 7.93 per farm. The hardware worked; the app went unopened, with weekly active farms at 94 of 410, or 22.93 per cent. Nilay Thatte, who runs sales, was sure growers distrusted the recommendation. Manjiri ran fourteen interviews from 2 March to Friday 20 March, eighteen days later, asking about the last three times they had opened a valve.

Both decisions turn on the same question: how do you reveal what a person did, when every force in the room rewards opinion?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A discovery interview is a semi-structured conversation whose unit of evidence is the episode: a bounded past event, locatable in time, involving named people and an observable action. Its purpose is to recover enough episodes that a team can say what happens, how often and at what cost before committing to a solution. The rest follows: open questions, because closed ones return a token not a narrative; silence, because the second half of an answer is usually the informative half; "why", because an episode without causation cannot be generalised; no speculation, because a forecast cannot be coded or checked.

The method exists because stated and revealed preference diverge, a gap mid-century market research exposed but mispriced. Four streams converged: ethnography, which insisted on observing action in context; jobs-to-be-done reasoning, from Clayton Christensen and Bob Moesta, which made the dated switch the unit of study and forced interviews into the past tense; Steve Blank's customer development; and Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test (2013), which reduced it to rules anyone could follow.

Believers in interviews split three ways. The episode-fundamentalist school counts only dated past behaviour. It signs: "a finding with no dated episode behind it is a hypothesis." It will not sign: "a hypothetical can substitute when no episode exists." The sense-making school treats meaning as data, since a grower's belief about why the app is wrong shapes behaviour even when mistaken. It signs: "the respondent's interpretation is part of the phenomenon." It will not sign: "strike every opinion." The measurement-first school treats interviews as hypothesis-generating only. It signs: "no interview number enters a business case." It will not sign: "interviews establish how common a problem is."

3. Mechanics, including the parts left implicit

The decision sheet comes first. Before recruiting, Nupur wrote one question at the top of a page — which adjudication stage consumes the most elapsed days, and can software move it? — then four rival causes: missing hospital documents, medical-officer wait, policy-terms ambiguity, payment-release approval, with a fifth line blank. A written list of rivals makes "none of these" possible, the only condition under which research can surprise you.

Talk share is the most diagnostic mechanic, and the transcripts measured Nupur's own behaviour.

Split the twelve at a 30 per cent interviewer share. The quieter six (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12) used 4,040 interviewer words against 17,500 participant words — 21,540 in all, a share of 18.76 per cent — and produced 28 episodes, or 4.67 each. The implicit step is the within-the-hour coding pass. Nupur coded each session before the next began, tagging every episode with one rival cause, a verbatim sentence and a date. Coding late lets a theory rewrite ambiguous episodes, and that drift runs one way.

The formal treatment is a coverage calculation, not a significance test. If a problem is present in a proportion p of the population and interviews are independent, the chance of hearing it at least once in n interviews is one minus (1 − p) to the power n.

They are poor for rare ones: at 10 per cent prevalence, 28.2 per cent go unheard. The table governs detection only, licensing no claim about size.

4. When the method applies, as testable claims

One: the behaviour has already happened, recently and memorably. At Nirnay every handler had closed a slow claim that week. At Mausam irrigation follows the season, so an episode from the dry fortnight before 2 March was retrievable and a monsoon one was not, which is why Manjiri capped her anchor at thirty days.

Two: the respondent can observe the behaviour you care about. Nirnay's executives saw reports about turnaround; the handlers saw the waiting, which is why seven of nine executives named medical opinion and the people doing the work did not. Mausam's growers could observe their valve work but not the sensor's calibration drift, which only the firmware logs saw.

Three: no instrumented record answers the question more cheaply. Nirnay held 48,000 claim records with stage timestamps, so the honest sequence was interviews to find which stages stalled, then logs to measure them; Mausam had telemetry on screens but none on its mechanical valves, so interviews were the only instrument. Four: the decision is still open. Nupur's was open only in that no contract was signed, and research after commitment yields confirmation or a political problem.

The method is actively misleading for new categories, where nobody has a relevant past; for magnitude questions, where vivid stories outrank a dull majority; and for price, the least reliable number in product work.

5. Hard edge cases

In multi-product firms the episode seldom respects the product boundary: a Nirnay handler's slow claim crossed the adjudication module, the hospital's portal and a scheme's eligibility check, and the team owning adjudication codes it to its own surface. The seam is where the time goes. In two-sided businesses one episode has two incompatible narrations — the billing clerk described sending documents twice and being told they had not arrived; a handler described never receiving them, and both are honest.

Regulated settings constrain the interview itself. Indian general insurance operates under IRDAI conduct rules, and a handler cannot read a live claim file aloud; Nupur's workaround was narration from a redacted screen, the compliance officer approving the protocol beforehand. The constraint costs detail; hiding it would cost credibility.

In hardware-plus-software products the gap between account and physical record is the finding: three Mausam growers called a sensor "dead" when the firmware log showed it reporting normally, outside the app's sync window — wrong about the cause, right about the experience. In AI-native products the respondent cannot reliably report what the system did, since it is non-deterministic and the output is gone; episodes need a saved session to anchor them. At organisational seams, mature firms describe one research function and run three — researchers, product managers, and sales contact nobody records. The better ones centralise coded episodes, not talking.

6. The nuances that separate the expert

The second question is more diagnostic than the first

Competent interviewers write good openers; experts care about the follow-up, which shows whether the interviewer was listening or waiting. The tell: every probe is "and why was that?" whatever was said. Consistency is not discipline: a probe names something just said.

Silence is an instrument, not a courtesy

The expert's pause after an apparently complete answer runs seven to ten seconds, feels interminable, and is where additions arrive. The tell: no gap over two seconds in forty minutes. Nirnay's interviews 4 and 8, at 60.3 and 67.8 per cent interviewer share, had none and each yielded one episode; in interview 8 Onkar sat in and Nupur filled the silences.

An episode's date is load-bearing

Asking "when was that?" tests whether the respondent is retrieving or constructing. The tell: no episode in the findings carries a date. Dates look like tidiness; in fact an undated episode cannot be audited.

The respondent's causal theory is data about them, not about the cause

Nilay Thatte's hypothesis — growers distrust the model — was also what several growers said when asked directly. It was false as an account of why the app went unused, true as an account of how they rationalise a product they never open. The tell: explanations promoted to findings.

Recruitment decides the answer more than the guide does

Had Manjiri recruited only from the 94 weekly-active farms, every episode would have come from people for whom the app already worked. The tell: a list drawn from a support queue or beta programme. The obvious reading, that engaged users give richer interviews, is true and is the problem.

Eight to fifteen interviews establish a ranking, never a share

The temptation to write "62 per cent of growers" after fourteen conversations is strong because percentages travel better than orderings, but Table 2 shows the sample is sized for detection, not estimation. The tell: a finding with two significant figures; an expert writes "most of what we heard", then instruments it.

Saturation is a property of the question, not of the method

Manjiri stopped at fourteen because interviews 11 to 14 added nothing — evidence about her question at her frame, not a universal number. Change it to how they choose what to buy and the curve restarts at zero. The tell: a fixed count in policy.

The blank fifth line matters more than the four hypotheses above it

Policy-terms ambiguity was on Nupur's list; the surprise was how much traced to one scheme's wording. A contaminated exchange in interview 2 was marked, not deleted, preserving the base rate of her errors. The tell: no "other" code, or one left empty.

7. What changes across product types and stages

In consumer products recruitment is cheap and recall poor, because the behaviour is habitual; anchor on an artefact such as a receipt. In B2B and enterprise the difference is structural: user, buyer and blocker are different people with different episodes, and a programme reaching only users misses the procurement, security and integration episodes that decide whether anything is bought — Nirnay spread its twelve across four roles and still omitted the IT security reviewer. In marketplaces each finding needs matching episodes from the other side; in hardware, the account can be checked against a device log; in AI products, it needs a retrievable artefact. By stage, what changes is who interviews: at seed the founder does and the risk is advocacy; at scale it is fragmentation, remedied by a shared repository. The technique does not change; claims that it does are claims about recruitment dressed as methodology.

8. Three worked examples

Nirnay: interviews rank, logs measure

Nupur's forty episodes coded as: missing hospital documents 17, medical-officer wait 11, policy-terms ambiguity 8, payment-release approval 4 — summing to 40, with shares of 42.5, 27.5, 20.0 and 10.0 per cent, summing to 100.0. She then pulled stage timestamps for the 48,000 cashless claims closed that quarter: 1,63,200 delay-days, an average of exactly 3.40 days per claim.

The disagreement on second place is instructive: interviews put the medical-officer wait second on 27.5 per cent of episodes, because waiting for a doctor is vivid, while the logs put it third on 18.00 per cent, behind policy-terms ambiguity on 27.00. The board pack rested on the vivid cause.

Nupur costed a document-chase workflow against the largest cause. Removing 60 per cent of missing-document delay is 0.60 times 71,040, or 42,624 delay-days — 26.12 per cent of all 1,63,200. Total delay falls to 1,20,576 and the average per claim to 2.512 days (1,20,576 divided by 48,000): a reduction of 0.888 days, the same 26.12 per cent of 3.40. The whole programme cost ₹3,21,184 — recruitment ₹42,000, incentives ₹24,000, transcription ₹8,184, time ₹2,09,000, travel ₹38,000 — or ₹3.21 lakh, ₹26,765 per interview.

Mausam shipped valve scheduling, not a better moisture model. Ten weeks later weekly active farms had risen from 94 of 410, or 22.93 per cent, to 263 of 410, or 64.15 per cent: 41.22 points, and 2.80 times the original count.

Mehnat Workforce Network: interviews run, and run badly

Mehnat Workforce Network, a blue-collar staffing marketplace, interviewed 22 employers in 2024 and concluded they wanted a rostering calendar. The interviews were real; the questions were not — nearly every one asked a variant of "would a rostering view help you?", and nearly everyone said yes. Mehnat built for nine months, July 2024 through March 2025, at ₹2.4 crore — ₹240 lakh.

The module shipped on 1 April 2025 to 7,400 employer accounts. Of those, 1,850 opened it at least once, or 25.0 per cent; of the 1,850, 296 used it more than once — 16.0 per cent of 1,850 and 4.0 per cent of 7,400. By 31 May 2025, sixty days after launch, 74 were still using it: 25.0 per cent of the 296 and 1.0 per cent of the original 7,400. Against ₹240 lakh of build cost that is ₹3,24,324 per retained account (2,40,00,000 divided by 74).

The recovery was the same research with the questions repaired. Across June and July 2025 Mehnat ran eighteen switch interviews anchored on a dated event — the last time an employer filled a shift off-platform — for ₹14 lakh. Employers were not planning rosters; they were replacing a worker who had not turned up, usually within ninety minutes. Mehnat rebuilt around same-day replacement for ₹62 lakh, shipping 3 November 2025. Of the same 7,400 accounts, 2,960 opened it, or 40.0 per cent, and by 2 January 2026, sixty days later, 1,184 were still using it — 40.0 per cent of 2,960 and 16.0 per cent of 7,400. At ₹62 lakh that is ₹5,236 per retained account (62,00,000 divided by 1,184): 61.9 times more efficient than the first attempt. Total spend was ₹240 plus ₹14 plus ₹62 lakh — ₹316 lakh, or ₹3.16 crore.

Mehnat lived in the after-launch cell: ₹240 lakh of build against a ₹3.21 lakh programme at Nirnay's rates — 74.7 to 1 — and row two of Table 5 would have caught it.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether hypotheticals have any legitimate place. The fundamentalist case: stated-preference error is bias with a known sign, so a hypothetical adds error in a predictable direction, and no data beats data biased towards yes. The opposing case: for products with no precedent there is no episode to recover, and a concept probe carrying a commitment cost recovers much of the signal. The fundamentalist is wrong if such probes predict behaviour as well as episodes do; the pragmatist is wrong if that gap persists however the probe is built.

Whether product managers should interview at all. The specialist position: interviewing is a trained skill, Table 1 is what untrained interviewing looks like, and letting everyone interview manufactures biased evidence at scale. The generalist position: a product manager who has never heard a customer struggle builds from abstractions, and the remedy is a recording norm and a talk-share check, not a licence. The specialist is wrong if recording and review close the gap; the generalist is wrong if untrained interviewers miss what trained ones find rather than just finding less.

A third quarrel: whether to publish interview percentages at all, since "11 of 14" survives being quoted out of context and "79 per cent" does not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this follows the rules visibly: past tense, open questions, no pitching. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They arrive with a written decision and rival explanations including a blank line, so the research can fail. They treat their own talk share, probe quality and coding drift as measured quantities. They keep separate what the respondent did, what the respondent believes about why, and what the interviewer concluded. And they are precise about the instrument's boundary: after fourteen interviews they will tell a sceptical executive that pump-power scheduling is almost certainly dominant and that its size is unknown.

12. What each of them decided

On Wednesday 18 February 2026, a week after her last interview, Nupur took Table 3 to Onkar. She did not argue the workbench was worthless; she argued it was third. She proposed building the document-chase workflow first, since it addressed 43.53 per cent of measured delay-days and could cut the average claim by 0.888 days, after four weeks interviewing hospital billing staff. The board pack was amended, not withdrawn: the workbench stayed on the roadmap, two quarters later.

Manjiri's decision contradicted both her colleague and her customers. On 20 March she recommended shipping valve scheduling and deferring the moisture-model work growers had asked for, with one safeguard: because labour for valve changes appeared in 64.3 per cent of interviews but was named most important by only 7.1 per cent, she instrumented valve events in firmware first, so the claim could be measured rather than argued. Nilay's objection — that they were building what growers had not asked for — went into the memo unresolved.

Three questions for discussion. First: Nupur's logs and interviews agreed on first place; had they differed there, which would you have believed? Second: Manjiri's curve flattened at interview 10, but her frame held only grape growers near Nashik — what would it do if interviews 15 to 20 came from another crop? Third: Mehnat's first programme ran 22 interviews and its second 18, yet only the second worked. What changed, and what would have caught it before ₹240 lakh was spent?

13. Going deeper

Designing an interview guide — talk share is a guide problem. Recruiting research participants — decides the answer more than the guide. How many interviews — formalises Table 2 and the curve. Cognitive biases in research — why interview 8 went as it did. Synthesising research — episodes into a problem statement. Switch interviews (JTBD timeline) — Mehnat's recovery technique. Willingness-to-pay probes in interviews — what interviews cannot answer. Observation and contextual inquiry — when respondents cannot see the behaviour. Solution interviews and concept tests, evidence strength: say, do, pay, qual + quant feedback loop and continuous discovery habits — the hypothetical, the vocabulary, the sequence and the cadence. Interviewing in B2B: users, buyers, blockers — the reviewer Nupur missed. Win/loss analysis, expert and analyst interviews, mining support tickets, reviews and sales calls and diary studies and longitudinal research — episodes interviews cannot reach. Qualitative vs quantitative research underpins it all; research operations and AI-assisted synthesis keep the repository alive.
